events.title: Category 2 Hurricane Isaias nears landfall, leading to production shut-ins
events.summary: U.S. Energy Information Administration - EIA - Independent Statistics and Analysis Browse by tag liquid fuels natural gas electricity oil/petroleum production/supply crude oil consumption/demand generation prices map states exports/imports international coal renewables weather forecasts/projections gasoline capacity steo (short-term energy outlook) Hurricane Isaias nears landfall, leading to production shut-ins Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, U.S. Energy Atlas map of hurricanes, cyclones, and typhoons ; National Weather Service’s National Hurricane Center Note: LNG=liquefied natural gas As of 4:00 a.m. central time on October 9, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration expects Hurricane Isaias to make landfall on the Gulf Coast late Friday or early Saturday, creating the potential for significant disruptions to energy infrastructure. Hurricane Isaias is the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season and will be the largest storm system to make landfall in the region since Hurricane Helene in September 2024. Hurricane Isaias’s forecasted path toward the Gulf Coast has already impacted crude oil and natural gas production in the region. The Marine Minerals Administration reports that as of Thursday, October 8, 130 production platforms and rigs have been evacuated or moved resulting in production shut-ins of about 1.3 million barrels per day of crude oil and 1.1 billion million cubic feet per day of natural gas. The U.S. Gulf Coast is home to a large portion of the U.S. refining fleet, and the impacts from Hurricane Isaias could affect refinery operations . events.title: Yvonne Bajela is bringing $17M in fresh capital to Europe’s startup scene
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Yvonne Bajela knew it was time to launch her own fund. She spent more than a decade as a VC, most recently at LocalGlobe and Impact X Capital Partners, where she made bets on now-unicorn companies like the fintech Wise, the insurance company Marshmellow, and robotaxi Mooves. On Tuesday, she announced that her own fund, Evertrue, officially closed an oversubscribed $17 million Fund I. “After more than a decade backing founders who bet everything on their ideas, it felt like time to make a bet of my own,” she said. “I wanted the independence to act on those convictions and build something that reflected my own approach to investing.” The firm, which has already backed seven companies, will focus on early-stage investing across the U.K. and Europe. The average check size will be around £350,000, she said, with plans to back at least 20 companies over the next three years. Perhaps unsurprisingly, she said this AI boom helped her realize that this was the right time to launch her own fund. Not only has it changed the economics of launching a company, she said, but it has created new opportunities for early-stage investors like herself. “The ability to build has been democratized,” she said. “But the ability to build something enduring remains rare.” As TechCrunch has previously reported, the U.K.’s startup scene is having a moment. King’s Cross, for example, is one of the world’s top AI hubs, while companies like Revolut, Synthesia, ElevenLabs, and the Bezos-backed CuspAI are redefining what it means to scale and attract success in the U.K. market. For someone like Bajela, this moment means there is an opportunity to snap up investments in the next generation of top British talent early. “I think more globally significant businesses will emerge from a wider range of starting points,” she said. However, this is also a tough market for emerging fund managers. In the U.S., it has been described as a barbell market where capital is concentrated at the top and among firms led by those who already have solid track records. Things may be slightly rosier in the U.K., as PitchBook data through the end of September shows that emerging fund managers in this region raised $7.4 billion, already surpassing the $6.2 billion they raised in all of 2025. Still Bajela said fundraising was a grind. The hardest rejections weren’t necessarily the outright nos. “They were the ones that came after months of conversations and significant time invested, only for the answer to ultimately be no,” she said. “Time is one of the most valuable resources a founder has, and a prolonged process without clarity has a real cost.” Still, she said the fund nabbed five institutional backers, including the British Business Bank and Basecamp, the fund-of-funds of the investment firm Phoenix Court, which is also home to LocalGlobe. Evertrue was part of the £400 million British Business Bank’s Investor Pathways capital initiative, which saw it pour £90 million to 10 first-time fund managers. Bajela said Evertrue wanted to raise around $13 million but saw a lot of investor interest. She decided to turn down additional investors rather than expand the fund size. “Fund size is a strategic decision, not a measure of success in itself,” she said. “I wanted enough capital to build meaningful positions in my highest-conviction investments without creating pressure to deploy capital simply because it was available.” Around 80% of Evertrue’s LPs are U.K. based, with the rest scattered across Europe, Asia, and the U.S. She said her international LP base represents the relationships she’s built “over more than a decade investing across markets.” It also reflects the fund’s global ambition, she said, especially since so many British founders keep their eyes on a U.S. expansion; more than half her portfolio already operates in the U.S. Evertrue will invest mainly across AI and fintech, she said, adding that she’s “particularly interested in people with a unique insight into a problem, an unusual ability to execute and the ambition to build something much bigger than their initial product.” “I also pay attention to the distance a founder has traveled, what they’ve overcome, and how that has shaped their perspective,” she continued. She’s lived in Japan as a senior investment manager at Mistusi and started her career as an analyst at Goldman Sachs. Throughout her career, she said she’s seen how “widely distributed ambition and talent are.” “I want Evertrue to be known for the quality of the founders I back and the businesses they go on to build.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. Dominic-Madori Davis is a senior venture capital and startup reporter at TechCrunch. She is based in New York City.

events.title: Vice-Premier He Lifeng vows support for Hong Kong as international financial centre
events.summary: At opening of investment summit in city, He says finance sector ‘plays an irreplaceable role in Hong Kong’s high-quality development’ Beijing says it will introduce extra measures, as needed, to bolster Hong Kong as an international financial centre, with Vice-Premier He Lifeng pledging continued support in a speech on Tuesday. Delivering a keynote speech at the opening of the 2026 Global Financial Leaders’ Investment Summit in Hong Kong via video link, He said finance was the most important leg of the city’s “four centres and one highland” agenda and stressed that using the advantages of the “one country, two systems” constitutional principle was key to their development. The vice-premier described “one country” as the “seed capital” and “two systems” as “the profit”, and said that, as any investor knew, seed capital needed to be protected before risks were taken to maximise returns.

events.title: UK and EU agree draft deal to scrap Brexit red tape over food exports
events.summary: Published 3 November 2026, 02:11 GMT The UK and EU have agreed a draft deal on removing post-Brexit checks from food and agriculture exports, ahead of the UK-EU summit later this month. The BBC understands the 200-page draft text for this so called "SPS" [sanitary and phytosanitary] agreement has been circulated to EU nations in Brussels for consideration at a meeting on Wednesday. Similar texts for deals on emissions trading and a youth travel and work scheme have also been circulated alongside a 15-page draft joint statement for UK and EU top leaders. The food deal is the most significant part of the so-called Brexit reset agreed so far, removing checks and red tape that hit exporters after the UK exited the EU's single market. The deal should remove the need for £200 Export Health Certificates, £25 Phytosanitary certificates, inspector fees, organic certificates, some port fees, sampling fees and other checks for exports and imports to and from the EU. UK exports to the EU of fresh sausages, burgers, shellfish from domestic waters and seed potatoes will also be able to resume. Each of the elements on the table was up for discussion under Sir Keir Starmer, and the summit would have taken place by now had Labour not replaced its leader in July. Under Andy Burnham, Britain's approach to post-Brexit relations with the EU have shifted significantly. Sir Keir said the UK would not rejoin the bloc in his lifetime, while Burnham has said he would like to see Britain back in the EU in his. As a result of the agreement, the government claims the UK economy will eventually see £5.1bn worth of annual benefits. It will also allow for passports for UK pets to be taken into the EU, while the UK will commit to observing and adapting to existing EU regulations on plant, animal and food trade standards. This process is called "dynamic alignment". European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen with Prime Minister Andy Burnham While UK rules remain mostly aligned with EU ones, there are some areas where England has diverged from the EU rule book, for example on "precision breeding" of plants, previously known as gene editing. In recent weeks, agreement has been struck on transition arrangements while the EU's new regulations come in to force. The government has already announced a European Partnerships Bill which will provide a legal mechanism for the application of new EU rules and regulations. This will also allow for the necessary alignments for the linking of the UK emissions trading scheme with the EU's, and save the need for UK exporters to pay the EU's new carbon border tax. The draft agreements will be discussed at a meeting of EU ambassadors called Coreper on Wednesday, with some key details on the planned numbers in a Youth Experience Scheme to be finalised at a political level in the coming days. A discount on full foreign student fees for EU students is likely to be pushed to next year alongside a plan to reconnect electricity markets. The BBC understands that the draft agreements will also include some references to UK involvement in defence cooperation schemes, access to law enforcement databases and some reassurances over the EU's "Made in Europe" plans . A food deal will have particular significance for Northern Ireland, radically reducing the impact of the post-Brexit Irish Sea border. Northern Ireland's Brexit deal kept it inside the EU's single market for goods. That means food products from elsewhere in the UK require paperwork and some physical checks when arriving at NI's ports. A deal will ultimately end those requirements. While the food trade plans have been backed by supermarkets and farmers representatives, some pro-Brexit campaigners have criticised the reapplication of EU rules. The post-Brexit trade deal signed by Boris Johnson's government prioritised regulatory freedoms for the UK over avoiding new regulatory red tape, checks and delays. But William Bain, the British Chamber of Commerce's (BCC) head of trade policy, told the BBC's Today programme that business overall thought that it was a "price is worth paying" to follow common rules, as companies would benefit from "lower costs, reduced delays [and] increased market access". At the moment, he said, the requirement for Export Health Certificates can add thousands of pounds of costs to each truck carrying goods, in addition "to the delays that people find at the ports or at the borders". "So we get lower exports because of the delays and the massive increases in costs that have come into the supply chain." The BCC has released a new analysis of its members' views suggesting options for a closer relationship. The business lobby group says the current trade relationship is "failing to deliver", leaving firms "struggling with a thicket of Brexit red tape" nearly six years after the UK's exit from the bloc.

events.title: From scooters to shampoo - the people saving hundreds from dumpster diving
events.summary: 'I've always looked in bins for clothes' Published 3 November 2026, 00:41 GMT Darryl Baker was shocked to see piles of clothes dumped beside the recycling bins outside her local supermarket. On several trips to the dumpsters she has also found a host of other items, such as "a perfectly decent" Ikea picture frame and children's scooters. Always on the lookout for ways to save money and appalled by the waste, the thrifty mother-of-two from north London asked supermarket staff if she could take some of it. Permission granted, "I got my children entire new wardrobes," says Darryl, 39, adding that she's stuff put away for years to come. During a six-month stint this year, "I have probably saved hundreds of pounds," says the freelance journalist. Darryl reels off the names of brands she has salvaged - Ralph Lauren, Nike and The North Face, among others. "My mind was blown," she says. "This stuff is just strewn all over the floor." Darryl Baker takes the clothes for herself and her children, and to sell In addition to finding clothing for her children and her nephews and nieces, she keeps some for herself. Others she donates or sells, including recently getting £30 for a men's Barbour jacket. Darryl has joined the ranks of so-called dumpster divers – people who rummage through commercial bins for treasures. Motivations include saving money, giving items to charity and disgust at how often perfectly usable items are being consigned to waste - or a combination of all three. Texan Jeff Ferrell has been rooting around in trash for more than 50 years. "I still dumpster dive every day by bicycle," says the 72-year old, who lives in Fort Worth, and has written books on the topic. "I still enjoy it as much, or more, than ever." Jeff considers himself a "bit of Robin Hood mixed with anarchist direct action", only scrounging in more affluent neighbourhoods and giving away many of his finds. "Almost everything in our home is scrounged, and I never buy, for example, soap or toiletries or medical supplies, or shoes and clothes and tools and garden supplies," he says. Jeff Ferrell sells some of what he finds, and gives away other items Jeff looks for discarded metal to sell at a scrapyard which, he says, earns him around $150 (£110) every two weeks. His wife sells his other finds, such as "an antique or piece of jewellery", on eBay. Through savings and selling the more valuable items, he estimates his finds are worth "tens of thousands of dollars a year". 'If something catches my eye, I'll grab it' While dumpster diving may have been considered taboo in the past, it's now something many people are proud to do and post about online. Millie Diamond, a London-based stylist, posts videos on TikTok of her rummaging through bins. But she has a very specific aim - to unearth fabrics and clothing that she can salvage and refashion into new items, some of which she then sells. Millie Diamond turns dumped textiles and clothes into new outfits She estimates that one dress she found was worth £600. "I'm a bit of a magpie. I like collecting things off the street or anywhere that there's a freebie. If I see something that catches my eye, then I'll grab it." Millie, 36, began bin diving after spotting some fabrics discarded by a business that had shut down. "I literally clambered into the bin. It turned out it was loads of vintage clothes." 'I haven't bought shampoo for years' For Charlotte Bayford in Essex it's all about timing. Her best finds come when students at Essex University head home for the summer and ditch anything they don't want to take with them. This includes half-filled toiletries. "I haven't bought shampoo for eight years," says the 44-year-old sales assistant. "I'd say that has saved me some money." Like other dumpster divers, Charlotte gives a lot of her finds to charity. But she has also filled her house with salvaged objects, and sells on some valuable items. Food, as long as it remains sealed, is fair game too. "I've found tins of Heinz baked beans, perfectly fine. I'm quite happy to eat those," Charlotte says. Charlotte Bayford gives some of her finds to charity But is taking things out of bins and keeping them acceptable in the eyes of the law? Jeff, who is professor emeritus of sociology at Texas Christian University, says many US cities have made the practice illegal, including New York, Cleveland and Wichita. "Dumpster diving is considered illegal [in such places] because that which is thrown away now belongs to the city... or to the private company that provided trash services," he explains. Any dumpster diver also risks trespass charges. In Fort Worth, where Jeff lives, items can only be removed from bins if they are on public land , external . In the UK, Sunjay Versani of Duncan Lewis Solicitors says it depends on the circumstances. "In many cases involving genuinely discarded goods, prosecution is unlikely," he says.

events.title: Saudi state oil company reports jump in profits despite attacks; Australian central bank lifts rates – business live
events.summary: 22m ago Introduction: Saudi state oil company reports jump in profits despite attacks; Australian central bank lifts rates Introduction: Saudi state oil company reports jump in profits despite attacks; Australian central bank lifts rates Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets and the world economy. The Saudi state oil company Saudi Aramco has reported that profits rose by more than a third in the latest quarter despite attacks on its facilities. The world’s top oil exporter posted a net profit of $3.25bn in the three months to September, compared with $26.9bn a year earlier. The US-Israeli war on Iran has reduced Aramco’s output, but this has been offset by higher oil prices. This morning, Brent crude climbed $2.38 a barrel to $107.15 a barrel, a 2.2% gain, after the ⁠US reportedly launched limited strikes on ​Iran’s Qeshm Island late on Monday. (Before the war, which started on 28 February, Brent traded around $72 a barrel.) However on Monday, the global oil benchmark plunged 11% to $103.28 a barrel after Donald Trump reportedly said he was willing to give diplomacy more time. Amin H. Nasser , Aramco’s president and chief executive, said: Geopolitical uncertainty and attacks on key energy facilities continued to amplify the global energy supply crisis in the third quarter of 2026, with serious implications for global energy security. Despite challenges, the unwavering dedication of our workforce, our operational excellence, the flexibility of our system, and the strength of a supply network built over decades enabled us to continue delivering reliably to our customers through this extraordinary period. We continue to explore additional overseas storage capacity and alternative export routes to further strengthen our global supply network, and our robust operational and financial performance during this volatile period demonstrates the value of our resilience. This means that the world’s biggest oil companies are on track for combined profits of around $100bn between July and September. Australia’s central bank has lifted interest rates for the fifth time this year, taking them to the highest level in 18 years. The Reserve Bank of Australia’s board raised its cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.85% and said it will continue to do what it considers necessary to bring inflation to target. However, it dropped its previous guidance that it would raise the cash rate further if needed. And a surprisingly narrow 6-3 vote indicated policymakers may be getting to the end of their rate hikes. Michele Bullock , the governor, said it was “not the news that many Australians want to hear”, but it would prevent “even worse pain down the track”. She said it was unclear what the next move in rates will be, adding that the three dissenting members stressed downside risks such as the weakening housing market and rising unemployment. After five rate hikes this year, she said it is an appropriate time to pause and assess how the economy is responding to the rate rises, but cautioned that there is still a bit of a skew on the upside to inflation risks, and we need to be alert to those materialising. Updated forecasts from the central bank show headline inflation hitting 4.5% in the fourth quarter, before easing back to the target range of 2% to 3% in the second half of next year. Unemployment is forecast to rise above 5% in the next couple of years. Ipek Ozkardeskaya , senior analyst at Swissquote , said: Higher energy prices… would strengthen the case for further monetary policy tightening by the Federal Reserve (Fed) and other major central banks . The Reserve Bank of Australia delivered a 25bp hike today, as expected, while the Bank of England (BoE) is widely expected to announce a 25bp hike on Thursday, following a rather uneventful budget announcement last week that allows the BoE to go on with its life — and take care of its inflation problem. Overall, if we take a step back and look at the bigger picture, the latest monetary policy decisions have brought either rate hikes or the prospect of tighter monetary policy to fight inflation fuelled by elevated global energy prices. On top of that, many developed-market bond yields face upward pressure from intensifying fiscal concerns, while large bond issuance by technology companies to finance their massive AI buildout could add to that pressure. The cryptocurrency exchange Binance said hourly deposits exceeded withdrawals this morning, suggesting flows are stabilising after its hack last week. This resulted in $6.3bn of assets being stolen from customer accounts. It has been described as the biggest heist in history; experts identified North Korea as the probable culprit . 3pm GMT: US JOLTs job openings for September 3pm GMT: US Factory orders for September

events.title: The US midterms will test the limits of Trump’s power
events.summary: Importance of governor races in midterms Control of Congress is at stake, but so is the ability of American institutions to withstand presidential pressure. On November 3, as Americans vote in the midterm elections, the United States faces a defining test of presidential power, constitutional accountability and democratic resilience. The election will determine control of Congress, but its stakes extend far beyond partisan fortunes. At issue is whether constitutional checks and balances can constrain President Donald Trump, whether election officials can withstand political pressure, and whether the government will respect the voters’ verdict when the outcome threatens its interests. The battle for control of elections The administration’s efforts to reshape election procedures have encountered substantial judicial resistance. According to an October 20 review by the Brennan Center for Justice, at least 34 federal district court decisions had temporarily or permanently blocked administration initiatives involving election procedures and demands for voter registration records. The rulings included decisions by judges appointed by presidents of both parties, including Trump himself. These decisions demonstrate that judicial oversight remains an important constitutional safeguard. Yet repeated litigation exposes a vulnerability: courts often intervene only after disputed measures have been introduced, leaving states to challenge policies that can generate uncertainty close to Election Day. The controversy intensified on October 26, when a federal appeals court declined to order California to set aside ballots from approximately 20,000 registered voters whom the Justice Department alleges may be noncitizens. The court ruled that the lower court had not been given adequate opportunity to consider the government’s request. The underlying dispute remained unresolved. The administration maintains that its actions protect electoral integrity. But investigating credible allegations of wrongdoing is fundamentally different from restricting eligible voters on the basis of unverified suspicions. Election security requires accurate voter rolls, but it equally requires protecting citizens from erroneous challenges. Repeated allegations of fraud can undermine confidence even when evidence fails to establish that an election has been compromised. The danger is that routine election administration becomes suspect in the public mind, regardless of the facts. Republicans hold narrow majorities in both chambers of Congress, placing control of the House and potentially the Senate within reach of Democrats. A Democratic House majority would strengthen the opposition’s ability to investigate administration policies, subpoena officials and scrutinise executive decisions. Immigration enforcement, election procedures, federal spending and the implementation of executive orders could face intensified oversight. Such scrutiny could expose misconduct where evidence supports it and compel officials to explain decisions otherwise shielded from meaningful examination. Yet investigations do not automatically produce accountability. Subpoenas can trigger prolonged legal battles, and congressional hearings alone cannot force policy changes. Control of the Senate would give Democrats greater influence over presidential nominations and judicial appointments. Nevertheless, Trump would retain his veto power and substantial executive authority. Even unified Democratic control of Congress would not automatically reverse his agenda. The deeper question is whether Congress will exercise its constitutional responsibilities independently or allow partisan loyalty to take precedence over institutional accountability. Checks and balances cannot function effectively if one branch declines to challenge another when circumstances demand it. Perhaps the most consequential confrontation will come after the ballots are cast. Trump’s response to his 2020 presidential defeat remains a critical precedent. He challenged the result, made unsubstantiated allegations of fraud, and pressured Georgia officials to find enough votes to reverse his loss. On January 6, 2021, a mob attacked the Capitol as Congress met to certify the presidential election. That history does not establish that similar events will recur in 2026. It does, however, make scrutiny of potential election disputes essential. The danger may lie not in a single intervention capable of changing the result, but in successive confrontations: challenges to ballot counting, pressure on state officials, demands for investigations and attempts to portray ordinary procedures as evidence of fraud. Even unsuccessful efforts can delay resolution and weaken public confidence. Candidates have every right to pursue legitimate legal challenges. Courts must consider credible evidence, and election officials must correct documented irregularities.

events.title: China’s ‘Lipstick King’ touts AI tokens in first for Singles’ Day festival
events.summary: Li Jiaqi, also known as Austin Li, hosting a live stream at the headquarters of MeiONE in Shanghai on Sept 7. Li sold 100,000 monthly memberships of Alibaba’s QwenWork office AI service within half an hour during a Taobao Live broadcast on Nov 2. China’s Singles’ Day added AI token packages as a major new product, moving beyond cosmetics and home appliances. It is the first time such AI credits were sold widely in the festival. Alibaba’s Austin Li sold 100,000 monthly memberships of QwenWork in 30 minutes. The stream also sold AI laptops and workplace devices, with Alibaba and JD.com launching AI token centres. AI token sales rose 450% from the previous month, and AI laptop sales jumped more than 300% in the first hour. Analysts said users may stock up, but fast AI change could make prepaid plans risky. BEIJING - The Singles’ Day shopping extravaganza in China unveiled a new attraction for 2026 as it graduates beyond a long association with cut-price cosmetics and home appliances: computing credits used to access artificial intelligence tools. The launch is the first time AI token packages have been offered as a significant consumer product category during Singles’ Day, the world’s largest shopping festival originally held on Nov 11 each year. Top live-streamer Austin Li sold 100,000 monthly memberships of Alibaba’s QwenWork office AI service within half an hour during a Taobao Live broadcast on Nov 2, the company said. That is equivalent to about two trillion AI tokens, or units of text processed by AI models. “Chinese consumers are now very accustomed to using AI productivity tools,” said Lian Jye Su, chief analyst at tech research firm Omdia. Frequent users can run short of credits, he added, which makes extensive purchases during a sales period “a very reasonable action”. It was unclear how much the token plans were discounted from normal prices, however. First sale of AI products for ‘Lipstick King’ The live stream marked the first sale of AI products by Li, who earned the “Lipstick King” moniker for amassing a huge following while selling vast volumes of lipstick online. It showcased QwenWork token plans, AI-enabled laptops and workplace devices. Chen Yusen, an Alibaba Group vice-president and chief executive of QwenWork, also made an appearance. Li asked Chen if AI could be used to build a digital avatar of himself to chat with fans around the clock. While AI could not replace Li, Chen responded, he hoped it could handle everyday tasks for users, freeing them to spend time with their families. Alibaba’s Tmall has launched an AI Token Center for the Singles Day festival, offering consumer token packages from Alibaba Cloud, MiniMax, Moonshot AI and Z.AI. Alibaba’s Tmall has launched an AI Token Center for the festival, offering consumer token packages from Alibaba Cloud, MiniMax, Moonshot AI and Z.AI, the e-commerce giant said. JD.com has also introduced an AI token section bringing together services from companies including DeepSeek, Z.AI and ByteDance’s Volcano Engine. Sales of AI token plans from Oct 1 to Oct 20 soared 450% from the previous month, Alibaba said, while sales of AI personal-computer laptops surged more than 300% year on year in the first hour of the Nov 11 checkout period. Su said the tokens’ relatively long expiry periods could spur users to stock up, but warned that rapid changes in AI products may make consumers wary of prepaying for services at risk of being replaced or retired. Singles’ Day, which has run since 2009 in an effort to spur consumer spending, earned total revenue of 1.70 trillion yuan (S$327.3 billion) across platforms in 2025, according to third party data provider Syntun. events.title: China regulator tells banks to pause IPOs: Report
events.summary: The move follows a sharp selloff that saw the blue-chip CSI300 Index slumping 8.5% in October, its worst monthly performance in more than a decade. China’s securities regulator told banks to pause IPOs and large share sales, The Financial Times reported, citing three sources. The China Securities Regulatory Commission gave informal “window guidance” after meetings with investment banks, Reuters could not verify the report. The move follows an 8.5% October fall in the CSI300, while regulators also launched market support steps on Nov 2 to stabilise shares. BEIJING – China’s securities regulator has told investment banks to pause initial public offerings and has suspended large share sales by existing shareholders until markets recover, The Financial Times reported on Nov 3, citing three sources with knowledge of the discussions. The China Securities Regulatory Commission held meetings with investment banks and gave informal “window guidance” over the past few days, the report added. Large sales by existing shareholders have also been temporarily suspended until the markets have recovered, according to the report. Reuters could not immediately verify the report. Chinese financial regulators did not immediately reply to a Reuters request for comments. Persistent weakness in the world’s second-largest economy, weighed down by frail consumption, a prolonged property debt crisis and a steep tech stock selloff, has sapped investor confidence. Chinese regulators rolled out a handful of measures on Nov 2, from conducting swap operations to upgrading a lending facility for stock buybacks by listed companies, as part of efforts to stabilise struggling capital markets. The effort to steady its sliding stock market struggled for traction on Nov 3, with AI-related shares leading declines as investors judged the financial support measures insufficient. China’s blue-chip CSI300 Index and the benchmark Shanghai Composite Index both dropped more than 1% in early trade, before paring losses to 0.1% and 0.7%, respectively, by midday. REUTERS

events.title: RBA interest rates: Bullock says ‘pain now’ will prevent worse later as Reserve Bank hikes rates for fifth time
events.summary: Reserve Bank of Australia increases official cash rate to 4.85%, bringing it to highest level since 2008 RBA interest rates live updates: Reserve Bank cash rate decision Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast The Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock has said that “some pain now will prevent even worse pain down the track”, after lifting official interest rates to an 18-year high of 4.85% in a bid to combat persistent inflation. The RBA’s decision to hit mortgage holders for a fifth time in 2026 will intensify pressure on indebted households, but there were signs that the central bank will at least now wait through summer to gauge the impact of higher interest rates on the economy. The decision split the monetary policy board, as six members voted for a hike, while three were in favour of a steady cash rate. Financial markets halved the probability of another rate rise before Christmas to 12%, but continued to price in a roughly 30% chance of a sixth hike by May. Speaking to journalists shortly after the rate decision, Bullock said: “I know this is not the news that many Australians want to hear, but it is what’s needed to get inflation down.” “Inflation is too high, and our forecast suggests it will stay higher for longer. Some pain now will prevent even worse pain down the track,” she said. The back-to-back hikes will heap more pain on over 3.3m households with home loans and turn the screws on a federal government under pressure for its economic management. The latest rate rise will lift the monthly interest payment on a $700,000 home loan by $107, according to Canstar, bringing the total rise in repayments over this year’s five hikes to $532. Jim Chalmers, the treasurer, said higher fuel prices due to the Middle East conflict were the “primary driver” for the recent inflationary surge. “Our budgets are not what’s putting upward pressure on inflation. But we can play a helpful role and that’s what we intend to do,” Chalmers said. With surveys showing Australians are increasingly inclined to blame the Albanese government for ongoing high cost of living, Angus Taylor, the opposition leader, said voters “deserved to hear the truth”. “Labor’s spending spree is driving up inflation, it’s driving up interest rates, and Australians are paying the price,” Taylor said. The RBA’s post-meeting statement removed an explicit reference to the need for further hikes – an omission that economists at UBS interpreted as “clearly dovish”. And with the cash rate now at its highest level since 2008, Cherelle Murphy, the chief economist at EY, said the RBA “is likely to take a wait-and-see approach over summer”, even as she said higher interest rates could not be ruled out. The RBA’s latest set of forecasts in its Statement on Monetary Policy (SOMP) showed a difficult period ahead for the economy. The forecasts suggested the country’s cost of living crisis would extend for another year, even as Australia struggles with below trend economic growth and climbing unemployment. Inflation will push higher through the final months of 2026 to about 4.5% and only return below 3% – within the bank’s 2% to 3% target range – by the end of next year, or nine months later than hoped. Global oil prices would ease over the coming 18 months, but still remain relatively elevated, according to the forecasts, suggesting limited relief from high fuel costs for motorists and ongoing high costs for businesses. “We view the risks to the inflation outlook as still skewed to the upside,” the report said. Alongside persistent cost of living pressures, the RBA also predicted weak economic growth through to the end of 2028. The economy would grow by 1.6% this year and by 1.3% in 2027. That would be well below an estimated potential growth rate of about 2%, but better than recent forecasts by bank analysts. And despite the risks associated with a housing downturn that “is one of the steepest over the past 50 years”, the central banks’ economists saw no evidence that the country was headed towards recession over the coming two years. Unemployment, now at 4.7%, would end next year at about 4.9%, before creeping over 5% in 2028.

events.title: Adnoc’s XRG to buy Australian LNG stake for $1.5bn
events.summary: XRG , the international energy investment unit of Adnoc, has agreed to acquire Shell’s stake in an Australian natural gas project for $1.5 billion, as the company seeks to diversify its portfolio amid disruption to global energy markets caused by the Iran war. Abu Dhabi-based XRG will buy the stake in Australia's North West Shelf LNG project, marking its first investment in the country's gas sector and opening up greater access to customers in the Asia-Pacific region, the company said on Tuesday. The deal, which is subject to regulatory approval, will give XRG access to one of the world's largest integrated LNG developments, with liquefaction capacity of 14.3 million tonnes per year and 4.4 trillion cubic feet equivalent of remaining resources. XRG has been actively increasing its portfolio of investments globally and plans to double its asset value over the next decade. Launched in 2024 as an international lower-carbon energy and chemicals investment company, with an enterprise value exceeding $80 billion, it has acquired stakes in several global gas projects. The latest acquisition strengthens XRG's position in the Asia-Pacific region. The North West Shelf project has been operating for more than four decades and plays a key role in the country's domestic gas supply and energy exports. The asset has supported domestic energy supply, jobs, international trade, and Australia’s emergence as a leading global energy exporter, XRG said. “This investment advances XRG’s strategy to build a leading international gas business serving growing demand across Asia-Pacific. The North West Shelf combines immediate production, strategic infrastructure, and future upstream development opportunities, making it a strong fit with our long-term ambitions,” said Mohamed Al Aryani, president of international gas at XRG. “XRG understands the importance of balancing export success with local energy needs. We believe continued investment in the North West Shelf can help sustain domestic gas supply, support regional energy security, create jobs, and deliver lasting economic benefits for Australia.” XRG said the project offers a combination of existing production, strategic infrastructure and opportunities for future upstream development. The company, which is wholly owned by Adnoc , has an enterprise value of more than $150 billion and invests across natural gas, chemicals and energy solutions.

events.title: When will we know the US midterm election results?
events.summary: Importance of governor races in midterms The first results are expected on Tuesday as polls begin to close at 23:00 GMT. But final results might take days. On Tuesday night, the United States – and many people around the world – will be following one of the country’s most closely contested midterm elections in recent years. All 435 seats in the US House of Representatives and 35 of the 100 Senate seats are up for grabs as Democrats hope to take control of both chambers from President Donald Trump’s Republican Party. list 1 of 4 How the president’s party has fared in every US midterm election since 1946 list 2 of 4 Trump, Vance campaign with candidates on last day before US midterms list 3 of 4 US midterms 2026: What polls reveal about Democratic, Republican voters list 4 of 4 Trump makes final midterms pitch at Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool Here is what we know about the results: When will the first results come in? The first results should be known on Tuesday after polls begin to close. Voting will end first in some jurisdictions on the East Coast at 6pm (23:00 GMT). Results will continue to come in throughout Tuesday evening, and some probably won’t be known until Wednesday or later in some races as more states finish voting and officials start releasing their vote counts. But the first reported results won’t necessarily mean that a winner has been announced. Election officials release vote counts as ballots are processed, and news organisations, like The Associated Press, then analyse them to determine how to call a race. A closely contested race could take hours to call – or even days. It might not be clear for days whether the Republicans will retain control of Congress or Democrats secure a majority in either or both chambers. What time do polls close in the US? The first polling stations to close will be in parts of Indiana and Kentucky. 6pm Eastern Standard Time (EST) (23:00 GMT) – parts of Indiana and Kentucky 7pm EST (00:00 GMT) – most of Florida, Georgia, South Carolina, Vermont, Virginia, and the remaining parts of Indiana, Kentucky and most of New Hampshire 7:30pm EST (00:30 GMT on Wednesday) – North Carolina, Ohio, West Virginia 8pm EST (01:00 GMT on Wednesday) – Alabama, Connecticut, Delaware, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Mississippi, Missouri, the remaining parts of New Hampshire, New Jersey, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Tennessee, Washington, DC, and parts of Florida, Kansas, Michigan, North Dakota, South Dakota and Texas 8:30pm EST (01:30 GMT on Wednesday ) – Arkansas 9pm EST (02:00 GMT on Wednesday) – Arizona, Colorado, Iowa, Louisiana, Minnesota, Nebraska, New Mexico, New York, Wisconsin, Wyoming, and the remaining parts of Kansas, Michigan, North Dakota, South Dakota and Texas 10pm EST (03:00 GMT on Wednesday) – Montana, Nevada, Utah, and parts of Idaho and Oregon 11pm EST (04:00 GMT on Wednesday) – California and Washington, and the remaining parts of Idaho and Oregon 12am EST (05:00 GMT on Wednesday) – Hawaii and most of Alaska 1am EST (06:00 GMT on Wednesday) – the remaining parts of Alaska, including the western Aleutian Islands Which states could take longer to count votes? Alaska : The state uses ranked-choice voting. If no candidate receives more than 50 percent of the vote, extra rounds of counting are needed to determine the winner. And while in-person early and Election Day voting are reported on election night, the mail-in voting results are released in the following days. In 2024, about 75 percent of the votes were counted by the morning after the election with the remaining votes reported over the following days. California: The state carries out elections primarily by mail. Large batches of ballots come in and are verified days after the polls close, so close House races can take days or weeks to resolve. Arizona: In some counties, voters drop off mail-in ballots on Election Day. These ballots must undergo signature checks before being counted, which can delay results by several days in close races. Nevada: All registered voters are mailed ballots. Mail-in ballots postmarked by Election Day can arrive up to four days later. Voters also have six days after Election Day to fix any signature problem, and this could delay results until the following week. Maine: Like Alaska, this state also uses ranked-choice voting. If no candidate receives more than 50 percent of the vote in a race with two candidates, ballots must be taken to Augusta, Maine’s capital, for further counting. This can delay final results. Washington: The state holds elections by mail. Ballots postmarked by Election Day can be counted in the following days, which can cause delays. Which states could report results earlier? Some of the states that could report results earlier include: Florida: Votes are usually counted quickly. In the 2024 general election, about 99 percent of the votes were counted by 10:51pm EST (03:51 GMT the next day), according to The Associated Press news agency.

events.title: Apple Watch’s AI features for rewinding and recapping conversations begin beta testing
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Apple’s AI-powered “Audio Intelligence” technology for the Apple Watch is now rolling out into beta testing, initially for developers in the iOS 27.3 update, after first being announced at the company’s Surprise and Shine hardware event in September. The technology includes a set of four opt-in AI features that allow Apple Watch Series 12 wearers to detect important sounds, identify songs, catch up on conversations, and take notes. The sound recognition feature will help deaf and hard-of-hearing users identify important sounds like sirens, alarms, or doorbells from their watch, while the song recognition feature taps into Apple’s Shazam app to detect music playing in the background and identify the song name and artist. However, the more potentially controversial features are those that listen to human conversations: Live Rewind and Siri Recaps. Given the backlash to AI recording devices, like Meta’s AI glasses and other AI wearables, Apple has attempted to carve out a space where the features can be useful to Apple Watch owners, while still respecting the privacy of those around them. With Live Rewind, the idea is to let you go back in time to see what someone just said, in case you missed it. For instance, if someone was giving you verbal directions or reading a long list of specials at a restaurant, you could double-press on the Watch’s digital crown to see what was said in the last 15 seconds as a text snippet displayed on the watch face. You can either view this snippet and then do nothing, and it will disappear permanently. Or you can save it to the standalone Siri app that shipped with iOS 27 for later access, which might be helpful if you’re trying to remember someone’s name or take a quick note from a fast-paced presentation. Apple says that users will also be able to tap an “Ask Siri” option that appears below the text snippet if they have questions about something that was said — like a technical term they don’t understand, or perhaps some sauce option the waiter mentioned that they’re unfamiliar with, among other things. When you double-press the digital crown, an audible chime appears and an animation displays on the watch. This is meant to signal to people through the combination of the gesture, sound, and the visual display that you’ve recorded something that was said. These snippets will be deleted automatically after 30 seconds if you don’t save them. The other option, Siri Recaps, takes this ambient listening technology even further by allowing Apple Watch owners to take high-level notes of their conversations. Importantly, Apple says it’s not identifying speakers, saving the raw audio, or providing word-for-word transcriptions. Instead, the feature summarizes a conversation with a short sentence and some bullet points that identify key points. For instance, depending on the topic, the bullet points might include things like important dates or deadlines, pricing or payment plan information, and other factual information. Apple suggested the feature could be used in scenarios like work meetings, parent-teacher conferences, personal training sessions, or other places where you may need to remember what tasks you have to complete or things that were said. Essentially, it’s supposed to mimic a user’s ability to jot down their own notes — without adding emotion or tone. This could be helpful particularly at times when you aren’t able to write up your own notes, either because your hands are full or you’re trying to concentrate on whatever’s being said at the time. The recaps won’t record conversations when you’re listening to music with your headphones or using their noise cancellation features. At the end of the day, you’re prompted to review your saved Siri Recaps when the feature is enabled, and then choose which, if any, you want to save. These notes can be saved to your Notes app or even exported to your Journal app, if they’re more personal in nature. If you do nothing, the recaps will delete themselves within seven days. This reminder to review the Siri Recaps you’ve recorded also appears when you first unlock your Apple Watch in the morning, too. Users can opt to enable the Siri Recaps manually, or they can configure a schedule, such as only having the recapping take place while at work, or making sure that they never run at night. Even if they’re running on a schedule, you can still turn off the recapping feature at any time from the Control Center. Apple notes that Siri Recaps has been designed to omit sensitive information like government-assigned identifiers, financial and authentication data, certain personal identifiers, and any language that would promote self-harm.

events.title: Aged over 50, experienced and looking for work. Will employers bite?
events.summary: Even as older workers are encouraged to remain in the workforce for longer, the question is whether employers are willing to hire them. Singapore will raise retirement age to 65 and re-employment age to 70 from Jan 1, 2029, as the Government backs plans to help older workers stay in work. Older jobseekers like Raj Bharij, Gurmit Singh Kullar and Jason say they face instant rejections, overqualification fears and long job searches after retrenchment or resignation. Data shows weaker hiring for older workers: 42% in their 50s and 39% over 60 found jobs within six months, versus 61% in their 40s; employers may still value contract roles and transferable skills. SINGAPORE – Raj Bharij lost his job in 2026 when his employer, a global bank, restructured. “I’m 50 years old,” he recalls thinking, when told of the retrenchment in April. “Is anyone going to actually hire me now?” Six months on and more than 100 applications later, the former transformation director is still searching for his next job. He has received “instant” rejections, within seconds, from some firms’ automated systems and radio silence from others. An artificial-intelligence chatbot tasked with helping to refine his resume suggested he take five years off his age. Bharij and other mature job seekers whom The Straits Times spoke to believe that being older and more experienced has somehow made their job search harder. Their experiences highlight a question facing Singapore: Even as older workers are encouraged to remain in the workforce for longer, will employers be willing to hire them? Singapore will raise its retirement age to 65 and re-employment age to 70 from Jan 1, 2029 – one year ahead of an earlier target. This was announced on Oct 26 when the Government accepted recommendations from the Tripartite Workgroup on Senior Employment aimed at helping older workers remain in meaningful employment for longer. The move comes as the Republic’s population ages . The share of workers aged 50 and above in the workforce grew from 34% in 2015 to 40% in 2025, and is expected to rise further, a report by the workgroup said. Gurmit Singh Kullar, 52, left his job as a marketing director in July 2024 after experiencing burnout. Re-entering the workforce after a six-month break has proven an uphill task. Many marketing roles these days, he found, merge what would previously have been three jobs into one, effectively denting the value of his past experience. He applied to more than 200 openings in less than two years. When he did not hear back from prospective employers, he widened his search to include more junior or mid-level roles that paid just half of what he had been earning. Still, they did not bite. Hiring managers sometimes commented he had too much experience. “Isn’t it better for you to have someone more qualified?” he wondered. He attended career counselling and a handful of courses to learn new skills, where he encountered other mature job seekers in a similar situation. “Have you heard this line from people, that you’re overqualified?” he was asked by a man who had been retrenched from the insurance industry. “All the time,” he replied. Older workers are taking longer than others to find new work after losing their jobs, data from the Ministry of Manpower shows. In the second quarter of 2026, 42% of people in their 50s and 39% of those over 60 found new jobs six months after a layoff, compared with 61% for those in their 40s. A study by researchers, including Lee Zeewan from the National University of Singapore, found that 47% of employers surveyed were likely to hire workers in their 50s, compared with 35% who were neutral and 18% who were unlikely to do so. That number fell to 33% for workers aged 60 and above, they said, in a paper published earlier in 2026. Kirsty Poltock, a country manager for Singapore at recruitment firm Robert Walters, notes that the difficulties which older job seekers describe come as the market grows tougher for candidates in general, and firms’ hiring slows. She surmises that the labour market has become “less forgiving about a mismatch” between job seekers’ existing experience and the skills which firms are looking for, but believes there are still opportunities for workers in their 50s, having regularly placed such candidates in new roles. Contract work is one area that could play to senior workers’ strengths, she said, as more companies hire for non-permanent roles on a one- or two-year horizon as the economic outlook weakens. People who can articulate how their experience can help firms transform their human resources or finance operations, for instance, are seen as valuable hires, Poltock added. As their search for new work continues, Bharij and Gurmit are also having to deal with the emotional toll that being unemployed later in life brings, after having grown accustomed to the rhythm of work over decades.

events.title: A response to Andy Burnham: We need an apology and reparations
events.summary: It is good news the British PM is open to calls for an apology for slavery. But debt restructuring instead of reparations won’t do. Vice-Chair of The CARICOM Reparations Commission. I read with interest the recent news that United Kingdom Prime Minister Andy Burnham is now open to calls for a formal apology for Britain’s role in the transatlantic trafficking in enslaved Africans and chattel enslavement. On the face of it, this is some good news. Only a full and formal apology can allow for the healing of wounds and the destruction of cultures caused by colonialism, chattel enslavement and other forms of oppression of peoples to begin. The Reparations Commission of the Caribbean Community (CRC of CARICOM) has been requesting a dialogue on apology and reparations for some time without success. Indeed, previous such demands have been met with expressions of deep sorrow and regret, but never an apology or even a promise of one. As a reminder, in 2015, British Prime Minister David Cameron rejected calls for slavery reparations. Instead, he announced a 25-million-pound UK-funded project to help construct a new prison in Jamaica, aiming to facilitate the deportation of Jamaican nationals serving long sentences in British prisons. The proposal caused much controversy. I suspect that, now that King Charles III will address the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Antigua on Tuesday amid civil society protests and calls for an apology and reparations, this promise has been squeezed out of the British prime minister before the event. I have often been asked why a formal apology for the transatlantic trafficking in enslaved Africans and chattel slavery in the Caribbean is so important to the reparations process, and what difference an apology can make in terms of acknowledgement, accountability, healing and repair. As CARICOM’s Ten Point Plan for Reparatory Justice emphasises, an apology is a formal gesture of goodwill and will foster better relations between the states of Europe and the Caribbean. It would acknowledge a shared history and interconnectedness to be mobilised towards justice and mutual respect. It would accept responsibility for these crimes, commit to non-repetition and pledge to repair the harms caused to the victims and their descendants. It would represent an ethical and legal acknowledgement of how present-day inequalities and racial injustices are rooted in the history of such criminal conduct; acts such as complicity in native genocide, the introduction and perpetuation of chattel slavery and violent oppressive colonisation. An apology would then have to be followed by meaningful reparations actions. Those actions, however, cannot be reduced to what Burnham proposes: improved debt repayment conditions. Here, it is important to remind ourselves of the debt Britain and other nations involved in enslavement have to repay. Sir Arthur Lewis, considered the father of the modern Caribbean reparations movement, conceptualised the call for reparations within the framework of social and economic development. In his book Labour in the West Indies: The Birth of a Workers’ Movement, published in 1939, Lewis insisted: “It is the British who by their action in past centuries are responsible for the presence in these islands of the majority of their inhabitants, whose ancestors as enslaved persons contributed millions to the wealth of Great Britain.” He further referenced the over 200 years of unpaid labour Britain extracted from millions of enslaved people in the Caribbean as “a debt that must be repaid – and which the British have yet to repay”. The British have not yet acknowledged or attempted to repay their “black debt”. Indeed, they have denied responsibility for reparations, even in the face of quantitative and qualitative evidence of how they benefitted from chattel slavery. Lewis’s economic development theories were grounded in the belief that the 20th-century economic transformation of the British colonies could not be realised without the coloniser acknowledging and honouring its “black debt”. Statements in the Ten Point Plan, Ghana’s March 2026 United Nations Resolution and the UN Committee on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination’s General Recommendation No 40 all express, in varying ways, that the transatlantic trafficking in enslaved Africans and chattel enslavement really broke the world. Together they created an unprecedented racialised regime of violence and governance that reduced Africans and their descendants to permanent, nonhuman property, barred them from civic life, and laid the blueprint for modern global power, economics, and enduring hierarchies of race and gender. What we, the descendants now living with the legacies of chattel enslavement and colonial terror, want is a conversation on actual reparations: debt cancellation rooted in the reality of the lingering legacies of colonialism.

Two helicopters have collided in Nepal’s Mount Everest region, killing at least one person and injuring two others. The crash happened on Tuesday as both aircraft were attempting to land just below Mount Everest base camp. events.title: Apple unsure when more foldable iPhones will be available after selling out
events.summary: Published 3 November 2026, 00:29 GMT The new head of Apple says the company is working to get its new foldable iPhones available to more people after the $1,999 smartphone quickly sold out when it was released just over a week ago. John Ternus, who in September took over the role as Apple's chief executive from Tim Cook, said on Monday that he was "thrilled" at the early reaction to the iPhone Duo. While the costly phone, which sells for £1,999 in the UK, immediately sold out, some buyers have seen their screens crack . The phones are still in high demand and Sabhi Kahn, Apple's new chief operating officer, said the technology giant did not know when more Duos would be available. "At this time, it's really hard to predict when supply and demand will be in balance," Kahn said during a call with financial analysts to discuss Apple's latest financial results. Apple executives did not mention during the call any issues with the iPhone Duo. But last week, the company said it would replace any phones that were impacted by an issue that caused a "small number" of the new phones to crack along the inside fold. Nevertheless, Apple said on Monday that over the last year it sold more iPhones globally than it ever has before. During the three months to 26 September, which did not include sales of the iPhone Duo that went on sale toward the end of October, Apple saw iPhone sales rise 17% to $57bn. Apple has boasted throughout the year that iPhone sales have been surging, despite the company's warnings that crucial components for the device, along with Mac computers and iPads, were constrained to the point of weighing down sales. Sales of Mac computers also grew during the quarter by 27%, hitting $10.7bn, another record for Apple. Overall sales at the company rose by 15% for the year, to $479bn. However, sales for both the iPad and Apple's wearable products, including its headphones and Watch fell by 10% and 7%, respectively. Kahn noted during the call that most Apple devices are still seeing supply constraints driven in part by difficulty in getting enough microprocessors with "advanced nodes." Those components are essentially computer chip technology that allows Apple's devices to operate more quickly, most of which Apple has manufactured through TSMC, which is based in Taiwan. Khan said that such supply constraints are expected to continue into next year, particularly impacting iPads and Macs. The situation has been made worse by what the company has repeatedly insisted is "unexpected demand" for its products. Ternus noted, too, that Apple is still seeing "unprecedented" cost increases for memory, or the ability of Apple devices to store data like apps, photos, and text messages. Much of that memory storage runs through data centres which have seen a huge boom in demand for space as artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots and platforms, including those developed by OpenAI and Anthropic, have become popular. As demand for memory has grown, storage prices have gone up for tech companies like Apple. Cook had earlier this year referred to the sudden increase in data centre costs that Apple was seeing as a "thousand year flood." It has led to the company raising prices on essentially all of its hardware products by around 20%. Sunil Krishnan from Aviva Investors told the BBC's Today programme that Apple posted "a reasonably solid set of results" with a "pretty good performance" from its iPhone business. While there were concerns over the company's guidance on profit margins and the cost of memory chips, Krishnan added that in the broader context, "margins well north of 45% for a very well-established company, I think, are pretty impressive". events.title: Poundland staff could be out of work for years if retailer collapses, founder says
events.summary: Steve Smith calls on owners to accept proposed buyout as 12,000 staff face uncertain future in run-up to Christmas The founder of Poundland has warned that staff at the retailer could be out of work for “years” if it collapses, as he called on the owners of the troubled chain to accept a proposed buyout deal. Steve Smith, who set up the firm with a store in Burton upon Trent in 1990, said: “Once these jobs are lost, they are lost” from Britain’s struggling high streets. His warning comes as the chain’s 12,000 employees face uncertainty over their future in the run-up to Christmas. Poundland’s future hangs in the balance after the retailer, which is controlled by the US restructuring specialist Gordon Brothers, filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators at the high court on Thursday, with the advisory firm AlixPartners lined up to run the process. The legal measure protects Poundland from the demands of creditors until 12 November while a solution to its problems is sought. However, the likelihood of it avoiding mass store closures and job losses diminishes by the day as suppliers have held back on deliveries, hurting its ability to trade . Poundland’s management is scheduled to meet Kate Dearden, the minister for the future of work, on Wednesday as political pressure mounts on Gordon Brothers to accept an offer from Northern Ireland’s Martin Property Group rather than calling in administrators to break up the retailer. The restructuring firm is understood to believe that it can raise more from a breakup of Poundland than through the Martin offer. Smith – who sold his final shares in Poundland for £250m in 2006 – said he was prepared to support that offer but Martin Property Group did not need his cash. “It was my baby,” he said, adding that he had put in an offer when Poundland was first put up for sale but had not heard back and it was too late to now launch his own bid. “If they have got offers on the table, why is Gordon Brothers not taking it and saving all these people? Retail is hard out there and if these people lose their job it could be a couple of years before they get jobs again. They work week to week and need their wages,” Smith said. “It is not just 12,000 jobs. Poundland has more than 2,000 suppliers, some only deal with Poundland and some employ hundreds of people.” He suggested that as many as 30,000 jobs could be at risk in Poundland’s supply chain, stores and at other affected businesses on high streets around the country. “Poundland brings in 4 million to 5 million customers every week to towns and shopping centres and retail neighbours are going to suffer as well,” Smith said. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning “Now it has been restructured and is turning a corner and starting to do well.” It is understood that talks continue about a potential deal under which Martin Property Group has offered about £7.5m up front and the same again in deferred payments over the next two years. That would pay off only half the £30m shareholder loan, the majority of which was taken on by Gordon Brothers when it bought the company. The deal would also include taking on a further, asset-backed loan worth about £90m, it is understood. This deal has been rejected by Gordon Brothers despite Pepco, a former owner of Poundland that holds the other £7.5m of the debt, being prepared to wait for repayment in the hope of saving the business, as first reported by Sky News. Gordon Brothers has been approached for comment.

events.title: Cities Worldwide Build and Scale AI Services With NVIDIA Physical and Agentic AI
events.summary: Cities generate enormous amounts of data from cameras, sensors and operational systems, but turning it into useful action — for planning, maintenance and public services — remains a challenge. Physical and agentic AI offer new ways to close that gap, from digital twins for infrastructure planning to vision and service agents, while keeping local governments in control of how sensitive data is processed and used. Building on initiatives announced at GTC Berlin , NVIDIA and its partners are expanding physical AI and AI agents to cities worldwide. Shared computing infrastructure gives city departments, neighboring municipalities and local developers a common foundation to build on — extending services without each organization having to acquire and manage resources of their own. From resident services to vision agents, cities are adopting NVIDIA agentic AI to deliver faster, more responsive public services. City teams don’t need a massive infrastructure investment to get started building these AI services: depending on the workload, NVIDIA RTX workstations or a small GPU system may be enough. In Spain, 1MillionBot combines open source ALIA models trained at the Barcelona Supercomputing Center with NVIDIA Nemotron and other models in resident-service agents for Madrid Digital (Comunidad de Madrid), Administració Oberta de Catalunya and 150+ deployments across Spain, handling municipal procedures, appointment requests, urban-planning incidents and service inquiries. In the San Francisco Bay Area , LiveX is bringing its AI City vision to life with NVIDIA Cosmos world models and Nemotron open models, and Omniverse and Metropolis libraries on NVIDIA RTX PRO GPUs. The interactive, conversational AI hosts understand people’s needs, provide answers and take action, and can be tailored to local languages and service needs in airports, hospitals, local events and other public spaces. Vision AI agents can turn existing city camera feeds into operational insights, helping teams identify mobility and safety issues and coordinate emergency responses across city services. In Wrocław, Poland , K2K is building shared AI infrastructure using NVIDIA accelerated computing, NVIDIA Cosmos world reasoning models, and NVIDIA Metropolis Blueprint for video search and summarization (VSS) to transform existing camera streams into actionable intelligence for mobility, safety and event response — using the same infrastructure across several city functions. In Malaysia , ITMAX bundles infrastructure and agentic AI applications into long-term managed services for cities, including for traffic management. Built with reference to Cosmos, Nemotron and the Metropolis VSS blueprint, ITMAX’s SamurAI V2 vision agents are scaling on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs to support 17,000+ cameras by 2027. ITMAX integrates TeraSim, an open source traffic simulation platform from Laplace Intelligence, to test signal timing, reducing peak-hour corridor travel times by up to 26%. Plan and Operate Critical Infrastructure With Digital Twins Beyond public-facing services, digital twins can help cities expedite infrastructure planning, minimizing disruption to local communities. City digital twins can also serve as a real-time operational simulation to facilitate faster decision-making. At Dangote’s Lekki refinery in Nigeria, Honeywell Technologies’ Forge Plant Cognition uses Nemotron-powered AI agents to understand operational data. A digital twin of the plant and its processes, built using Omniverse libraries, is also planned to support simulation and training. The platform, built on Dell PowerEdge servers with NVIDIA RTX PRO accelerators, helps operators identify bottlenecks, anticipate equipment and process issues, and optimize plant performance. In Taiwan , Linker Vision and Dutch architecture firm MVRDV are using NVIDIA Omniverse and Nemotron to build environmental, social and governance agents that can assess the environmental impact of various urban planning scenarios, simulating 15-year outcomes of an urban forest canopy in 10 minutes — increasing design iteration speed from two weeks per iteration to less than an hour. Cities can extend AI to more services by building on infrastructure already in place and adding capacity. Shared resources and managed services can help extend those capabilities across departments and municipalities. At Morocco’s Tanger Med port, Cires Technologies is expanding a sovereign AI factory for planned applications in worker safety, congestion analysis, cargo routing and port operations. Cires Technologies is also building an ecosystem of application providers to develop local models and applications for ports and cities. Beyond city services, Barcelona Supercomputing Center’s AI Factory Accelerator Programme gives startups access to sovereign computing, technical support and training. BSC AI Factory also supports research and innovation for startups — spanning agriculture, medical imaging, knowledge access and speech services. Learn how NVIDIA and its ecosystem are bringing physical AI, agentic AI and local AI factories to cities worldwide at Smart City Expo World Congress, running Nov. 3-5 in Barcelona, where NVIDIA Vice President of EMEA Paolo Guglielmini will deliver a keynote address followed by a panel moderated by Charbel Aoun, director of smart city and spaces for EMEA at NVIDIA. events.title: Australia’s High Court hears bid to overturn under-16s social media ban
events.summary: Online giant Reddit and advocacy group Digital Freedom Project argue ban is unconstitutional. Australia’s world-first social media ban for under-16s faces its first major legal test in the High Court, almost one year after taking effect. The challenge was brought on Tuesday by online platform Reddit and Australian advocacy group Digital Freedom Project. list 1 of 3 Meta’s $18bn settlement: How social platforms will change for child users list 2 of 3 Australia seeks big tech support for internet safety, AI regulation list 3 of 3 Greece joins push to ban social media for minors Reddit has highlighted a number of issues in its written submission to the court, pointing to problems enforcing the ban and a lack of scientific evidence about the harms of social media. “The evidence so far is that the effectiveness of the ban has been limited,” Reddit’s submission reads. Social media companies were forced to delete millions of accounts after Australia banned those aged below 16 from the likes of Facebook, TikTok, YouTube and Reddit last December. The platforms are responsible for identifying and deleting the accounts of underage users, and face hefty fines if they are found in breach of their obligations. Reddit argued this approach was actually more dangerous, as registered accounts were governed by in-built safety features. Material posted on many online platforms and social media sites could still be accessed without an account, Reddit said. “Young people using other platforms without an account are also unable to be protected from exposure to particular harmful content as they previously had been,” its submission read. Australia said its restrictions would protect young users from graphic content and online predators. While there is a growing body of evidence about the harms of social media, Reddit argued there was no “scientific consensus”. A team of Australia-based researchers published a study in August that found little evidence to suggest teenagers have stopped using social media despite the ban. Digital Freedom Project, led by New South Wales politician John Ruddick, believes the ban is unconstitutional because it restricts teenagers’ ability to take part in political discourse. “Social media is an important means of accessing news and engaging in political communication for young Australians, including children under 16,” the advocacy group argued in written submissions. “The restriction also risks removing beneficial sources of connection, support and participation,” it added. Digital Freedom Project, according to its website, comprises a group of Australians who are concerned about increasing government intervention and censorship in the digital space. Reddit and the Digital Freedom Project separately announced last year they would challenge the ban. It was unclear how long the court would take to consider the case. The Australian government has stepped up online and social media restrictions to protect young people from pressures and risks they could be exposed to while logged in to social media accounts, according to the online regulator, eSafety Commissioner. The government has also proposed opt-out laws which would force social media companies to give users the choice to turn off their algorithm. Meta and its social media platforms Facebook and Instagram are facing a class action lawsuit in Australia over allegations that addictive design features are harming children and teenagers. The class action suit was filed on behalf of eight plaintiffs who allege they were harmed by Meta while they were below the age of 18.

events.title: AFC reschedules Asian Cup 2027 in Saudi Arabia amid regional conflict
events.summary: Start date for AFC Cup 2027 moved from January to December due to ongoing Houthi attacks on host nation Saudi Arabia. Football’s upcoming Asian Cup 2027 tournament in Saudi Arabia has been rescheduled from a January start to December due to the ongoing conflict in the region, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) has confirmed. The 24-team competition, which was due to get under way in Riyadh on January 7, 2027, will now begin on December 23, the AFC said in a statement on Tuesday. Asian football’s governing body announced the decision following “extensive discussions and close consultation with the Local Organising Committee (LOC) of the AFC Asian Cup Saudi Arabia 2027 and the Saudi Arabian Football Federation (SAFF)”. The tournament will now run from December 23, 2027, to January 21, 2028. “The organising committee for the AFC Asian Cup approved rescheduling the tournament in light of the current exceptional circumstances arising from developments in the region, including substantial logistical complexities and travel disruptions,” the AFC’s statement added. Saudi Arabia has repeatedly come under attack from Yemen’s Houthis since September, with the capital Riyadh among the cities repeatedly hit by missiles. The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen reported on Friday that it “intercepted and destroyed” a drone launched by the Houthis towards Saudi Arabia’s Mecca region . It was also reported that a missile aimed at western Saudi Arabia was earlier brought down, as hostilities between the Riyadh-backed Yemen government and Iran-backed Houthis continue to escalate . The tournament’s fate hung in the balance in the past weeks, with several participating nations expressing concerns about the security situation. The AFC said while “exceptional circumstances” had been created for the organisation and delivery of the competition as originally scheduled, the postponement became necessary “in the interest of all participating teams, officials, spectators and other stakeholders”. The AFC will submit the new tournament dates to FIFA for approval from football’s global governing body.
