events.title: Russian strikes choke Ukraine’s economy as steel shuts down and grain exports stall
events.summary: Ukraine's economy is struggling as Russia's air war targets industries, logistics networks and ports needed for exports KAMIANSKE, Ukraine -- The furnaces are cold, the factory floor deserted, and twisted metal litters the grounds of Kamet Steel, a vast industrial complex that once helped power Ukraine’s economy but closed after a Russian attack . Across the country, grain — a key export — piles up in fields and silos as farmers struggle to find routes safe from airstrikes and wait for prices to rise. Russia’s intensified air campaign is slowly strangling Ukraine’s economy, targeting industrial and energy plants and the logistics networks, railways and export routes that keep it afloat. The near-daily strikes with ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones disrupt production and drive up transport costs. As a result, Ukraine’s government faces a deepening cash crunch as the air war chokes its revenue from steel, agriculture and other key sources. The damage ripples across interconnected sectors just as Kyiv faces uncertainty over future U.S. support . Ukraine’s central bank last week forecast a 0.4% economic contraction in 2026, reversing its previous projection of 1.8% growth, due to the attacks and a surge in global energy prices. Gov. Andriy Pyshnyy said the bank had also raised its inflation forecast to 12.5%, from 10% in July. Ukraine spends some 40% of its gross domestic product on defense — far beyond what it can cover alone, notes Torbjörn Becker, director of the Stockholm Institute of Transition Economics. Raising taxes only would bring in a fraction of what is needed. Missile strikes have halted steel production across Metinvest Group, the country’s mining and metals giant. Kamet Steel, in the industrial city of Kamianske, accounted for more than a quarter of Ukraine’s steel output in 2025. The complex employed thousands producing steel and pig iron for domestic construction. It also supplied semi-finished steel to Metinvest’s facility in Bulgaria for the market there and elsewhere in Europe. But five ballistic missiles struck the site on Sept. 5. Its closure has hurt Ukraine’s industrial economy, affecting construction, mining, engineering, energy and logistics. Ukrzaliznytsia, the national railway operator, relies heavily on steel transport and other freight revenue. Businesses that rely on the plant could lose jobs and face bankruptcy, said Oleksandr Tretyakov, Kamet Steel’s CEO. European Union trade restrictions could hinder recovery by narrowing the market for Ukrainian steel exports, he said. “This is the worst situation since the Second World War,” Tretyakov said, noting that steel once accounted for about 6% of Ukraine’s GDP. “It did,” he said. “Right now, it’s zero.” Agriculture accounts for up to 60% of Ukraine’s foreign currency earnings, making it critical to the wartime economy. But Russian attacks on Black Sea shipping have sharply reduced traffic through Ukraine’s deep-water ports just as farmers need cash to prepare for the next planting season. Ukraine’s Black Sea trade has collapsed with attacks on ports, vessels and logistics infrastructure, according to maritime data and analytics company Lloyd’s List Intelligence. There were only 21 ship arrivals at Black Sea ports in August, down about 90% from a year earlier. Soaring insurance premiums and the constant threat of Russian strikes deter shipowners. Dozens of sailors have been killed in attacks this year. “All our developments and all the innovations we achieved will be crossed out by this situation and we will need to start from zero later,” said Volodymyr Scavinskyi, trade director at Nibulon, one of Ukraine’s leading agricultural exporters. Learjet with 9 aboard crashes in Palm Beach County, Florida: FAA Sen. Chris Murphy hospitalized after suffering a stroke, chief of staff says 2 college students found dead after going missing while hiking, police say Ship traffic from Ukraine's lower-capacity ports on the Danube River to the Black Sea has surged, even under the threat of Russian bombardment. But it is costly. The Danube delta's Sulina Channel is too shallow for the largest vessels, and dozens of ships often wait days to enter or leave the river. Record low Danube water levels due to drought also constrain the route. Barges that once carried 1,500 tons are loading only 800 to 900 tons, Scavinskyi said. Nearly twice as many barges are needed to move the same volume, raising costs. Transporting each ton of corn from central Ukraine to Spain cost up to $50 earlier this year. Now, it can reach $150, he said. “It’s still risky and you don’t have any guarantees that your voyage will be successful,” Scavinskyi said. For Olena Shelest, commercial director at HarvEast, a major agricultural holding, the immediate challenge is finding buyers. HarvEast is holding wheat in enormous silo bags, waiting for market prices to stabilize. But the grain must be sold by year's end to free up cash for next year’s planting.

events.title: Palestine weekly: Election deadlock meets West Bank sieges, Gaza killings
events.summary: Will Israel’s election change life in Gaza? As Israel grapples with an inconclusive election, Palestinians face West Bank closures and Gaza killings. The election night highs for Palestinian citizens of Israel – Arab-led parties won a record 19 seats – turned into a week of delegitimising rhetoric from Israeli politicians. Nearly 840,000 people voted for Ra’am and the Joint List, a 64 percent increase on 2022 , and adding them to opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot’s bloc would give an anti-Netanyahu coalition 67 seats; without them, only a unity deal between the main Zionist blocs or another election is possible. list 1 of 3 Displaced in Hebron: Picking up pieces after Israeli siege list 2 of 3 Al Jazeera condemns Israeli ban extension, calls for its immediate lifting list 3 of 3 Arab parties back Eisenkot: What’s the latest in Israel’s coalition talks? Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud alleged the election had been “stolen” by Palestinian parties with unproven claims of Qatari financing. Qatar denied such accusations , as police sources told The Times of Israel that there was no evidence of widespread fraud. By Sunday, election committee chairman Noam Sohlberg declared the election “conducted properly”. However, the rhetoric delegitimising the Palestinian vote is now being reflected in the coalition negotiations under way. Avigdor Lieberman, leader of the right-wing Yisrael Beytenu party, has ruled out Palestinian partners, and Eisenkot has presented four conditions for anyone joining his coalition that would be anathema to the Palestinian parties, including recognising Israel as “a Jewish, democratic, liberal, and egalitarian state”, and mandatory national service for all citizens, including Palestinians. However, Palestinian politicians continue to express a willingness to back an Eisenkot government from outside – if only to enable the departure of Netanyahu and the far right. Meanwhile, thousands rallied in Tel Aviv for a coalition that includes the parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel. While the Israeli electorate was consumed by the election’s unclear results, Palestinians in the occupied West Bank continued enduring a variety of sieges, most prominently in Hebron. By October 29, Al Jazeera’s data unit counted 10 entrances sealed and about 5,000 people displaced. The city saw at least 120 arrests and 13 businesses demolished by Friday, when the army also blew up the homes of two men it blamed for an attack. Palestinian officials accused the government of using the operation to win settler votes ; no Israeli official has said so outright. On November 2, Governor Khaled Dudin announced the army had withdrawn from Hebron, and that displaced families could return. The Jerusalem Post reported that the army’s chief of staff recommended leaving Hebron before the election, but that Netanyahu refused. But even with the operation over, the damage remains following more than 120 arrests and daily economic losses the governor put at 10 million to 12 million shekels ($3.2m to $3.8m) in a city responsible for about 40 percent of Palestinian industrial output. Sieges in homes, expulsions from land But Hebron was only the largest of many closures that continue to plague the West Bank. In Masafer Yatta, at least 12 villages were cut off , and the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported that forces detained 10 teachers from the Jinba school on Sunday. Yousef Shanaran – who has been besieged in his home with his family in Wadi Rakhim for four weeks now – told Al Jazeera on Monday that settlers have now poisoned the well outside his family home, which the family already was unable to access for days at a time due to the siege. “No water, no food, nothing at all I’ve got,” he said. “Nobody is allowed to bring anything to us.” These sieges continue as settlers, and increasingly Israeli forces, disrupt the olive harvest across the West Bank. United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) documented 397 settler attacks causing casualties or damage in the first 26 days of October – a monthly high since OCHA began tracking such incidents in 2006. Across villages, a familiar pattern has emerged: settlers attack pickers, the army declares a closed military zone and orders the farmers out, and the harvest is lost. Amid reports of detentions and deportations of solidarity activists who came to the West Bank to assist in the olive harvest in recent days, activists accused settlers of assaulting three activist journalists at Umm al-Khair , and Israel revoked Brad Lander’s travel authorisation after he was detained while harvesting olives two weeks ago. In Gaza, attacks continued on a daily basis as the UN human rights office warned on October 30 that Palestinians are being pushed into an ever smaller area, calling the “ Yellow Line ” a “kill zone” that is moving westward. By November 2, the Ministry of Health put the death toll since last year’s ceasefire at 1,593.

events.title: North Korea denies links to Binance hack as researchers trace stolen billions
events.summary: North Korea denied allegations linking it to the $6.3 billion Binance hack, calling it a "grave political provocation." Hackers moved stolen funds through roughly 12,000 wallets and 40,000 transactions across 11 blockchains, with about $2.85 billion frozen or seized, according to Elliptic. North Korea-linked actors began moving stolen funds onto Solana after draining $500 million from Tron staging wallets, according to Chainalysis. North Korea rejected allegations linking Pyongyang to the estimated $6.3 billion Binance hack, calling the accusation a “grave political provocation,” according to state media. Kim Yo Jong, sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, denounced the FBI's attribution of the attack to North Korea-linked hacking group TraderTraitor, Yohnap reported Tuesday, citing the state-run Korean Central News Agency. Blockchain analytics firms including Elliptic and Chainalysis have also linked the attack and subsequent movement of the stolen funds to North Korea-linked actors. "The FBI is trying to brand the DPRK as a 'cyber criminal state', claiming that it obtained information that a hacking organization 'supported' by the DPRK was involved in the incident," Kim said, according to KCNA. She accused Washington of misleading international public opinion by portraying cybercrimes around the world as the work of North Korea. Separately, Binance said Tuesday it would begin progressively reopening withdrawals for additional crypto assets across more networks, expanding its phased restoration of services following last week's hack. The denial comes as blockchain analytics firms trace billions of dollars in cryptocurrency stolen from Binance through thousands of wallets across multiple blockchains. Elliptic and Chainalysis said hackers linked to North Korea have used increasingly complex techniques to obscure the trail of the funds. In the first four days after the attack, the hackers used roughly 12,000 wallets across 11 blockchains and conducted more than 40,000 transactions, Elliptic said in a report Monday. The activity appeared highly complex and automated, with an average of one new wallet used every 25 seconds. Much of the laundering activity initially took place on the Tron blockchain, where stolen funds were distributed across about 7,700 addresses before being moved to Ethereum through cross-chain bridges, according to Elliptic. At least $147 million had been transferred out of Tron through such bridges. The hackers also used decentralized exchanges to swap stolen stablecoins into cryptocurrencies that cannot be frozen by their issuers, including ether. Elliptic said roughly $786 million in stablecoins was converted before issuers including Tether and Circle froze the remaining assets. The laundering operation has since expanded to other blockchains, including Solana . Chainalysis said North Korea-linked actors had begun a new phase of laundering after moving more than $500 million through intermediary wallets on Tron. Elliptic also identified the first signs of bitcoin mixing, a technique designed to make transactions harder to trace. About 28 bitcoin, worth $2.2 million, had passed through 18 mixing transactions as of early Monday, the firm said. Despite the extensive movement of funds, about $2.85 billion — or 44% of exactly $6.43 billion stolen as reported by Elliptic — has been frozen or seized, while roughly $3.24 billion remains in addresses linked to the theft, mostly in bitcoin and ether. The firm said only a negligible amount of stolen funds appeared to have been cashed out, with most of the activity involving transfers or conversions between cryptocurrencies rather than exchanges into spendable funds. Elliptic said the laundering has moved slower than after the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025, when North Korean hackers moved all the stolen ether within 10 days. It expects the remaining funds to be gradually converted into bitcoin and potentially cashed out through over-the-counter brokers and exchanges over several months. Binance added it has covered about 95% of the affected amount, with the remaining 5% consisting of less liquid tokens that take longer to source. The exchange said it was working with industry partners to acquire the remaining assets.

events.title: Chalmers promises to be 'helpful' on inflation but rejects blame for rate hike
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Government will play 'helpful role' on inflation but not at fault, Jim Chalmers says Jim Chalmers pointed to evidence that public sector demand was easing. ( ABC News: Ian Cutmore ) Jim Chalmers says the government's budget is "not what's putting upward pressure on inflation" after a fifth rate hike this year. The Reserve Bank made the widely expected move on rates. The government has promised fresh savings in the mid-year budget update next month. Treasurer Jim Chalmers has again denied his budget is the cause of persistent inflation, after the Reserve Bank raised interest rates for the fifth time this year. Facing political pressure over the level of government spending, the treasurer seized on the bank's assessment that public sector demand was "weaker than expected" in early 2026, the period when inflation began its resurgence. "Public demand growth has eased quite substantially at a time when private demand has tripled," he said. "Our budgets are not what's putting upward pressure on inflation, but we can play a helpful role and that's what we intend to do." RBA lifts interest rates to try to dampen inflation The RBA lifts interest rates to the highest level in 18 years in a majority decision by its board. Mr Chalmers has promised fresh savings in next month's mid-year budget update, but could not say whether the savings would be enough to outweigh new spending, a feat the Albanese government has not managed in any of the five years it has overseen. "We take responsibility for our part of the fight against inflation," he said. "We're helping with the cost of living at the same time as we manage the budget responsibly." Reserve Bank Governor Michele Bullock maintained her longstanding practice of avoiding direct comment on the government's budget, saying overall demand, combining public and private, remained too high across the economy. "It's up to the government, the elected officials, to decide what they want to do with the budget," she said. "Independence is a two-way street. I don't tell them what to do with fiscal policy. They don't tell me what to do with interest rates." Public demand eases, but question marks over role of NDIS Ms Bullock said the decision on rates, which was not unanimous, was motivated by the ongoing consequences of the Middle East and domestic factors. The main domestic driver, though not the sole one, has been artificial intelligence investment. The bank's updated forecasts predict business investment will grow by 12 per cent this year and public demand by just 2.1 per cent. The "weaker" public result was partly due to "the ending of some temporary cost-of-living measures", a staff note explained. Also cited was a "moderation" in spending on defence, disability and aged care. The largest single category of savings by far under the Albanese government has been to the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS), with $36 billion saved over four years in the May budget alone. But fresh doubts have been raised over whether that saving can be achieved, after the publication of preliminary findings from the Australian Government Actuary that the $36 billion figure was subject to "considerable uncertainty". Though cautioning that he did not have "sufficient detail" to draw a firm conclusion about the costings, actuary Guy Thorburn noted several risks, including an assumption of the numbers of children with autism entering the scheme not yet borne out by reality. The government has not been specific about where further savings will be found in the budget. Finance Minister Katy Gallagher said she was "looking across government" for ways to cut back, but that these would be "difficult decisions". "We have to respond to the economic circumstances we face … [But] we're also mindful of the fact we need to support people through this as well," she said. "I hear a lot of calls for cuts to government spending, I don't hear as many specifics about where." Could government spending cuts fight inflation? The Reserve Bank is tipped to increase interest rates tomorrow because of an ongoing concern that inflation is not under control. But is there an alternative? Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson said the government had a "spending addiction" and was fuelling inflation. "[It] will never pull in its belt, but it keeps telling Australians to pull in theirs. It stokes inflation, taxes inflation and spends inflation," he said. While public demand is growing much slower than private demand in the Reserve Bank's forecasts, the bank does expect it to grow faster than the economy overall.

events.title: North Korea denies being behind record $6.3bn Binance hack
events.summary: Kim Yo Jong, the sister of North Korea's leader Kim Jong Un Published 3 November 2026, 00:56 GMT North Korea has denied claims that it was behind the record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance , calling the allegations "absurd rhetoric". Kim Yo Jong, a top Democratic People's Republic of Korea official and the sister of leader Kim Jong Un , said on Tuesday that the accusations are another "sinister attempt" by the US to damage Pyongyang's public image. The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the Secret Service and cyber analysts have said North Korea orchestrated the hack, which has been described as the largest in history. This is the latest hack to be linked to North Korea, which has been accused of relying on cyber-crime to help finance its sanctioned economy. Blockchain analysts and the FBI have said the attack was led by state-backed hacking group TraderTraitor. The FBI has called on industry partners to help block transactions involving cryptocurrency accounts linked to the group. "The US has made a trite provocation of linking it with the Democratic People's Republic of Korea again," Kim Yo-jong, the director of North Korea's General Affairs Department, said in a statement. "It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads the international public opinion as if all the cyber crimes in different parts of the world are our deeds," she said. Why North Korea's 'elite' hackers are the prime suspect in major Binance hack Published 3 days ago Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far Published 3 days ago But Pyongyang has been blamed for a number of major cyber attacks in recent years - accusations that it has denied. The TraderTraitor unit, which is also known as the Lazarus Group, was blamed for a then-record $1.5bn hack of crypto exchange Bybit in 2025. Pyongyang has systematically built its cyber operations, recruiting promising students from universities and sending them to hacker units overseen by North Korea's intelligence agency, research groups like the S Rajaratnam School of International Studies think tank have said. The country has consistently denied such claims. Kim Yo Jong said "it is the consistent policy stand of the DPRK government to resolutely oppose all sorts of malicious acts in cyberspace". Kim Yo-jong: North Korea's heir apparent? Published 16 June 2020 Who is Kim Yo-jong? Video, 00:02:32 Who is Kim Yo-jong? Published 16 June 2020 The BBC has contacted Binance for comment. Since the hack, the crypto giant has largely focused its public statements on the technical nature of the breach and its response to protect users. The company said last week that initial checks indicated that an engineer's laptop had been compromised, enabling an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals. Trading in major cryptocurrencies on Binance has since resumed after the exchange worked with issuers to freeze assets impacted by the hack. A net $5.27bn has been withdrawn from the exchange since transactions resumed on Sunday, according to data posted on Tuesday by Binance. It also said the level of transactions has now stabilised. The company has repeatedly said it would cover all of the losses linked to the attack and that it has so far covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Models are commodities, harnesses are the valuable part A whopping 3% of boardroom execs spy productivity and costs savings from AI 6 days ago Alibaba's Qwen AI caught trying to contact server in China 7 days ago IBM CEO says open weight models are now irresistibly good and cheap on-prem 12 days ago Nvidia woos wary Europeans with more open weights models 12 days ago The AI math isn't mathing as infrastructure spending forecast to outstrip expected revenue 19 days ago For-profit model-makers, many of which are spending billions on AI infrastructure, will be chasing revenue from just ten percent of steps involved in agentic AI workflows, according to analyst firm Gartner. “Nine in 10 agent workflow steps are routine, and open-weight models handle them at parity for a quarter of the price of the cheapest closed model,” the firm’s senior director Mark Petty and group vice president Raymond Paquet wrote last week in new document titled “Open-Weight Models Will Run 90% of Enterprise Agentic Workflow Steps.” “Typical operational workflows involve hundreds of routine executions, such as classification, tool calling, passing, validating and reconciling data,” the pair observe, before suggesting open-weight models “can handle hundreds of these routine steps for every one that needs frontier reasoning.” “Against the cheapest closed model at the same score, the open model costs a quarter as much. Against a frontier model run on every step, it costs as little as a twentieth,” the pair add. Those are the best-case numbers, because the analysts admit “Current open models can be more verbose and retry more often, so the saving per task against a frontier model is closer to five or six times.” That’s still a lovely saving, but the analysts rate it as the welcome by-product of moving to open models rather than an end in itself. “Years of workflow history are a large part of what an acquirer pays for in a SaaS company and every routine step sent to a frontier API moves a slice of it outside your perimeter,” the pair wrote. “Open-weights preserve your control. The cost saving is a bonus.” The two analysts therefore offer the following strategic planning assumption: “By 2030, 90% of enterprise operational agent workflow steps will execute on open-weight models.” They argue that enterprises will mostly adopt domain-specific open-weight models, because they do well “in scenarios where a small number of highly stable steps run millions of times a month.” Most models, however, are already commodities. Harnesses, the tools that run agents and manage agents, are the source of value in AI products, because one of their roles is to route work to the most appropriate model for a job, without users noticing any impact. A good harness saves money, imposes strong guardrails, and manages agent fleets. Less powerful harnesses leave users with more to do. The paper suggests frontier models will continue to have a role as the engine of research and development and are effectively capital expense. Community venues and libraries across the county will offer free hot drinks and the opportunity to connect with others until 31 March 2027. The service in over 100 venues available across Surrey, with those taking part shown on a map , external on the authority's website. The project, which has run since 2022, will also offer energy advice and help to access other support services. It is being supported by the Crisis and Resilience Fund, a government funded scheme that helps people on low incomes. events.title: Brittany Snow says she learned to have a different kind of relationship with her father after his Alzheimer’s diagnosis
events.summary: Brittany Snow said her father was diagnosed with Alzheimer's in 2020. Gilbert Flores/Variety via Getty Images Brittany Snow said her father's Alzheimer's has brought a "prolonged grief." But it has also made her appreciate the small moments they still share. Their relationship has taken a different shape, she said, but they're still close. Brittany Snow , 40, says her father's Alzheimer's diagnosis taught her to appreciate the time they still have. On Monday's episode of " Armchair Expert with Dax Shepard ," Snow spoke about her relationship with her father, who was 48 when she was born. "My dad and I had an interesting relationship growing up, and then when I was doing the soap opera when I was 12, it really shifted for me, and we got really close," the "Guiding Light" actor said. "We were so close." Snow said her father was diagnosed with Alzheimer's in 2020, and his condition is "pretty extreme at this point." "I shouldn't refer to it as 'we were close' because we are close, but you know, it takes a different shape," Snow said of her current relationship with him. She said navigating her father's illness has brought a mix of emotions, from sadness and grief to gratitude for the time they have together. "I got six years that I wouldn't have had if he got cancer or something like that, and I got to really be present in those years because I knew it was happening," Snow said. "I really don't take that for granted." She said her father's condition has brought a form of "prolonged grief," but has also given her time to make sense of the loss instead of being hit by it all at once. "You're sort of mining all the stuff before," she said. Snow has opened up about her father's diagnosis in past interviews. In a 2024 appearance on the " Broad Ideas with Rachel Bilson & Olivia Allen " podcast, Snow said leaving after visiting her father is difficult because he didn't understand where she was going. She added that she has to remind herself that he would want her to continue living her own life too. "It's a baffling disease to witness, but it's really, really interesting and beautiful to get to see someone still there, but in a different version of themselves," Snow said. events.title: Victorian farmers blindsided by approval of 155-turbine wind farm ahead of election
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Victorian farmers blindsided by wind farm approval on eve of election caretaker period A 155-turbine wind farm has been approved for Victoria's north. ( ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding ) The Victorian government has approved the controversial Meering West Wind Farm, which could include up to 155 turbines, a day before entering caretaker mode. More than 100 objections had been lodged and neighbouring farmers say their concerns have been ignored. The project's future could hinge on the November 28 state election, with the Coalition pledging to scrap the VNI West transmission line the project intends to connect to. The Victorian government has signed off on a large wind and battery project for the state's north, on the eve of entering caretaker mode ahead of this month's state election. Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny signed off on a planning permit for the Meering West Wind Farm on Monday, just a day before the caretaker period came into effect. The facility to be built at Meering West, about 140km north-west of Bendigo, would be one of Australia's largest, incorporating up to 155 wind turbines. Construction on the project, which would deliver 1.3 gigawatts of generation capacity and 1,000 megawatt-hours of battery energy storage, is due to start in 2029. Like other similar facilities, it has been deeply controversial among local residents, with many farmers rallying against its approval. The timing of the approval is further complicated by the facility's intention to tap into the VNI West transmission line, which is yet to be built and would be scrapped if the Victorian Coalition came to government. Tyler Nelson is one of many neighbouring farmers who have objected to the project. He said he was not surprised the government had signed off on it at the last minute. "I'm very disappointed, but at the same time I can't say I'm shocked with the behaviour of the Labor government," he said. "It's well established that there are a lot of projects being rushed through at the 11th hour and there's been a pretty poor process involved for quite some time." Tyler Nelson is among the many farmers who oppose the Meering West wind farm. ( Supplied: Tyler Nelson ) Mr Nelson said he and other neighbours had been unaware of the project until it was well advanced. "Most neighbours and those affected found out pretty late in the piece, once there were contracts and caveats in place," he said. Mr Nelson said more than 100 people had objected to the project, with concerns including noise, shadow, flicker, land devaluation, fire risk and impacts on the natural environment. He said their objections and requests, including removing turbines from the project footprint close to objecting neighbours, had not been adopted. The wind farm at Meering West would have 1.3 gigawatts of generation capacity. ( Supplied: Pixabay / JACLOU-DL / License /File ) Mr Nelson was reluctant to comment on the community divisions the project had created. "I've tried not to let it affect me, but it's difficult not to," he said. "Communities that usually stand together and talk, when that's taken away, it seems a bit odd." Victoria's election is nearly here — it's time to have Your Say Before Victorians head to the polls on November 28, we want to hear about what matters to you most. Given the Coalition has committed to scrap VNI West, Mr Nelson said he hoped there would be a change of government on November 28, but he was not convinced it would leave the Meering West project dead in the water. "It would be nice to think that is the case, but what we're learning is we never know what's happening with backroom deals," he said. "Yes, scrapping VNI West is a good move by the Coalition, but what does it mean for this project? "It's my understanding that [project proponent Virya] will continue to develop on somehow, but I don't know what that looks like." The Victorian government, Meering West Wind Farm representatives and developer Virya were contacted for comment.

events.title: Russia is hiding anti-Starlink jammers in parking lots and trailers on the front lines: Ukraine drone expert
events.summary: A Ukrainian soldier operates a GARA long-range drone. Dmytro Smolienko/Ukrinform/NurPhoto via Getty Images A top Ukrainian drone expert says Russia is deploying more jammers to counter Starshield. These Volna Kupol Garant systems beam interference at specific satellites as they pass overhead. They first emerged in 2024, but Russia said this August that it's begun serial production of the system. Russia is rolling out more trailer-mounted jammers designed to prevent Ukraine's attack drones from connecting to SpaceX's satellites , according to a top Ukrainian analyst. Each jammer can provide point defense covering about 25 square kilometers, or about 9.6 square miles, said Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, a Ukrainian presidential advisor on drones. "Russia has covered nearly all important sites in Crimea with this type of EW and is increasingly deploying it along the front line," Beskrestnov wrote on Monday on his Telegram channel. He said the Kremlin was deploying the systems to counter Ukraine's use of Starlink over Russian-held territory. Ukraine's forces rely on the military version of the SpaceX service, Starshield, for strike and deep-recon missions. Starshield, as well as onboard artificial intelligence, has been crucial to helping Ukraine control mid-range attack drones and receive intel from recon drones flying behind Russian lines. Beskrestnov advised Ukrainian drone pilots to look out for truck or trailer parking lots as an "ideal place" for Russia to conceal its jammers. "Of dozens of trucks, three to six may have the system installed. Also watch for small trailers attached to passenger cars," he wrote. "The complex can even operate from generators," Beskrestnov added, saying that Ukrainian drone teams could look for polycarbonate panels, plastic sheeting, or greenhouses that can obscure the jammer. The system mentioned is the Volna Kupol Garant, which targets the satellite instead of the drone or ground terminal. It uses dish antennas to beam powerful radio interference at individual low-Earth-orbit satellites, aiming to create a local bubble in which satellite links such as Starlink struggle or fail to work as they pass overhead, per ODIN, the US Army's public database. Ukraine reported Russia's first use of the system in Kharkiv in 2024, but it's been deployed in greater numbers since the start of this year, as Starshield has increasingly allowed Ukraine to strike deeper into Russian-held territory with drones. In August, the Russian state media outlet TASS reported that serial production of the Volna Kupol Garant was underway to build more countermeasures. One jammer system typically consists of six trailers, each with two antennas. Ukrainian forces attacking jamming sites previously uploaded drone footage showing these trailers sitting neatly in two rows. But Beskrestnov said on Monday that Russia had recently developed versions that use only one antenna per trailer and was learning to spread them out and conceal them. Still, analysts believe one jamming system can target only a single low Earth orbit satellite at a time. Open-source trackers estimate that Starshield, which is owned and operated by the US, uses a constellation of at least 240 satellites. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: How a Harvard dream ended in tragedy for a Pakistani family
events.summary: A 24-year-old physics graduate dies after her family pays millions to a man who lied about getting her admitted into the university. Islamabad, Pakistan – The sign above the Rana Malik Center, a dairy shop in Islamabad’s G-10 neighbourhood, advertises milk, fresh yoghurt, lassi and desi ghee. Rana Muhammad Ijaz has lived with his family in the apartment above for more than three decades. Sitting outside his shop in late October, Ijaz recalled how his youngest daughter, Laiba, would make tea for him every morning and then again at night before bedtime. “She used to massage my shoulders before I went to bed too.” he told Al Jazeera. Ijaz sat outside his shop, remembering her. “Now that she is gone, I miss it all.” Laiba Ijaz, 24, a physics gold medallist from the publicly funded International Islamic University Islamabad (IIUI), was found dead near her home on October 9. According to the initial findings of a police case, she likely died by suicide after she and her family were defrauded of millions of rupees – tens of thousands of dollars – by a man who promised her admission to Harvard University in the United States. Muhammad Noman, accused of the fraud, was arrested two days later. He died on October 20 after being shot while in police custody. Police said his accomplices had opened fire to free him. On October 21, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi visited the family and handed over more than 5 million rupees ($18,000) that officials said had been recovered from Noman. But that money means little to Ijaz and his family. What mattered most – his daughter – is gone. Ijaz studied until the eighth grade and his wife until grade 10, but all four of their daughters went to university. Two of the sisters studied mathematics while one of Laiba’s elder sisters spent a year in China on a scholarship, learning Mandarin. Laiba, too, studied on scholarships, her father said, and won the gold medal at her university. “The day she got it, Laiba danced and jumped in front of her sisters,” Ijaz said. Laiba later taught science at an Islamabad school and gave out-of-school tuition classes to children between grades 2 and 6. IIUI offered her a scholarship to study in Saudi Arabia, but she wanted to pursue higher studies in the US, her father said. She asked him to pay for her studies abroad. “’I did all the work myself, and I teach tuitions too, so can’t you do this for me?'” she asked her father, he recalled. He told her: “My dear daughter, I will.” “From there, we started preparing,” Ijaz said. Then they met Noman, and the dream grew. Unknown to the family at the time, it was built on hollow promises and outright lies. Laiba met Noman this year at a call centre where she worked in Islamabad’s Blue Area, the capital’s main business district. Her hours were late, and most of her colleagues were male. Ijaz was uncomfortable with Laiba’s work environment and encouraged her to leave. She quit the job. But Noman then began coming to the shop to buy milk and yoghurt. During his visits, Ijaz said, he asked about Laiba’s plans to study in Saudi Arabia. “No, we will not go to Saudi Arabia. We will go to America,” Ijaz said he told Noman. Noman claimed to work at the Supreme Court, showed Ijaz a service card and said he needed no licence because he was a government employee. “The card looked right to me too. I showed it to the people next to me,” Ijaz said. Noman offered to help Laiba with her application. Ijaz and Laiba decided to accept his offer. “That was our biggest mistake,” the father said. The family paid in stages, starting with 2.2 million rupees ($7,900) for university fees, Ijaz said. Noman later claimed Harvard needed a statement proving 7.2 million rupees ($25,900) in funds, which he insisted had to pass through his account to be converted into dollars. “To help my daughter, I sold a plot which I owned. I also sold the [family] jewellery, so I could complete the demanded 7.2 million rupees,” he said. Documents shared with Al Jazeera appear to trace a real application: Harvard offer and scholarship letters, a US immigration form with an official-looking stamp, a sponsor’s affidavit from a New York relative, an embassy record bearing Laiba’s photograph and a business-class ticket to Boston. The final file, handed over in late September, also contained a bank statement in Laiba’s name and an October 12 visa interview date, Ijaz said. In early October, Ijaz said he called Noman to help prepare his daughter for the interview. Noman told him he was in Quetta and would return the next day. Suspicious of his evasiveness, the family showed the documents to a travel agent and discovered the Boston ticket was fake. A lawyer neighbour checked the file and told them none of the documents was genuine. They learned the truth about October 6, Ijaz said. The family was shattered. “I used to tell her, ‘What had to happen has happened,'” Ijaz said.

events.title: North Korea says it wasn’t behind the $6.3 billion Binance hack and claims the US blames it for “all the cyber crimes”
events.summary: North Korea is denying being involved in the hack on Binance. Korea Summit Press Pool/Getty Images North Korea denies involvement in Binance's $6 billion crypto theft. Kim Yo-jong accused the US of using cybercrime allegations to harm North Korea's global reputation. Binance detected a $6.3 billion breach and said it would cover losses. North Korea has denied that it was behind the $6.3 billion theft from cryptocurrency exchange Binance , calling the FBI's allegation a "grave political provocation." In a Tuesday statement, Kim Yo-jong, the sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, said: "The FBI is trying to brand the DPRK as a 'cyber criminal state,' claiming that it obtained information that a hacking organization 'supported' by the DPRK was involved in the incident." The statement was carried by the state-run Korean Central News Agency and republished by South Korea's Yonhap News Agency. "It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads the international public opinion as if all the cyber crimes in different parts of the world are our deeds," she added. Kim also said Washington was using cybercrime allegations to damage North Korea's reputation. She said the Trump administration had announced plans to confiscate illicit cryptocurrency and use it as a strategic reserve, and suggested that who ultimately received "the so-called stolen cryptocurrency" could offer "a clue about who is behind the hacking incident." This statement comes after a few days of disruption for Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange. On October 29, Binance said it discovered unauthorized withdrawals worth about $6.3 billion. The company initially said the breach may have involved a compromised laptop used by a DevOps engineer, though it later said it had identified additional points of intrusion. Binance said it found no evidence that wallet private keys had been leaked. The exchange temporarily suspended withdrawals and said about $3 billion in assets had been frozen as it worked to investigate the attack. On October 31, the FBI said North Korea was responsible for the theft and identified the alleged operation as "TraderTraitor," a name it has previously used for North Korea-linked crypto thefts. The agency said it had observed the actors converting stolen assets primarily into ethereum and warned industry companies to block transactions connected to listed wallet addresses. Binance began restoring withdrawals in phases on November 1 and said it saw a net outflow of about $3.64 billion in under 10 hours. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Hope for house hunters amid slump as realtor warns optimism premature
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Perth property price slump provides glimmer of hope for homebuyers Vanessa Bray says a drop in Perth house prices has given her hope of finding a home for her family. ( ABC News: Madigan Landry ) Home buyers are hopeful a drop in Perth property prices will help them break into the market. New data shows the city's median dwelling value has fallen to $942,018, but that is still 68 per cent higher than it was five years ago. A Perth realtor warns the optimism of those trying to buy a home may be premature, saying the figures do not represent the true state of the housing market. After years of searching for a home as Perth property prices continued to rise at an unprecedented rate, Vanessa Bray finally feels like she has a fighting chance of securing one. The single mum has been buoyed by new figures showing Australia is tracking towards its biggest housing market downturn in 40 years, with Perth's house prices dropping 5.7 per cent over the last three months. Data from property research group Cotality shows Perth's median dwelling price has fallen to $942,018 — a drop of nearly $100,000 since peaking at more than $1 million in April. Meanwhile, economists at the Commonwealth Bank today released an updated forecast predicting Perth property prices would plummet 18 per cent from that April peak, before prices begin to stabilise in the second half of 2027. For Ms Bray, the easing market spells hope of finding a home for her and her sons. Vanessa Bray is feeling a lot more positive about buying a home in light of recent data. ( ABC News: Madigan Landry ) "I can't even begin to describe the relief that I feel for myself and my kids that we could maybe have a home of our own," she said. "It's close. I feel like it will happen instead of the despair that I had that it was never going to happen." National house prices have fallen for a seventh consecutive month, according to property research group Cotality. Ms Bray has been looking for a family home since she and her partner separated four years ago. She needs to find something in their school catchment while staying under the $850,000 cap needed to qualify for the federal government's Help to Buy Scheme. Ms Bray said her experience of trying to buy a home had been '"devastating" and like being on a "rollercoaster". "[I've gone from] thinking, 'right, this could finally be it. I'm going to make it. I'm going to have long-term security for me and my kids' to the devastation of 'I've missed out again'," she said. Perth's median dwelling price has fallen by almost $100,000 in six months. ( ABC News: Gian De Poloni ) While the recent slump in prices represents a glimmer of hope for those trying to break into the market, the softening represents a small dent in the meteoric rise in Perth's property prices, which have risen 93 per cent in a decade, including 68 per cent in the last five years. Perth realtor Kyle Peters warned the optimism of those trying to enter the market could be premature. Mr Peters said the recent figures were not a good representation of the true state of Australia's housing market. "It would be an interesting anomaly that a housing market would crash when we have a housing crisis and don't have enough houses for people to live in," Mr Peters said. "At the rate things were ramping up before, there needed to be some abatement, but certainly we [still] have a housing shortage." REIWA president Rob Mandanici said even if prices did not continue to fall on the same trajectory, the slowing market still provided benefits for those entering the market. REIWA President Rob Mandanici says the easing should give buyers some breathing space. ( ABC News: Madigan Landry ) "They can take a little bit more time to make that purchasing decision and not feel that immense pressure to rush into a decision," he said. "The buyers themselves haven't disappeared, they've become more selective." House prices are falling all around the country. ( ABC News: Charlotte Wilkes ) Mr Mandanici said there was no doubt Australia was experiencing "a little bit of a market slowdown", but said the dip in prices did not amount to a crash. "We are seeing some prices across multiple Perth suburbs pull back, but a lot of those suburbs are coming off highs," he said. "We've got a lot of buyers sitting on the sidelines and I think today's interest rate decision will just give buyers the certainty that they want moving forward." On Tuesday the Reserve Bank increased interest rates by 0.25 percentage points, lifting the cash rate to 4.85 per cent, the highest it has been since 2008.

events.title: ‘Going hungry’: Garment workers in Bangladesh say wages barely cover needs
events.summary: Tens of thousands of workers in the world’s second-largest apparel exporter nation hit the streets to demand better minimum wages. Dhaka, Bangladesh – Laili Begum can no longer afford to keep her two children in school. There are days when the 37-year-old garment worker struggles to put even one proper meal on the table. An experienced sewing operator at Virtual Bottoms Limited, a ready-made garments factory near Bangladesh’s capital Dhaka, Begum earns around 15,000 taka ($121) a month, which sometimes rises to 18,000–20,000 taka ($145–$161) when she works overtime. list 1 of 4 Bangladesh garment factories disrupted as protests continue for third day list 2 of 4 Bangladesh forms wage board as garment workers protest list 3 of 4 Bangladesh garment exporters fear $1bn losses after huge airport fire list 4 of 4 Bangladesh per capita GDP forecast to outstrip India’s: What does it mean? Her 15-year-old daughter and 12-year-old son dropped out of school earlier this year because she could not afford their education. “We can barely afford one proper meal a day. This morning, we had only puffed rice and Bombay mix [a snack]. There was nothing for lunch. We’ve been going hungry, hoping to have a proper meal tonight. Yesterday was the same. This is how we survive now,” she told Al Jazeera. “My son is so thin that you can count every rib in his chest. What else can I do?” Begum is among approximately four million garment factory workers in Bangladesh, half of them women. They are now protesting for better wages . Bangladesh, the world’s second-largest apparel exporter after China, is a key supplier to global fashion brands such as H&M, Zara, Levi Strauss, Walmart, and Primark. The country’s ready-made garment sector accounts for more ⁠than 80 percent of its export earnings, which touched $39bn last financial year. Yet, the people sewing those clothes say their pay no longer covers basic living costs. A Muslim-majority South Asian nation of 170 million people, Bangladesh has one of the world’s lowest wages among apparel-producing countries. Cambodia has a minimum wage of $210 a month for garment workers, Vietnam’s range from $140-$210, while wages at China’s manufacturing hub of Guangdong range between $286 and $378. That disparity – worsened by rising inflation and the growing cost of living – pushed the workers to strike and hit the streets on Saturday to demand a minimum wage of 30,000 taka ($241), more than double the current wage of 12,500 taka ($102). On Sunday, Begum joined one such protest in the Jamgora part of the Ashulia industrial area on the outskirts of the capital Dhaka, with the police firing tear gas and stun grenades to disperse the protesters, and arresting dozens of them. The ⁠Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association said the demonstrations disrupted operations at 529 factories on Sunday and affected nearly a million workers. Later that day, the government announced the formation of a six-member wage board to review the workers’ demands. But that did not stop the garment workers from returning to the streets for a third straight day on Monday. In northern Dhaka’s Gazipur area, the workers blocked the Dhaka-Tangail highway, and vandalised and torched several vehicles, while clashes with police were reported from the neighbouring Mirpur district. “The government only makes promises,” Begum told Al Jazeera. “They haven’t told us when wages will increase and by how much.” Rasel Khan, a 30-year-old garment worker at Ashulia, told Al Jazeera his monthly earnings of 18,000–20,000 taka ($145–$161), including overtime, were no longer enough to support his family, which included his mother and younger brother besides his wife and child. As living costs soar, he has accumulated a debt of about 100,000 taka ($805) to meet his needs. “It’s impossible to support a family on this income anymore. Prices keep rising, and we have to borrow money just to survive,” he said. The last revision of the minimum wage in the garment sector took place in December 2023. Since then, prices have continued to climb. Official data put annual inflation at 8.34 percent in September, including 7.22 percent for food and 9.30 percent for non-food expenses. Begum says she pays 3,500 taka ($28) as rent for a single room shared with her mother and children. Her father, living in their village in the central district of Sirajganj, also depends on her income. She says she is burning discarded paper and other materials to cook because she is not able to afford a gas cylinder that costs about 2,200 taka ($18). Zahid Hussain, a former lead economist at the World Bank’s Dhaka office, said persistent inflation over the past five years has sharply eroded the purchasing power of low-paid workers. “When real income falls, they have to cut their daily living standards,” he told Al Jazeera. “They don’t have any surplus income.

events.title: Adnoc Gas to supply TotalEnergies with up to 1.6 million tonnes of LNG in five-year deal
events.summary: Adnoc Gas has signed a five-year agreement to supply up to 1.6 million tonnes of liquefied natural gas to France's TotalEnergies, as the Abu Dhabi company expands its share of the global LNG market. The deal builds on a long-standing partnership between the two companies and reflects growing demand for LNG and confidence in Adnoc’s ability to deliver reliable supplies, the company said on Tuesday. “ Global demand for LNG continues to grow, and Adnoc Gas is well-positioned to capture that opportunity,” said Fatema Al Nuaimi, chief executive of Adnoc Gas. “This agreement reflects the strength of our LNG business, the competitiveness of our supply offering and our ability to secure long-term partnerships that support growth, enhance resilience and create lasting value for shareholders.” Adnoc Gas has continued to execute its long-term growth strategy this year, despite operational constraints. The company awarded $8.2 billion in engineering, procurement and construction contracts, part of its largest capital investment, for the second and third phases of the Rich Gas Development project – $3.9 billion for Phase 2, and $4.3 billion for Phase 3, the company said in August. These contracts build on Phase 1, announced in June 2025. The Rich Gas Development is a multi-phase, $13.2 billion capital investment programme by Adnoc Gas to expand gas processing and liquid recovery infrastructure across the UAE. The latest move strengthens Adnoc Gas’s commercial position at a time when demand for LNG is rising across Europe and Asia. Asia remains the main destination for LNG, accounting for about 65 per cent of global imports in 2025, while Europe has become a major buyer as it replaces Russian pipeline gas and manages storage needs, according to the International Energy Agency’s latest gas market report. “Thanks to its perfect location between Europe and Asia, this new supply will enable TotalEnergies to confirm its position as one of the main LNG portfolio suppliers,” said Stephane Michel, president of gas, renewables and power at TotalEnergies. TotalEnergies is both a shareholder in Adnoc Gas and a partner in the Ruwais LNG project. Adnoc Gas said it expects the planned integration of the Ruwais LNG project to significantly increase its production capacity, supporting its ambition to become one of the world’s leading LNG suppliers. The agreement between Adnoc Gas and TotalEnergies comes as Adnoc scales up a new global LNG marketing and trading platform that combines the marketing activities of Adnoc Gas and investment arm XRG with the trading capabilities of Adnoc Trading . The platform is aiming to reach 47 million tonnes per annum of marketable LNG beyond 2030, a level intended to place it among the world’s leading LNG marketing and trading businesses, Adnoc Gas said on Tuesday. Adnoc Gas supplies about 60 per cent of the UAE’s sales gas needs and supplies end-customers in more than 20 countries.

events.title: California’s Bay Area debates data centres ahead of US midterm elections
events.summary: Importance of governor races in midterms Seven Bay Area cities have passed data centre moratoriums, despite the region’s reputation as a hub for AI innovation. Oakland, California – Protesters dressed as cardboard robots chanted and danced to a drumbeat as they protested against new data centres outside Oakland City Hall last month. Their concerns largely focused on how the centres — which process large amounts of digital information — might strain the energy grid. list 1 of 3 Supreme Court rejects Trump request to set aside California ballots list 2 of 3 Mamdani’s progressive allies vie for seats in Congress list 3 of 3 Trump makes final midterms pitch at Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool The result, they argued, would not only be environmental harm but also sky-high electricity bills for local households. “Power prices have gone up so much in Oakland that some people are thinking of shutting off their power,” said Carlos Gutierrez, an activist for Communities for a Better Environment, an environmental justice group. “And the city is planning to provide power to a data centre instead.” Opposition to data centres is growing across the United States, as residents express concern about their rapid expansion. More than 3,000 data centres already operate in the country, with more than 1,500 others in development, according to the Pew Research Center. But the backlash is perhaps most striking in California’s San Francisco Bay Area, a region considered to be the heart of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom. Major AI companies such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta are based in the Bay Area, and the industry’s growth has been credited with fuelling a local economic renaissance. Data centres house the advanced computer chips and servers needed to run AI-powered services such as Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI’s ChatGPT. But they also require 24-hour power and a large supply of water to cool their processors. Even with such cooling technology, data centres are notorious for emitting heat, leading to an increase in land surface temperatures as high as 9 degrees Celsius (16 degrees Fahrenheit). Concerns about the cost of rapid data centre growth, both environmentally and financially, have catapulted the issue into the discourse around Tuesday’s midterm elections. In the final two months before the vote, at least seven Bay Area cities, including San Francisco and Richmond, have passed temporary moratoriums on data centre construction. They include Oakland, which passed a data centre moratorium on October 6, after days of protest. Local politicians competing in Tuesday’s midterms have also used the topic as a wedge issue, to rally support among certain pockets of voters. One of the most closely watched races in the Bay Area is for the seat left vacant by longtime Democratic leader Nancy Pelosi. After 39 years in the House of Representatives, Pelosi is retiring at the end of the year. Two Democrats are competing in Tuesday’s election to fill her position in Congress: San Francisco Supervisor Connie Chan and state Senator Scott Wiener. Each one has staked out a different position on AI data centres. Wiener, for instance, opposes any ban on data centres. “A blanket data centre moratorium could undermine AI regulation,” he told the publication Mission Local. Chan, meanwhile, has pledged to seek a nationwide moratorium on data centres, at least until responsible AI regulation is put in place. “Let’s start with a moratorium on data centres. Allow us to have that moment to regulate artificial intelligence,” she said at a debate in October. Chan played a leading role in passing San Francisco’s moratorium in early October. A poll from the University of Southern California showed Wiener leading Chan 47 percent to 41, as of mid-October. “Right now, data centre opposition is an issue that unifies the US public like no other,” said Shum Preston, a political analyst based in San Francisco. So far, there has been relatively little opposition to the data centre moratoriums in local hearings. But he speculates that there may be several reasons for the lack of pushback to the bans. Among them are the surveys indicating widespread public backlash to data centre creation. An October CNBC poll found that 63 percent of registered US voters oppose building data centres within 16 kilometres, or 10 miles, of their homes. “Data centres poll very poorly, and developers probably don’t want to put their supervisor friends in trouble ahead of elections. So they probably let this pass,” Preston said. He also signalled that the short-term nature of the moratoriums may be a factor. Certain Bay Area cities like San Francisco, Brisbane and Oakland paused construction on data centres for 45 days, with the option to extend the ban later. Opponents of the moratoriums “will be more vocal when” the 45 days end, Preston said. By that time, the heat of the midterm election season will also have settled, he added.

Overall, Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has killed at least 74,609 Palestinians and wounded 175,872 people. The latest attacks came amid efforts to secure shelter for displaced Palestinians before winter. Israeli Army Radio reported that Nickolay Mladenov , the high representative of the Board of Peace, established by the US to oversee a so-called peace plan in Gaza, arrived in Israel on Monday to seek permission to bring in tents and push for steps to accelerate reconstruction. The scale of the need in Gaza remains vast. The United Nations migration agency said on October 9 that nearly two million people required shelter assistance and half of Gaza’s tents and makeshift shelters needed replacing, leaving families exposed as winter approached.

events.title: Taiwan’s AI stock boom is making early-stage startups a harder sell
events.summary: Taiwan's stock market has surged this year as investors chase the country's broad AI supply chain. I-Hwa Cheng/AFP/Getty Images Taiwan's stock market has surged as investors pile into companies powering the global AI buildout. The rally is giving local investors a liquid alternative to early-stage startup bets. For early-stage founders, that can mean looking abroad for capital. Taiwan’s AI stock boom is creating more ways for investors to profit from its chip supply chain, making early-stage startups a tougher pitch. Taiwan’s benchmark Taiex index is up more than 50% this year, making it the world’s best-performing major index after pulling ahead of South Korea’s Kospi. The gains extend well beyond Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., spanning chip design, advanced packaging, networking, and server companies. About 7% of Taiwan-listed stocks have doubled this year, compared with 3% in South Korea. That wider exposure has made Taiwan a preferred Asian AI trade. A September Bank of America survey found that 35% of fund managers expected Taiwan to benefit most from the next phase of the AI cycle, tying it with the US. Just 5% chose South Korea. For startups, the appeal of those public-market returns can reshape the funding calculation. For Anderson Chen, the founder and CEO of Operon Solutions, a Y Combinator-backed industrial AI startup, that calculus was part of what shaped how he raised money. Chen said he chose to raise Operon’s $700,000 pre-seed primarily from Silicon Valley investors, leaving room for Taiwanese friends and family to participate. “The market in semiconductors is just too good, and you can get 10X returns from the stock market,” Chen told Business Insider. In his view, even a successful startup IPO might generate only a two- or threefold return for investors. The hunt for a first check That creates a challenge for startups trying to build Taiwan’s next generation of winners. Caleb Chu, an early-stage investor and founder of Taiwan-based Nova Studio, which backs young founders, told Business Insider that the stock rally had drawn many Taiwanese investors toward listed shares and away from venture capital and startups. Findit, a government-commissioned platform that tracks Taiwan's startup ecosystem, found that seed and angel rounds made up 38.4% of investment deals by Taiwanese VC firms in 2021. By 2024, their share had fallen to 17.1%. By contrast, B- and C-round deals accounted for 39 deals, or 29.1% of the total, in 2024. Chu said Taiwanese investors had increasingly favored B- and C-round and pre-IPO companies, where the route to returns was clearer. Private-equity funds face a related, though not identical, pressure. A March report by KPMG Taiwan said TSMC’s share-price strength had created a “crowding-out effect” for private funds, as investors favored liquid public AI stocks over funds with longer lockups and less certain exits. US venture data shows a different, if still uneven, mix. PitchBook and the National Venture Capital Association said early-stage dealmaking was more favorable for AI startups than for non-AI peers in the first quarter of 2026. In a separate report, they found that 87.5% of US venture dollars invested in the first half went to rounds of $100 million or more. “When you look at the statistics around the world, the world is leaning toward early stage because investors realize it can generate much higher returns. Taiwan is the opposite,” Chu said. For founders, that can mean looking abroad for early backing. Operon's Chen said fundraising had become easier overall for Taiwanese deep-tech startups seeking overseas capital, helped by Taiwan’s technical talent and semiconductor expertise. His startup's $700,000 pre-seed round closed within three days. “It's gotten easier to fundraise in general, but maybe not necessarily in Taiwan,” he said. events.title: UK job satisfaction at record low amid rising frustration over pay and flexible working
events.summary: Resolution Foundation study finds workers are less willing to go ‘above and beyond for employers than a decade ago’ Job satisfaction among UK workers has dropped to a record low, according to a study that shows a growing frustration with employers over pay and flexible working. Analysis by the Resolution Foundation thinktank shows that a lack of flexible working, insecure jobs and a loss of independence have undermined how workers feel about their employment. Based on the 2025 British Social Attitudes survey, the study found a sharp fall in satisfaction at work that translated into British workers being less willing to go “above and beyond for their employers than they were a decade ago”. Job satisfaction fell from 81% in 2015 to 74%, the lowest figure recorded in the British Social Attitudes survey since 1989, when the question was first asked. Fewer workers said they had an interesting job or one that offered the chance of advancement. The proportion of workers who said they would work harder than required to help their employer succeed fell from 69% in 2015 to 55% in 2025. The Resolution Foundation said its analysis would give policymakers an insight into how they could reverse decades of slowing productivity growth, low levels of job mobility and high economic inactivity among some groups, most notably younger people . Only 4% of workers said there was “little intrinsic value” from working – a figure that has remained flat over time. What has declined, the thinktank said, was the number of people feeling positive about the jobs they do. The proportion saying they have an interesting job fell over the decade from 74% to 63%. Hannah Slaughter, an economist at the foundation and co-author of the report, said there was a rise in the number of workers who said they suffered from low pay and this concern spanned all the pay scales. She said decades of low pay-rises and the spiralling cost of living was affecting the outlook of all groups, though the demand for greater flexibility was equally pronounced. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning “Workers increasingly want jobs that provide flexibility, independence and financial security. But many feel those expectations are not being met,” said Slaughter. “The result is rising frustration among workers, who report lower job satisfaction, declining willingness to go above and beyond, and a reduced appetite for full-time work. This ‘dissatisfaction drain’ is self-evidently bad for workers, but it also doesn’t bode well for productivity and labour supply, both of which are vital for lifting living standards in the years ahead.” Separate polling by Ipsos dating back to the 1980s supported the foundation’s study, with workers reporting much lower satisfaction this year than when the same question was asked in 1976 and 1986. In 1976 it found 83% were very or fairly satisfied with their work compared with 69% in 2026. John Curtice, the Strathclyde professor and pollster who is co-editor of the British Social Attitudes report, said the findings showed young people had not become more work-shy, “nor have workers in general become more reluctant to change jobs. But if workers are to be fully engaged in their work, it has seemingly become more important for employers to provide jobs that are both financial rewarding and have flexible work hours.”

events.title: ‘It brings soul into this sterile world’: the Birmingham clubbers fighting to save their patch – and Britain’s nightlife
events.summary: Digbeth is the city’s most thriving party district, but railway upgrades could tear it apart. Here, clubbers explain why they are doing everything to stop that happening H ouse beats ring out through the open air while a heaving crowd of young partygoers dance. Suddenly, they begin to chant: “Richard Parker, Richard Parker!” You might think he is the next DJ on the set list, but in fact he is the mayor of the West Midlands and this block party has been assembled to send him a message: leave Digbeth alone. It’s Sunday night and I’m in Birmingham’s trendy party district. It’s filled with bars, warehouse clubs and storied music venues. The 1,800-strong crowd of mostly twentysomethings at the Parker event fits right in. But buzzy scenes like this may soon be a thing of the past. Under plans proposed by the Midlands Rail Hub Alliance – including Network Rail, which owns and manages railway infrastructure in Great Britain – seven nightclubs, including XOYO Birmingham, Mama Roux’s and Club Colette, could be demolished from 2030. The aim is to expand a nearby viaduct, allowing more trains to run through Moor Street station rather than the more congested New Street, but striking a blow to the city’s nightlife. Ravers want Parker, who leads the region’s strategic transport agenda, to use his power to lobby against these plans. The proposal comes at a testing time for the industry. More than 26% of all late-night venues across the UK closed for good between 2020 and 2025, according to the Night Time Industries Association . Birmingham has been hit harder than any other major city, experiencing a 28% drop in the number of bars, clubs and other establishments where you might grab a late-night drink. But Digbeth, a former industrial centre where metal sheets, Typhoo Tea and Bird’s Custard were once manufactured, has stood strong as the city’s cultural bright spot – far cooler than Broad Street, Birmingham’s main clubbing strip, which has the vibe of a street-long All Bar One. It’s where some of the names now headlining electronic music festivals around the world caught the raving bug. The Birmingham DJ Fleur Shore, 30, has been coming to Digbeth since she was 15. “Here is where it all started for me,” she says from behind her decks. “Without Digbeth, I wouldn’t be where I am now. I get to go all over the world and do my job.” Shore has played gigs in the Argentinian countryside, the historic Plaza de España in Seville, Spain, and the mountains of Gran Canaria. But the UK has not always made it easy. “The UK is so strict,” she says. “They don’t embrace this part of people.” The Parker party is a way for young ravers to revolt, she says: “This country doesn’t value younger people who want to go out, let loose and socialise. When everybody’s all together, dancing to the same thing, it’s powerful.” The mooted demolition of Digbeth’s bars and clubs is just one example of the threats to British nightlife. In central London, a bitter battle is playing out between venues and the Soho Society, a community group aimed at “preserving the character of Soho”, which routinely objects to new bar and restaurant licences, often backed by Westminster council. Venues say the restrictions could “destroy Soho’s reputation on the international stage”, while the mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, has criticised the council’s “breathtaking arrogance” . In Manchester, meanwhile, the famed music venue Night & Day cafe was threatened with closure after noise complaints from neighbours in new flats. After a three-year row, it was told to limit noise in the small hours. There is no doubt that noise can be a nuisance, but it is hard to understand how anyone who moves next to a decades-old venue in an area known for nightlife can claim to be shocked by it. The value of a good night out is being forgotten, says Shore: “There’s so much pressure in life. People come to these places to breathe, dance and not think about their problems. I feel like, the way things are going, we’re going to be a soulless nation.” Lina and Johnny, who are part of the crowd making its way down the Digbeth strip, agree. “People from all walks of life come together here to move our bodies and exist in harmony,” says Johnny, 24. “If this street is demolished, that will be a lot harder to do.” Lina, who is also 24 and a musician, says she has met “so many other beautiful, talented people” in the area. “Where would all these creative people go? It brings soul into this sterile world,” she says. Among a group who met only hours earlier are Hood Ssengendo and Daniel Wright. “The fact they want to demolish this whole thing is pointless,” says Wright, a 24-year-old music producer. “There is still a club scene, ravers and people that want to have a good time.” Ssengendo, a 25-year-old welder, says: “For most young people, this is their hotspot for a night out and to make friends.” For many marginalised communities, the district remains a safe haven for a night out.

events.title: What time do polls open and close in the US midterm elections 2026?
events.summary: Importance of governor races in midterms The first set of polls are set to open in Vermont at 5am (1000 GMT). Voting in New Jersey, Virginia, Connecticut and Kentucky will start at 6am (1100 GMT). Why the US midterms matter even if you don't live in America More than 230 million eligible voters across the United States can head to the polls on Tuesday to decide who will represent them in Congress. All 435 House of Representatives seats and 35 of the Senate’s 100 seats are being contested . Voters in 36 states will also elect governors. Republicans currently hold both chambers. list 1 of 3 As Islamophobia ramps up in US midterms, Texas Muslims eye local stakes list 2 of 3 Trump, Vance campaign with candidates on last day before US midterms list 3 of 3 Judge dismisses charges against FBI agents involved in Hunter Biden case Here is what is expected on the day: Voting hours are determined and set by each state. The first polls are set to open in Vermont at 5am (10:00 GMT). Voting in New Jersey, Virginia, Connecticut and Kentucky will start at 6am (11:00 GMT). Voting in Georgia, Florida, Pennsylvania and New York will start between 6am (11:00 GMT) and 7am (12:00 GMT), while Ohio and North Carolina will see voting start at 6:30am (11:30 GMT). In Michigan, polls will open at 7am (12:00 GMT). Polls close in waves across the country, with the earliest closures at 6pm (23:00 GMT) in Indiana and Kentucky. Voting in Michigan closes at 8pm and in Kansas at 7pm local time (both 01:00 GMT on Wednesday), while polls in Iowa close at 8pm (02:00 GMT on Wednesday). Alaska is the last to close, at around 1am Eastern Time (06:00 GMT) on Wednesday. The first results could start arriving on Tuesday as polls begin to close. Results will continue to come in throughout Tuesday evening, and some on Wednesday as more states finish voting and officials start releasing their vote counts. However, the first reported results will not necessarily mean that a winner has been announced. Election officials release vote counts as ballots are processed, while news organisations such as the Associated Press analyse the results and determine when a race can be called. Closely contested races could take hours, or even days, to call. It might not be immediately clear which party will control Congress. How does the American voting system work in the midterms? Voters can cast their ballots by mail, early or in person on election day, which is Tuesday. Many mail, provisional and other ballots are counted after election night, which is why tallies can take a few days, or even weeks, to finalise. Senate Democrats need a net gain of four seats to reach a majority. House Democrats need three seats for a majority. Here are a few key races to watch as the two parties go head-to-head: In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers are locked in a closely watched race after Democratic Representative Haley Stevens decided to endorse Rogers on Sunday. In Florida, Democrat Angie Nixon is challenging Republican Senator Ashley Moody. In Georgia, Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff will face Republican Mike Collins. In Maine, Republican Senator Susan Collins is up against Democrat Troy Jackson. In New Hampshire, Democratic Representative Chris Pappas is on the ballot against Republican John Sununu, a former senator. In North Carolina, Democrat Roy Cooper and Republican Michael Whatley are on the ballot.
