events.title: UK to double wait for permanent residency, with exemptions for care workers
events.summary: Under the new rules, most foreign workers will have to wait 10 years to settle in the UK, but higher earners can qualify sooner. Al Jazeera investigation exposes paramilitary hitman linked to Turning Point UK The United Kingdom has revised its immigration rules, doubling the time most foreign workers must wait to qualify for permanent residency to 10 years and making refugees who arrive on “small boats” wait as long as 30 years. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood, speaking in Parliament on Monday, said hundreds of thousands of care workers will be exempt from the hardline rules, offering a concession amid a political outcry within the governing Labour Party. list 1 of 3 UK gov’t condemns masked anti-immigrant protesters blocking Dover port list 2 of 3 Net migration to the UK falls by nearly 50 percent amid tighter policies list 3 of 3 UK jails teen asylum seeker for steering overcrowded Channel migrant boat Permanent residency, known in the UK as indefinite leave to remain, carries the right to work, study, use the free National Health Service and claim welfare benefits. Until now, it has been granted after five years. The new rules, set to take effect next year, tie eligibility for permanent residency to income. People who earn more than 50,000 pounds a year ($67,000) will still be able to apply after five years, and those earning more than 125,000 pounds ($167,500) after three. Everyone else will be placed on the 10-year path. The median salary in the UK is about 39,000 pounds (roughly $52,000). The rules will apply retroactively to workers already in the country. “Settlement should not be automatic. It should be earned,” Mahmood, the home secretary, told Parliament, adding that the changes would restore fairness by linking the right to settle to what immigrants contribute. “Those who contribute most will settle fastest,” she said. “Those who don’t play by the rules will be refused or wait longer.” The UK government first proposed last year that lower-skilled workers wait 10 to 15 years for permanent residency. But the plan drew fierce opposition from unions and parts of the Labour Party, particularly over its effect on care workers, who are often poorly paid and work in a sector that has long struggled to fill vacancies. Many of them arrived in the early 2020s, as the country was reeling from the COVID-19 pandemic, to fill gaps left by European workers who had departed after Brexit. Under the revised plan, care workers will be able to settle after five years if they have met the conditions of their visas and earn at least 25,000 pounds ($33,500) a year. Mahmood said the rules would offer a path for care workers “who worked hard and answered our call when we needed them”. As for refugees, those who arrive through one of the government’s “new safe and legal routes” will be able to settle after five years, she said. For other refugees, the standard wait will become 20 years, reduced to 10 years for those who work or study. Anyone who arrived by an “illegal method”, such as by small boat, could wait up to 30 years for settlement, she said. Under the new rules, applicants will also be disqualified if they have a criminal record, cannot speak English “to a high standard”, owe money to the government, or have not made at least three years of national insurance contributions. Mahmood said the overhaul would mean that half a million people would settle later than they otherwise would have, saving the government billions of pounds in benefits. In total, the government estimates that as many as 1.4 million people will receive settled status between 2026 and 2030. The changes, announced after a 12-week public consultation that drew more than 200,000 responses, are part of a broader effort to tighten immigration rules after arrivals surged following Brexit. They are a response to political pressure, including from Nigel Farage’s populist Reform UK party, which has surged in popularity in recent years with calls for stricter migration controls. Reform UK has sought to depict the arrivals of refugees on small boats across the English Channel as a crisis, and anti-immigration activists have staged protests, including outside facilities that house asylum seekers. Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government has said that increased law enforcement cooperation between the UK and France has helped reduce the number of people making the crossing so far this year by more than 40 percent compared with 2025.

AI 15 hours ago 'Mother of all editors' Emacs is 50 1 day ago AlpineBSD announced – an AI-free FOSS OS 3 days ago Howler will have AI answer your questions, then burn the chat 4 days ago Ubuntu 27.04 may bring a preview of the long-awaited Core Desktop 4 days ago A cloud architect has created an open-source alternative to VMware’s Virtual Disk Development Kit (VDDK), which the virtualization giant recently withdrew from public downloads. VMware describes VDDK as “a set of libraries and utilities that enable software developers to create applications that can access and manipulate virtual disks” and “a valuable tool for developers of storage and backup applications.” Users, along with VMware’s rivals, had another use for VDDK: migrating VMs to alternative virtualization platforms. In August, VMware restricted access to VDDK downloads to its partners, meaning VMware customers couldn’t access the tool and some of its rivals’ migration tools became less effective. Cloud architect Andrija Panić decided to do something about it. “Many tools that have nothing in common except VMware use the same small library to read a virtual machine’s disks: virt-v2v and nbdkit, the importers in Forklift/MTV, Proxmox VE and Apache CloudStack, and countless in-house scripts,” he told The Register by email. “When public VDDK downloads ended, all of them became harder to install and run.” “I didn’t think it was fair that people’s ability to move or protect their own data should depend on a download page.” He describes the project as “an independent drop-in for libvixDiskLib.so.8.0.3, the disk library that VMware backup and migration tools load to read virtual disks. It was written from scratch, using only public documentation and black-box testing, and contains no VMware code.” Panić told The Register he wrote the tool in Go, with a thin C layer that exposes exactly the same C interface, library name and symbol versions as VMware’s code. The tool cannot write disks, just read them for backup and migration purposes. In his email to The Register , Panić said he has successfully tested OpenVDDK on vSphere versions 6.7 U3, 7.0.3, 8.0.3, 9.1.1. He said that tests in his lab with the latter version, accessing OpenVDDK through vCenter on a standalone ESXi host, saw every disk read match. “Independent testers have reported successful use with Forklift (VMware to KubeVirt, cold and warm), MTV on OpenShift (cold and warm), a Proxmox VE pipeline and custom nbdkit-based tools,” the architect told The Register . “I've received reports of production use, including a German cloud provider migrating a large file server with V2K Migrate and a US-based company migrating to Apache CloudStack/KVM.” Panić was at pains to point out that the reports of successful use are “not independently audited customer endorsements or a guarantee of suitability for every production environment.” As is often the case with FOSS tools. OpenVDDK is not the only option for migrating away from VMware without VDDK. KVM-based OpenNebula has a tool called OneSwap that it says has a 96 percent success rate. Nutanix recently tweaked its “Move” migration tool so it can do the job without VDDK. Red Hat is working on a fix but has provided details of a workaround . Panić made OpenVDDK available under an Apache license, so perhaps Red Hat and others will find it useful as they re-jig their VM migration tools.

events.title: US midterms present a test for Republican redistricting in Texas and beyond
events.summary: Importance of governor races in midterms Partisan redistricting has transformed election for Black voters in Houston as Democrats seek new pathways to victory. Houston, Texas – The gospel music from Mount Hebron Missionary Baptist Church spills into the streets of Sunnyside, a predominantly Black neighbourhood in southern Houston. It is a familiar scene on any given Sunday: hands in the air, immaculate bow ties on starched shirts, fabric flowers adorning perfectly pastel hats. But with the US midterm elections just two days away, the service held a special significance on the front line of a US redistricting battle . list 1 of 3 US midterms: What to know about independent voters and candidates list 2 of 3 How the president’s party has fared in every US midterm election since 1946 list 3 of 3 US midterms: 1 day to go – Democrats rally around El-Sayed amid attacks Mt Hebron had long been located in the ninth congressional district, its politically engaged Black voters for two decades helping to elect Democrat Al Green, a flamboyant presence in Congress known for his cane-waving opposition to US President Donald Trump. But following an appeal from Trump, the Republican state legislature last year conducted rare mid-decade redistricting, redrawing the church and its Black community into the Black-majority 18th district. Critics call the process “cracking and packing”, diminishing the representation in Congress of minority groups, particularly heavily Democratic Black communities, by consolidating their voting power into fewer districts. “It’s kind of one and the same when we talk about the voting and the civil rights,” said Pastor Max Miller, who has served at the church for 18 years. “They are trying to manipulate and monopolise the vote and minimise the people who are in those districts,” said Miller. “We see so much rolling backwards that it looks like they’re trying to take a script from an old song and turn back the hands of time.” As a result of the redistricting, Green was forced to run in a primary against 18th district incumbent Christian Menefee, another Black Democrat. He lost, and Houston lost one of its Black representatives in Congress. The ninth district, meanwhile, was redrawn to favour Republicans, one of at least five US congressional seats the party hopes to pick up in the midterm vote. The machinations have resonated with worshippers at Mt Hebron. “I don’t like the redistricting at all because Al Green was moved out,” said 97-year-old Alice Jefferson, who had followed the congressman throughout his political career. “He always had good advice for the people.” Janice Ray, a 61-year-old home health aide and entrepreneur, said state lawmakers were “trying to move people out of the district that they’re familiar with”. “To me, it was all a bunch of BS,” she said. “There was no reason for it.” “But we’ll stand firm, regardless of what they try to do,” Ray added. “Because just like it was changed, it can always be changed back.” The redistricting process has undergone a generational transformation this election season, one that, experts say, has degraded longstanding guardrails protecting minority voting power. “In political science, we have what we call descriptive representation,” Michael Adams, a professor at Texas Southern University in Houston, told Al Jazeera. “In terms of descriptive representation, minorities and others feel that if they can elect someone who reflects their values, for example, and who may look like them, their voting can be defined as one voice.” “And certainly with not having an additional Black member of Congress representing Houston, a significant segment of Black voters may feel that their voices have been weakened,” he said. This year Republican and Democratic state legislatures across the country joined the spree: Republicans successfully redistricted in Missouri, North Carolina, Tennessee, Louisiana, Alabama, Florida and Ohio; Democrats did so in California, while a court-ordered map in Utah handed Democrats a favourable seat. A Democratic push in Virginia was subsequently invalidated. Redrawing maps mid-decade, and not waiting for the latest demographic numbers from the US census, was already atypical. But many of the maps drawn this year would have been deemed illegal in previous cycles. Section 2 of the landmark Voting Rights Act of 1965, initially passed to counter blatantly racist voting practices in the US, had long prohibited redrawing congressional maps to dilute the electoral power of minority voters. In April, the conservative-dominated US Supreme Court ruled that anyone challenging such a map must prove “racist intent”. Critics have said the ruling effectively allows for racial gerrymandering, with proving such an intent an unreasonably high bar. But critics of Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act have said drawing maps to protect minority voting power is in itself discriminatory.

events.title: U.S. reportedly strikes Iran's Qeshm Island as Vance hopes for ‘negotiated settlement’ with Tehran
events.summary: U.S. military carried out attacks on Iran's Qeshm Island on Monday, a Wall Street Journal report said. U.S. Vice President JD Vance on Monday said he was optimistic about reaching a 'negotiated settlement' with Iran. Vance said the Iranians are "unpredictable" and U.S. President Trump retains "kinetic and non-kinetic" options against Tehran. The U.S. reportedly carried out strikes against Iran on Monday even as Vice President JD Vance expressed hopes of reaching a "negotiated settlement" with Tehran. America attacked Iran's Qeshm Island on Monday, U.S. officials told The Wall Street Journal, which added that Washington has been carrying out "limited strikes" against the country in recent weeks. The military campaign against Iran has been kept quiet on purpose so as not to signal any intention of major combat escalation, the report said, quoting an unnamed official. Qeshm Island, off Iran's southern coast, is the largest island in the Persian Gulf. Located near the Strait of Hormuz, it has emerged as a potential U.S. target amid reports that anti-ship missiles, mines, drones and attack craft are being kept there in underground tunnels. President Donald Trump's administration has been talking down risks of an all-out war with Iran, with Vance being the latest to claim "good progress" in talks with Iran. "The president and I both feel really good about the prospect of potentially coming to a negotiated settlement," Vance told CNN on Monday. He added, though, that Iranians are "unpredictable" and Trump retains "kinetic and non-kinetic" options against Tehran. Vance said that Washington has not set any deadline for reaching a peace deal with Iran. Trump said earlier Monday that the U.S. had to go to war with Iran to stop the country from having " a nuclear weapon ," that "we're not going to allow Iran ever to have a nuclear weapon. And they understand that." Last month, the president had said the U.S. will not attack Iran before the midterm elections, after polls ahead of the ballot showed that support for the war had dwindled, with only 31% of Americans supporting the military action. Trump told Fox News in an interview Monday night that the U.S. had to take a "little detour" to Iran to stop the country from having nuclear weapons. The president said that the U.S. has bombed out all of Iran's potential nuclear power, but he might target Pickaxe Mountain next. Located south of Iran's Natanz enrichment plant, Pickaxe Mountain houses an underground nuclear facility. "We might have to go after Pickaxe, but that's not a big deal," Trump said, adding the U.S. could destroy it in one hour. On Nov. 1, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio had also said Trump would like to resolve the Iranian war "diplomatically," and prefers not to use military force .

events.title: China to raise FX reserve requirement to slow yuan’s rally
events.summary: The People’s Bank of China said it would raise the foreign exchange reserve requirement ratio by 2 percentage points to 6% from 4%, effective on Nov 15. China’s central bank will raise the FX reserve requirement ratio to 6% from 4% on Nov 15 to slow the yuan’s strong rally and absorb US dollar liquidity. The move may remove about US$24 billion from the system and sent the onshore yuan down 0.37% to 6.6728 per dollar, its sharpest daily fall in six months. Markets see the step as mainly symbolic. The yuan has still risen more than 5% in 2026, backed by exports, trade surpluses and corporate FX sales. BEIJING - China is raising the amount of foreign currency that financial institutions must hold as reserves, in one of the strongest moves to slow the pace of a long rally in the yuan, setting the currency on course for its sharpest one-day drop in six months. The People’s Bank of China (PBOC) said in a statement on Nov 3 it would raise the foreign exchange (FX) reserve requirement ratio (RRR) by 2 percentage points to 6% from 4%, effective on Nov 15. The adjustment would result in an extra US$24 billion (S$30 billion) being withdrawn from the financial system, according to a Reuters calculation based on official FX deposit data. The decision to raise the ratio is “aimed at strengthening the management of foreign exchange liquidity in financial institutions”, the PBOC said. The onshore yuan weakened as much as 0.37% against the dollar to a low of 6.6728 per dollar, the weakest level since Oct 23, following the announcement. And it looked set for the biggest one-day drop since May 15. Its offshore counterpart also followed the weakening trend. “The PBOC is responding to strong market-driven yuan appreciation,” said Marco Sun, chief financial market analyst at MUFG (China). “By absorbing part of the available US dollar liquidity in the banking system, it is attempting to reduce the momentum behind yuan appreciation and prevent the market from developing excessive one-way expectations.” The yuan has gained more than 5% against the dollar so far in 2026, reaching its strongest level since 2022 and becoming one of Asia’s best-performing currencies. Its strength has been underpinned by robust exports, big trade surpluses and heavy corporate FX conversion. The FX RRR hike on Nov 3 would be a policy reversal of the PBOC’s decision in September 2023 to lower the FX RRR, which was a move to stem the yuan’s rapid losses and capital outflows. However, market participants do not expect the move to reverse the yuan’s upward trend. Xing Zhaopeng, senior China strategist at ANZ, said the move was likely to “carry greater symbolic significance” for the market. Corporates’ heavier FX settlement into yuan had “resulted in the current imbalance conditions of excess supply over demand”, Xing said. He added that the increase in the FX RRR would not be enough to ease the oversupply. Separately, the PBOC lowered its midpoint rate for a second day in a row on Nov 3 to 6.7150 per dollar, 661 pips weaker than a Reuters estimate - its largest weak-side deviation since Sept 10. The central bank has been gradually strengthening its daily yuan official guidance in 2026, but at levels weaker than market expectations, suggesting it is seeking to manage the pace of appreciation, market watchers said. Meanwhile, PBOC deputy governor Zou Lan reiterated the central bank’s stance on the currency. “China has promoted high-level opening-up and insisted that the market play a decisive role in the formation of the exchange rate,” he told a financial forum in Hong Kong on Nov 3. events.title: I lived in Shanghai in my 20s. Now, at 34, I'm back in China to start a business.
events.summary: After college, Alex Greenberg moved to Shanghai, then returned to the US. Now, at 34, he's giving life in China another try. Provided by Alex Greenberg After graduating from college, Alex Greenberg moved to Shanghai to teach skateboarding. He planned to stay for a year, but "the city felt so alive" that he stayed for five. After a few years back in the US, he returned to China last month to start a company in Chengdu. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Alex Greenberg, an American founder living in Chengdu, China, who runs Observed Media, a creative studio. He is also the creator of the Instagram account @shanghaiobserved. His words have been edited for length and clarity. As graduation from college in Vermont approached, I had no idea what I wanted to do with my life. I'd studied abroad in Australia during my junior year and knew I loved traveling, but I drew a blank on what to do next. Then, in November of my senior year, I received an offer to teach skateboarding in Shanghai. It was my only job offer; I hadn't applied to much else. Teaching skateboarding in China wasn't exactly what I pictured doing with a college degree, but I figured it would make for an interesting gap year . I arrived in January 2015 speaking zero Chinese. More than a decade later, China has shaped my career. When he arrived in China, he spoke zero Chinese. Provided by Alex Greenberg Shanghai felt like a place where anything could happen Shanghai had become a magnet for street skaters, and most of my friends came through skateboarding and the video production world. It was one of the best social periods of my life. I remember constantly thinking, "What am I doing? This is wild." I'd chosen this completely unexpected life, and somehow it was working. After my one-year contract ended, I expected to go home. But by then, I'd built a network and a life in Shanghai . Leaving didn't make sense. I also had the safety net of teaching English. The US job market felt like a mystery to navigate, so I stayed. Not knowing what I wanted to do became an asset Career-wise, I was throwing everything at the wall. I started juggling English teaching and private skate lessons. At the same time, I started Shanghai Observed on Instagram as a daily photography project for fun. There wasn't some grand business plan behind it; I was just walking around Shanghai and documenting the city. In 2016, I got an internship at PUSH Media and eventually worked my way up to project manager. We produced campaigns and events for brands like Adidas, Vans, and The North Face. Have you relocated abroad — especially to Asia — for career opportunities, retirement, or lower living costs? We want to hear from you. Fill out this short form to share your story. Meanwhile, Shanghai Observed continued to grow alongside my career. Today, it has over 280,000 followers and gets millions of views a month, mostly from people outside China who are curious about everyday life. It's never been my primary source of income; it's always been more of a passion project. But it opened a lot of doors. A trip home unexpectedly turned into years away from China I flew to the US for Christmas in December 2019 and planned to return after Chinese New Year. Then COVID hit, and I couldn't get back. I spent about 15 months living with my parents in New York. After that, I went to Kauai to work on a pineapple farm. I was only supposed to be there for three months. China still hadn't reopened, so I stayed in Hawaii for two years. I converted a school bus into a tiny home on a friend's farm, worked as a drone pilot, and spent my free time surfing, playing poker and casual baseball games, and having dinner at friends' houses. Then, in 2023, I moved to San Diego for a remote brand manager role. I had built an entirely different life and career in the US, but China never really disappeared from either, and I continued running the Instagram account. He converted a school bus into a tiny home on a friend's farm in Hawaii. Provided by Alex Greenberg Moving back started making sense By the end of my time in California, I was paying $2,400 a month in rent, including utilities, for a small one-bedroom place in Encinitas. I loved living near the ocean, but I started thinking about what the same money could buy me elsewhere. I realized I could base myself in China again, build my own media business, and have considerably more money left over to travel. This September, I finally moved back — but instead of returning to Shanghai, I chose Chengdu, a major city in southwestern China. Despite not having lived there before, I had friends there, the creative scene seemed exciting, and it's a much more affordable place to build my business and study Chinese . Shanghai has more opportunity, but also more competition. Chengdu's pace feels slowe r. The city prides itself on tea houses, long dinners, and relaxing. There's a real emphasis on quality of life and comfort. Right now, I pay 3,000 Chinese yuan, or $420 a month, for a furnished studio on a month-to-month lease. A bowl of noodles costs around $2, and a coffee costs $1.50. Greenberg says he wants Shanghai Observed, his platform, to remain a window into the human side of China. Provided by Alex Greenberg I'm running a creative studio on my own I'm producing stories for brands and creators. Shanghai Observed was where I learned how to do it; Observed Media brings it all under one roof. The thread connecting everything I've done — from skateboarding and sharing day-to-day life content in Shanghai to my days in California — has been paying attention to culture and turning it into stories people want to watch. Shanghai Observed is still where I experiment. It's a mix of my own photography and footage, submissions from followers, and content I discover through WeChat groups . When I first moved to Shanghai at 22, I thought I was taking a one-year skateboarding job while I figured out what I wanted to do next. Instead, that spontaneous decision shaped my friendships, my career, the business I'm building, and the way I see the world. More than a decade later, I'm 34 and back in China, starting another chapter. And, strangely enough, I have that same feeling I had when I first arrived: What am I doing? This is wild. Only this time, I have a much better idea of what I'm doing here. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Here’s who is falling in line for Trump’s “Super Intelligence” loyalty test
events.summary: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . At the end of September, President Trump signed an executive order that contained just one directive, ordering government agencies to rebrand what they had been calling artificial intelligence as “Super Intelligence.” That term beat out other contenders, including “Extreme Intelligence” and “Supreme Intelligence,” offered by the president in a poll on X a couple of weeks earlier.  Rebrands are, of course, now a White House tradition: Trump has changed names to project US dominance of certain bodies of water (the Gulf of America and Lake America), to signal new institutional priorities (Department of War), or simply to leave his mark on storied places (see the ongoing fight over renaming the Kennedy Center).  The stated reason for this name change is that today’s AI systems “amplify human ingenuity” rather than merely “imitate” intelligence, and the government’s terminology should reflect that. But if this rebrand follows the pattern of others, its effects will extend beyond government.  It will turn a choice of words into a political loyalty test: Those who use the new term demonstrate allegiance to the administration, and those who don’t become marks for attacks (recall that the Trump administration barred the Associated Press from some White House press events after the news outlet did not adopt the term “Gulf of America”).  But most Americans go months without ever pondering what to call the major lake between New York and Canada. AI, on the other hand, is at the center of our national conversation and a technology two-thirds of Americans report interacting with multiple times a week. It might be the boldest rebrand yet.  So one month in, who’s on board? Let’s start with the government itself. The term “Super Intelligence”—or simply “SI”—now appears more often on government solicitations, like a new request by Immigration and Customs Enforcement for companies to build “SI-powered” surveillance for ICE detention facilities. The new term has been swapped in silently on most government websites. Some, including that of the National Institutes of Health, now include a banner warning visitors they might see both the new and the old terms during the transition period. There have been hiccups. A day after the rebrand order, the Pentagon announced an ambitious new initiative to study the future of warfare, called Project Meridian; it used the old terminology. A Federal Trade Commission press release last week used “superintelligence” instead of the two-word, capitalized version ordered by the president, and recent press releases from Health and Human Services show no sign of the new language.  The term “AI” will likely stick around given the countless AI-related offices, initiatives, and programs that have sprung up in recent years, like the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office at the Pentagon (the executive order says it doesn’t apply to previously issued regulations or documents). As for government employees, it appears to be taking time for “SI” rather than “AI” to roll off the tongue. One researcher at a national lab I interviewed a few weeks ago used “AI” repeatedly before sheepishly acknowledging the slip-up. Even Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth used “AI” in an interview on October 3.  But Trump’s other rebrands suggest the goal isn’t merely to change the government’s vocabulary. It’s to change how the rest of us speak, too. In the past couple of weeks, most of President Trump’s posts on Truth Social have been endorsements for candidates in the midterms. But on October 27 he took a break from electioneering to criticize the Wall Street Journal for not using “Super Intelligence,” “the name which virtually everyone else is using, or soon will be.” He suggested that a new rule will soon go further than the executive order to outright ban “artificial intelligence” from government documents.  But the Wall Street Journal is not alone: Even Newsmax, an outlet whose founder described it as “supportive of the President and his policies,” isn’t using the president’s preferred term.   Are Big Tech executives falling in line? It’s complicated. The same day that President Trump signed the rebranding order, he also released a nonbinding statement on AI safety, the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, signed by six of the most powerful people in tech: Sundar Pichai of Google, Dario Amodei of Anthropic, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, Greg Brockman of OpenAI, Elon Musk of xAI, and Jensen Huang of Nvidia. But even among this group—three members of which attended Trump’s inauguration—the term has not caught on.  In an analysis of third-quarter earnings calls, CNBC reported that only Zuckerberg and Musk used the term consistently. But Zuckerberg doesn’t quite count: Meta has been saying “superintelligence” since last year anyway. Musk’s companies seem to use the term the most—and he even pledged to rename SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI. Musk himself still mixes SI and AI when posting on X.  Executives from Amazon, Microsoft, and Alphabet used “AI” in their calls, though Microsoft’s recent letter to shareholders referred to the “Super Intelligence era.” Huang has referenced the term but still uses AI too . One objection to this rebranding project is that it will cost time and taxpayer dollars. It is Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff’s prerogative to decide that SIForce is a better name than AIForce and direct his company to implement that change. But government employees are now spending time writing guides on how departments should navigate the rebrand. And, per the executive order , leaders of federal agencies will be required to put their heads together to draft a new legislative definition of “Super Intelligence” to be run by the president by the end of this month. But I’m more worried about what this does to our national conversation about AI than I am about the potential waste of time and money. Surprisingly often I overhear strangers at a grocery store or coffee shop who have struck up a conversation about AI. The substance of the conversation is rarely uplifting—they most often talk about a jobs apocalypse or AI-powered warfare—but what is heartening is how often I see a widespread desire among people to have a say in how this technology transforms their lives.  People may have wildly different feelings about AI, including outright hostility, but those differences don’t yet map neatly onto the partisan divisions that make it awkward for strangers to discuss immigration or climate change. If “Super Intelligence” turns into a loyalty test, this will cease to be the case. events.title: El-Sayed, Rogers hold dueling rallies as bitter campaign comes to a close
events.summary: Importance of governor races in midterms The events come as Haley Stevens opined on why she withdrew support for the US Senate Democratic nominee. On the eve of the consequential midterm elections in the United States, candidates in Michigan’s bitter, hard-fought US Senate race have made their final appeals to voters in a contest that could help determine control of Congress. During duelling campaign rallies on Monday evening, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers offered contrasting visions to the state’s voters. Despite dramatic, late-breaking developments, polls suggest the tenuous race has slipped further out of reach for the Republican Party. list 1 of 3 As Islamophobia ramps up in US midterms, Texas Muslims eye local stakes list 2 of 3 US midterms: 1 day to go – Democrats rally around El-Sayed amid attacks list 3 of 3 Trump, Vance campaign with candidates on last day before US midterms As Tom Petty’s I Won’t Back Down played in the background, Rogers took the stage in Rochester Hills, Michigan, to talk about the race he described as a battle for the “heart and soul of the country”. “Are you guys ready to fight for freedom tomorrow?” the former congressman asked the crowd. “Are you ready to send a message to the rest of the country that we are the ones that defeated the Democrat Socialists of America?” Half an hour away in Detroit, at a rally with members of the United Auto Workers labour group, El-Sayed focused on his cost-of-living platform. He touched on the barrage of dark themes that have reverberated across the state – and the nation – in the closing days of the campaign, including a litany of anti-Muslim rhetoric. “You might think that in a moment when gas is too expensive and people can’t afford their groceries, that if you wanted to win an election, you might want to talk about gas and groceries,” El-Sayed told rally attendees. “They don’t wanna talk about gas and groceries. They wanna talk about me and my name and my faith.” The primary instigator of those attacks, US President Donald Trump, has said that El-Sayed, whose family emigrated from Egypt, would “invite hordes of jihadis” to the US. Trump has also frequently purposefully misnamed the Democrat, calling him “Abdul Ramadan”, or emphasising his middle name, “Mohammed”. “I don’t even care if [Trump] knows what my name is,” El-Sayed said. “Because after tomorrow, we’re gonna make sure he calls me senator.” But a shocking endorsement of El-Sayed’s opponent from a fellow Democrat may prove pivotal, as late-deciding Michiganders prepare to enter the voting booth on Tuesday. Representative Haley Stevens, a Democrat who lost to El-Sayed in the race for the US Senate nomination during the state’s primary earlier this year, sent shockwaves across the country on Sunday when she broke ranks and threw her support behind Rogers. Stevens, who had struggled in a series of interviews to explain why she decided to back the Republican in the race, posted a lengthy message to social media Monday detailing what went into her decision. She said it was based on an advertisement unaffiliated with El-Sayed’s campaign that tied US support for Israel to rising grocery costs, as well as being “shut out” of the campaign. “Mike Rogers and I disagree on many things. But Michigan has to elect a senator and there is no neutral choice that absolves me of responsibility,” Stevens wrote on X. “Once I concluded that Abdul El-Sayed is not fit to serve in the United States Senate, I had to confront who should.” Stevens, who chided her fellow Democrats for their reaction to her endorsement, hinted at possible future political plans when she leaves office in January. “We can build a stronger, more welcoming, more courageous Democratic Party,” she said. “And I plan to help lead that effort”. Attendees at Rogers’s rally applauded when he highlighted Stevens’s and other Democratic endorsements he had received. “That is a special kind of courage,” he said of Stevens. The crowd then burst into chants of “Haley!” A New York Times-Siena poll released on Sunday suggested El-Sayed is leading Rogers by 11 percentage points – 53 to 42 percent – among likely voters. The poll had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.6 percentage points.

events.title: Australia hikes rates to 18-year high to fight inflation
events.summary: The move was a split decision, with six members voting for the increase and three opting for a hold. The central bank has also upgraded its inflation projectons, saying that inflation is not expected to reach its 2%-3% target range till late 2027. This was due to higher fuel and other commodity prices, but other factors including AI-related investment is driving rapid growth in prices for technology-related goods, the RBA said. Australia's central bank raised its benchmark cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.85% on Tuesday, the highest level since November 2008. The Reserve Bank of Australia's move was in line with expectations from economists polled by Reuters, and marked its fifth rate increase this year. In its statement, the RBA said that the move was a split decision, with six members voting for the increase and three opting for a hold. This also comes as the country continues to grapple with high inflation, with the consumer price index rising 4.3% in September, up from 4% in August and marking its highest level since March. The central bank also said inflation is now expected to "remain elevated through much of 2027," and not expected to fall back into its 2%-3% target range till late 2027, three quarters later than previously forecast. This was due to higher fuel and other commodity prices, in addition to factors including AI-related investment, which is driving rapid growth in prices for technology-related goods, the RBA said. In its September decision, RBA governor Michelle Bullock said that inflation is "too high," driven by higher oil prices from the Iran War and stronger domestic spending. "We're seeing signs that upside risks to inflation are materializing," she added, saying that additional hikes will come "if that's what's needed to get inflation down." Growth has slowed in the first two quarters of 2026. Australia's GDP rose 2.1% in the June quarter compared to a year earlier, down from 2.5% in the March quarter. The RBA is trying to bring inflation back under control while higher borrowing costs and cost-of-living pressures weigh on households and activity. When asked if she sees a recession for Australia, Bullock said that it is "not our base case at the moment."

events.title: SATS redeploys staff to baggage handling amid MOM probe into contracted firms
events.summary: Some SATS employees have taken on additional responsibilities or been temporarily redeployed to help the ground handler keep its baggage-handling operations running. SINGAPORE – Ground handler SATS has temporarily redeployed some employees and assigned others additional responsibilities to keep its Changi Airport operations running smoothly, amid investigations into possible work pass violations involving workers employed by its contractors and sub-contractors . In an e-mail sent to all staff and seen by The Straits Times on Nov 3, SATS thanked its employees for helping out and supporting the company through the “operational adjustments required in recent weeks”. “Some employees have taken on additional responsibilities or been temporarily redeployed to help ensure our operations continue to run safely and smoothly. Your dedication, flexibility and professionalism have been instrumental in maintaining service to our customers, and we thank you for your support.” The e-mail addressed to SATS employees also outlined a broader context on actions the firm has taken to “enhance verification process controls” to make sure contractor workers are deployed according to their work passes. “We are rectifying compliance deficiencies in accordance with MOM’s guidelines,” said the company spokesperson in the e-mail, urging employees to reach out to team leaders if they have questions or want to clarify facts after reading media reports on the investigation. A SATS employee who did not want to be named said employees, including those from non-operations departments, were encouraged to step up on a voluntary basis to help with baggage-handling services, especially to fill slots for the upcoming Deepavali long weekend. ST understands that employees who volunteer for additional 2½-hour block duties will receive $15 in NTUC vouchers, time off in lieu and transport allowance. SATS said on Nov 3 that it is regular practice for the company to invite employees across the organisation to volunteer their support during peak travel periods, and that the request for volunteers did not come as a result of the probe. The request for volunteers can include customer service and premier services ambassadors, as well as support for baggage services, added the SATS spokesperson. Vouchers or time off in lieu will typically be provided as a gesture of appreciation. “This provides colleagues from non-operational functions with opportunities to gain first-hand experience of frontline operations, while supporting operational teams and enabling frontline employees to take well-deserved breaks.” Responding to queries from ST, a spokesperson for Changi Airport Group (CAG) said it is working closely with SATS’ management team to “minimise the impact of the manpower situation on airport operations”. “CAG expects SATS and other operators at Changi Airport to strengthen the oversight of companies they contract with and to ensure that these companies comply with applicable manpower laws and regulations.” MOM said in a media statement on Nov 2 that it has identified around 270 workers, employed by SATS’ contractors and sub-contractors, whose deployment may not have been in compliance with work pass regulations. MOM said the ministry found Employment Pass holders deployed to perform baggage-handling services during a recent inspection. SATS’ share price fell 3.01% after market opened on Nov 3, with about four million shares worth about $14.2 million changing hands as of 10.40am. Sharon Salim is a business correspondent at The Straits Times, with a focus on jobs, workplace culture and trends.

events.title: Most of our stuff is still on the Villa Vie Odyssey. We're on another cruise, waiting to see what happens next.
events.summary: Travel vloggers Dwight and Sheila Greene have been aboard Villa Vie Odyssey for over a year. All Over The World with Dwight and Sheila Dwight and Sheila Greene have been living aboard the Villa Vie Odyssey for over a year. When it abruptly halted operations in Cambodia last week, they left most of their belongings aboard. They're now on another cruise, waiting to see what happens to the Odyssey. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Dwight Greene, 64, a Villa Vie Odyssey passenger from Fort Worth, Texas. He and his wife, Sheila, are travel vloggers. It has been edited for length and clarity. My wife, Sheila, and I have always loved to travel and have been on plenty of cruises. It was our friends who first told us about the residential ship . In May 2025, we flew to Acapulco, Mexico, and sailed for a week to Mazatlán through Villa Vie Odyssey's "try before you buy" program. We loved it so much that we decided we wanted to be a part of it. Six weeks later, we came home from a separate trip to Europe and had two weeks to pack for the move. We kept our house in Texas. We had been traveling with Villa Vie Odyssey for over a year. The couple, from Fort Worth, Texas, boarded the cruise ship in August 2025 when it was in Japan. All Over The World with Dwight and Sheila We joined the ship in August 2025, when it docked in Yokohama, Japan. I had only been to Tokyo once before, over three decades earlier, so I was excited to return to this part of the world. We flew over with seven giant suitcases. The day the ship was supposed to arrive in Yokohama, it was raining. We put on ponchos and walked around, trying to see whether we could spot it. We came to a clearing on a bridge overlooking the water, and there she was. When we finally went aboard, I remember thinking it was the greatest day of our lives. We found a community aboard The Villa Vie Odyssey didn't feel like any other cruise we'd been on. What really got us was the people. On other cruises, nobody ever talked to us. It's like we were invisible. But on the Odyssey, people would come up and say, "Hello, welcome aboard. Let's introduce ourselves." We made friends in one week. A lot of people rotated tables, and we would eat dinner with different people each night. Sometimes we would just be walking by, and someone would say, "Have dinner with us." There was a buffet and a sit-down restaurant with tablecloths and silverware. We drank wine every day. The couple found a community aboard the Villa Vie Odyssey. All Over The World with Dwight and Sheila We put on our own shows, too. I had been a stage actor, so when someone dropped out of a musical, they roped me into it, and it was a blast. Staying on the ship full time would have been too restrictive for us. We like to bop around. We use it like an aircraft carrier, getting off to do deep dives into other countries as it travels the world. Then, we'll come back to our "home," except it's in a cruise cabin . For example, when the ship changed its New Zealand itinerary in March, we got off in Dunedin with two friends, rented a car, and spent a couple of weeks traveling around the country before flying to Melbourne to meet the ship again. We had already set off on our own By the time the Villa Vie Odyssey halted operations in Cambodia last week, Sheila and I had already gotten off. They were already off the ship when the announcement came that the Odyssey was halting operations. All Over The World with Dwight and Sheila The first time the ship docked in Sihanoukville in late September, we got off to travel through Cambodia. In early October, we met the ship again in Laem Chabang, near Bangkok, to pick up a few more things from our cabin. That was the last time we were aboard. By then, everyone knew the ship was having fuel issues , and people had started talking about it more seriously. While in Bangkok, we were also told that several ports would be dropped from the itinerary, leaving the Odyssey at sea with only a brief refueling stop. With little to no internet expected during that period, and no certainty that we'd be able to get off in time to fly to Singapore for a Royal Princess cruise we had booked months earlier, we decided not to stay aboard. We got off and traveled around Thailand instead, before making our way to Singapore for our cruise. The cruise we're on now is supposed to end in Singapore on November 10, around the time the Odyssey was originally scheduled to arrive. We thought, "They'll arrive, we'll arrive, and we'll just change ships." Now, the couple is on another cruise, and waiting to see what will happen with the Odyssey. All Over The World with Dwight and Sheila That was the plan. Then, we got the announcement that the Odyssey was halting operations . We were fortunate that our travel plans were already in place, so we had somewhere to go. We knew other passengers were in a much harder position . When we got off in early October, we took the important stuff we needed. I left most of my things on the ship, including a full-size refrigerator and a big-screen TV we put up. I have been angry before, when I was younger, and I did not like the person it made me. Now, I am a positive person. I try to look for what is good in every situation. My wife and I are both that way — it's how we go through life. If the ship is in Singapore when we arrive in mid-November, we'd love to hop back on board. For now, we're waiting to find out what happens next. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: RBA lifts interest rates to highest level in 18 years to try to dampen inflation
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts The RBA's monetary policy board has increased interest rates for the fifth time in 2026. ( Reuters: Jason Reed ) The Reserve Bank's monetary policy board has lifted interest rates by 0.25 percentage points. The decision lifts the cash rate target to 4.85 per cent, up from 4.60 per cent. It is the highest cash rate since late 2008. It is the fifth interest rate increase in 2026, and the RBA has left the door open for more rate hikes. The Reserve Bank has lifted interest rates to their highest level in 18 years, while acknowledging it will take much longer to drag inflation down than it was expecting a few months ago. It has increased rates by 0.25 percentage points, which lifts the cash rate target to 4.85 per cent, up from 4.60 per cent. The cash rate has not been this high in Australia since late 2008. It is the fifth time the bank has lifted rates in 2026. The brutal redistribution at the heart of the RBA's interest rate policy RBA officials argue the hit to borrowers' income isn't the main way rate rises lower inflation. But they often omit a key fact. The RBA board's decision to lift rates was not unanimous. Six members voted to increase the cash rate target by 25 basis points to 4.85 per cent, while three members voted to leave the cash rate target unchanged at 4.60 per cent. The majority decision will be another blow to households with mortgages. But individuals who have high-interest savings accounts will see their savings accruing more interest after today's decision, if their bank applies higher rates to their accounts. In a statement , the RBA board said inflation was now forecast to remain high throughout much of 2027 and was not expected to fall below 3 per cent until late 2027, which is "around three quarters later than previously forecast". "This presents upside risks to inflation expectations," it said. In recent weeks, RBA officials have been signalling their intention to lift rates at today's meeting, arguing that they can not afford to see peoples' inflation expectations drift higher. The RBA wants annual inflation in consumer prices to be around 2.5 per cent on average over the cycle. "There is an increasing share of businesses who are thinking that maybe 3 to 3.5 per cent is the new normal [for inflation]," RBA deputy governor Andrew Hauser warned last month . It takes between 12 and 18 months for a change in interest rates to flow completely through the economy, so we will not know what total impact this rate hike will have on economic activity until 2028. Economy slowing, house prices falling, unemployment rising The RBA Monetary Policy Board said the cumulative rate hikes this year have tightened financial conditions in Australia. It says the economy is slowing, housing prices have fallen significantly this year, and the unemployment rate has risen. Why housing's the great Australian talking point Why are Australians obsessed with property? Because we have to be. And there are big reasons why it's always on our minds. Its new economic forecasts see growth in output slowing even further over the coming year, which is expected to reduce capacity pressures and help return inflation to target. It says employment is expected to keep growing, but the unemployment rate is projected to rise by more than expected. In August, it was forecasting the unemployment rate to average 4.8 per cent in the December quarter of 2028, but now it was forecasting it to average 5.1 per cent in that period. The unemployment rate is currently 4.7 per cent . But the RBA board has also acknowledged that there continue to be "heightened uncertainties" about the outlook for inflation and the economy. "The Middle East conflict remains unresolved, and there are scenarios where inflation is higher and activity lower than forecast," it warned. "Global oil supply disruptions are maintaining upward pressure on global and domestic energy prices and inflation. "A period of prolonged uncertainty may also cause growth to be lower overseas and in Australia. "To date, however, growth in Australia's major trading partners has been stronger than expected, as the boost from AI-related investment has outweighed the adverse effects of the Middle East conflict," it said. Is the RBA pushing the economy into recession? In her post-meeting press conference, RBA governor Michele Bullock left the door open for more rate increases. She was then asked if the RBA was risking pushing Australia's economy into recession with more rate hikes. The Reserve Bank doesn't want consumer prices to come down, but to rise more slowly.

events.title: Google takes Dreambeans to India in bid to bring AI-generated personal stories to the masses
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Google has launched its experimental AI app Dreambeans in India, its first market outside the U.S., as the company looks to tap the world’s second-largest internet market to bring personalized visual stories drawn from users’ digital activity to a broader audience. On Monday, Google expanded Dreambeans, available on Android and iOS, to India with support for 13 local languages, including Hindi, Punjabi, Tamil, Telugu, and Bengali, alongside English. The launch comes less than two months after Google made the app available to all eligible U.S. users aged 18 and older. Introduced in June, Google’s Dreambeans uses information from connected Google services, including Calendar, Gemini, Gmail, Photos, Search, and YouTube, to proactively generate personalized, illustrated stories about users’ interests and everyday lives, without requiring them to enter a prompt. The app initially featured static, AI-generated illustrations, but Google recently added a feature that uses its Veo video-generation model to even animate images in select stories. Google said it chose India as Dreambeans’ first international market because of strong interest from Indian users seeking access to the app and the widespread use of its services in the country. India stood out for its high overlap of users across Gemini, Gmail, and Google Photos, Google product manager Gozde Oznur said during a press briefing. Dreambeans has recorded nearly 55,000 downloads in the U.S. since its June debut, according to estimates from market intelligence firm Sensor Tower shared with TechCrunch. About 63% of those downloads came in September, when Google opened the app to all eligible U.S. users aged 18 and older. However, downloads dropped 84% month over month to about 5,500 in October. In the first 30 days after Google opened Dreambeans to all eligible U.S. users, the app recorded an estimated 29,000 downloads, compared with 7.4 million for Meta’s Muse, 2.8 million for ChatGPT, 362,000 for Grok Bot, and 155,000 for Claude during their respective first 30 days after launch, Sensor Tower estimates show. However, unlike those general-purpose AI apps, Dreambeans focuses on generating personalized stories instead of responding to a broad range of user queries. Even though Dreambeans supports many widely spoken Indian languages, users can select only one language at a time for their generated stories. The app can draw on information across Google services in multiple languages, but it cannot currently generate stories that mix languages, Oznur said during the briefing. That could limit Dreambeans’ appeal in India, where many people regularly switch between languages, including Hindi and English, often mixing the two in what is commonly known as Hinglish. Dreambeans’ dependence on information from users’ Google accounts also raises questions about privacy and data access. The app uses Google’s Personal Intelligence technology to draw on connected services and personalize its AI-generated stories. Those services can contain sensitive personal information that some users may not want to share with an AI app just to receive personalized content. Users can choose which Google services to connect to Dreambeans and disconnect them at any time, Oznur said. They can also delete their Dreambeans data from within the app. Moreover, Oznur asserted that information deleted from the underlying connected services is also removed from Dreambeans’ personalization system. Users, Oznur said, can tell Dreambeans to avoid certain subjects, including business-related information, and the app will try to adjust its stories accordingly. She added that Dreambeans is available only to personal Gmail account holders, not enterprise users, and that generated stories are visible only to the account holder. Dreambeans’ proactive approach also carries the risk of surfacing memories that users may find upsetting. Oznur acknowledged that Dreambeans could generate stories involving people who have died, for instance. She said users can tell the app to stop showing certain subjects, comparing the feature to controls in Google Photos that let users limit which memories appear. Oznur told reporters that Google is exploring ways to make Dreambeans more actionable, moving beyond personalized stories and recommendations to help users act on the app’s suggestions. events.title: EQT seeks joint AI and data centre deals with Saudi and UAE sovereign investors
events.summary: EQT , Europe’s biggest private markets investment firm, is in talks with sovereign investors in the UAE and Saudi Arabia to explore joint artificial intelligence and infrastructure investment opportunities in the Arab world’s top two economies, its global chair has said. The company with $400 billion in assets, which has been raising funds from Gulf investors for decades, is keen to now deploy capital in the region , home to some of the biggest sovereign wealth funds in the world, Jean Eric Salata, told The National . “Here [in the UAE] I would say, and we've also been talking to Saudis as well, looking at opportunities there. Those are the two big areas that we're working on right now,” Mr Salata said of the continuing AI co-investment conversations with sovereign investors. “We're most excited about, which I think aligns with the strategic goals of the UAE, is the whole infrastructure, particularly data infrastructure and data centres, where we have globally one of the largest footprints.” The Stockholm private equity company plans to expand its AI infrastructure footprint in the Gulf through its portfolio firm EdgeConneX, which owns more than 106 data centres across 25 countries, he said. AI opportunity EQT, which currently manages more than $100 billion in digital and energy assets across markets, is the latest global investor looking to the rapidly developing AI and digital infrastructure sector in the region. AI has become a central plank of economic diversification efforts of the oil-rich Gulf economies that have already announced mega AI infrastructure projects. The UAE is leading the way with a planned five-gigawatt UAE-US AI campus in Abu Dhabi, which includes Stargate UAE – a massive 1GW computing cluster anchored by a $20 billion data centre investment. UAE Tech investors Khazna and G42 are working on these projects alongside global leaders such as OpenAI, Oracle, Nvidia and Cisco, and investors such as SoftBank. Saudi Arabia, the largest Arab economy, has rolled out Project Transcendence, a $100 billion scheme to scale domestic AI and data infrastructure. The kingdom’s $1 trillion Public Investment Fund has also set up Humain to build out national cloud infrastructure in the country. Qatar’s sovereign arm, the Qatar Investment Authority, has also launched Qai, a $20 billion AI infrastructure partnership, to build out domestic GPU and data centre footprints. Since last year the three Gulf states have announced AI investment plans worth $120 billion, which exceeded 5 per cent of their gross domestic product, according to International Monetary Fund estimates. The sheer scale of investment required for AI development and data centres creates a huge opportunity for global investors such as EQT. The $1.3 trillion Blackstone Group has already struck a $3 billion deal with Saudi Arabia’s Humain, while tech giant Microsoft has committed over $10 billion towards data centres and related infrastructure across UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and Kuwait through to 2030. “There are many conversations that are ongoing right now with potential partners, both here [in the UAE] and elsewhere in the region,” Mr Salata said. “This is a sector that is capital constrained and is really, if you think about the AI build-out, the core, the key constraint in building the infrastructure is actually physical. It's the physical constraint around chips, energy, and data centres.” There is no shortage of demand for compute, hence a very strong investment case for building the power generation capacity and rolling out data infrastructure, he said. “I think that's where a lot of investment opportunity is right now for providers of long-term capital that can invest on a 15-year investment horizon,” he said. UAE SWF partnerships EQT opened an office in Abu Dhabi’s ADGM in September, joining the roster of trillion-dollar investors and asset managers including BlackRock, State Street, Blackstone Group, PGIM , Nuveen and Capital Group . A base in Abu Dhabi gives global investors opportunities to expand in the region and work closely with sovereign funds, large family offices and institutional partners. EQT is already working closely with the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, and Mr Salata said the firm is keen to expand that relationship. “They are one of our most important partners, and we're very excited to be working with them in, I would say, ever-increasing dimensions. We not only manage investments for Adia in our funds, but we also do a lot of co-investing together,” Mr Salata said. Adia is one of EQT’s largest co-underwriters in some of the European firm’s largest deals to take companies private in Europe. In June, Adia, along with Abu Dhabi’s $385 billion sovereign investment arm Mubadala Development Company, joined EQT’s £9.5 billion acquisition bid for the UK’s Intertek Group. Over the years, EQT has executed several co-investment deals with Mubadala, including the 2022 acquisition of Envirotainer, a biopharmaceutical industry solutions company. In 2025, Mubadala took a $600 million stake in Nord Anglia Education, and has been “a significant partner of ours all over the world”, he said. Deeping ties Establishing its first Middle East office in Abu Dhabi, Mr Salata said, was necessary to deepen its ties to the region, where it has active relationships with “many of the other sovereign wealth funds”. “The plan is to continue to develop those relationships regionally and use this office as a base to access them on a more regular basis,” he said. Forty EQT portfolio companies already have a presence in the Gulf, and with a local footprint, it expects more investments from regional sovereign investors to flow into those companies. “The logical place for us to start is with our existing portfolio companies,” Mr Salata said. “We really want to try and figure out how we can become more deeply involved in the investment ecosystem here,” he said. Over time EQT plans to bring more of its portfolio companies to the Gulf, and Mr Salata believes that the number will grow two or three-fold over the five to 10-year horizon. The sectors it seeks to invest in are “very much aligned with some of the longer-term trends in the region”, including infrastructure, education and health care, as well as technology and energy, where “the government policy is supportive”, he added.

events.title: OpenAI hires former U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll for national security role
events.summary: Driscoll will join OpenAI as senior counselor for national security modernization, the company said. He will advise OpenAI's leadership on AI applications in national security and cyber security, according to the company. Driscoll resigned as Army secretary following reported tensions with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Reuters reported. OpenAI has hired former U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll as senior counselor for national security modernization, a newly created role at the company . Driscoll will focus on how artificial intelligence can be used to strengthen U.S. national security and cybersecurity, OpenAI said, while his updated LinkedIn profile also lists his new position. He will work with OpenAI's senior leadership and external partners, with a particular focus on helping U.S. allies adopt advanced AI responsibly. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said the U.S. has "an extraordinary opportunity to work with other countries to spread the adoption of democratic AI," and that Driscoll's appointment would help strengthen American leadership in the technology. "National security requirements are changing faster than at any time in the past fifty years," Driscoll said. He added that AI could help reduce paperwork, process information and deliver answers more quickly to those working in national security. The appointment comes after Driscoll stepped down as Army secretary earlier this year after months of reported tensions with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. An Iraq war veteran, Driscoll pushed efforts to modernize the U.S. military, including expanding access to drone and counter-drone technologies among U.S. allies, according to a previous U.S. Army announcement. Driscoll also met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv in November 2025 to discuss a U.S.-proposed peace plan aimed at ending the war with Russia, according to a statement from the Presidential Office of Ukraine. At OpenAI, Driscoll will work with government officials, industry leaders, academic institutions and allied organizations to advance what the company calls "democratic AI." He will also help internal teams understand the operational needs of national security institutions, building on OpenAI's efforts to strengthen cyber resilience and protect essential services through its Daybreak program .

events.title: ‘Fastest entertainment property in history’: GTA VI arrives to test a thin November box office
events.summary: A nearly three-hour documentary about Elizabeth Holmes was the No. 1 movie in America over Halloween weekend. That’s a triumph for A24, and a scary harbinger for theaters heading into a thin November that faces competition from an entirely different corner of entertainment. A24’s You Can See Everything , directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, took in $11.4 million in its third weekend, narrowly edging DC Studios’ Clayface , according to Monday’s final figures reported by Variety . It had finished second in each of its first two weekends, behind Street Fighter and then Clayface . Its domestic total now stands at $64.7 million. It is the first documentary outside the concert genre to top the box office since Michael Moore’s Fahrenheit 9/11 in 2004. But its lack of direct competition is telling. No studio opened a wide release, and overall ticket sales came to about $56 million, down more than 40% from the prior weekend and the second-lowest total of the year, according to studio estimates. Why Halloween weekends sink the box office Unlike Christmas, Thanksgiving, or the Fourth of July, Halloween doesn’t boost the box office when it lands on a weekend. People don’t get an extra day off, and they’re more likely to spend peak moviegoing hours trick-or-treating or at parties. The last Saturday Halloween, in 2020, came while most theaters were shuttered. The one before that, in 2015, was the weakest weekend of that year to that point: three new wide releases flopped, and The Martian stayed on top in its fifth week, as Fortune reported . A thin November slate This year’s quiet Halloween also foreshadows a challenging month. The biggest swing is Lionsgate’s The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping on Nov. 20, the sixth film in the franchise and an adaptation of Suzanne Collins’ 2025 bestseller. Boxoffice Pro’s long-range tracking puts its opening at $55 million to $65 million; the last installment, 2023’s The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes , opened to $44.6 million. Thanksgiving week brings Disney’s animated Hexed and Universal’s Focker In-Law , both on Nov. 25. Focker In-Law is a greater gamble: the fourth film in the franchise that began with 2000’s Meet the Parents arrives 16 years after Little Fockers , which opened to $30.8 million in 2010. Warner Bros.’ animated The Cat in the Hat and Searchlight’s Wild Horse Nine open Nov. 6, and smaller titles like Ebenezer: A Christmas Carol and I Play Rocky are sprinkled through the month. But the box office’s most likely competition comes from the video game business: Rockstar Games releases Grand Theft Auto VI on Nov. 19, one day before Sunrise on the Reaping opens. The month’s biggest launch isn’t a movie The sixth game in the series arrives 13 years after Grand Theft Auto V , and anticipation has been building for years. Rockstar confirmed development in February 2022; that September, a hack leaked roughly 90 clips of early footage, and in December 2023 the first trailer leaked hours before its scheduled debut. The game promises a more expansive setting than any previous Grand Theft Auto title. Grand Theft Auto V generated $800 million in sales in its first 24 hours in 2013 and passed $1 billion in three days, which publisher Take-Two Interactive called the fastest any entertainment property had reached that mark. It has since sold more than 230 million units, according to Take-Two’s August 2026 earnings report . GTA VI is poised to beat those numbers. Analytics firm Sensor Tower estimates it had drawn 6.45 million digital pre-orders worth about $630 million as of Oct. 20, excluding physical copies. That global, pre-launch haul already tops the roughly $625 million domestic run of Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey , the year’s second-highest-grossing film behind Spider-Man: Brand New Day . It is also more than 11 times what every movie in North American theaters grossed over Halloween weekend. For Take-Two, which reported $6.66 billion in revenue in its fiscal year ended in March, the launch underpins a forecast of $8 billion to $8.2 billion in net bookings this fiscal year. Video games may draw a narrower audience than theatrical films, but a release this size is bound to occupy the attention of millions later this month. That’s likely to pull some of them away from the big screen for at least a weekend, leaving a notable dent in the fall box office. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Frantic Binance hackers created windfall for crypto traders
events.summary: Blockchain data firm Bitquery estimates the attackers lost about US$119 million through poor execution in their haste. Binance was hacked for US$6.3 billion, and North Korean hackers rushed to move stolen funds before stablecoins were frozen and withdrawals were halted. Their panic created sharp price gaps in Ether, TRX and other tokens, letting fast traders and bots make big profits from the chaos. Bitquery said hackers lost about US$119 million through poor execution, while Binance later restored withdrawals and said it had frozen about US$3 billion in affected assets. SAN FRANCISCO – For most crypto investors, the theft of US$6.3 billion (S$8.07 billion) from Binance was a reminder of the risks that still surround digital assets. For a small group of fast-moving trading firms and skilled investors, it was a chance to make a quick buck. As apparent North Korean hackers rushed to convert funds stolen from the world’s biggest crypto exchange, they accepted punishing prices. That handed well-prepared traders a fleeting but lucrative opportunity. Bitquery, a blockchain data firm, estimates the attackers lost about US$119 million through poor execution in their haste. “The hack created sharp price volatility and a single, large, price-insensitive seller moving through thin liquidity,” said James Aitchison, chief investment officer at Caerus Global Management. That aggressive, one-way torrent distorted crypto prices across disparate venues and blockchains, he said, adding: “We traded the event and found several attractive dislocations.” After gaining control of Binance funds on Oct 29, the attackers focused on getting rid of the stablecoin portion of the haul, knowing issuers would soon begin freezing those stolen tokens. Within roughly half an hour, they began aggressively swapping stablecoins such as USDT into other cryptocurrencies like Ether, which cannot be frozen, buying the tokens wherever they could and jacking up the price. Tether and Circle froze roughly US$1.8 billion worth of their stablecoins about 40 minutes after the main Ethereum leg of the hack began, according to blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs. Binance, meanwhile, stopped withdrawals while it investigated the breach. That disrupted the usual flow of money between trading venues and allowed price gaps that normally disappear in seconds to remain open far longer. Luca Parlamento, founder and chief investment officer of D2 Finance, said his firm spent the night “on the other side of the thief’s trades”. Parlamento said the attackers paid an average of about US$2,657 for Ether through decentralised exchanges such as Uniswap, well above the roughly US$2,300 price on Hyperliquid, a crypto derivatives platform. “The gap was ours to close,” Parlamento said. For traders with funds already sitting on such venues, the basic trade was straightforward: sell Ether where the hackers’ frantic buying had pushed the price unusually high and buy it where the price remained lower. Annanay Kapila, a former quant trader who runs derivatives exchange QFEX, was working in his central London office on the night of Nov 29 when he noticed that the price of Ether had skyrocketed on decentralised exchanges, reaching over US$3,000 in some cases. Kapila began to borrow large amounts of Ether on decentralised lending platform Aave, depositing stablecoins in return. He then sold his Ether on exchanges where its price was highest. Kapila said he made a 25% profit on the trades within five minutes. Crypto’s lack of persistent volatility in recent years means this kind of window is increasingly uncommon, Kapila said, with the last such event being when prices collapsed in October 2025. “Crypto’s been a little bit dead this year. Anytime there’s big dislocation, there are big opportunities,” Kapila said. “I’ve been around since 2021 where this was almost a weekly occurrence, stuff like this. But nowadays, it’s relatively rare.” The scale of the price gap showed the extent to which crypto’s typical market structure had been weakened. Achieving a fair price usually depends on traders being able to move coins quickly from one venue to another. Binance’s suspension of withdrawals also did not help, with locked funds preventing more traders from cashing in on the opportunity. The dislocations spread quickly to other tokens. One of the largest appeared on Tron, another blockchain network. Aitchison said the attackers swapped about US$234 million of USDT for 638 million TRX, Tron’s native token, in 16 trades. The average purchase price on a small venue called SunSwap was about 36.7 US cents, compared with a wider market price near 33 US cents. The buying briefly pushed the main trading pool as much as 18% above the broader market, and the gap took roughly 10 hours to fully disappear, he said.
