events.title: Feeling isolated? Half of in-office workers describe their desk jobs as 'remote,' NY Fed survey finds
events.summary: Corporations have made the case that in-office work is critical to the collaboration and productivity that fuels business growth, but new research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York pokes holes in this push, citing a "staggering share" of office-based workers who describe isolated roles. Researchers at the New York Fed find in a survey of college-educated workers that roughly half say in-office days are dominated by Zoom calls, Slack threads, and few actual interactions with colleagues. There are multiple reasons, the NY Fed research indicates, including fully remote colleagues, teams that are geographically sprawling, the technology tools that isolate workers, worker failure to comply with mandates, and employer failure to force adherence. Many workers across the U.S. are now back in-office a majority of the time, and they are feeling more isolated than ever. A recent survey from researchers at the New York Fed finds that roughly half of workers based in-office don't describe a daily experience on the job that matches the goal many corporate employers stated in upping in-person mandates. Whether three-, four- or five-day mandates , companies have cited the importance of creative collaboration for business productivity and growth, as well as mentorship opportunities. Yet workers surveyed by the NY Fed describe endless Zoom calls and Slacks, and little actual face time. "Days in the office often lack human contact," the researchers write. Specifically, 48.8% of survey respondents said they had no in-person meetings, either with teammates or non-teammates, on the days they were most recently in the office. There are a variety of reasons for the disconnect between in-office work mandates and actual experience. Roughly one in four workers are now fully remote, according to U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics data cited by the NY Fed, but they say that alone likely "understates the explosion in the experience of remoteness from colleagues." With teams being spread across more offices — an effect they say has become more pronounced in the post-Covid organizational structure — many workers "no-showing" on mandates, and employers not enforcing mandates strictly, the result for in-office workers, according to the researchers, is that "they commute in just to take Zoom calls and answer Slack messages from their cubicles." The NY Fed paper, by NY Fed research economist Natalia Emanuel and University of Virginia economics professor Emma Harrington, concludes that "a staggering share of the workforce experiences this form of in-office remote work." The survey was conducted in September among a final sample of 1,835 college-educated workers. The researchers chose September, they say, to generate a "conservative estimate," since many companies push in-office attendance after summer ends, and the period between Labor Day and Thanksgiving has less remote work than holiday periods. The survey found that on in-office days, 70.6% of workers had at least one teammate who was not in the office; while half had no in-person meetings with all participants present, and over a third had neither in-person or hybrid meetings. "Amazingly, 37% of respondents reported that they had at least one meeting that was virtual, even though all the participants were in the same office that day. In short, many workers' commutes are simply yielding a new background for their Zoom calls," they write. They cite the example of Zoom CEO Eric Yuan , who said in 2023, "On Zoom, it's really hard. We cannot have a great conversation. We cannot debate each other well." But the researchers conclude, "if the debates in the office are also happening over Zoom, the benefits of the office may not be so large." The authors say that separate information collected on a Fortune 500 company employee base to which they had personnel data and badge swipe data shows that nearly half of corporate employees have at least one teammate who is out of the office on their in-office days. They say additional data from the BLS's American Time Use Survey similarly show that "Americans now spend more time physically alone on days they go into the office than they did before the pandemic." Other recent polling data from Gallup found worker sentiment to be at a 15-year low . The NY Fed authors caution that their research does not capture relationships with non-teammates, or worker's in-person interactions with clients, often outside the office. They also stress that workers who come to the office often cite seeing colleagues as a major draw. "But since the rise of remote work, the office increasingly fails to deliver this benefit," they write. They contend that the research has practical implications for both employers and employees. For one, the experience of remote work is much more widespread than understood, which could have many repercussions not being dealt with effectively now, such as mental health issues.

events.title: US urges Venezuela to follow phased plan for democratic transition
events.summary: Trump, Netanyahu and the Iran question How Iran war fallout may shape US elections This comes as leading opposition leader, Maria Corina Machado, returns to Venezuela and hints at criticism of Trump administration. The United States has urged Venezuela to continue on a phased plan of economic recovery and political reconciliation before embarking on democratic elections. Secretary of State Marco Rubio discussed the gradual plan during a meeting on the country’s political future with Venezuelan Minister of Foreign Affairs Oliver Blanco on Monday. The meeting comes nearly a year after US forces abducted former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro from Caracas and brought him to the US to face drug trafficking and other charges. list 1 of 3 Trump touts Venezuelan oil at Texas rally ahead of US midterms list 2 of 3 Venezuela’s Machado says she hasn’t spoken to Trump since October list 3 of 3 Venezuela’s Machado lauds Trump for ‘freedom’, urges 2027 elections Neither Rubio nor Blanco spoke to the media after the meeting, but in a readout. The State Department said in a readout that Washington had reaffirmed President Donald Trump’s “three-phase plan for Venezuela: stabilization, economic recovery and political reconciliation, and democratic transition”. Last week, Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado returned to her country, thanking the US president and Rubio for their support. Machado, a Nobel Peace Prize laureate who gifted her medal to Trump in 2025, said she had come to organise a movement in preparation for Venezuelan elections. Rubio “has set out a sequence of events aimed at moving toward a democratic transition that makes clear the holding of presidential elections in 2027”, she said. Machado is balancing an election campaign with a Trump administration that has sought to extract oil from Venezuela by striking deals with the government of interim President Delcy Rodriguez, who served as Maduro’s vice president and took over after his abduction. In September, the Trump administration said it had struck a deal with Venezuela that would give Washington a stake in about one-fifth of the country’s oil resources. The US said it was creating a joint venture with North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), owned by Venezuelan businessman Alejandro Betancourt, which is the second-largest private oil operator in Venezuela, behind Chevron. Under the deal, Caracas is giving the company 100-year rights over 17 oilfields with proven reserves of 65 billion barrels. The Pentagon will have a 35 percent stake in NABEP, and the US will be guaranteed the right to buy 20 percent of its oil output at cost, the Trump administration has said. Shortly before Machado’s statements on Thursday, Rodriguez assured the nation that elections would be held in Venezuela “with the world as witness”, but did not specify a date. When asked about a possible meeting with Rodriguez, Machado said she had not received any message from the interim president or from Washington. In remarks after returning Venezuela, Machado seemed sceptical of the oil agreement with the US. “This agreement does not reflect the levels of transparency that Venezuelan society wants,” Machado said.

events.title: Christmas 2026 stamps unveiled by Royal Mail
events.summary: Two stamps from the Royal Mail's annual Christmas collection Royal Mail has unveiled its Christmas stamps for this year - featuring scenes from the Nativity. The series of five stamps have been jointly created by graphic designer Gareth Howat and illustrator Rebecca Sutherland. The stamps depict familiar scenes of Mary and Joseph travelling, baby Jesus, an angel, the shepherds and the Three Wise Men. This year's collection marks the 60th anniversary of the first-ever Christmas special stamp. Sutherland said it was an "absolute honour" to be given the opportunity to illustrate the Christmas stamps for the Royal Mail. She said she has loved stamps since she was a child and had even collected them. "Being asked to create a set myself feels incredibly special," she added. The Christmas stamps from recent years have featured snowy scenes of UK cathedrals, or lyrics from famous carols - although 2025 also showed scenes from the Nativity. The first Christmas stamp collection came out in December 1966 after a children's art competition was announced by the then-postmaster Tony Benn. David Gold, of Royal Mail, said: "We hope this year's Christmas stamps will add an extra touch of festive magic to the millions of greetings sent to family and friends at home and around the world." events.title: Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies
events.summary: Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines. A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co. , a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “ XCPE ” (named after one of the malware’s core code components). The global distribution of XCPE botnet infections. Image: Google Threat Intelligence Group. The report said the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. As detailed in several stories here over the past year , residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects. “Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the GTIG post reads, noting that Google took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install additional malware. “A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors.” The report notes that while TV boxes made up the the majority of the botnet, the same XCPE malware was found in other Android-based IoT products, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and even digital signage systems . Google said it requires all Android device makers to pass compatibility and security tests to ensure their products don’t harm users, but that Videostrong nevertheless found a way to load their malicious software immediately after a user boots up one of these devices for the first time (Google says it has since addressed that weakness). The GTIG report calls out a number of residential proxy providers whose software development kits were routinely downloaded by devices infected by the XCPE botnet. Those include AppSalt , also known as Honeygain , which is owned by the Vilnius, Lithuania-based Oxylabs . In October 2026, Oxylabs was relaunched under a new brand called Source , after receiving $130 million in funding from private equity firm Warburg Pincus that reportedly valued the business at $3.6 billion. Oxylabs did not respond to a request for comment. Another provider linked to the botnet was NetNut , a once sprawling residential proxy company operated by the publicly-traded Israeli company Alarum Technologies . In July 2026, the FBI worked with industry partners to seize hundreds of domains associated with NetNut , saying the company was responsible for operating a separate botnet called Popa that enslaved TV boxes as residential proxies. Other proxy providers named in the GTIG report include EarnFM , Traffmonetizer , Jaguar , LINKFOG , BMW/IPWeb and GaGaNode . Google’s announcement credits a number of industry partners, including Synthient , a startup that tracks proxy providers. In January 2026, Synthient published research into the rapid spread of the Kimwolf botnet, which at the time was hammering networks worldwide with record-smashing DDoS attacks . Synthient documented how Kimwolf infected millions of Android set-top boxes virtually overnight, using a widespread vulnerability in these residential proxy services to compromise other Android-based devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting TV box users. Synthient’s research caused dozens of residential proxy providers to patch their networks, which helped to fragment the Kimwolf botnet into much smaller pieces that made its incessant and disruptive DDoS attacks far easier for network operators to manage. It also attracted the attention of the Motion Picture Association (MPA), a trade group representing the major Hollywood studios, which partnered with Synthient to purchase and tear apart a number of popular Android TV set-top boxes — including some that were being infected by Kimwolf and other IoT botnets. In a report published today, Synthient examined a popular, pre-infected TV box sold under the brand MECOOL by a publicly traded company in China called Skyworth Technology , concluding that MECOOL also bundled the malware from Videostrong Technology Co. and likewise installed AppSalt/Honeygain and other proxy components. The MECOOL storefront and marketing. Image: Synthient.com. Synthient founder Ben Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity that Videostrong’s malware also distributed software for the proxy service Grass . In our November 2025 story, “ Is Your Android TV Streaming Box Part of a Botnet? ” we quoted a researcher from Censys who found the popular Superbox TV streaming device bundled Grass’s residential proxy software. We also quoted the Grass founder, who denied any affiliation with the TV box maker. That November 2025 story noted that Superbox and similar Android TV set-top boxes gain new customers primarily by engaging influencers on Tiktok and other social networks who praise the product’s ability to offer hundreds of (pirated) pay TV streaming services for a one-time fee. Likewise, Synthient’s report observes that the MECOOL set-top boxes exploded in popularity after the product was mentioned in 2023 by the Youtube channel Linux Tech Tips, which has an audience of nearly 17 million subscribers [Linux Tech Tips said in a statement shared with Synthient that it has since updated the video to explicitly frame the product as a scam and have removed all associated affiliate links]. The popular Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips discussing MECOOL TV streaming boxes. events.title: Before the tragic Learjet crash, Adam Robinson had a message for startup founders: You don't need VCs to get rich
events.summary: Adam Robinson, right, poses with his wife Helen Sharp and the couple's two young children. Courtesy of the Robinson family Adam Robinson, who died in the Florida Learjet crash on Sunday, was a serial entrepreneur. Robinson's career in finance ended with a spiritual upheaval and a pivot into tech startups. An evangelist for bootstrapping, he leaves mourners in Aspen, Austin, and across the internet. Before this weekend's tragedy, Adam Robinson was carving out a picture-perfect life and a contrarian lane in tech entrepreneurship. The 45-year-old tech founder died in a private plane crash on Sunday near Greenacres and Palm Beach, Florida, along with his wife, their two young children, their nanny, and two friends. They were flying from Austin to the Bahamas when the plane went down. All nine occupants of the Learjet died, including the two pilots . "It's an unspeakable tragedy," Brett Hurt, a friend and mentor of Robinson's from Austin, told Business Insider on Monday. Robinson was an "amazing conscious capitalist," Hurt said, and a "beacon" for other startup founders learning how to bootstrap their own businesses. Robinson leaves behind a career that carried him from the halls of Wall Street during the 2008 financial crisis to serial entrepreneurship in Austin's post-2020 tech wave. In recent years, he had relocated to Aspen, Colorado, and crystallized an ideology that runs counter to Silicon Valley's VC-friendly ethos. On social media and in podcasts, Robinson evangelized for the idea that startups should run lean and earn their own keep . His companies, Retention.com, RB2B, and MoltSets, released a joint statement on Monday calling Robinson "a friend, a mentor and a bold, outspoken leader who lived life to the fullest." "His loss is deeply felt across our team and the tech community, as we collectively mourn," the statement said. Robinson's journey from Wall Street to tech Robinson grew up in the Houston suburbs and attended Rice University, where he was a guard on the basketball team. After college, he moved to New York City to work as a credit trader at Lehman Brothers. He stuck around until the 2008 financial crisis and then beyond, when Barclays absorbed much of Lehman after its bankruptcy. The Wall Street gigs made Robinson millions of dollars, he said on the ProfitLed podcast earlier this year. After around a decade, he'd also realized the lifestyle wasn't what he wanted and that he didn't have the invigorated energy of someone who truly loves their work. New York had given him another lesson, with a window into the tech startup world. His original roommates in the city had started Vimeo in their Tribeca apartment. "These guys were making just as much money, and it just appeared like they loved it," Robinson said on ProfitLed. "Everything they were dealing with just seemed so interesting to me." In his early 30s, unmarried, and with money in the bank from Wall Street, Robinson went through a bit of spiritual upheaval, he said on the Fulfillionaire podcast last year. He read former Zappos CEO Tony Hsieh 's "Delivering Happiness," various Buddhist texts, and John Mackey and Rajendra Sisodia's "Conscious Capitalism." He said he realized that money shouldn't be the end-all, be-all motivator; he needed to start working with more purpose. He made the leap into startups. Robinson's early days in tech were a slog At the time of his death, Robinson was a bona fide serial entrepreneur, with a cluster of businesses — Retention.com, RB2B, and MoltSets. The same group of 32 people runs those businesses, and Robinson has said they bring in $35 million in annual revenue. They offer products for identifying website visitors and accessing contact information. It'd taken a bit of grind. Robinson's first startup, an email service provider called Robly, burned through his and his brother's money for its first few years. On ProfitLed, he said he had to lay off 27 of the company's 35 workers at one point; after paying severance, the company was profitable, yet its customer count was slowly shrinking. Thankfully for Robinson, they were on to an idea. A feature built at Robly to snag people's email addresses became popular with customers, and Robinson and the other founders spun the business off into a company called GetEmails. He described the tactic in a 2023 interview with Practical Ecommerce as "email laundering" — placing a pixel on customers' sites and then collecting email addresses from their anonymous web traffic. Robinson said on ProfitLed that he realized the product would be "10 times better of a business." From there, the business grew. GetEmails became Retention.com, and the team launched other companies. The day Robinson's plane crashed, he'd posted on LinkedIn that RB2B had hit $10 million in  annual recurring revenue  and MoltSets had nearly reached $1 million in ARR. Robinson explained the split between firms in characteristically bombastic style: "I think all-in-one platforms ALWAYS turn into garbage." He wrote that he would host a debate about keeping the companies separated on Tuesday. Robinson was an evangelist for bootstrapping More so than for his actual businesses, Robinson's star rose on the internet with a canny content-creation strategy and a no-holds-barred embrace of bootstrapping companies, or building them without outside capital. He accumulated 13,000 followers on X, and more than 160,000 on LinkedIn, presenting as a techie, brand-building thought leader. He often posted and spoke about the merits of the bootstrapping approach , arguing that it led companies to waste less on extraneous bets, keep their ambitions in scope, and more quickly identify the actual value of their product. This mindset contrasts with tech's typical embrace of venture capitalists, who Robinson often poked at in posts and interviews. "Bootstrapping to $10M ARR is easier and less risky than creating a VC-backed unicorn, with a far higher probability-weighted outcome," he wrote on X in January. In April, he posted: "You don't need to crash a plane to learn to fly ... and you don't need VC to build a business." And he often tied bootstrapping to an exhortation for founders to seek true financial freedom . "If you can hold out on investment long enough, the freedom you will have as a bootstrapper will give you the life you wanted when you started on this path in the first place," Robinson wrote on X in September. "VC will not." A wave of heartbreak in tech Figures in the tech world who'd interacted with Robinson or admired his bootstrapping enthusiasm expressed their grief on Monday. Hurt told Business Insider that when he visited Robinson in Aspen a few months ago, he was taken with how happy his friend seemed about his children, wife, and community in the Colorado mountain town. "He was a genuinely good, loving guy that just loved his family and loved the community so much, and did so much for everyone around him," Hurt said. "It's just absolutely tragic." Larry

events.title: HashKey Adopts Tokenised Deposit for Cross-Market Treasury and Liquidity Management on Standard Chartered's Blockchain Platform
events.summary: [The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.] Hong Kong, November 2, 2026 — HashKey Group (3887.HK), a leading Asian digital asset company, today announced that, its is among the first institutional clients to adopt Standard Chartered’s newly launched institutional tokenised deposit solution. HashKey is using the solution to support its institutional treasury management and settlement use cases. Tokenized deposits are the digital representations of commercial bank deposits on the blockchain. Built on Standard Chartered’s blockchain infrastructure, they enable eligible clients, such as HashKey to use their bank deposit balances within an approved blockchain-based environment, while retaining the characteristics of commercial bank money. By combining the trust of bank deposits with blockchain-enabled programmability, speed and extended availability, Standard Chartered’s tokenized deposits can facilitate near real-time movement of funds, and support more efficient cross-border liquidity management with extended availability. For HashKey, which operates across multiple jurisdictions, the ability to move liquidity across markets outside traditional banking hours is particularly important. While digital asset activity takes place around the clock, the movement of funds between HashKey’s entities has traditionally been constrained by banking cut-off times. Tokenised deposits help bridge this gap by enabling near real-time, extended-hours movement of funds, giving HashKey greater flexibility to manage treasury positions across markets and entities, reduce funding friction and deploy working capital more efficiently in support of its global operations. Haiyang Ru, CEO of the HashKey Exchange BG, stated: "As more assets move on-chain, fund and settlement systems also need to evolve synchronously. The significance of tokenized deposits lies in connecting funds within the banking system more directly to the on-chain environment. Being among the first institutional clients to adopt Standard Chartered’s newly launched tokenised deposit solution is an important step in strengthening HashKey’s institutional financial infrastructure. We look forward to exploring more efficient fund-flowing methods with global financial institutions, providing more comprehensive infrastructure support for institutions participating in on-chain finance." Mark Willis, Head of Emerging Payments, Transaction Services and Digital Assets, Standard Chartered, said: "Tokenised deposits can play an important role in connecting commercial bank money with the digital asset ecosystem, giving clients greater flexibility in how they move and manage liquidity across markets. Our work with HashKey demonstrates how this technology can support near real-time, extended-hours movement of funds, helping clients manage treasury and liquidity more efficiently while supporting their digital asset activities. This is about bringing the trust of bank deposits together with the speed and programmability of blockchain to solve real-world treasury needs." In recent years, HashKey has continuously promoted the construction of institutional-grade digital asset infrastructure, expanding its business network with its "Asia Interconnected" strategy, and deepening its business layout and financial connections in major Asian markets. Relying on the group's cross-jurisdiction compliant license layout, institutional customer service capabilities, and continuously expanding global financial institution partnership network, HashKey continues to expand channels for institutional funds to enter the digital asset market, enhancing cross-market capital management, trading, and settlement capabilities. Based on HashKey's long-term business experience in serving institutions and professional investors, HashKey will further improve its global treasury management capabilities, strengthen the infrastructure connection between the traditional financial system and the digital asset market, and provide more efficient fund-flowing support for tokenized assets and other on-chain financial applications. In the future, HashKey will continue to deepen cooperation with global financial institutions, explore the practical applications of tokenized deposits in institutional business, and promote the further connection between the traditional financial system and on-chain financial markets. HashKey Group（“HashKey”, the Company, Stock Code: 3887.HK） is a leading digital asset company in Asia with a global footprint, providing end-to-end financial infrastructure, technology and investment management to create a digital assets ecosystem. The Company offers a licensed digital asset platform to provide transaction facilitation services, on-chain services, and asset management services. We are a leading international banking group, with a presence in 55 of the world’s most dynamic markets.

events.title: Fox-Roku deal poised to clear Justice Department scrutiny under consent decree
events.summary: The Scoop Fox’s $22 billion acquisition of Roku is poised to clear Justice Department scrutiny and move forward under a consent decree, according to people familiar with the deliberations, despite efforts from a right-wing ally of President Donald Trump to hold up the deal. It’s unclear what a consent decree would entail, or what terms are being considered. It’s possible the DOJ could change course, the people said. Fox declined to comment. Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward also declined to comment on the deal. “However, we can affirm that this DOJ under President Trump’s leadership will continue to prioritize affordability for all Americans across our economy,” he said in a statement. The deal, which would unite Fox’s content empire of news and sports with Roku’s dominant connected-TV operating system, had worried rivals who fear that Fox will favor its own content. Roku’s free, ad-supported channel also competes for viewers and content with Tubi, which Fox owns. Fox CEO Lachlan Murdoch has said his “expectation” is to run the two businesses separately while selling advertising across them. Semafor first reported in September that antitrust regulators were widening the inquiry into the deal, days before the two companies confirmed the deeper probe, known as a “second request.” That enhanced scrutiny came in part because of pressure from Newsmax majority owner Chris Ruddy, who bills himself as a Trump confidant and has had a long-running spat with Fox owner Rupert Murdoch, Semafor later reported. Rohan’s view Ruddy, briefly a reporter for Murdoch’s New York Post in the 1990s, has been feuding with Fox for more than a year over streaming access to his media assets. Murdoch’s camp has previously dismissed Newsmax’s efforts as a bid to “sue their way out of their own competitive failures,” and Murdoch himself has dined with Trump more than once. But it’s clear that Ruddy has been a headache for the Murdoch clan. Investors have fretted about the possibility that Fox’s deal for Roku could get tied up as a result of Ruddy’s efforts. Those worries were exacerbated after Fox ousted business anchor Maria Bartiromo following an internal investigation into allegations she leaked internal network information and communications to the Trump administration, a claim her lawyers have disputed. But if the deal goes through, it’s more evidence that the Murdoch name still carries a fair amount of weight in Washington.

events.title: New Apple CEO John Ternus chalks up some early wins, but the honeymoon is over
events.summary: John Ternus, Apple’s new CEO, has spent the first two months in his new post celebrating a batch of fresh products, particularly the release of the foldable iPhone Duo . On Monday, the 51-year-old executive introduced himself to Wall Street for his first quarterly earnings call. The reception was not so friendly. While Apple beat September-quarter earnings expectations, investors traded the stock down in after-hours trading due to the company’s outlook on margins , which it said will continue to be squeezed by a shortage in memory chips, and slowing growth in its Services segment without a clear answer to how that may rebound. The company has also attempted to tell its AI story through its revamped Siri AI product, but investors don’t seem convinced yet that Apple has the winning formula for the AI age. On the call with analysts following earnings, Ternus fielded some questions but also delegated answers to Chief Financial Officer Kevan Parekh and Chief Operating Officer Sabih Khan, who Apple said would participate in earnings calls moving forward, something the company hasn’t done for years. Ternus projected confidence on the call, but he appeared to stick mostly to scripted marketing points, such as “Apple is the greatest company in the world,” that subdued the conversation. By some measures Apple is performing at its best ever (its September iPhone sales set a record), but the more nuanced reality is that the $4.9 trillion company has had to offset surging memory chip prices by raising its own prices, and it is relying on its massive install base to carry it forward. Compounding the pressures are supply chain shortages for products that include the iPhone Duo, with new orders for the phone not arriving until the end of January. “What we’re seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented,” Ternus told analysts on the Monday call. “That has put pressure on our prices.” He added that beyond the December quarter, the company expects the pricing for memory purchases to continue to increase. Apple said it expects its gross margin for its December quarter to be between 45% and 46% after posting a margin of 47.9% for its September quarter, when tariff refunds provided an approximately one-percentage-point boost. The decline, the company said, reflects the continued cost of memory, as well as costs associated with ramping up Siri AI. “We’re going into this [holiday period] with more downside than upside,” Apple investor Gene Munster told Fortune in an interview prior to Apple’s earnings. On X, Munster wrote after the earnings posted that, “It’s clear they don’t want to talk about personalized agents. They’re the biggest risk to the Apple ecosystem.” The Siri situation Ternus and Parekh offered few details when asked by analysts about the roadmap for Siri AI, the company’s revamped assistant . When asked about the industry shift toward consumer AI agents such as Meta’s Muse assistant, Ternus noted that Siri is “primarily request-based today,” though he said the assistant is built on an architecture that makes it possible to substantially expand its capabilities over time He described agentic capabilities as “promising tools for users,” but cautioned that users must be fully aware of what access they grant, and he stressed user security and privacy. Apple has touted Siri AI, which has been rolling out to users in beta mode, as a key upgrade that is central to new products such as the home devices it recently launched, which included its first smart home display. The new Siri is designed to understand what is on a user’s screen and act on it, help with writing, and search a user’s device for context, among other features. Reviews have been mixed on the revamp. Some analysts have said they liked the new features, but overall, the assistant has lagged well behind leading chatbots from OpenAI and Anthropic, as well as a wave of personalized agents from Meta and others that have ushered in a new kind of AI assistant capable of shopping, checking bank statements, and other tasks on its own. “Siri AI is much more capable and functional today, but how do you take it to the next level?” Wamsi Mohan, an analyst at Bank of America , told Fortune . Asked about Apple’s plans to handle its slowdown in its Services unit, which includes iCloud, the App Store, and other services, and how the company may find new revenue streams, Ternus and other executives on Monday mostly spoke about the company’s active installed base surpassing 2.5 billion devices, which they said will lead to future monetization possibilities. They added that there will be some usage limits on features that rely on AI that does not run locally, and that iCloud tiers historically focused on storage will evolve.  A wave of hardware The start of Ternus’ tenure has mostly comprised a new wave of hardware. In early September, at his first public event as CEO, Ternus unveiled the iPhone Duo. The phone has shown strong demand, with orders backed up, but supply constraints have made it difficult to gauge the scale of sales. Some units dealt with cracked screens, which Apple acknowledged and said it was replacing. When an analyst asked about the rollout of the Duo phones and hinted at “supply chain” issues, Ternus let Khan respond. The product ramp is going well, Khan said. “It’s really hard to predict when supply and demand will be in balance.” Analysts at Yorkville Ives predict Apple can sell roughly 10 million Duos over the next few quarters. Apple has moved to a staggered iPhone release, with its Pro, Pro Max, and Duo models now available but the base model and iPhone Air not expected until the spring. The approach, together with the rising component costs and a slowdown in Services growth, could affect its future performance, according to BofA’s Mohan. Sales in Greater China, a key market for Apple, jumped 21% year-over-year in the September quarter, though the sum was $1 billion short of Wall Street targets, according to Bloomberg estimates. Apple also plans to launch AI features for China-based iPhone customers after working out a deal with Alibaba Group Holding following a long period of negotiations, though the launch is not equivalent to a full Siri AI experience for Chinese customers. “We have everything we need to be extraordinarily successful,” Ternus said. “With this team, this vision, this mission, and these values, I have no doubt that we will.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: North Korea denies role in Binance heist as customers withdraw billions
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts North Korea dismisses Binance heist allegations as 'absurd' US rhetoric Kim Jong Un is the leader of North Korea, which has been accused of orchestrating the largest crypto heist in history. ( KCNA via Reuters ) North Korea has denied FBI allegations accusing the country of stealing $US6.3 billion from crypto exchange platform Binance. Ruling party official Kim Yo Jong dismissed the allegations as "absurd rhetoric and nothing new" from the US. Binance customers have withdrawn $US4.64 billion after the company lifted a temporary suspension on withdrawals. North Korea has denied US allegations that it was behind the $US6.3 billion ($9 billion) heist of cryptocurrency exchange platform Binance as "absurd rhetoric" and proof that Washington remained hostile towards the country. In a statement published by North Korean state media, Kim Yo Jong , the influential sister of leader Kim Jong Un, denied the country was responsible for carrying out last week's hack, thought to be the largest financial heist in history. Who is behind world's largest crypto heist? Almost $9 billion in cryptocurrency was hacked from exchange company Binance, but who was behind the attack? Ms Kim also warned the country had "issues to reconsider" over US hostility. "The FBI is trying to brand the DPRK as a 'cyber criminal state,' claiming that it obtained information that a hacking organization 'supported' by the DPRK was involved in the incident," she said in the statement. "But the US assertion is absurd rhetoric and nothing new. "It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads international public opinion as if all the cyber crimes in different parts of the world are our deeds." On Saturday, the FBI accused a North Korean state-sponsored unit known as TraderTraitor of carrying out the hack and stealing billions in crypto. The FBI says North Korean state-sponsored hacking unit TraderTraitor is behind the heist. ( Pexels: Tibe De Kort ) The US bureau said it had observed TraderTraitor converting stolen assets into a cryptocurrency called Ethereum and expected it to launder the assets further. "The FBI maintains its commitment to protecting the virtual asset community by identifying, mitigating, and disrupting North Korea's illicit cybercrime and virtual asset theft activities," a statement read. Cybersecurity experts said North Korean hackers were among the world's most prolific crypto thieves, with the proceeds used to help fund the country's weapons programs. North Korea has denied all allegations of its links to cryptocurrency theft and other cybercrimes. Ms Kim said North Korea would reconsider unspecified issues in light of the "very unpleasant US hostile attitude". It comes as Pyongyang remains silent on US President Donald Trump's offers to resume US-North Korea summit diplomacy. Experts have indicated Pyongyang may be weighing its options. Binance customers withdrew about $US4.64 billion ($6.6 billion) worth of assets after the company lifted its temporary suspension on Sunday. Zhao Changpeng is the founder and CEO of Binance, which has moved to reassure its users following the hack. ( Reuters: Benoit Tessier ) "Between 06:00 and 15:30 UTC on November 1, we processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits, resulting in a net outflow of approximately $3.64 billion," the company said on X. "Our team continues testing rigorously the remaining networks and assets. "Rest assured that market conditions are stable." The company said it had recovered 90 per cent of the stolen assets by using company money. events.title: What we know so far about the Learjet 60 private plane that crashed in Florida
events.summary: Roads are closed after a jet crashed on November 1. Saul Martinez/Getty Images A private jet crashed in South Florida on Sunday, killing all nine people aboard. Weather data at the time of the crash shows thunderstorms and moderate turbulence in the area. NTSB officials said there is evidence of the jet breaking apart before impact. Nine people aboard a private jet were killed when it crashed and exploded in a fireball near Palm Beach, Florida , Sunday afternoon. The plane, a Learjet built in 2004 and registered as N722BD, had departed from Austin and was en route to the Bahamas. Tech entrepreneur Adam Robinson and his wife Helen Sharp died in the crash, as did their children, their nanny Anita Maria Cetina, and their friends Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr, the victims' families shared. The plane's two pilots also died. Authorities have not said what caused the crash. "Please join me in praying for the families and loved ones of those we lost," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy wrote on X on Sunday. National Transportation Safety Board Member Tom Chapman said during a press conference on Monday that access to the crash site is challenging because of the bad weather on the ground, causing the impact crater to fill with water. Officials also said crash debris was scattered across fields, homes, and businesses. The crash occurred less than 10 miles from President Donald Trump's Mar-A-Lago resort . Trump left West Palm Beach around noon aboard Air Force One to attend a rally in Iowa, according to White House pool reports. What we know about the flight Aviation-tracking data from FlightRadar24 showed the plane descending from 41,000 feet to about 35,000 feet as it entered Florida, then crossed the state before plummeting about 27,000 feet in about a minute to the ground near Palm Beach. The plane was about two hours into the flight to North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas when it crashed. In the minutes before the crash, a pilot can be heard on air traffic control recordings reporting the air temperature outside as -47 degrees Celsius (about -52 degrees Fahrenheit), as well as icing, precipitation, and moderate turbulence. The pilot later said "mayday," saying the plane was descending at 10,000 feet per minute, and moments later, reported an overspeed condition before impact. Video footage shared online of the crash shows that part of the Learjet's T-tail may have separated from the plane. Chapman said there is "some evidence that there was some breakup of the aircraft before impact" and the NTSB is "still seeking to determine that." He also said the agency hopes to recover the cockpit voice recorder, but it's unclear if the particular jet had one installed. NTSB investigator Timothy Monville said during the briefing that the Federal Aviation Administration and the manufacturer Learjet, which is now a part of Bombardier, will assist the NTSB with the investigation. "We at Bombardier are deeply saddened by this tragic event and extend our sincerest sympathies to all those affected," Bombardier said in a statement. "We cannot comment on the potential cause of this accident until the investigation is complete and we will fully support the investigating authorities and cooperate as needed." What we know about the weather Widespread thunderstorms moved through South Florida on Sunday afternoon. Aviation weather data for the area showed heavy rain, low visibility, and turbulence around the time of the crash. "The weather conditions are a major focus of the investigation," Chapman said. "You all saw what the weather was like here at the surface; what we have to determine is what the weather conditions were like at altitude." There were thunderstorms in the area at the time of the crash. Saul Martinez/Getty Images It's not yet known what caused the crash, but retired Delta Air Lines pilot Mark Stephens told Business Insider that icing can occur at any altitude and, in some circumstances, cause a wing to lose lift and an aircraft to stall. "If there was a failure on one wing, meaning that wing iced up, then the good wing would still fly, but the other would lose lift," he said. "You'd have such an uneven lift that it would basically do close to exactly what the Learjet did; it can flop out of the sky." Stephens warned against immediately placing blame on the pilots, adding that anti-ice and weather radar systems can fail and that a number of factors beyond human error could have contributed. 'She was doing her job' Jared Isaacman, the NASA administrator and pilot, shared his personal thoughts on the crash on X and urged the public not to criticize the woman pilot in the ATC calls. "She was the second-in-command (SIC), and while she was empowered to point out mistakes as part of good crew resource management, she was doing her job, communicating with ATC right to the end in a terrifying situation," he wrote. He added that she "likely knew before many of those calls that she was going to die," and the public does not know factors such as the jet's maintenance history, or whether there was structural failure and why. Isaacman also said that charter companies often hire commercial pilots "very early in their careers to gain experience," alongside airline-qualified captains. "She would still have the appropriate training, qualifications, and checkouts by an FAA examiner or designee," he said. "Let people investigate, learn, and share the facts. Be respectful to those who perished and the families who carry their memories." This is a developing story. Check back for updates. Read the original article on Business Insider

The ABC has confirmed that David Jones just missed a deadline to file its most recent financial year reports to the corporate regulator, ASIC. Meanwhile, there is ongoing media speculation that the retailer is going to call it quits on several stores inside Westfield shopping centres. It currently has 38 stores nationally. Suppliers have also already been put on extended terms this year to give David Jones more time to pay for stock. David Jones was first founded as a corner shop in Australia in 1838 and today has multi-level department stores across Australia that sell everything from cosmetics to shoes and fashion. Its main rival is the ASX-listed Myer, which early last year voted to merge with Solomon Lew's apparel brands Just Jeans, Jay Jays, Portmans, Dotti and Jacqui E . That merger was billed as a way for Myer to keep relevant in a changing retail landscape, where younger generations are increasingly shopping online or opting for second-hand apps such as Depop. events.title: Indonesia’s severe drought threatens to disrupt China’s vast battery industry
events.summary: A severe drought in Indonesia is slowing output of a crucial material used to make electric vehicle batteries A severe drought in Indonesia is slowing output of a crucial material used to manufacture electric vehicle batteries, creating risks across China’s vast electric car supply chain. Indonesia is a vital link in the global electric car supply chain. The Southeast Asian nation is the world’s biggest production hub for nickel, a metal that is converted into a component used in lithium-ion batteries. But a sharp drop in rainfall in the country is causing local nickel refineries to reduce output, a move that could “add uncertainty … across the battery materials value chain”, according to market analysis firm CRU Group.

events.title: Apple may try to increase revenue by doing…something with third-party AI apps
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Apple’s services business remains at record levels, but it’s facing growing pressure . The central part of that business, Apple’s App Store, has faced regulatory pressure and a slump in mobile gaming, which have hurt services growth . However, on Monday’s earnings call, Apple signaled that it may look to boost services revenue through third-party apps. What does that mean, exactly? Unfortunately, it’s not entirely clear. When discussing how AI could potentially “contribute to revenue growth over time,” Kevan Parekh, Apple’s chief financial officer, said: “On the product side, you know, we feel AI offers a compelling reason for customers to upgrade and switch in order to get the latest capabilities, and we also feel there’s opportunities across third-party apps and partnerships as well as first-party opportunities.” Parekh did not elaborate on what sorts of opportunities might be available via third-party apps. However, Reuters reported Monday that investors are wondering whether Apple could profit by distributing third-party AI agents through the App Store and taking a cut of the revenue they generate. Regulatory and legal changes have cut into App Store commission revenue in some markets, even as Apple’s services business as a whole continues to grow. Third-party estimates in August, for example, suggested the company had seen an 18% drop in U.S. commission revenue, with declines also in Brazil and Japan after those countries introduced new regulations. Apple has traditionally controlled payments within its app marketplace tightly, taking a cut of all App Store transactions. But a lawsuit by Epic Games ultimately forced the company to allow apps to redirect users to outside payment systems. Other legal challenges throughout the world have further hampered the business. During the earnings call, Parekh referenced Apple’s App Store woes and returned to the idea that the company’s service business could expand into new territory. “We’ve also seen some factors that impacted the performance of the App Store, and during the September quarter, the performance on the App Store was similar to the prior year, and we had a record number of paid subscriptions with double-digit growth for third-party apps on the App Store,” Parekh said. “At the same time, we did see some headwinds in mobile gaming that we’ve talked about before, and expect to see those continue into the summer quarter.” Parekh added: “As we move ahead, we expect services growth to to be between 8 to 9% [in the December quarter]. This outlook contemplates our best estimates on sequential headwinds, primarily from third-party licensing and the additional half percentage point of foreign exchange I just mentioned.” TechCrunch has reached out to Apple for more information and will update this story if it responds. events.title: Oil rises after report of US strike on Iran’s Qeshm Island
events.summary: Earlier, US and Iran signalled that diplomatic talks are continuing. Oil prices rose after a Wall Street Journal report said the US struck Iran’s Qeshm Island, lifting fears of wider conflict and oil supply disruption. Brent crude rose 0.5% to US$105.25 and WTI rose 0.5% to US$96.93, after Brent had fallen 7.63% the day before. Tehran said talks with the US continue, while Trump said a deal may still happen and the US-Iran war keeps pressure on Strait of Hormuz traffic and petrol prices. Oil prices rose in early Asian trade on Nov 3 after a report that the US had struck Iran’s Qeshm Island, raising concerns about an escalation of the eight-month long conflict and prolonged disruptions to Middle East oil supplies. Brent crude futures rose 48 US cents, or 0.5%, to US$105.25 a barrel by 1.04am GMT (9.04am Singapore time), while US West Texas Intermediate crude was up 47 US cents, or 0.5%, at US$96.93 a barrel. Brent crude futures settled US$8.66, or 7.63%, lower to US$104.77 a barrel on Nov 2. The United States struck Iran’s Qeshm Island, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing US officials. Some of the officials described the assaults as defensive in nature to prevent Iran from having the freedom to attack commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz. “The report added a degree of risk premium back into the oil price. Just when markets were starting to price in a more diplomatic path, this reminder of ongoing military activity has flipped the tone,” said Tim Waterer, chief market analyst at KCM Trade. Meanwhile, Tehran said on Nov 3 that contacts between Iran and the US to end their war are continuing, after days of Iranian talks with Qatari mediators ended with altered proposals but no breakthrough. Trump raised doubts on Nov 3 about whether he would follow through on a threatened resumption of military strikes against Iran and said a deal with Tehran could happen. The US-Iran conflict that began in late February has sharply reduced traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, which previously carried about a fifth of global crude oil and natural gas supplies. The Iran war is a leading cause of high petrol prices that are weighing on voters in the US ahead of the midterm elections on Nov 3, and Trump is under pressure to end the conflict. Brent ended October at its highest in six months on concerns that the Middle East conflict could escalate again after the vote. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei had granted the government certain authorities for peace talks. Additionally, the US will bring together delegations from Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi on Nov 10 and 11 to discuss ending Moscow’s war against Ukraine, post-war security agreements and de-escalation. The SA government earlier confirmed the Torrens to Darlington Alliance, tasked with delivering the road corridor upgrade, had cancelled its contract with Career Boss on the grounds the company had not been "proactively disclosing" its involvement in a civil legal suit. State parliament's budget and finance committee has summoned the alliance to answer questions over its due diligence processes. A second company has been suspended from the Torrens to Darlington project, because of what the government says is a common shareholding with a labour hire firm that had its contract terminated amid a civil suit surrounding alleged bikie threats. The SA government said small cleaning subcontractor LYLA was not the subject of any allegations of criminal wrongdoing but had been "suspended from all work" on the $15.4 billion road corridor project. It said that step had been taken purely out of an "abundance of caution because of the common shareholding" with Career Boss, which has since had its contract terminated after it was suspended last month. A watered down ICAC gets called up for a full-bodied political scandal The government asking the state's anti-corruption watchdog to look at the $15.4 billion South Road project has been spun as a proactive step against potential bikie infiltration, but there is devil is in the detail. "Whether you have any link whatsoever to Career Boss, the message from the government is very clear: there is no place for you on the T2D, there is a zero-tolerance approach," Transport Minister Joe Szakacs said. On its website, LYLA Services lists an address at a Salisbury commercial building which is also home to Career Boss. The building has exterior signage for Career Boss, but LYLA Services is not publicly displayed. The ABC has sought a response from LYLA Services. The government said there was "no suggestion of wrongdoing by LYLA, its shareholders, directors, or owners". "This common shareholding of this company LYLA shows that we won't tolerate companies that have any association with anything that might be considered inappropriate for the North-South corridor," Treasurer Tom Koutsantonis said. "Sometimes, people will think this is unfair. We don't care. "There will be new tenders that go out and new companies will tender. There will always be an ongoing assessment of every single company that is working on this." Joe Szakacs says the government is taking "a zero-tolerance approach". ( ABC News: Che Chorley ) The government reiterated that SA Police last week had found "no evidence of organised crime on any public infrastructure project", including the T2D. Late last month, the SA premier wrote to SA's Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) requesting an evaluation of the Torrens to Darlington project. ICAC commissioner Emma Townsend later confirmed she was "independently of the view" it was in the public interest to evaluate the Department for Infrastructure and Transport's policies. Opposition leader Ashton Hurn said today's developments further demonstrated the need for a "forensic audit of every single contract". SA Opposition Leader Ashton Hurn has repeated a call for a forensic audit of contracts. ( ABC News: Che Chorley ) "Since day one, the government has not got its story straight on who knew what when," she said. "[It's] this type of absolute chaos that allowed billions of dollars in Victoria to flow to the very wrong people. We don't want to see that happen in South Australia." events.title: Supreme Court rejects DOJ's bid to block California from counting disputed ballots
events.summary: The Supreme Court denied the Department of Justice's bid to temporarily block California from counting the mail-in ballots of about 20,000 voters whom it suggested may not be U.S. citizens. The DOJ's petition to the Supreme Court came three days after the 9th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals rejected the department's bid to overturn a federal district court judge's ruling that allowed the ballots to be counted. The petition comes a day before Nov. 3, Election Day. The Supreme Court could act on the petition at any time, but there is no deadline. The Supreme Court , in an order Monday evening, denied the Department of Justice's last-minute request to temporarily block California from counting mail-in ballots from about 20,000 voters who it suggested may not be U.S. citizens. The one-sentence order came hours after the DOJ sought the injunction, and on the eve of Election Day. The Supreme Court did not explain its reason for the denial, and it did not note any dissents. The order came after Justice Elena Kagan presented the DOJ's request to the full court, which includes three appointees of President Donald Trump . The swift ruling was the latest courtroom blow to the Trump administration, which is engaged in multiple other legal fights related to the midterm elections. Those contests will determine which political party holds majorities in the House and Senate. Pollsters and analysts widely predict Democrats will make significant gains. On Sunday, a federal judge dismissed a DOJ lawsuit that sought to block Alaska election officials from immediately certifying the result of the U.S. Senate election there if incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses that race by a margin that could be attributable to voter confusion about another candidate with his name. California Attorney General Rob Bonta told CNBC that Monday's denial by the Supreme Court was "completely appropriate, very expected." "This was a Hail Mary. It was baseless," Bonta said in a phone interview. "And the U.S. Supreme Court's response showed just how baseless it was." The attorney general noted both the speed of the Supreme Court's order and the fact that it was issued without the court first asking California to respond to the DOJ's request. "That is very rare," Bonta said, adding that, "We haven't seen this type of order where they didn't even ask for a response since 2018." The DOJ's application to the Supreme Court came three days after the 9th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals rejected the department's attempt to overturn a federal district court judge's ruling that allowed the California ballots to be counted. That same day, another federal district judge in a separate case in California barred DOJ from threatening election workers with criminal prosecution for refusing to stop processing ballots or resisting other demands. During a hearing Monday in that second case, a DOJ lawyer admitted to Judge Trina Thompson that the lists of purported noncitizens on California's voter rolls had a "high error rate," MS NOW reported. But that lawyer also argued the errors are evidence of why election officials need to examine those rolls and make sure that everyone on them is a U.S. citizen. Trump focuses on Reflecting Pool in final public speech before midterms How the 2026 midterms could affect defense, healthcare, crypto and AI stocks DOJ asks Supreme Court to block California counting disputed mail-in ballots Solicitor General D. John Sauer, in his application Monday morning asking the Supreme Court to enjoin counting of the mail ballots, said, "In this case, this Office has been informed that the United States has identified more than 20,000 individuals who appear to be registered to vote in California based on publicly available information at the time that information was received, but who, in the United States' view, are likely not U.S. citizens." Sauer said "the United States is likely to succeed on the merits of its appeal" of the lower court ruling denying the DOJ's request. "The district court concluded that the United States lacks Article III standing to bring this suit, but the United States suffers a judicially cognizable 'injury to its sovereignty' from the 'violation of its laws,'" Sauer said in the petition. "Once California commingles the challenged ballots with lawful ones, there is no way to get the challenged ballots back." The DOJ sued California on Oct. 15 in U.S. District Court in Los Angeles. The complaint sought to prevent state election officials from tabulating mail-in ballots "from likely non-citizens in the upcoming federal election until the voter's citizenship status can be determined." The DOJ previously gave Los Angeles County officials a thumb drive containing names of voters the department suggested could be noncitizens, who by law are barred from voting in federal elections.

events.title: GOP's midterm blame game starts early
events.summary: Republicans don't know if they'll lose big or small on Tuesday, but they're already bracing for an epic blame game. Why it matters: Privately, Republicans acknowledge it's not a complicated version of Clue. The leading suspect: Mr. President , in the Oval Office, with an assortment of weapons — and one war. Returning Republican senators are unlikely to blame President Trump publicly. There's a price for that. And don't expect Trump to shoulder the responsibility. But do expect departing GOP lawmakers to take shots at Trump or his team, and Trump to fire back at Senate Republicans, whom he's never been shy about torching. The irony of Trump's second midterm: With Republicans privately resigned to losing the House, Trump can still credibly claim victory if they hold the Senate. "It's Donald Trump's midterms. He gets all the credit if we win. He gets all the credit if we lose," one national GOP strategist told Axios. The Iran war: From Alaska to Maine, Trump's decision to go to war with Iran — and the resulting spike in gas and diesel prices — has become a major political liability for Republican Senate nominees. "It's not tariffs … it's the war, it's gas prices, it's diesel," Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton said at a closed-door fundraiser in September, Axios reported last month . Tariffs: Trump's trade policies have compounded Republicans' affordability problems, particularly in farm country, where producers have faced higher costs and uncertainty over export markets. "We need to end this tariff war now," former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) , the GOP Senate nominee, said in an October campaign ad, breaking with Trump over his tariffs on Canada. Bad candidates: Trump's preferred nominees are also drawing blame, GOP strategists tell Axios. Paxton in Texas and Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina have forced Republicans to spend heavily defending races that should have been easier — and where the party had other options. Complacent incumbents: Sens. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) and Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-Miss.) are facing accusations of "arrogance" and "laziness" from Republicans frustrated that their once-safe seats have become late-breaking battlegrounds — exactly the complacency NRSC Chair Tim Scott warned against. Weak governors: Underperforming gubernatorial nominees in Iowa, Michigan and Ohio threaten to drag down Republican Senate candidates. Vivek Ramaswamy, for example, saw his polling crater in the final weeks . Recruitment failures: Republicans couldn't persuade Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp to run for Senate, and in New Hampshire settled for their second-choice Sununu — former Sen. John Sununu — instead of his brother, former Gov. Chris Sununu. Meanwhile, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) landed marquee candidates in Alaska, Ohio and Iowa — though Michigan and Maine proved more difficult. MAGA money: Trump's political operation amassed an enormous war chest, but some Republicans complain the money arrived too late to rescue vulnerable candidates. Distractions: Trump's focus on D.C. construction projects, the Kennedy Center, Sen. Jon Husted's (R-Ohio) backside and the SAVE Act has frustrated Republicans desperate for a closing message focused on the economy. "Reflecting Pool presser was an interesting choice for closing message," another national GOP strategist said of Trump's Monday news conference.

events.title: Dodge announces return to NASCAR Cup Series beginning at Daytona 500
events.summary: Dodge is returning to the NASCAR Cup Series in 2027, a year earlier than initially expected LAS VEGAS -- Dodge is returning to the NASCAR Cup Series in 2027, a year earlier than initially expected. The Stellantis-owned Dodge brand announced its return at the SEMA Show in Las Vegas on Monday. Dodge will once again give the Cup Series four manufacturers, joining Chevrolet, Ford and Toyota in fielding entries to compete in a 36-race schedule that begins in mid-February and crowns a champion in early November. Kaulig Racing will use the Dodge Charger to field a two-car team beginning at the Daytona 500. AJ Allmendinger and Ty Dillon are expected to fill those seats. “Dodge’s return to the NASCAR Cup Series is a significant milestone for the sport,” NASCAR CEO Steve O’Donnell said in a statement. “This commitment speaks to Dodge’s belief in our sport and gives fans another reason to be excited about what’s ahead. “The partnership between NASCAR, (Ram CEO) Tim Kuniskis and the entire team at Stellantis has been nothing short of phenomenal. They have a deep passion for NASCAR and its ability to showcase the world’s top brands, and we can’t wait to see Dodge on the racetrack for the Daytona 500 and beyond.” Dodge raced in NASCAR through the 2012 season and left the same month it celebrated the Cup title with Brad Keselowski and Penske Racing. It was Dodge’s first Cup championship since Richard Petty’s sixth of seven titles in 1975. Dodge re-entered the NASCAR Truck Series with its Ram brand in 2026, with eyes on expanding to the premier Cup Series in 2028. Kuniskis vowed to be disruptive while doing it “unlike anyone else.” Learjet with 9 aboard crashes in Palm Beach County, Florida: FAA Sen. Chris Murphy hospitalized after suffering a stroke, chief of staff says 2 college students found dead after going missing while hiking, police say Kuniskis said Ram planned to tap into NASCAR’s estimated fan base of 20 million “and turn it into 80 or 100 million.” Kaulig had five trucks race this season, all of which are outside the top 10 in the series standings heading to the season finale at Homestead, Florida, this weekend. Normally, it would have taken Dodge two years to get ready for the Cup Series. But Dodge bypassed part of the timeline required to develop a new engine by partnering with Earnhardt Childress Racing to build Dodge-spec powerplants alongside its regular Chevrolet operations. Chevrolet, Ford and Toyota allowed that unique partnership in part because they believed a fourth manufacturer in NASCAR would be good for the overall health of the racing series. events.title: PBOC to raise banks’ forex reserve requirements to ease appreciation pressure on yuan
events.summary: The People’s Bank of China says it will increase the reserve requirement ratio on foreign exchange deposits later this month The People’s Bank of China announced on Tuesday that it would raise the reserve requirement ratio on foreign exchange deposits by 2 percentage points. The ratio would be 6 per cent, effective November 15, the central bank said in a statement, calling it a move to strengthen the liquidity management of financial institutions. The policy, which would require banks to hold a larger share of their foreign currency deposits in reserve at the central bank, is expected to tighten onshore foreign-currency liquidity, potentially easing appreciation pressure on the yuan. The currency recently broke through the 6.65 per US dollar mark to reach its strongest level since June 2022.

Ukrainian drone teams have a new way to spy on the drones that spy on them. A Kyiv equipment startup called CODE380 has been gaining attention for a pocket-sized receiver, the D·Vision SDR, that picks up live camera video from many Russian drones and shows it on a screen. Those drones send their video over the air without any scrambling, so anyone with the right receiver can watch along. A Ukrainian unit can see where a drone is heading and what its pilot is aiming at before it hits. According to Defense News , the device is light, at about 10 ounces, which is less than half the weight of competing Ukrainian models, one of which weighs a couple of pounds. It also listens on the radio channels Russia’s newer Molniya drones started using for video in June. Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, a radio specialist who advises Ukraine’s president, said in a June Facebook post cited by Defense News that “most detectors don’t see these frequencies, or see them poorly.” He warned that putting too much trust in a detector could prove fatal. Beskrestnov has also warned that digital video could one day replace analog, which would blind receivers like this one. The New York Times reported in August that some Molniyas are AI-guided, using Nvidia chips and emitting no signals . events.title: Asian stocks fall on US tech jitters and yuan weakens
events.summary: In a sign some investors are looking to buy on dips, US stock futures gained. Japan is closed for a holiday. Asian stocks fell as US chipmaker losses deepened and investors waited for the US midterm elections. South Korea’s Kospi dropped almost 4%, led by Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. China’s market support steps failed to lift shares, with the CSI 300 down 0.1%. The renminbi ended 13 straight gains after the People’s Bank of China asked banks to hold more foreign currency reserves. Oil steadied after an 8% fall, while Apple shares slipped on a mixed outlook. Analysts said markets are in a “risk-off mood” because of AI worries, politics, and geopolitics. Asian stocks fell as a sell-off in US chipmakers deepened and investors grew reluctant to trade ahead of the US midterm elections. The MSCI Asia Pacific gauge dropped almost 1% with South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi Index sliding almost 4% . The decline came after a gauge of US chipmakers extended a three-day rout, bringing its losses to 12%. The Nasdaq 100 has now declined 10% from its peak, entering a technical correction. Japanese markets were closed for a holiday. Chinese equities fell even after the central bank said it would encourage financial institutions to make greater use of stock-support tools and optimise their terms as the authorities seek to bolster market stability. The renminbi ended its longest winning streak in three decades after the People’s Bank of China moved to cool its rally by asking banks to hold more foreign currencies in reserve . The renminbi weakened as much as 0.4% to 6.6728 per dollar, halting 13 straight days of gains, which was the longest streak since 1996. Kieran Calder, head of Asia equity research at Union Bancaire Privee, said: “Markets are mostly in a risk-off mood against the background of increasing AI concerns and the US midterm election . “We have looked at all US midterm elections since 1950 and found that the S&P 500 was higher six months later in each case. If this trend persists, we expect markets should move higher into year end but it could be a rocky week.” Korea’s Kospi Index led declines in Asia, with shares of the two chip giants, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, both dropping more than 4%. Hebe Chen, market analyst at Vantage Global Prime, said: “Korea’s semiconductor-heavy market is back on the front line of the global AI trade’s repricing. “The divergence on Wall Street, where tech heavyweights are losing ground even as broader market breadth improves, suggests investors are rotating away from crowded AI trades rather than abandoning equities altogether.” Brent crude steadied after plunging almost 8% on Nov 2, as the US and Iran both signalled a willingness to pursue peace talks as the war in the Middle East enters its ninth month. The global benchmark was near US$105 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate was below US$97 after its biggest decline in three months on Nov 2. Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian said his government had been granted more authority by the nation’s supreme leader to negotiate , while US President Donald Trump hinted at progress in talks. Still, simmering hostilities are keeping the market on edge. Apple’s shares fell in late US trading after the company delivered a mixed outlook to investors in its first quarterly report under chief executive John Ternus, with narrower profit margins overshadowing an upbeat sales forecast. Elsewhere, Anthropic disclosed a twelve-fold increase in quarterly revenue while outlining plans to spend more than US$895 billion (S$1.14 trillion ) in the coming years. China’s CSI 300 Index slipped 0.1% amid scepticism about the latest market support measures from the authorities. The two liquidity-injection tools – a swap facility and relending operations to encourage more stock purchases – reappeared with some adjustments as the authorities sought to bolster market stability and confidence. Chinese shares have been mired in a slump since the summer, weighed down by a weak economy and doubts over AI earnings. Previous attempts to revive the market – including a round of buying by the so-called national team starting July, and regulatory guidance to curb selling last month – have fallen short. Elsewhere, a Bloomberg gauge of the dollar edged higher, while US Treasury 10-year futures slipped 3/32. There was no trading of cash Treasuries in Asia owing to the holiday in Japan. Australia’s dollar fell after the central bank raised its key interest rate to an 18-year high, as economists forecast, in a split vote. The Aussie dropped as much as 0.5% to 69.99 US cents. US job openings data due on Nov 3 are expected to show that listings edged higher in September, while weekly jobless claims due on Nov 5 are seen remaining near historically low levels. Economists expect the Nov 6 payrolls report to show job growth more than doubled to 65,000 in October, with the unemployment rate holding at 4.2%.

events.title: Apple says it's 'really hard' to predict when iPhone Duo supply will catch up to demand
events.summary: Apple said it can't predict when the iPhone Duo supply will catch up with demand, as customers who placed orders online face a long wait time. Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images Apple said it can't predict when the iPhone Duo supply will catch up with demand. Online delivery estimates for the iPhone Duo were pushed to late January 2027 after preorders opened. Memory shortages spurred by AI demand are constraining Apple's product supply and raising costs. If you're considering Apple’s first foldable iPhone , know that getting your hands on it could take a while. During Monday's earnings call , Sabih Khan, Apple's chief operating officer, told investors that the company couldn’t say when supply of its new iPhone Duo will catch up with demand. “So we're thrilled with the initial response on the iPhone Duo. iPhone Duo is constrained as of today,” Khan said in response to questions from a JPMorgan analyst. “The ramp is going well, and we're working hard to get this revolutionary new product into the hands of our customers as quickly as possible," Khan added. "But at this time, it's really hard to predict when supply and demand will be in balance." The Duo was released on October 23, following preorders on October 16. The folding phone starts at $1,999 and opens like a book to reveal a 7.6-inch screen. Customers ordering online quickly faced a long wait, with delivery estimates slipping into late January 2027 shortly after preorders opened. The supply squeeze extends beyond Apple’s newest phone. Khan said that while strong demand constrained supplies of iPhones, Macs, and iPads during the September quarter, the biggest bottleneck was access to the advanced chipmaking technology used to produce Apple’s processors. “For the December quarter, we expect constraints on Mac and iPad, primarily driven by memory , as demand has been higher than what we expected,” Khan said. Apple is competing for memory with tech giants who are pouring money into AI data centers. Business Insider previously reported that Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron supply chips for both consumer gadgets and AI infrastructure , and as manufacturers shift production toward the booming AI market, device makers face tighter supplies and higher costs. The costs are already weighing on Apple. The shortages accompanied an otherwise strong quarter. Apple reported $114.5 billion in revenue, beating Wall Street’s estimates, with iPhone sales reaching $57.58 billion.
