events.title: Disney eyes thousands of layoffs, with managers asked to cut 20%
events.summary: The 20% in annual cost savings could come from job eliminations as well as from expense reductions. Disney is planning thousands of job cuts, with some managers told to find 20% annual cost savings through layoffs and lower spending. Chief executive Josh D’Amaro wants to use some savings for film and TV content, technology, theme parks and cruise ships. The cuts follow years of cost reductions across Disney, as traditional TV weakens and streaming growth slows; Disney had 231,000 staff worldwide last year. BURBANK, California – Walt Disney is moving towards thousands of job cuts, with the entertainment giant asking some managers to target 20% in annual cost savings, according to sources familiar with the matter. The savings could come from job eliminations as well as from expense reductions, said the sources, who asked to not be identified because the discussions are private. Some of Disney’s operations, from theme parks to TV network to the movie studio, will be affected disproportionately. Chief executive Josh D’Amaro aims to reinvest a portion of the savings into film and TV programming, technology, and the theme parks and cruise ship businesses, the sources said. The company has promised double-digit growth in adjusted earnings per share in the current fiscal year. A representative for Disney declined to comment. Disney has cut billions of dollars worth of costs and eliminated thousands of positions in recent years, with reductions impacting every division including ABC, Pixar, ESPN, the film studio and the experiences unit. The company had 231,000 people worldwide at the end of the last fiscal year. The Wall Street Journal reported on Oct 1 that Disney was planning a restructuring of its TV division, and cuts at the company’s legal and global affairs unit. Other entertainment companies including Netflix, Sony Pictures Entertainment, and Skydance’s Paramount and Warner Bros. divisions have also cut jobs as revenue from traditional television declines and streaming subscriber growth slows. They also have to cope with more viewers tuning to social media, online videos and streaming services backed by tech giants like Amazon.com and Apple. At the Bloomberg Screentime conference in Los Angeles in October, Disney president Dana Walden said: “There is a need to constantly evaluate how you’re structured and how big is the organisation. Technology set their sights on our business and we must survive and thrive and grow, and that’s what we’re going to do.” BLOOMBERG

events.title: Y Combinator’s Garry Tan uses AI agents so much, he spends up to $200K a year on tokens
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan has, in the past, jokingly admitted that he’s suffered from “cyber psychosis” and sometimes barely sleeps because he’s so excited to be working with his AI agents. On a new episode of Walter Isaacson’s podcast The Builders , set to publish on Tuesday, Tan put a price tag on his passion. “I spend about maybe $100[,000] to $200,000 a year on tokens,” he told Isaacson. He uses agents for countless work projects and coding tasks and has freely shared his set of 23 Claude Code skills, called gstack , on GitHub — an effort to help teach others what agents can do, he said. On the one hand, he uses his agent the way many people use AI: to help him research Isaacson’s podcast and prep for the kinds of questions he might be asked. On the other, his agent also helps him run his life. “It’s read all of my email and all of my Dropbox. It’s read, like, all of my Apple Notes, even my therapy notes going back 20 years,” he said. He describes using AI agents as getting help with “almost anything that you do in your day-to-day life, and for it to do it somewhat more autonomously. Think of it as a Jiminy Cricket on your shoulder at all times. Like, almost anything you want to do, it knows you, and it’s there to help. And it will actually sort of run ahead and say, ‘What about this?’ Or it’ll help you see around corners.” As an early OpenClaw adopter who is now a power user, Tan says one thing he’s learned is not to treat AI agents like traditional software. Some people are so worried about “repeatability and safety that they actually trade off all of the beautiful parts of working with an AI agent, which basically can be so similar to a human,” he said. For instance, Y Combinator is also using an agent that is “rebuilding the way we operate at YC,” he said. “We now have an internal AI agent, for instance, named Stray Light that kind of has a personality, and then it has a company brain. Like it actually has the total context of every founder we’ve ever backed, anyone who’s ever emailed us, like all the applications.” Tan, who is, naturally, an avid lover of technology (as anyone running Silicon Valley’s famed startup accelerator would be), believes personal AI agents will eventually become mainstream, if one major problem is solved: Costs have got to come down. “It’s too expensive right now,” he said, adding that he knows the amount of money he spends on AI agents is “a crazy privilege that not everyone can do.” But freebie agents controlled by Big Tech maybe aren’t the answer, either. When discussing the future he’d like tech to build, and how Meta as a social media company has impacted us, he said, “This is a huge company that controls the algorithm, and we all wish that they didn’t at some level,” he said. “So you could imagine a personal AI that you control, that you program.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Hinge tests a cheaper plan as users become more fed up paying for dating apps
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Hinge is testing a cheaper subscription plan as its parent company Match Group looks for new ways to get users to pay for dating apps at a time when people are increasingly tired of subscriptions and, in some cases, dating apps altogether. During its third-quarter 2026 earnings call on Monday, Match Group said the new Hinge tier will include features such as additional filters and custom location boundaries, giving users more control over who they see and where they meet people. “It’s designed for women in particular, but also for price-sensitive users,” said Steve Bailey, chief financial officer of Match Group. “Remember that Hinge is one of the highest-priced products we have. The revenue per payer, for example, at Hinge is almost twice that of Tinder, around $30. It also has one of the lower payer penetrations. Its payer penetration is only slightly more than half that of Tinder.” Match Group didn’t share how much the new subscription will cost. TechCrunch has reached out to the company for more details. The move comes as dating apps continue to struggle to convince people to pay for services they’re growing tired of using. Between subscription fatigue, endless swiping, and frustration with the overall dating experience, users are increasingly questioning whether premium dating features are worth the money. Interestingly, Hinge is making this move despite being one of Match Group’s strongest performers. The app had a much better quarter than Tinder, with global monthly active users growing 12% year over year, direct revenue increasing 19%, and paying users rising 23% to 2.3 million. The app generated $221 million in direct revenue and had 2.3 million paid subscribers as of the end of the quarter. Direct revenue is money earned from subscriptions and in-app purchases. By comparison, Tinder brought in $480 million in direct revenue but experienced a slight 2% decline year-over-year, although it has 8.9 million paid users, a 4% decline from a year earlier. The lower-priced subscription could help Hinge build on that momentum by converting more users into paying customers without requiring them to spend as much upfront. The move also marks a shift in Hinge’s subscription strategy. In 2023, the company experimented with a more expensive tier aimed at users willing to pay extra for features designed to help them get more out of the app. Now, it’s testing whether a more affordable option could appeal to a broader audience. Still, cheaper subscriptions alone are unlikely to solve the bigger problem facing dating apps: user fatigue. Match Group says it’s seeing some signs of improvement, partly thanks to efforts to make its platforms feel less like traditional dating apps. Recent initiatives include Group Hangouts and Events , which offer users alternative ways to connect beyond the usual one-on-one matching experience. Match Group plans to ramp up those efforts in the fourth quarter. Another initiative on the horizon is real-time adaptive recommendations, which the company plans to begin testing in the fourth quarter. Announced during its CEO Connection presentation in September, the feature will allow Tinder to respond to user actions within seconds rather than hours, with the goal of making recommendations more relevant and personalized. events.title: We're married airline pilots. We travel the world for free — but can go a week without seeing each other.
events.summary: We've traveled all over the world, from Tanzania to the Dolomites. Tyler Bell Tyler Bell and Jenn Hoare are married airline pilots who live near Boston with their two cats. They plan date nights at airports between flights and often feel like a long-distance couple. The two have traveled to Tanzania, Italy, and beyond, thanks to their jobs' free travel benefits. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Tyler Bell, 28, a first officer at JetBlue Airways, who is married to Jenn Hoare, 33, a first officer at Breeze Airways. It has been edited for clarity and length. All cockpit photos were taken in accordance with applicable federal regulations and company policies. My wife, Jenn, and I recently had an unusual date night: Better Buzz, a coffee shop inside the San Diego airport. Not idyllic, but our best option as two working airline pilots . Our trips overlapped, barely. She had time between flights, so I arrived early to meet her before mine. We spent an hour catching up over coffee before going our separate ways. While our hectic flight schedules can often make us feel like we're in a long-distance marriage, we get to live our flying dreams and travel the world together for free. We met at an airport and got married in a hangar Jenn began her aviation career in 2016 as a JetBlue flight attendant and was encouraged by the pilots she met to consider flying. She went on to complete pilot training at the flight school in Massachusetts where I was an instructor. My interest in flying began as a toddler, and I became an instructor after years of training and flying small planes. It wasn't until after Jenn got her pilot's license that we started dating, hiking in the Berkshires and taking short trips together. She eventually joined Breeze Airways, and I now fly for JetBlue Airways. We spent a lot of time flying small planes before transitioning to passenger jetliners. Tyler Bell In 2025, we married at the New England Air Museum in Connecticut, by Bradley International Airport near Hartford. It's only natural we'd have our wedding at an airport. We held our ceremony, cocktails, and reception across the museum's 100,000 square feet of connected hangars, surrounded by more than 100 historic aircraft. Signature drinks were served from galley carts. We're long-distance one week and nonstop together the next We split our time between our Boston-area apartment with our two cats, Ellery and Noogit, and crew hotels across the Americas. We might spend five straight days together at home, then go a week without seeing each other. We both love our jobs , but it's like toggling between a long-distance relationship and being tied at the hip. We met at an airport, got married in a hangar, and are now both airline pilots. Tyler Bell Every month, we block off birthdays, holidays, and family events when bidding for trips, yet workdays pile up in between, and flight delays, cancellations, or weather disruptions can mean we sometimes don't make it home at all. It's not unusual for one of us to come home as the other heads out the door. Still, as pilots, we can turn a long overnight into a mini-vacation: Jenn once joined me for my 28-hour layover in Aruba between flights. Shared interests and overcommunicating help us make it work Among aviators, there's a common understanding that a pilot career can be hard on marriages. We've each sat next to pilots in the cockpit telling stories of broken promises, financial strain, and divorces. We started our marriage by committing not to become one of those statistics. If we make one mistake, we're likely to over-communicate. It may not sound romantic, but discussing bidding plans and flight patterns in airport coffee shops keeps us grounded and the information flowing. Fortunately, we share similar interests. As Jenn points out, "Having shared values, interests, and hobbies is key: We both really like being active, skiing in the winter and hiking in the summer, and love to travel." Free flights mean spontaneous trips all over the world One of the best perks of the job is that we get standby travel benefits that let us fly for free, paying only a small listing fee and taxes. Because seats aren't guaranteed, we plan ahead with plans A, B, and C — but it's worth it. That's how we spent 12 days in the Faroe Islands this spring, living out of a camper van and hiking. We traveled to Italy this summer, eating our way through southern Italy and then hiking in the Dolomites. We just returned from our delayed honeymoon to Tanzania, Africa, where we summited Mount Kilimanjaro . For seven days, we climbed the Machame route with nine other hikers and a crew of guides, porters, and cooks. We summited Mount Kilimanjaro on our first wedding anniversary. Tyler Bell Summit night brought eight hours of steep, dusty trudging in the dark at 14 degrees Fahrenheit, with every breath a struggle at nearly 19,000 feet. It was the hardest thing either of us has ever done, but we reached the top on our first wedding anniversary. We originally imagined going on a safari for our 25th anniversary, but as Jenn reminds me, "Why wait? This adventure is best done when we are at our physical peak." Still, we hope to start a family someday and recognize that our lifestyle will change. Until then, it's just us, our cats, and a long list of places to visit. events.title: John Lewis Christmas ad stars Kristin Scott Thomas as glamorous granny on a gift hunt
events.summary: Company tugs at heartstrings with Pickles the talking toy dog as it celebrates 20 years of blockbuster festive ads John Lewis has turned to a celebrity best known for playing aristocrats to put a playful but rather upmarket spin on the countdown to Christmas with this year’s festive ad, which features a toy dog called Pickles and a glamorous granny. Kristin Scott Thomas, known for playing upper-crust characters in films such as Four Weddings and a Funeral and the Apple TV show Slow Horses, is cast as Gloria, a grandmother searching for gift inspiration, with the tagline “don’t give up on giving”. In the 20th version of its blockbuster Christmas ad, the department store kickstarts the official countdown to Christmas by tugging at the heartstrings, with Pickles, voiced by the comedian Paul Whitehouse, challenging Gloria to “do better than cash” when choosing a gift for her grandchildren. Pickles drags Gloria out of the house on a last-minute mission to find gifts, and after rejecting options in other shops, she sets off on a magical tuk-tuk ride to John Lewis, where she snaps up some disco balls and fairy lights to create a “gran cave” to hang out with her grandchildren, Freddie and Maggie. Rosie Hanley, the marketing director of John Lewis, said the retailer had increased its spend on this year’s festive ad as the cost of production had risen and it wanted to “push the boat out” for its 20th year. However, she said the company was confident it would see “a really strong return on our investment” as it tries to grab shoppers’ attention before the Black Friday discount period later this month. She said the company had wanted the ad “to be more joyful” this year because “things are tough for lots of families”. Despite concerns among British households about higher energy bills and housing costs, Hanley said spending on Christmas-related gear at John Lewis was already up on last year. The ad, set to a Sam Fender version of the Rolling Stones song You Can’t Always Get What You Want, features a range of John Lewis products in different price brackets, including the £12.99 Fisher-Price pull-along toy dog and a £255 Weekend Max Mara top and matching £290 skirt worn by Gloria. The three-minute ad will launch on social media on Tuesday morning, including Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and YouTube, before a 60-second version airs for the first time on TV in the ad breaks for ITV’s Coronation Street and Channel 4’s The Great British Bake Off on Tuesday evening. John Lewis will also erect a giant Christmas tree outside its store on London’s Oxford Street to mark the recent pedestrianisation of the road . The company said the numbers of visitors to its store on the street last week were up by more than a fifth on the same week last year. This year’s ad, created by the Saatchi & Saatchi agency, returns to a formula of using a cute character – such as Monty the penguin in 2014 and Buster the boxer in 2016 – after two years foregrounding other family relationships. However, it has the twist of focusing on the relationship between Pickles and a grandmother rather than centring on cute children. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Hanley said the ad was inspired by research which had revealed that 52% of grandparents give cash as presents because they are not sure what youngsters really want. “People want to give thoughtful gifts but can often lack confidence, so resort to giving cash,” she said. Now considered a national moment which invites social media comment and skits, the first big-budget John Lewis festive TV ad launched in 2007, soundtracked by a piece of music by Prokofiev. Previous John Lewis Christmas TV ads have been soundtracked by covers including the Smiths song Please, Please, Please, Let Me Get What I Want and Together in Electric Dreams by Giorgio Moroder and Philip Oakey. Last year’s ad included the 1990s club classic Where Love Lives by Alison Limerick. This year’s track, which features the choir from the John Spence community high school, which Fender previously attended, and the Easington Colliery Band, will be released on vinyl later this month, with proceeds going to Action For Children. Pickles the dog is based on an existing Fisher-Price pull-along toy called Little Snoopy that is celebrating its 60th year. The John Lewis ad launch comes hot on the heels of other festive ads for most of the big supermarkets that kicked off last weekend. Total ad spending across the festive period is set to reach £14bn, up 8.2% year-on-year according to the annual review by the Advertising Association and research group WARC. That growth is led by an 18.5% year-on-year surge in social media spend, while total TV spending is expected to be up by 1.6%.

events.title: AI-powered malware ‘highly likely’ to be used to hack UK infrastructure by 2028
events.summary: National Cyber Security Centre expects attacks on critical facilities such as power stations, airports and hospitals AI-powered malicious software is “highly likely” to be used in hacking attacks against the UK’s power stations, airports and hospitals by 2028, according to the state cybersecurity body. The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) said AI will probably enable a ransomware attack against critical national infrastructure [CNI] between now and 2028. The UK’s definition of CNI covers a range of facilities and services across sectors including energy, transport, defence, food, health and finance. The warning from the NCSC, part of the GCHQ spy agency, was published in the organisation’s annual review, which also warned that Russia and China will start using AI “routinely” in cyber-attacks. “It is … highly likely that between now and 2028, AI-powered malware will have been used in a ransomware attack on UK CNI,” said NCSC. Ransomware has become a cornerstone of the criminal hacker’s repertoire and is a signature ploy of gangs that typically operate out of former Soviet Union states. After gaining access to a victim’s IT systems, the attackers then encrypt files with bespoke malicious software – or malware – and then demand a payment in cryptocurrency to unlock the crippled systems and return any stolen data. UK ransomware victims include Royal Mail , outsourcing firm Capita and various public bodies, including councils . AI is set to enhance the ransomware threat by helping attackers with tasks such as scouting targets, locating weaknesses in IT networks and writing malicious code, said the NCSC. Last month, the government urged Britons to stock up to nine litres of bottled water and three days’ worth of food in order to ensure that households can survive a weather, cyber or other serious emergency. Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, said as the Be Ready campaign was launched that Britain needed to prepare for the threat of “state-sponsored terrorism” by Russia or other hostile powers targeting everyday infrastructure. NCSC’s chief executive, Richard Horne, will warn the public in a speech accompanying the review on Tuesday that AI is going to unleash a wave of cyber-attacks imminently. “In the coming months, we face a real prospect of an unprecedented rise in the number of cyber incidents,” he will say. Horne will attribute the threat to the technology’s ability to uncover weaknesses in IT systems that have been “tolerated for far too long”. An example of AI’s capacity to root out previously undetected vulnerabilities came last month, when the technology helped discover a critical weakness in PHP , a computer language used by almost 70% of the world’s websites . Alan Woodward, a professor of cybersecurity at Surrey University, said NCSC’s warning underlined the need for nation states and companies to access cutting-edge AI technology. Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters “AI can help people find these flaws and patch them, but if we don’t get the access the bad guys will beat them to it,” he said. So far, leading AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic have given some companies advanced access to their most powerful models in order to help them identify serious IT glitches. Horne will also say in his speech that communications networks used by the British military are subjected to daily attacks that are “persistent” and “sustained”. Horne will say Russia was one of the perpetrators, but the attacks have deliberately not crossed the line into warfare, with Moscow carrying out “notable campaigns” that “intentionally fall below the threshold of armed conflict as they escalate their attempts at hybrid warfare”. Horne will add that recent cyber-attacks on supermarket fridges in Europe , which have seen fridge temperatures raised by hackers to more than 50C, are a warning to companies and organisations to invest strongly in cyber resilience. “For decades we have collectively got away with tech on the cheap,” he will say.

"Discussions will focus on post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps toward peace," Witkoff said in a statement. Witkoff added that lower-level U.S. officials will meet this week in Brussels with representatives from France, Germany, the United Kingdom, the EU, and NATO to discuss security guarantees for Ukraine, Europe's post-war security architecture, and economic opportunities to support Ukraine's reconstruction. "We look forward to building on the progress made in Kyiv, Oslo, and St. Petersburg toward a comprehensive, durable peace agreement that delivers lasting security for generations to come," Witkoff said.

events.title: British Airways lost my father’s vital life-saving machine
events.summary: He needs a dialysis machine to survive, but on a flight it was first damaged, then it was lost My father suffers from terminal renal failure and relies on a highly specific dialysis machine every night to survive. British Airways’ check-in staff twice insisted on checking this fragile 20kg lifeline into the aircraft hold where it was first damaged, then lost. When his outbound flight arrived at Heathrow, it was returned broken resulting in a frantic search for a loan unit and hours spent in A&E so my father’s blood could be monitored. On the return flight to Rome, the machine could not be found. My parents waited until 2am before being told to go home without the equipment that keeps my father alive. He had to borrow another unit from a hospital. His was finally delivered three days later with the protective case unsealed and critical internal components disconnected. The sheer terror and stress of missing a treatment, not knowing if the A&E could accommodate him in time, and fearing that his health had already been severely compromised, was indescribable. British Airways has missed all deadlines to address our complaint and is now ignoring our correspondence. DL , London Your father did not need to use the fragile unit during the flight but was concerned, rightly as it turned out, it might suffer damage in the hold. BA, in common with most airlines, allows vital medical equipment to travel for free along with its owner, provided it does not exceed the dimensions of cabin baggage. It’s essential for safety reasons that belongings can be stowed under a seat or an overhead locker. Your father’s device was too large, and I believe it was reasonable for BA to check it into the hold if the flight was full. If, however, there were spare seats, it could have allowed it to travel on one. It has since told you a seat could have been bought. The real shocker is that such vital kit was mishandled not once, but twice. The impact on your father could have been grave had loan units not been found. BA’s response was, at best, cavalier. When you wrote to me, a month had passed since your initial complaint and you’d heard nothing besides auto-generated acknowledgments. The company got its act together when I questioned its attitude. An operative called you to apologise and it managed, at last, to reply to your emails. However, you are unimpressed by its offer of £300 in e-vouchers to, in its words, “put things right”. I’ve suggested it convert this into cash and consider a sum that better reflects the impact on your father. It told me it will be in touch to discuss a “gesture”. events.title: Final polls, models and markets see a "blue tsunami"
events.summary: The threat of a blue tsunami is bearing down on President Trump's Washington, with virtually every major indicator forecasting a Democratic rout in Tuesday's elections. Why it matters: Expectations for the midterms have soared so high that some Democrats fear disappointment is inevitable, particularly if the party falls short of winning the Senate — a prize that seemed beyond reach just months ago. By the numbers: Five key metrics help distill the extraordinary consensus taking shape on the eve of the midterms. 🔮 95% and 80%: The probability of Democrats winning the House and Senate, respectively, according to election forecaster Nate Silver , whose model projects an average gain of 25 House seats. Silver says Democrats could now withstand a modest polling error and still capture the Senate — a remarkable cushion given the GOP's history of outperforming polls in the Trump era. 🗺️ 7 for 7: Democrats lead in every Senate battleground state surveyed in the final New York Times/Siena polls , including by 11 points in Michigan and seven in Texas. Trump carried six of those seven states in 2024, though five of the Democratic leads — Maine (+6), Kansas (+5), Ohio (+5), Alaska (+2) and Iowa (+1) — remain within the polls' margins of error. 🏛️ 240: The number of House seats Democrats could win under the upper end of Cook Political Report's forecast — potentially their largest majority since the first year of Barack Obama's presidency. Reaching that mark would require Democrats to sweep all 18 toss-up races. Cook already favors them in 222 districts, four more than needed for a majority. 🎲 73%: The probability of Democrats winning both chambers of Congress, according to Kalshi . After correctly favoring Trump in 2024, prediction markets have become a closely watched barometer of political expectations. Nearly $100 million in contracts have traded on Kalshi's congressional control market alone. 📊 +14: Democrats' lead on the generic congressional ballot in the final poll from AtlasIntel , which became the nation's highest-rated pollster after its remarkably accurate 2024 performance. Reality check: Even the pollsters forecasting a Democratic landslide are haunted by the possibility that they're still missing Trump voters. New York Times polling chief Nate Cohn warned that white Democrats were roughly 30% more likely than white Republicans to respond to the final Times/Siena surveys — a slightly wider gap than in 2020, when polls overstated Democratic support. Washington Post pollsters raised similar alarms after finding Democrat Adam Hamilton leading Republican Sen. Roger Marshall by nine points in Kansas, where registered Democrats were more than twice as likely as Republicans to participate. What they're saying: Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson have accused pollsters of deliberately manufacturing the appearance of a Democratic wave to suppress Republican turnout. "They're trying to create this idea of a blue wave and they're using the poll numbers to do it," Johnson said Monday , claiming conservatives distrust polling calls because they believe "it's a psyop." Between the lines: Prediction markets are sometimes touted as more accurate than polls because bettors have money at stake. But their odds often reflect the same polling data and political sentiment, leaving them vulnerable to the same blind spots. In Wisconsin, Kalshi gave state Rep. Francesca Hong a 96% chance of winning the Democratic gubernatorial primary the day before the August election. She lost to Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley. In Brazil, Kalshi gave Trump ally Flávio Bolsonaro an 84% chance of defeating President Lula ahead of last week's runoff. Lula won, prompting MAGA influencers to amplify baseless claims that the election was rigged. The bottom line: Voters will ultimately deliver the only verdict that counts. But on the eve of the election, the polls, forecasts and betting markets are all pointing in one direction.

events.title: Jim Cramer says these six fashion stocks are buys beyond the AI trade
events.summary: CNBC’s Jim Cramer highlighted six fashion stocks he likes as investors look beyond the struggling AI trade. His picks include Ralph Lauren, Tapestry, Levi Strauss, VF Corp, Kontoor Brands and Reformation. CNBC's Jim Cramer highlighted six fashion and apparel stocks on Monday for investors looking for alternatives to the struggling AI trade. While technology stocks have come under pressure in recent weeks, consumer stocks have been resilient. The SPDR S&P Retail ETF (XRT) gained 10% this quarter, while the Technology Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLK) fell 11%. Cramer said falling interest rates could provide an additional boost to apparel companies heading into the holiday shopping season. "Ralph Lauren, Tapestry, Levi's, VF Corp, Kontoor Brands and Reformation are some of the fashion stocks that we think look best right now," the " Mad Money " host said. Ralph Lauren remains Cramer's favorite apparel stock, thanks to its consistent growth under CEO Patrice Louvet. The company has continued gaining momentum across women's apparel, accessories and outerwear, and has been strengthening its international presence, particularly in Asia. Although the stock pulled back in August and September, it has since recovered, and Cramer is optimistic ahead of Thursday morning's earnings report. Tapestry , the parent of Coach and Kate Spade, also reports Thursday. Cramer likes Coach's position in the accessible luxury market, particularly its popularity among younger female consumers. However, shares have fallen 20% since the company's August earnings report, when guidance failed to impress investors following a massive multiyear rally. "I hope this Thursday's report can represent the start of a comeback for Tapestry," he said. Levi Strauss is another potential turnaround story. Shares fell below $20 following disappointing earnings a few weeks ago, but CEO Michelle Gass told Cramer that the company had moved quickly to address inventory shortages in popular styles. The stock has since rebounded more than 20% from its post-earnings low, though Cramer still considers it inexpensive at roughly 14 times earnings, with a 2.8% dividend yield. "I think this is a good option to play the broader strength in denim that we keep hearing about," he said. VF Corp , which owns The North Face, Vans and Timberland, is showing signs of improvement after years of struggles, particularly at Vans. Cramer pointed to encouraging results from a recent Piper Sandler teen survey and a strong quarterly report as evidence that the sneaker brand's turnaround may be gaining traction. Shares have risen roughly 14% since he recommended the stock about two weeks ago . Kontoor Brands offers another opportunity tied to denim and corporate restructuring. The company plans to sell its Lee brand for up to $1 billion, allowing it to focus on Wrangler and outdoor apparel maker Helly Hansen. Cramer expects the sale to be followed by substantial share repurchases and said the remaining businesses have room to grow. Shares trade at roughly 14 times earnings and offer a dividend yield near 3%. Cramer's more speculative pick is Reformation . The women's fashion brand initially struggled after its IPO in late July, but Cramer said it "has great growth, it's profitable, and it has a differentiated shopping experience with a technology kicker." Cramer highlighted the stock in late September; shares surged more than 31% in October. events.title: Grab Holdings boosts 2026 forecasts on strong delivery, ride-hailing demand
events.summary: Grab is South-east Asia’s biggest ride-hailing and delivery company. Grab raised 2026 revenue to US$4.15 billion-US$4.20 billion and EBITDA to US$790 million-US$800 million after strong ride-hailing and delivery demand. Its financial services unit posted its first core profit in Q3, as more drivers and merchants used loans, insurance and other products. Q3 revenue rose 27% to US$1.11 billion and monthly transacting users hit a record 57 million, even with high fuel costs and wider economic pressure. Grab Holdings raised its full-year revenue and profit forecasts after quarterly earnings beat estimates, signalling confidence that rising ride-hailing and food-delivery demand across South-east Asia will offset regulatory hurdles. Sales will rise to US$4.15 billion (S$5.31 billion) to US$4.2 billion in 2026 , while adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation will be as much as US$800 million, the company said on Nov 3. In August, it had forecast sales of as much as US$4.15 billion and earnings on that basis of up to US$740 million. The stock rose about 2% in after-hours trading. Grab added about 3 million monthly users in the quarter through September for a total of 57 million, suggesting that it is succeeding in fending off intense competition from the likes of Indonesia’s GoTo Group. Demand for ride hailing and food delivery is rising in South-east Asia as more people go online. Meanwhile, higher fuel prices are raising ride and delivery costs across the region of about 700 million people. Platform companies are offering incentives to drivers and customers to soften the blow, but that risks squeezing already thin margins. Regulators are also piling on pressure. Indonesia, one of Grab’s biggest markets, has already cut the maximum commission companies can charge on scooter rides, and is considering further rules in areas like food delivery by the end of 2026 . Competition remains intense, with rivals such as GoTo and new entrants like Green & Smart Mobility vying against Grab in populous markets like Indonesia and Vietnam. Uber Technologies, one of Grab’s backers, could also be a looming threat – its planned acquisition of Delivery Hero opens up a path for Uber Eats to re-enter South-east Asia. Alphabet’s Waymo also plans to launch robotaxis in Singapore in 2028 . The company, meanwhile, is striking deals to spur growth beyond its core business. In September, it agreed to acquire a majority stake in buy-now-pay-later platform Atome Financial for US$1.49 billion, after buying US-based Stash Financial for an enterprise value of US$425 million. But not every deal has gone to plan. In October , Taiwan’s Fair Trade Commission blocked Grab’s roughly US$600 million purchase of Foodpanda’s local delivery operations on antitrust concerns. In the latest quarter, adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda) rose 74% to US$237 million, the Singapore-based company said. Analysts projected US$194.2 million on average, according to Bloomberg-compiled data. Revenue grew 27% to US$1.1 billion, roughly in line with estimates. To add users, Grab has expanded its product offering to include more affordable and premium options. It is also expanding into games and microdramas, partnering with other platforms to keep users on its app for longer. Bloomberg Intelligence analysts Jason Low and Nathan Naidu said that despite its failed acquisition of Foodpanda Taiwan, Grab is positioned to maintain its 2028 adjusted Ebitda guidance, given the roughly US$60 million the business would have contributed is small relative to its US$1.7 billion target. More details on Grab’s acquisition of Singapore-based buy-now-pay-later and digital lending platform Atome Financial could be disclosed at the earnings announcement. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Apple sales meet estimates, though China is a weak spot
events.summary: Revenue from the iPhone grew 17% to US$57.6 billion during the quarter, topping an average estimate of US$56.5 billion (S$72.3 billion). Apple’s September quarter revenue rose 12% to US$114.5 billion, just above estimates, but sales growth slowed and China was a weak spot. iPhone and Mac sales beat forecasts, while services matched estimates; iPad and wearables were weaker, with wearables down 7.9%. New CEO John Ternus faces holiday-quarter questions on the foldable iPhone Duo, supply, and how new products will lift future sales. Apple posted September quarter revenue that narrowly topped analysts’ estimates, even as sales in the key Chinese market fell short of projections. Revenue rose 12% to US$114.5 billion during the fiscal fourth quarter, which ended Sept 26, the company said in a statement on Nov 3. Analysts had estimated US$113.5 billion on average, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. The quarterly report – the first under new chief executive John Ternus – offered a mixed picture to investors. Sales growth decelerated from a 16% clip in the June quarter, and results from Apple’s iPad and wearables businesses were particularly weak. But the iPhone, the company’s biggest moneymaker, remained strong. Apple shares climbed less than 1% in late trading after the report was released. They had gained 24% in 2026 through the close. Ternus became CEO on Sept 1, putting him in charge for the final month of Apple’s fourth quarter. He has since overseen the unveiling of the foldable iPhone Duo , touch-screen MacBook Pro and HomeView hub , though none of those products went on sale until the current quarter, which runs through December. Apple typically provides revenue guidance for the current period during its earnings call. Wall Street will be closely watching for signs of how much the foldable iPhone could contribute to holiday-quarter sales, as well as commentary on when Apple expects supply of the device to catch up with demand. Apple itself had projected fourth-quarter revenue growth of 9% to 11%. Though sales from greater China increased 21% to US$17.5 billion, that was more than US$1 billion short of estimates. Revenue from the iPhone grew 17% to US$57.6 billion during the quarter, topping an average estimate of US$56.5 billion. That shows the company is weathering a schedule change in its product releases. Apple typically launches multiple new iPhones in September, but this time released only the iPhone 18 Pro line . A regular iPhone 18 and new iPhone Air are not arriving until the first half of 2027, while the foldable iPhone Duo did not launch until Oct 23 – deep into the quarter. Services, a segment that includes music streaming, the App Store, iCloud subscriptions, Apple TV and other digital offerings, rose 9.8% to US$31.6 billion. That matched estimates. Earnings came in at US$2.10 a share, topping an estimate of US$2. Mac revenue climbed 24% to US$10.8 billion, smashing the average projection of US$9.7 billion. And a wave of new products should help keep momentum going. The company’s touch-screen MacBook Pro, refreshed iMac and new low-end MacBook Pro ship on Nov 6. Apple is planning to keep updating the Mac in the coming months. That includes a new MacBook Neo and MacBook Air early next year, Bloomberg News has reported. The iPad brought in US$6.23 billion, missing an estimate of US$6.9 billion. A new iPad mini is launching in the current quarter, while a new iPad Air, low-end tablet and iPad Pro refresh are coming in 2027. The wearables, home and accessories category brought in US$8.3 billion, declining 7.9% from a year earlier. That missed a prediction of US$9 billion. The company launched the AirPods 5 earbuds and two smartwatches in the fourth quarter, but all the updates were relatively minor. BLOOMBERG

It just doesn't want the people who built it 20 hours ago Google's AI satellite sends a very expensive haiku to Earth 2 days ago Amazon sends chills through its workforce with mixed message memo about AI use 2 days ago Anthropic has published a regulatory filing revealing nearly $900 billion in compute and infrastructure commitments, with additional estimated payments potentially pushing the total beyond $1 trillion. The Monday filing reports that Anthropic expects to pay nearly $70 billion in contractual obligations by September 2027, with a total of roughly $447.5 billion in commitments expected to be incurred by the end of 2030. That's assuming of course its revenues continue their upward trajectory, which the prospectus warns is far from guaranteed. "In the nine months ended September 30, 2026, our revenue was $33.2 billion, representing a year-over-year growth rate of 1,206%," the prospectus reads. "We do not expect our revenue will continue to grow at comparable rates, and we cannot assure you that it will continue to grow at all." "Our ability to meet the substantial and growing financial obligations of these requirements to secure compute depends on our ability to generate significant revenue growth," the filing reads. Which is to say, if Anthropic's revenues don't grow faster than its compute commitments, it could end up falling into a nasty spiral. And while Anthropic has several options, including debt and equity financing, relying on these long term could dilute existing shareholders or force the company to borrow on unfavorable terms. Every IPO filing reads a bit like this because no company can guarantee eternal success and growth. A lot of this filing's language, as damning as it might sound, is therefore just Anthropic covering its butt. However, even though the company is still growing steadily year-over-year, the latest filing shows revenue growth is already slowing. Between Q1 and Q2 of this year, revenues grew nearly 2.5x. Yet in Q3, Anthropic's reported revenues of nearly $17 billion represented an increase of just 46 percent from Q2. In the same period, Anthropic's compute and infrastructure costs grew 77 percent and it kept signing deals that commit it to more expenditure. Last week, we reported that Anthropic's purchase commitments exceeded $800 billion over the next decade or so. Anthropic now says its commitments are closer to $895 billion. Roughly $320 billion of those commitments relate to existing contractual obligations. Another $451 billion covers leases Anthropic has signed, but that have yet to commence, with the company expecting them to begin between 2026 and 2028, although some remain subject to termination rights or other conditions. Overall, however, Anthropic's compute spend is on track to increase substantially over the next few years. And that's not even counting the blank checks Anthropic has written to secure adequate compute, which it values at $150-$175 billion, putting Anthropic's total compute tab at somewhere north of $1 trillion. Anthropic can't walk away from some of this spending because its deals with Microsoft, Google, Amazon, and Broadcom, which now total $437 billion, are non-cancellable. Some require payment regardless of whether Anthropic lights up a single GPU. The AI upstart estimates that of its $895 billion in contracts, only about $213 billion worth allow it to avoid payments. The revised S1 filing also offered insights into the company's customer base, including a major reliance on cloud service providers for distribution.

events.title: Trajectory raises $45M to make AI model training accessible to nontechnical experts
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Whether developed by OpenAI or Anthropic or built on open source alternatives, current AI models share a critical limitation: They don’t learn from their mistakes without further training. Businesses adapting these models for specialized fields, such as law and finance, typically get around this by fine-tuning general models. However, that often requires hiring internal research teams or relying on expensive consultants, commonly known as forward-deployed engineers (FDEs). Trajectory , a startup founded about a year ago by three Stanford classmates with experience at Google DeepMind and Apple, wants to automate that process, allowing AI models to learn from feedback and continuously improve at specialized tasks. The 18-person company just announced that it raised $45 million in a Series A round at a $300 million valuation, led by Sequoia, with participation from Nvidia, Bessemer Venture Partners, and Bain Capital Ventures. Trajectory co-founder Ronak Malde compared foundational models to a very smart PhD student who’s always starting a new job. “But what the economy values is someone who worked on the job for 30 years,” he told TechCrunch. The startup aims to solve this problem through an approach known as continual learning. Businesses using Trajectory can start with an open source AI model and connect the platform to their applications, allowing it to collect feedback on how the model performs. Trajectory then uses that information to retrain the model, helping it improve at specialized tasks over time. With Trajectory, lawyers, doctors, and other specialists can improve the models near automatically themselves, Malde said. That capability could make deploying specialized AI faster and cheaper. Companies like Harvey and Rogo are already using Trajectory’s platform to post-train open source models, helping them perform more like experienced lawyers or financial analysts by learning from previous tasks, such as reviewing a particular type of legal contract or valuing a company using a specific methodology. Trajectory’s other customers include Decagon, Mercor, and Nvidia. The startup is now making its post-training platform publicly available. The people using Trajectory decide “what good looks like for their organization and can turn that into improvements for their model,” Malde said. Trajectory’s approach to continual learning shares some similarities with recursive self-improvement (RSI), the idea that AI systems can improve their own capabilities. But co-founder Michael Elabd argues that keeping humans involved in the training process makes Trajectory’s approach safer, since autonomous self-improvement could lead to unintended or even dangerous outcomes. Trajectory isn’t the only startup trying to automate post-training. Other companies going after this market include Thinking Machines Lab, founded by former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati and the company behind the fine-tuning platform Tinker, Applied Compute, which was valued at $3.25 billion last month, and Prime Intellect , a platform that helps companies build and train their own AI agents. Malde believes the startup’s biggest advantage is its team . He was among the handful of researchers Google DeepMind acqui-hired from Windsurf. Elabd also worked at DeepMind, while Trajectory’s third co-founder, Arjun Karanam, previously worked on generative foundation models at Apple. The startup has also recruited researchers and product designers from OpenAI, Stripe, and Netflix. Why does design matter so much to a company focused on AI training? Karanam says the startup has developed an interface that makes post-training more accessible to its nontechnical customers. events.title: Stock market after midterm elections: What S&P 500 history shows
events.summary: The S&P 500 averaged a 13.7% one-year gain after 11 midterm elections since 1980. After divided-government outcomes, the index averaged a 15% one-year gain, compared to 11.5% under single-party control. Fed policy, earnings and the AI trade may matter more than the election result. Markets are sweating it out ahead of the midterm elections, but the event historically heralds strong performance for stocks — regardless of whether it's a red or blue wave, split decision, or status quo in Washington. The S&P 500 tends to perform well after both midterm and presidential elections. According to a CNBC analysis of S&P 500 returns after elections from 1980 through 2024, the index rose an average of 0.2% after one day and one week, and 1.1% after one month across both presidential and midterm elections. A year later, the index gained an average of 13.7% after midterms and 13.8% after presidential elections. Returns were positive in 91% of cases. And the S&P 500 was up after all 11 midterms from 1982 through 2022. Short-term returns were less reliable, particularly after presidential contests, which produced slightly negative average returns after one day and one week. "There's some anxiousness before these elections," Ryan Detrick, CNBC contributor and chief market strategist at Carson Group, told CNBC. "Once you are through it, it's a big relief and markets tend to do pretty well." Still, the market usually prefers divided government: one party in charge of the White House and the other holding at least one house of Congress. Across 10 midterm and five presidential elections that left no single party in charge, the S&P 500 rose an average 15% after one year. One-year returns were positive in 14 out of 15 cases. By comparison, the index gained an average of 11.5% over the year after elections that resulted in single-party control. "If you have a huge red wave or a big blue wave, markets actually kind of don't like that as much because you have too much spending one way and too much power," Detrick said. Leaving Democrats in control of Congress with a Republican in the White House — a scenario that may emerge from the elections on Tuesday — was also positive. A CNBC analysis found that after the three midterms (1986, 1990 and 2006) when Democrats controlled both houses and a Republican held the presidency, the S&P 500 averaged a 0.5% decline on the reaction day but was up 3.4% a month later and 10.9% after a year. Granted, elections may be coincident events to factors that matter far more for market performance. The S&P 500 plunged 22.1% in the year after the 2000 elections due to the dotcom bust, marking the worst post-election performance since 1980. Conversely, the S&P 500's best post-election year was a 38.3% gain after the 2020 elections, when markets mounted a massive comeback from the COVID-induced selloff. Investors should bear in mind that Federal Reserve policy and the corporate earnings cycle ultimately matter more than elections, according to Société Générale. Stocks declined in the aftermath of the 2018 midterms, for instance, when Democrats wrested control of the House during President Donald Trump's first term. More importantly, the Fed tightened monetary policy that year, raising interest rates four times, and the S&P 500 ended the year down 6.2%, though the market was up 11.7% a year after the election. The big swing factor now is AI and whether declines in tech will continue. As long as the AI wave is still moving and the economy keeps growing, "this bull market is probably still alive and well," Detrick says. But a Democratic sweep of the House and Senate would almost certainly pressure the AI infrastructure buildout and could lead to more retrenchment. The bond market is also skittish with yields rising globally and a mini debt crisis in France. And the war with Iran could get worse post-election if President Trump follows through on threats of more strikes or Iran escalates. "Seasonality isn't destiny, and worries around Iran, AI and France won't mysteriously vanish," said Jim Reid, Deutsche Bank's global head of macro and thematic research, in a note. If history is any guide, we could see a Santa rally and S&P 500 gains after the midterms. But this is still an AI-driven market, with geopolitics, the Fed, and bond market very much in charge. — CNBC's Chris Hayes contributed reporting.

events.title: SCOTUS rejects Trump's bid over disputed California ballots
events.summary: The Supreme Court denied the Trump administration's request Monday to hear its case regarding more than 20,000 California ballots that President Trump claims were cast by noncitizens . Why it matters: It's a blow to the administration, which has been tussling with the state in what it says is a fight to ensure all eligible voters can vote and have their ballots counted, as the law requires. What they're saying: " The application for injunction pending appeal presented to Justice Kagan and by her referred to the Court is denied, " an unsigned order from the court read . Catch up quick: The Trump administration sued California in mid-October, arguing that it had identified more than 20,000 noncitizens on the state's voter rolls. Judges have consistently rejected the administration's argument, finding that its lists contain factual errors and risk disenfranchising eligible voters. One judge even noted that when the administration claimed it had specifically verified more than 100 people as noncitizens in Nevada, the state proved they were, in fact, citizens. Zoom out: The court has often sided with Trump, but has notably broken with him on cases involving voting access. The president has no constitutional authority over elections. That power largely rests with the states and Congress. The White House and the Department of Justice did not respond to Axios' request for comment. Apple’s stockpiling of inventory, particularly computer memory, continued in its fiscal fourth quarter, according to earnings reported Monday. The company reported that its inventory increased significantly in the quarter, growing from $11.09 billion in Q3 to $14.54 billion in Q4, a jump of 31.1%. Year-over-year, inventory grew 154.3% from $5.72 billion in the fourth quarter of 2025. Apple’s forecast of a 45% to 46% gross margin in the December quarter was largely attributed to the impact of higher memory costs. The company reported a gross margin of 47.9% for the September quarter. “What we’re seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented,” said Apple CEO John Ternus, speaking to analysts on the call. “As we said earlier in the September quarter, we did see higher memory costs as compared to the June quarter, which were partly offset by the benefit of carrying inventory and lower costs on certain non-memory components.” He said that the company expected “even higher memory costs” in the December quarter, which would be partially offset by price increases implemented earlier this year on some devices, including Mac and iPad at the end of June and iPhones in September. Ternus also said that beyond December, Apple expects memory costs “continuing to increase.” “As we said before, we do believe we’ll see a decreasing benefit from the carry-in inventory on memory over time,” he noted, adding that the company was increasing its purchases of this key component. “As we work to improve supply, our manufacturing purchase obligations have increased by 33 billion dollars from June to the September quarter, which you’ll see in our annual filing when it comes out tomorrow.” Apple also brought COO Sabih Khan, who oversees the company’s supply chain and manufacturing, onto the call to address questions about memory. He reiterated the increased purchase obligations but did not rule out future price increases on Apple devices. The company also blamed supply constraints for weak iPad sales in the quarter. The iPad was one of the only product segments that didn’t grow, even as iPhone and Mac sales beat estimates. iPad revenue was $6.2 billion, below analysts’ expectations of $6.7 billion. events.title: CNBC's The China Connection newsletter: Nvidia's humanoid push relies on China-made robot hands
events.summary: Nvidia's latest humanoid robot reference platform uses hands from Chinese startup Wuji A similar humanoid platform earlier this year used hands from China-linked startup Sharpa. The news comes as Xiaomi recently revealed progress on its own humanoid hand. Hi, this is Evelyn, writing to you from Beijing. Welcome to the latest edition of The China Connection — a snapshot of what I'm seeing and hearing from local businesses. Chinese robot companies still underpin many U.S. tech endeavors, especially when it comes to the pain point of robotic hands. Who is one of the latest on Nvidia's radar? In just a few months, Nvidia has showcased two humanoid robot training packages: one with mechanical hands from Sharpa , and another with hands from Wuji . Both have ties to founders in Shanghai. Pan Yunzhe founded Wuji in 2019, eventually moving much of the team to Shenzhen and drawing backers such as Ant Group, HSG and Future Capital, according to PitchBook. A demo video last week claimed a Wuji Hand 2 could autonomously spin a pen, despite interference . The Wuji Hand 2 made it onto a slide Oct. 21 behind Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang as he told a crowd in Berlin about a new humanoid hardware system for training the robots on Nvidia software. The robot body comes from Agile Robots, which has offices in Germany, China and the U.S. "It will be the flywheel by which we can accelerate development of robotics," Huang said of the hardware system, called Agile One SN. Agile Robots announced the system, which uses Nvidia's Isaac robotics software and Jetson Thor computing platform. Research institutions, such as Stanford and ETH Zurich, can likely start using the Agile One SN system in early 2027, according to Nvidia . Stanford and ETH Zurich were also among the institutions Nvidia named in connection with its first reference humanoid design, announced May 31. That system uses a body from Chinese humanoid company Unitree and mechanical hands from Sharpa. It was scheduled for delivery from late 2026. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on whether deliveries had begun, or whether the researchers would try both reference robots, or just one. Sharpa, headquartered in Singapore, was co-founded by David Li, CEO of Shanghai-based lidar company Hesai . Sharpa has said its manufacturing R&D is in Shanghai . While these are just two of the many robotic hand makers in China — and globally — they've grown so much in prominence that Google DeepMind research lead Keerthana Gopalakrishnan directly compared the two startups in a podcast last month . Sharpa Wave is a bit stronger than Wuji, which is closer in size to a typical human hand but has the strength of a ten-year-old, she said. It was not clear whether she was testing the Wuji Hand 2 or an earlier version. In September, humanoid startup JoyIn's Zhu Mingxuan told me she found Wuji's mechanical hands very light and very good at completing tasks, but prone to heating up while doing so. She said Sharpa's performed better, but were far more expensive. Hardware is limiting humanoid development, and hands are the main challenge, she said. Zhu said she left U.S. humanoid company Figure last year, where she had also worked on models to help humanoid robots mimic human actions. As China pushes its humanoid industry to develop more core technologies , mechanical hands are one way companies can try to stand out in the robot race. Consumer electronics company Xiaomi said last week that, by testing its robotic hand in its car factory, it found that most of the tasks it tested required only a specific range of movement. And in another sign of just how far along the tech may have come in China, Meta has worked with Chinese startup Fourier for a humanoid prototype, The Information reported Oct. 31, citing sources. Neither company immediately responded to a request for comment. events.title: How Trump’s trade policy is handing Asia to Beijing
events.summary: For a decade, Washington urged the world’s manufacturers to move their factories out of China and into friendly Southeast Asian states—only to attack the very countries and companies that answered the call. Usually, U.S. economic statecraft is designed to help American companies succeed abroad. President Donald Trump’s punitive trade program is having the reverse effect. Broad-based import taxes have jolted manufacturers across ASEAN (the Association of Southeast Asian Nations), including American ones. Rather than checking China, trade policy is alienating regional partners, harming supply-chain diversification, and eroding America’s influence over the bloc’s trade decisions. The U.S. is engaged in what Evan Feigenbaum, a veteran diplomat and former Republican, terms a “ reverse pivot .” Bogged down in foreign crises elsewhere, Washington now projects hesitation and retreat in Asia rather than dynamic leadership. In the months after President Trump’s April 2025 announcement of “Liberation Day” tariffs, some of ASEAN’s non-tariff barriers fell. A few countries used the exogenous threat to bring about needed reforms.  Deals were done, including Boeing sales and–at least prospective– LNG contracts . It appeared that coercion worked, at least in the short term. In February the Supreme Court struck down much of the initial tariff regime and the administration pivoted to workarounds: 150-day emergency measures under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, and expansive Section 301 investigations into forced labor, intellectual property violations, and “excess capacity.”  America’s labor, intellectual property, and excess-capacity concerns are really about China, not Southeast Asia. The administration substituted an improvised China policy for a coherent Southeast Asia policy—a strategic blunder. By treating regional partners as collateral damage to show that China isn’t singled out, Washington is undercutting its most reliable partners and allies.  Nowhere is the absurdity of this approach more evident than in the supply chains themselves. For nearly a decade, multinational corporations have redirected capital and manufacturing from China into Vietnam, Malaysia, India, and the Philippines. The goal of these “ China plus one ” strategies was to insulate critical industries from geopolitical risk and move them into friendly states.  Washington’s tariff regime now undercuts this strategy. Southeast Asian export hubs suffer far more than the United States when Chinese firms attempt illicit transshipment, while subsidized Chinese overcapacity squeezes local producers. The broader reality, though, is not widespread evasion but deep and legitimate supply-chain integration. By imposing blanket punitive duties, Washington is tightening the vise on the very partners helping achieve that diversification.  As Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation, has observed , Washington created the incentive structure for alternate supply routes and is now penalizing regional partners for using them.  These tariffs aren’t even achieving Trump’s stated goals. Higher costs and a shortage of skilled domestic labor mean production lines won’t magically shift to U.S. shores. Bilateral trade deficits with Southeast Asian economies remain largely unchanged; regional exporters, U.S. importers, and consumers are simply absorbing higher costs.  ASEAN nations have long been masters of dynamic hedging—exemplified by Vietnam’s “ bamboo diplomacy ”—balancing China against the United States. None of them want to be dominated by Beijing, making Washington their natural partner. Yet as U.S. policy grows increasingly erratic and punitive, it inadvertently pushes them to hedge elsewhere.  As Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney warned at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January , the weaponization of economic tools forces middle powers to organize: “If we are not at the table, we are on the menu.”  Coercive tactics failed with Canada, and they will fail in Asia. Recently, politically appointed U.S. ambassador to Singapore Anjani Sinha told local and international business leaders that he received orders from the President to “bring home the money,” so they needed to double their U.S. investments.  The demand went over like a lead balloon. Capital flows are not surging into the United States; they are pivoting further into Asia . This friction runs counter to decades of bipartisan precedent. Since the 1985 Plaza Accord , which catalyzed an era of industrial integration in Southeast Asia, American leaders have recognized that regional partners thrive under predictable, rules-based frameworks rather than blunt coercion. Today’s transactional posture risks creating a durable trust deficit that will penalize American enterprise for a generation.  Since America pulled out of the Trans-Pacific Partnership in favor of country-by-country negotiations, its absence at the table has been filled by others. ASEAN is now building institutional networks that bypass Washington altogether. Member states are working with accords like the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) and the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP).  American companies have not forgotten the benefits of clear rules of the road in a multilateral context. They have worked closely with ASEAN negotiators toward the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement ( DEFA ). Spanning 11 nations, nearly 700 million consumers, and an estimated $2 trillion digital marketplace, DEFA would establish comprehensive standards for cross-border data governance, cybersecurity, digital identity, and artificial intelligence.   As Washington retreats behind tariffs and procedural disputes, Southeast Asia—with input from U.S. companies—is writing the regulatory architecture of the 21st-century digital economy.  Washington builds walls while ASEAN builds architecture.  Southeast Asia does not wish to decouple from the United States. Four ASEAN nations—Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia, and Singapore—rank among America’s top 20 bilateral trading partners . Private enterprise, investment flows, and educational links remain extraordinarily resilient.  But in statecraft, trust is the ultimate currency. U.S. influence in the Indo-Pacific was never sustained through sheer market size or coercive leverage alone; it thrived because Washington offered an institutional vision grounded in mutual benefit and reliable rules. If Washington continues to treat its Asian partners as transactional pawns in a zero-sum struggle with Beijing, it will discover they have other trading partners. America risks economic isolation and strategic diminishment in the century of the Pacific Rim. events.title: Max-severity bug in widely used OT programming tool exploited to deliver Linux malware
events.summary: Unknown criminals are exploiting a maximum-severity vulnerability in Node-RED, a flow-based programming tool that is widely used in critical infrastructure, to deploy a flow that downloads and runs a Linux bot. Node-RED is commonly used for workflow automation in industrial control systems (ICS) and operational technology (OT) environments. It’s built on top of Node.js and is used in commercial products including Siemens SIMATIC IoT2050 . In August, Siemens assigned the vulnerability identifier – CVE-2026-58115 – to describe the bug and explain its perfect 10-out-of-10 CVSS rating. Affected Siemens devices do not enforce authentication on the Node-RED HTTP interface, allowing unauthenticated access to programming nodes that can execute system commands on the device. This means unauthenticated remote attackers can create malicious flows, which is what VulnCheck researchers began documenting last Friday. “On October 30, 2026, one of our canaries caught an attacker exploiting CVE-2026-58115,” VulnCheck researcher Patrick Garrity warned in a Monday advisory, adding that two Node-RED built-in nodes make this vulnerability “trivial to weaponize.” One is an inject node, which fires a message either on a schedule or once at startup. The second, an exec node, can run shell commands. “Wire one to the other and the flow executes a command as soon as it is deployed, with no further interaction,” Garrity said. Plus, these exploits come as criminals increasingly look to target internet-exposed OT and ICS devices , allowing their cyberattacks to impact the physical world and produce real-life harm. Case in point: the ongoing refrigeration controller hacks across Europe and the attacks on wa ter systems across at least 12 US states over the summer. The activity observed by VulnCheck came from a single IP address, 4.201.105[.]116, which sits in Microsoft’s AS8075 network and geolocates to Brazil. “It didn't just scan us. It sent the complete exploit, flow and dropper, in a single POST /flows,” Garrity wrote. While there’s a lot that the researchers don’t yet know about the attacks - they didn’t retrieve a binary or staged scripts to analyze - the filename, bot-linux-amd64, indicates that the malware targets Linux running on AMD64 processors. It also suggests the malware operator may have other builds. “We did not fetch the binary, so we can't say what it does once running,” Garrity noted. Between October 30 and November 1, the researchers saw this IP address target the same Node-RED vulnerability 16 times, and log 125 hits against eight different CVEs across their wider canary network. Among the targets of the attack were a seven-year-old Apache Solr flaw tracked as CVE-2019-17558 – affecting Camunda, Gitea, MLflow, Traefik, and Joomla, alongside Node-RED. All this suggests “opportunistic mass scanning rather than a targeted attack,” according to the researcher. One of these hits delivered a different payload pointing to a separate server (85.215.73[.]250), which VulnCheck now tracks - but doesn’t have any telemetry other than the URL. “Because the download host is a different machine from the one that sent the exploit, the likely setup is a scan-and-infect arrangement: the hosts that find and exploit vulnerable instances pull the implant from a separate, dedicated server,” Garrity wrote. The mix of old and new bugs across unrelated products indicates “opportunistic mass scanning rather than a targeted attack,” Garrity wrote. “If you run Node-RED anywhere, including inside OT environments, check today whether it’s reachable from outside your network, apply updates where available and implement detections to reduce the risk of exploitation,” he added in a LinkedIn post. While the bug has been added to VulnCheck’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, it hasn’t appeared (as of press time) in the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s KEV.®

The company has seen a boost from heightened demand for artificial intelligence tools. Palantir beat Wall Street's third-quarter estimates after the bell on Monday, with U.S. commercial revenue topping government for the first time as businesses adopt more of the company's artificial intelligence tools. Here's how the company did compared to LSEG estimates: Earnings per share : 44 cents adjusted vs. 41 cents expected Revenue : $2.31 billion vs. $2.18 billion expected Revenue nearly doubled from a year ago and blew past $2 billion for the first time ever, Palantir said. Net income more than doubled to $1.13 billion, or 44 cents per share, from about $476 million, or 18 cents per share. "I don't believe anyone's had consistent results like this in the history of software AI, ever," CEO Alex Karp told CNBC's Seema Mody in an interview, adding that the business is succeeding without salespeople. Palantir has long been known for its strength in the government sector, but its commercial segment caught up in Q3. U.S. commercial revenue jumped 148% to $984 million, surpassing U.S. government revenue of $953 million, which was up 96%. The company's U.S. commercial revenue has more than quintupled over the last two years. Palantir lifted its guidance, saying it now expects U.S. commercial revenue "in excess of" $3.56 billion for the full year. Last quarter, the company boosted its forecast to $3.42 billion. The company projects about $2.65 billion in revenue for the fourth quarter and about $8.53 billion for full-year 2026. Karp has openly supported the use of open-weight models and criticized leading AI labs, which he told CNBC earlier this year are forcing businesses to sell their data sovereignty. Karp, on Monday, also reiterated recent calls to nationalize AI labs, calling it the "only realistic way" to manage liability. In September, Karp joined major tech CEOs at the White House as calls for regulation mounted following claims from AI researchers that the technology has a more than 10% of killing humanity . "My message to everybody is: Beware of thinking you can delay the future in AI," he told CNBC. "The future is here. The political ramifications of it are here." events.title: Another judge blocks DOJ ballot demands in California
events.summary: A federal judge on the eve of Election Day barred the Trump administration from demanding California officials set aside ballots from registered voters it suspects are noncitizens, finding the effort likely violates the Constitution. Why it matters: Courts had already rejected the Justice Department's attempts to force California to separate the ballots. Monday's ruling goes a step further, directly barring federal officials from making those demands even as DOJ turns to the Supreme Court to compel the state to comply. Driving the news: Chief U.S. District Judge James Boasberg ruled Monday that the Trump administration likely violated the Constitution by pressuring California officials to change how they count ballots. His order prohibits the Justice Department and the Department of Homeland Security from demanding officials set aside ballots or depart from existing state election procedures based on federal lists of suspected noncitizens. Boasberg found that the Constitution gives states and Congress, but not the executive branch, authority over election rules. The federal ban on noncitizen voting does not mean the administration can rewrite those rules. By the numbers: The DOJ claims it identified more than 20,000 suspected noncitizens on California's voter rolls. After Boasberg ordered DOJ to turn over its list, an expert found that at least 22 members of the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights — all known U.S. citizens — were wrongly included. The expert found another 66 members were almost certainly on the list. Boasberg found the expert credible and concluded the list's errors posed a real threat to eligible voters. What he's saying: "The President evidently believes that it would be good public policy for more stringent procedures to be put in place," Boasberg wrote. "No matter how strong that policy case may be, however, it does not justify overstepping the bounds of the Executive Branch's limited constitutional authority in this domain." The White House referred Axios to the Department of Homeland Security for comment. DHS and the Justice Department did not immediately respond to Axios' requests for comment. Catch up quick: In a separate lawsuit , DOJ sought to force California and Los Angeles County to segregate ballots from suspected noncitizens. A federal judge rejected that request Wednesday, as did an appeals court on Friday. Monday's ruling is different in that it restricts the federal government from making its demands rather than simply refusing to order California to comply. It also follows a broader nationwide temporary restraining order Friday that prohibits similar demands and threats of prosecution against election workers. Yes, but: Boasberg did not prohibit federal officials from investigating illegal voting or compiling lists of suspected noncitizens. Federal law makes it a crime for noncitizens to vote in federal elections, and DOJ can prosecute people who knowingly break that law. But that doesn't give DOJ the authority to order states to change how they verify voter eligibility or count ballots, Boasberg wrote. California can continue following its election procedures while federal prosecutors pursue illegal voting, Boasberg said. What's next: The Supreme Court could still order California to set aside the disputed ballots.
