events.title: AI could break legal systems by finding previously hidden loopholes
events.summary: If AI can find the holes in programming code, it can do the same with legal code, paving the way for chaos. Felix Ringe, a visiting fellow at Stanford Law School’s liftlab and legal scholar, suggests large language models (LLMs) have become potent enough that they could break legal systems by identifying exploitable inconsistencies at scale. "Legal systems encode the foundations of social order in natural language," Ringe and collaborator Linus Folkerts argued in a blog post last week. "Similar to computer systems, the written law can contain vulnerabilities that invite exploitation." Ringe contends that while courts tend to pave over these text vulnerabilities through statutory interpretation, the ability to discover adversarially useful inconsistencies in the law in an automated way risks overwhelming the legal system's ability to bridge the gaps. To buttress his thesis, he points to recent work by other legal scholars that frames laws as vulnerable code, such as " Legal Zero-Days : A Novel Risk Vector for Advanced AI Systems" and " Hardware and Software Bugs in the Legal System " [PDF]. The analogy dates back at least to 1999, with Lawrence Lessig's Code and Other Laws of Cyberspace [PDF] and Code Is Law: On Liberty in Cyberspace . Lessig credits William J. Mitchell, in City of Bits: Space, Place, and the Infobahn (1995), with the idea that code is cyberspace's law, adding that he "drew the metaphor from others as well." Ringe has turned this on its head by proposing that law is code. The analogy between programming code and legal code works reasonably well, up to a point. Law and code both have their share of formatting pedantry and ritual. The mapping breaks down when courts get cast as a runtime environment – non-deterministic trial outcomes don't work for production applications. Discontinuities aside, Ringe's point is that AI models can surface statutory gaps at a scale that may bring the chaos currently seen in the software security ecosystem to the legal world. To demonstrate that, Ringe and Folkerts cite several potential gaps in German law that they uncovered with the help of LLMs, noting that they're only sharing legal exploits they believe could not cause serious harm. For example, an amendment to Germany's Occupational Diseases Regulation (BKV) is subject to a constitutional requirement to cite its statutory authority. But Ringe and Folkerts argue that the amendment omits a required reference. So, in theory, a journalist could request an unpublished statement submitted to Germany's occupational-diseases advisory council under freedom of information rules, challenging a confidentiality provision that the researchers argue may be invalid. Another example cited describes a transit visa rule that may be invalid because the government failed to identify the authority under which the rule was made. "We believe that with cheap legal reasoning proliferating, AI systems could jeopardize the functioning of today’s legal systems," they wrote. "In such a world, lawmakers would need to significantly harden the process of legislation, for example by leveraging advanced AI themselves." Wendy Musell, a San Francisco-based employment law attorney and partner, told The Register that the use of AI in the legal field is expanding rapidly. "Some California Courts, including LA Superior Court, are testing the use of AI as law clerks," said Musell. "Generally law clerks would assist the Court by researching and drafting opinions for the judge's review. That means AI is serving that role in certain courts. Litigators now must consider how AI is analyzing motions and cases. "This is the case even where I personally have found different AI sources to appear to have a slant or bias, and often fail to accurately analyze legal issues. It was just a matter of time before AI came for the legislative process." Eric Goldman, associate dean for research and professor of law at Santa Clara University School of Law, told The Register that Ringe's argument has some merit. "I think the methodology of using AI to identify potential statutory gaps is logical," said Goldman. "However, it will require careful human review to determine if the AI-identified gaps are in fact actually gaps. Statutory gaps also may have no legal consequence, or at least none of significance; and legislatures will often correct any major gaps once they are identified." Goldman said the idea that legislators should use AI during the drafting process is ambitious, at least in the short term. "Legislators often draft laws with a range of goals and priorities, and avoiding statutory gaps is rarely a high priority," he explained. "But many legislatures have legislative counsel who are responsible for converting draft bills into final legislative text, and I could see where legislative counsel could benefit from using AI to identify drafting gaps as part of their standard cleanup protocols." ®

events.title: Student-loan borrowers face 'imminent' harm from Trump's plan to limit borrowing for advanced degrees, judge says
events.summary: A federal judge said the Trump administration's plan to limit student-loan borrowing for advanced degrees is an overreach of authority. Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images A federal judge recently ruled that Trump's plan to cap borrowing for professional degrees was an overreach. It's the third ruling that blocked Trump's plan to limit higher borrowing to 11 professional programs from taking effect. The judge said that students and colleges would face "imminent" harm and revenue loss from the caps. A federal judge dealt another blow to the Trump administration's plans to cap student-loan borrowing . US District Judge Michael Simon ruled that the Department of Education exceeded its authority when it intended to restrict access to federal lending for certain professional degrees. It's the third ruling by a federal judge blocking the department's plan from taking effect. The department had planned to implement a new rule on July 1 that would have limited professional degrees to 11 programs, including dentistry and medicine, while excluding others like nursing and social work. Only these programs would qualify for a $200,000 lifetime borrowing cap, while other advanced programs would receive a $100,000 lifetime cap. The department's proposed list of professional degrees sparked pushback from lawmakers and advocates, who said some programs excluded from the list required higher borrowing caps to ensure sufficient funding for students in those programs. The ruling in Oregon last month related to the naturopathic medicine field. The plaintiffs, including colleges and students in naturopathy, said that the department's decision to exclude the field from the professional degree list risked pushing students into private student loans, which often have higher interest rates and are ineligible for federal loan forgiveness programs. Additionally, naturopathy associations said the caps could harm revenue should students choose not to enroll due to the borrowing caps. Simon, the judge, said the harms posed by the caps to both students and schools are "imminent" because students are deciding whether they can afford to enroll in the program for the coming academic year. He placed a preliminary injunction on the department's proposed definition of "professional" and ordered it to qualify naturopathic medicine for the higher borrowing limit. The department wrote in a notice on Federal Student Aid that it encourages students to contact their school to see how the court ruling affects them. At the end of June, a separate court decision blocked the department's narrowed definition of a professional degree from taking effect. As a result of that ruling, the department released an updated list of 30 programs that would qualify for a higher borrowing limit as the litigation progresses. It said at the time that it's confident the narrowed definition is "lawful and will continue to defend it." Have a story to share about student loans? events.title: Binance clients pull US$4.7 billion after hack as crypto world studies fallout
events.summary: Binance said net outflows represented 3% of the assets on its platform, suggesting customer confidence has largely held up. SINGAPORE/PARIS/NEW YORK - Binance’s customers have withdrawn a net US$4.72 billion (S$6 billion) from the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange since it reopened, after hackers stole around US$6.3 billion of crypto from the platform in what could be the largest-ever financial heist. The exchange froze withdrawals for more than two days after the hack, which the FBI said was carried out by North Korea, then started allowing customers to withdraw again on the morning of Nov 1. The theft has underlined the vulnerability of digital assets to attacks and raised questions about the impact of the hack on Binance, which has vowed to repay customers in full. Binance said the net outflows amounted to around 3% of the assets on its platform, a relatively modest figure that analysts said suggested customer confidence had largely held up. Most withdrawals from the platform were in the form of Tether’s USDT stablecoin, Binance added. The outflow compares with about US$7 billion withdrawn from Circle’s USDC stablecoin over a week after the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank in 2023. Binance itself processed net outflows of about US$6 billion over 72 hours in 2022 after the collapse of FTX. The attack marks a step-up in North Korea’s crypto thefts. Blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs said North Korea-linked hackers have stolen US$7.4 billion so far in 2026. Analysts and crypto experts said the fallout appeared limited so far, and there was little sign of an impact on broader financial markets despite deepening ties between crypto and mainstream finance in recent years. “Binance will absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds, not our users,” the company said in a statement on X. Binance said it was covering the losses with company funds and had already raised US$6 billion from its corporate treasury, an insurance fund and reserves set aside for security breaches. “It has not yet triggered widespread panic or a massive, concentrated withdrawal,” said Tim Sun, a senior researcher at HashKey Group, a digital asset financial service company in Hong Kong. Binance, which says it has more than 335 million users worldwide and average daily trading volumes of US$95 billion across digital assets and derivatives, said it had also seen US$2.7 billion in customer inflows since Nov 1 and that withdrawal volumes were stabilising after an “initial spike.” Data from data analytics provider DeFiLlama showed several crypto exchanges received notable inflows to their platforms since Binance opened withdrawals, although it was unclear what share came from users moving funds off Binance. OKX recorded US$284.87 million in inflows in the last 24 hours, followed by Gate with US$93.22 million in inflows and Bybit, which saw US$29.25 million in inflows. Representatives for OKX, Gate and Bybit did not respond to requests for comment. Some traders told Reuters they were keeping their accounts on Binance. Ryan Tan, a Binance user, said he was in no hurry to withdraw his funds from the platform, as he had already kept his account fairly light since the collapse of FTX four years ago. “After the FTX collapse, I decided to hold everything on my wallet instead of leaving them on exchanges,” said the 39-year-old. After hitting a six-week low on Oct 30, bitcoin prices recovered through the weekend to trade above US$77,000 on Nov 2, while ether also rebounded from a two-month low. Stablecoin market capitalisations, often viewed as a gauge of money moving into and out of crypto markets, have fallen since Oct 30, suggesting some investors have shifted funds into cash or traditional assets. Binance started allowing US dollar cash withdrawals again on Nov 2. The FBI said on Oct 31 that the North Korean state-sponsored group TraderTraitor was responsible for the attack . Researchers describe the group as highly sophisticated and say its activities help fund the country’s weapons programmes. Analysts said the attack’s scale could curb institutional appetite for cryptocurrencies. Spot bitcoin ETFs recorded outflows of US$643 million on Oct 30, the largest daily withdrawal in October, while more than US$1.3 billion in leveraged positions were liquidated, according to Ari Redbord, global head of policy at TRM Labs. “A hack at a crypto exchange is bank robbery at the speed of the internet, which creates an unstable risk profile for anyone responsible for other people’s capital,” he said. About half of the stolen funds were held in stablecoins and have been frozen by issuers including Circle, which said on Nov 2 it had frozen more than US$1.1 billion in USDC. According to blockchain analytics firm Elliptic, the hackers still control around US$3.28 billion, mostly in bitcoin and ether, and only a negligible amount has been cashed out of crypto and into fiat currency.

events.title: Oracle files to sell $20 billion in new stock, bonds to finance AI buildout
events.summary: Oracle filed plans on Monday to issue $10 billion in stock and $10 billion in bonds, it said in a filing. The plans were outlined last week at its investor day. Oracle filed plans on Monday to issue new stock and more debt to finance its artificial intelligence buildout. The hyperscaler will sell $10 billion in common stock and $10 billion in senior notes, according to filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. While the fundraising was already outlined at an investor day last week , shares tumbled 8.8% Monday. "This seems to be exactly what they previewed," said Rob Oliver, senior research analyst at Baird. "So I'm not sure why the market is freaking about it." Oracle said it plans to use the proceeds for general corporate purposes, which may include capital expenditures, repayments of debt and future investments. The hyperscaler's stock initially bounced after last Wednesday's investor day, when Oracle also issued a revenue forecast of at least $225 billion for fiscal 2030. At the time Oracle also said it was limiting its additional capital market funding for the fiscal 2027 to 2030 investment cycle to that $20 billion. "This is a major relief given concerns about the state of debt markets and the cost of capital (although UBS has argued that these debt market concerns have been over-stated)," UBS analyst Karl Keirstead said in a note on Thursday. Oracle plans to turn to vendor financing, customer-provided hardware and customer prepayments to help it transition to positive free cash flow, which it expects to reach in the second half of 2028. Stock and bonds in Oracle, co-founded by former CEO Larry Ellison, have been under pressure amid growing investor concerns about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure. Oracle shares are down 33% in 2026 and 50% over the past 12 months. The yield on its investment-grade 4.95% bond due in 2031 is currently 7.276%. The sentiment shift is also seen in Oracle's five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default. The spread sits at 292, up 265% in one year. That's more in line with a high-end junk bond rating, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence's Gavan Nolan. While still an investment-grade credit, Oracle was downgraded by S&P to a BBB- in July, one rating level above high yield. It has $125.34 billion in debt, as of Aug. 31, with the bulk in senior notes. What ultimately matters for Oracle is execution, Pat Nerney, head of investment solutions at Dynasty Financial Partners, said in an email to CNBC Monday. "Can they do what they say they are going to do? We view this as the narrative across the AI space," he said. "If this gets executed according to plans laid out, they will be rewarded. If they have to come back to market in the back half of '27 after telling everyone this was the last of the capital needed ... look out." — CNBC's Seema Mody and Ari Levy contributed reporting.

events.title: Trump to Axios: "No rush" to decide on bombing Iran again
events.summary: President Trump told Axios in a phone interview Monday he's "in no rush" to decide whether to resume fighting in Iran . Why it matters: The midterm elections have been seen as an inflection point for Trump on whether to unleash a massive bombing campaign to try to bring the war to an end. But it appears the president, at least for now, will continue on dual tracks — letting negotiations play out while preparing to go back to war if he concludes a deal isn't reachable. What he is saying: "One way or the other, we will do something, but there is no rush. We crippled them financially. They have no money, no gasoline and their people are getting very tired of it," Trump said in the interview. Driving the news: Qatari mediators have written a draft agreement outlining a three-day sequence of confidence-building measures aimed at resuming direct U.S.-Iran negotiations, according to regional sources. A diplomat with knowledge of the situation said the Qatari mediators are waiting for feedback from the U.S. and Iran. Qatari mediator Ali al-Thawadi traveled to Tehran on Monday to continue talks on the draft agreement and the diplomat said progress is building. Trump is giving diplomacy a chance but is clear-eyed about the chances of reaching a deal. "We are talking to them. It's going fine. The problem with them is ... they try and tap tap tap [us along]. There's less urgency [on the Iranian side] than you think there would be, but they want to make a deal more than they ever wanted," Trump said. The latest: Hours after the interview, Trump posted on Truth Social: "Oil Prices are DROPPING LIKE A ROCK, down almost $10 a Barrel, A RECORD, because people feel that there will not be a War with Iran. Iran wants a settlement, as soon as possible. It could happen!" Between the lines: Trump is weighing three courses of action, backed by three different camps: 1. Make a deal: Vice President JD Vance and White House envoy Steve Witkoff are urging him to move toward a deal because a renewed war might not change the situation for the better. Most Gulf countries support this position and have communicated that to Trump, sources say. 2. Go back to battle: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu wants to resume combat, as does Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. They argue that Iran can't be trusted to make a deal let alone abide by one, and that Trump should finish the job militarily. 3. Maximum economic pain: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, CIA Director John Ratcliffe and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are advising Trump to maintain the "no war, no deal" status quo and allow the economic pressure campaign to continue, sources said. Ratcliffe told Trump that prolonged economic pain will induce Iran to make more concessions — or create enough instability inside the country that citizens revolt, a source with direct knowledge said. The CIA declined to comment. The other side: Iran's civilian leadership sounded hopeful on Monday about the prospects of reaching a deal. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei "granted the government certain authorities" to try to reach an agreement through diplomacy. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Monday that the diplomatic exchanges "have become very intensive." "Qatar and Pakistan are playing very active roles as mediators. We have presented our conditions and our proposal, and everything depends on Washington's political rationality. If they choose genuine diplomacy, we are ready to engage. But if they intend to engage in deception and military operations, they will face a response more painful and severe than in the past," he said. Araghchi said that if the U.S. accepts Tehran's conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, then "negotiations will resume." "Otherwise, the current situation will continue, and Iran will not bow down," he said. The big picture: Russia and China are taking an active role in the effort to reach a deal. Russian President Vladimir Putin spoke by phone Monday with Iran's Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council Gen. Mohsen Rezaei. The two discussed the efforts to reach a diplomatic agreement. Rezaei, who is very close to Khamenei, was also the recipient of a letter Vance sent recently proposing to resume negotiations. Russia has also offered to be part of any nuclear agreement, including by receiving Iran's enriched uranium stockpile. At the same time, Rezaei's deputy visited Beijing on Monday and met with the Chinese foreign minister. China is also urging the U.S. and Iran to resume direct negotiations to end the war. What they're saying: Vance told reporters on Monday that he and Trump "feel pretty good about the prospect of reaching a settlement" with Iran. "We made some progress and we will see if we can make some more," Vance said. He added: "We haven't set deadlines (for resuming strikes). We want to make sure the Iranians don't rebuild or try to rebuild their nuclear program. We do think there is a pathway there but it requires a firm and verifiable commitment that they don't rebuild their nuclear program."

events.title: Lumentum CEO touts 'enormous' opportunity in massive AI connectivity deal with Marvell
events.summary: Marvell will acquire Lumentum in an all-stock transaction. The deal will expand Marvell's push into optical connectivity for artificial intelligence data centers. Marvell's takeover marks one of the most significant bets on AI in 2026. Marvell Technology 's deal for optical components maker Lumentum will create an "enormous" opportunity to address growing connectivity demands from the artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout, Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston told CNBC on Monday. "You need scale-up technology that needs semiconductors and optical working seamlessly together," Marvell CEO Matt Murphy told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." "We are going to create a new category of company here." Since the tie-up is a fixed-ratio deal with no cash, the value will depend on the price of Marvell shares. The company said the transaction has an implied enterprise value of $115 billion for Lumentum, in a release. Marvell shares slumped 13% in trading Monday, while Lumentum's stock sank nearly 19%. But both stocks have been huge winners in the artificial intelligence boom, with Marvell more than doubling in the past year, prior to Monday's sell-off, and Lumentum quadrupling over that stretch. Through the acquisition, Marvell said it can combine electrical and optical technologies to meet accelerating and shifting AI connectivity demands across regions and systems. Companies are increasingly relying on optical connections to piece together chips used to run and train large language models. "We're actually going to create solutions around those that are highly sticky, and the reason that they're sold out is because the demand is exploding, and we don't see that changing anytime soon," Murphy said. Humans are still doing the work behind some AI agents OpenAI pares fundraising goal, now seeking up to $20 billion in latest round Binance resumes withdrawals following $6.3 billion hack, says 90% of stolen user assets are covered Why AI is boosting Meta’s ad business while hurting Google search Lumentum shareholders will receive 4.5 Marvell shares for each Lumentum share under the agreement. The deal is expected to close during the first half of 2028. Marvell's takeover marks one of the most significant bets on AI in 2026 and comes despite recent concerns over the long-term sustainability of infrastructure spending. This isn't the company's first bet on AI growth. This year, the company closed a multibillion-dollar deal for Celestial AI, a startup focused on optical interconnectivity technology. Marvell 's Murphy also shot down concerns about Nvidia's circular dealmaking, given the leading AI chipmaker's recent multibillion-dollar investments in both companies. In a bid to further support the data center infrastructure that houses its AI chips, Nvidia has positioned itself as a central cog in a network of related companies, investing in several technology companies that purchase its chips or neoclouds that rent out computing capacity. That's sparked criticism that companies like Nvidia are virtually funding themselves by taking stakes in customers. "This is a double down on supporting Nvidia, who is the ecosystem leader in this area," Murphy told CNBC. "We're very committed to that partnership, and I think having two of the key suppliers come together, that support that ecosystem, is going to be a big benefit for them." Marvell has seen its market value more than triple over the last three years, buoyed by unrelenting AI enthusiasm. Lumentum's stock has more than doubled in 2026 alone. A previous version of this story incorrectly cited the Marvell CEO.

events.title: Why Relationships Still Matter in the Digital Age of Banking
events.summary: As technology reshapes trade finance and global commerce becomes more complex, Habib Bank AG Zurich’s Hong Kong CEO says the winning formula is not scale alone – but responsiveness, judgment and trusted relationships. When Sachil Dagur took charge of Habib Bank Zurich in Hong Kong in 2018, he saw a bank with valuable strengths already in place: a niche in trade finance, deep ties to the trading community and a footprint across markets important to its clients. The opportunity, he believed, was not to reinvent those strengths, but to connect them more effectively and help clients make better use of them. Dagur, CEO of Habib Bank Zurich (Hong Kong), had spent more than two decades at Axis Bank, including senior roles in India, Singapore and Hong Kong. His career gave him a close view of corporate banking across Asia and shaped his belief that, while technology and trade routes may change, clients still value sound advice, relevant information and someone who answers the phone. “If they know they can reach out and somebody’s going to pick up the phone or call back immediately,” he says, “it gives great comfort.” For Dagur, the future of banking is not a choice between technology and relationships. It is about using one to strengthen the other. According to Dagur, technology may have transformed banking, but clients still want a bank that understands their problems and offers solutions. Personal accessibility remains a competitive strength, with customers valuing clear points of contact. This relationship-led approach, he explains, is what builds loyalty. In fact, he notes that about 40 per cent of Habib Bank Zurich’s clients have stayed for more than a decade. Trust, however, is not built on goodwill alone, he says. It requires continuity, knowledge and delivery. “The continuity of people is the most critical part,” he says. Clients should not have to repeatedly explain their business to changing relationship managers. Staff must also understand banking products as well as the markets and industries in which their clients operate. “You would always love interacting with people who provide additional knowledge to you,” Dagur says. That knowledge is particularly important in trade finance, where clients may be exploring unfamiliar destinations, counterparties or supply chains. Habib Bank AG Zurich’s presence in 11 markets including Bangladesh, Turkey, Pakistan, South Africa and Kenya gives it local insight that can help clients assess opportunities and risks. Dagur takes a similarly pragmatic approach to technology. No bank can ignore digital change, but not every institution needs to be first in every innovation. “If a tiger is chasing you, don’t be the last guy,” he says. “If you can’t lead, at least hang around at the front end of the crowd.” For Habib Bank Zurich, this has meant digitising internal processes such as letters of credit and invoice discounting while monitoring blockchain-based trade finance. Dagur believes blockchain may become important, but adoption remains limited. The immediate priority, he says, is to ensure that internal processes can be fully digitised before moving further. The bank is not yet blockchain-ready, he says, but it is watching the space and will be ready when the market is. As supply chains shift and companies rethink trade routes, banks cannot control geopolitics. They can, however, help clients understand change earlier and respond more intelligently. For Dagur, knowledge will be a key differentiator. “What do you know better and faster than others?” he asks. “That is going to be the differentiator.” Habib Bank AG Zurich’s representative offices in Bangladesh, Turkey and China, alongside its presence in several other countries, help the bank build deeper market understanding and share relevant intelligence with clients. This can be valuable for Chinese companies as they seek overseas markets and trading businesses look for new destinations. The challenge is no longer simply to provide financing. Banks must help clients decide where to trade, whom to work with and how to adapt when conditions shift. Risk management, he notes, is central to that role. Dagur has placed greater emphasis on larger, highly rated corporate clients, regular staff training and sustained attention to compliance. Risk and compliance, he believes, cannot remain the responsibility of a specialist department; they must become part of the institution’s culture. “If risk and compliance becomes a culture, it becomes a non-issue,” he says. His view was partly shaped from his early days in a military school, where the motto was “Play the Game”: which translates to “If you’re playing the game, play by the rules that the game has.” In banking, that means compliance is non-negotiable. Rules governing anti-money laundering, liquidity and financial crime controls must be followed, and employees need to understand why they matter.

events.title: Outback helicopter firm grounded over 'serious and imminent risk to safety'
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Outback chopper firm Fortescue Helicopters grounded over safety breaches CASA found Fortescue Helicopters has been operating with "a deliberately and systemically non-compliant safety culture". ( Supplied: Fortescue Helicopters ) The Civil Aviation Safety Authority (CASA) has grounded Sky High Helicopters for a series of serious safety breaches. CASA says the breaches included directing its pilots "not to accurately record the total time in service for aircraft operated by the company". The company's suspension comes a year after CASA warned the watchdog would crack down on helicopter pilots over safety regulations. An outback Australian helicopter company has had its fleet grounded and its air operator's certificate suspended immediately over a "serious and imminent risk to safety". Sky High Helicopters Pty Ltd, which trades as Fortescue Helicopters in Western Australia and Queensland, has been grounded by the Civil Aviation Safety Authority (CASA). In its findings published yesterday, CASA said the company had been operating with "a deliberately and systemically non-compliant safety culture". Fortescue Helicopters operates in Western Australia and Queensland. ( Supplied: Fortescue Helicopters ) Corporate documents show the chopper company was first registered in 2008, offering aerial mustering, charter flights and mining support from the Pilbara mining town of Newman. It also has other bases in Perth, Broome and Far North Queensland. Owned by WA cattle producer and pilot Weldon Percy, Fortescue Helicopters lists among its clients mining giants Fortescue Metals Group (FMG), Rio Tinto, Glencore and Hancock Prospecting. On its website, the business says it has a fleet of 22 aircraft. "Safety, for our pilots and clients is our number one priority," the company's website states. "We believe safety is a company culture, not just a practice." It is not yet clear how long Fortescue Helicopters' suspension will last. ( Supplied: Fortescue Helicopters ) Fortescue Helicopters is not affiliated with the similarly named FMG, although it lists the company founded by billionaire Andrew "Twiggy" Forrest as "an important client of ours". It is understood Fortescue has used Fortescue Helicopters on an ad hoc basis but it is not its primary provider. CASA said in its findings the company had committed a series of serious and systemic intentional safety breaches, including that its pilots had been "directed not to accurately record the total time in service for aircraft operated by the company". Other breaches detected by CASA included pilots being "directed not to record maintenance defects on aircraft maintenance releases" and operating "aircraft with outstanding maintenance requirements". It also said personnel at the company were being ordered to perform unauthorised maintenance activities and had failed to comply with the company's operations manual. CASA has previously pledged to crack down on safety compliance in the northern Australian chopper industry. ( ABC News: Michael Parfitt ) CASA also said "pilots' flight and duty time limits are regularly and deliberately exceeded" by the company. Mr Percy hung up when the ABC contacted him for comment. Fortescue Helicopters was also separately contacted but has not responded. Suspension follows safety crackdown pledge The grounding of Sky High Helicopters comes a year after CASA's chief executive Pip Spence warned the watchdog would crack down on helicopter pilots who tried to "game the system" over safety regulations . She made the comments in the aftermath of the month-long trial of celebrity crocodile wrangler and chopper pilot Matt Wright in the Northern Territory Supreme Court last year, in which he was sentenced to prison for five months. Wright trial exposes cowboy chopper culture The trial of celebrity crocodile wrangler Matt Wright unearthed a culture of helicopter maintenance and safety breaches by his company, which some say have been ongoing in Australia's north for decades. Wright's trial for attempting to pervert the course of justice heard accounts of frequent under-reporting of helicopter flying hours within the northern Australian aviation sector, with pilots regularly disconnecting the devices used to record their hours. Separate to his criminal trial, Wright's company, Helibrook, was grounded in late 2024 over numerous breaches , including failing to record accurate flight times, reckless operation of aircraft, and the falsification of maintenance records.

events.title: I bonds now pay 5.51% — but there are trade-offs. What to know before buying
events.summary: Newly purchased Series I bonds will pay 5.51% through April 2027, up from 4.26% through October. The variable part of I bond interest rose to 4.08%, and the fixed part increased to 1.40%, the highest since 2006. But there are key things to know before buying I bonds, experts say. Now that Series I bonds pay higher interest , the government-backed, nearly risk-free asset could be more attractive for certain investors. But I bonds have downsides, and there are alternatives to consider. Newly purchased I bonds currently pay 5.51% annual interest through April 30, up from the 4.26% yield offered on purchases made through October. Amid rising inflation , the variable part of I bond interest rose to 4.08%, while the fixed part increased to 1.40%, the highest since 2006. Combined, the 5.51% composite rate is the biggest yield since November 2022. The new I bond rate is "very attractive," according to Ken Tumin, founder of DepositQuest.com, a blog that tracks I bond rates, among other deposit accounts. The variable part of I bond interest resets every six months, based on the consumer price index. For the next six months after purchase, I bonds look "very competitive" compared to other shorter-term options for cash, such as savings accounts or certificates of deposit, according to Tumin. Midterm election: How affordability and the economy could affect voters' decisions These Senate races may help determine the fate of Social Security Social Security: How much money beneficiaries may lose if Congress does nothing Trump Account holders to receive SpaceX stock from Gwynne Shotwell in December CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 ranked CNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026 Meanwhile, the I bond's 1.4% fixed rate stays the same for as long as you own it, which could appeal to longer-term investors, he said. But I bonds aren't right for everyone. Here are some key things to know before purchasing. I bonds can be a 'secondary emergency fund' Investors can buy $10,000 of electronic I bonds per person per calendar year via their TreasuryDirect account . You can open additional TreasuryDirect accounts for other family members or businesses to buy more. I bond interest is tax-deferred until redemption and is not subject to state or local taxes. You can also avoid federal taxes if you use the money for qualified education expenses . But experts say there are some downsides. The funds are locked up for 12 months from purchase, and you'll lose your last three months of interest if you redeem within five years. Advisors typically recommend keeping at least three to six months of living expenses in cash for emergency savings . I bonds could boost those reserves, experts say, as long as you keep enough readily accessible cash elsewhere. "I always say [I bonds are] a secondary emergency fund," said David Enna, founder of Tipswatch.com, a website that tracks Treasury inflation-protected securities , or TIPS, and I bond rates . Once you own I bonds for five years, you can redeem the money as needed, penalty-free. With I bond purchase limits, restrictions and some TreasuryDirect complaints , advisors often recommend other options for clients who want to preserve purchasing power. "For most of my clients, I bonds are more hassle than they're worth," said certified financial planner Eileen Olson, founder of advisory firm Emerald Wealth in Daufuskie Island, South Carolina. "The amount is too small to matter." On a $2 million portfolio, the $10,000 annual purchase limit is only 0.5%, and it earns about $550 in a year before federal taxes, she said. "That won't protect anyone's lifestyle from inflation." Instead, Olson prefers TIPS , which don't have purchase limits and can be bought alongside other assets, outside TreasuryDirect. TIPS have five- , 10- and 30-year terms, with yields ranging from about 2.3% to above 3% for the 30-year term, as of Nov. 2. However, the right option depends on your investing goals and timeline, experts say. "For short-term cash, Treasury bills and high-yield savings are simpler," Olson said. Also backed by the U.S. government, Treasury bills , or T-bills, have terms ranging from four weeks up to 52 weeks. As of Nov. 2, some T-bill yields were well over 4%. By comparison, the top 1% average of high-yield savings accounts were paying above 4% , according to rate comparison site DepositAccounts. Some one-year certificates of deposit were also offering rates over 4% , the same day, according to Bankrate. Money market funds are another option. Some of the biggest funds were paying around 4%, as of Nov. 2, according to Crane Data .

events.title: Trump pre-election pitch: Reflecting Pool, pipes and a new promenade
events.summary: President Trump extolled his administration's Reflecting Pool project , dug up debunked claims of vandalism and applauded the new White House helipad in a Monday pre-Election Day speech. The big picture: Trump's deep focus on remaking the nation's capital has taken center stage as the clock ticks down to midterm elections. Driving the news: "The pool is now better and more beautiful than it's ever been before, and we're very proud of it," Trump said in Monday's speech, adding, "We went through a lot with vandalism." But Trump's own Justice Department dropped vandalism charges against former Olympian David Hearn , whose case was later killed by a judge after prosecutors acknowledged that faulty installation caused the damage to the Pool. Trump added the administration was "giving serious thought" to renaming the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool to the "Trump Reflecting Pool," before later saying he was kidding. Throughout the speech, he held up printed images he identified as pipes, joints and other Pool materials. He also showed an image that appeared to show "8647" sprayed onto the base of the emptied pool, claiming "that was a Comey phrase" — a reference to his former FBI director and top foe. Zoom out: He also discussed his White House renovation projects, including the recently installed helipad and Scotts Miracle-Gro's lawn restoration after the UFC fight on White House grounds. Friction point: Trump's projects, including his D.C.-area arch and White House ballroom, have been broadly panned by Americans in polling. "This project should be a project that unites all Americans," Trump said Monday of the newly reopened Reflecting Pool, which stood empty for an extended period earlier this year. Zoom in: His pre-election pitch at times sounded more like a typical rally speech, where he touted his immigration policies and war with Iran while slamming Democrats as "a party that hates America." This is the last day before the midterm elections, the most important midterm I believe in our lifetime," he said. "The Democrat Party has nominated the most extreme and dangerous slate of candidates in American history." He also reiterated his pitch to distribute $5,000 checks should Republicans win in the midterms. What's next: After inviting Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to speak, Trump then touted his planned " triumphal arch ," detailed plans for a "promenade" from the Lincoln Memorial to the Potomac River and teased his golf course renovation . "We have a lot of great things planned for Washington, and I could get into the nation, but for that you don't have enough time," Trump said. He ended his closing argument by lauding a "golden age," saying, "We were laughed at like we were stupid people. We were laughed at by every ruler, every president, every prime minister, every king, every queen. But they don't laugh anymore." Axios' Josephine Walker contributed to this report. events.summary: Traders on Kalshi see a 74% chance of Democrats winning the Senate. The higher odds come after a New York Times and Siena University poll found Democrats are leading in seven battleground states. Momentum for Democrats is building on Kalshi, with traders on Monday seeing a 74% chance of the party winning control of the U.S. Senate — the highest odds seen for the party on the platform since the market first opened. The higher odds come after The New York Times reported Sunday that a poll it conducted with Siena University found Democrats are leading in several battleground states, strengthening Democrats' path to a possible Senate majority. The contract asks "Who will control the Senate?" and will be verified by the Library of Congress after Tuesday's vote. Since it opened in 2024, Republicans dominated the market for Senate control in 2026. The gap between the parties' odds narrowed shortly after the U.S. and Israel first launched strikes on Iran on Feb. 28, though the chances for Republican control jumped up to 60% in July before reversing in mid-September. Markets on separate Senate races have also seen major movement in favor of Democratic candidates in the last 24 hours. Traders on Kalshi now see a 74% chance of Democrats winning the Senate race in Texas, up from 68.4%, over the past 24 hours. The market on the Senate race in Iowa jumped to 50% from 42% on Polymarket in favor of Democrats. In Kansas, which has not elected a Democratic U.S. senator since 1932, odds of Democratic candidate Adam Hamilton winning over Republican Roger Marshall are up to 63% from 52%. events.title: Scoop: Senate GOP makes massive bet on streaming
events.summary: The top Senate GOP super PAC has nearly tripled its spending on streaming and social media platforms this election cycle to more than $200 million, Axios has learned. Why it matters : In a record cycle for ad spending, more political money is shifting to streaming, where super PACs have greater freedom to target voters, bargain and experiment — but platforms have more power to set the rules. In some states, streaming and social media have swallowed half of the Senate Leadership Fund (SLF) budget, according to a source familiar with the group's spending. SLF's $200M+ total for the 2026 cycle (up from $71M in 2024) includes tens of millions of dollars funneled through the SLF-linked Texas PAC and its affiliated nonprofit One Nation. The other side: The top Senate Democratic super PAC declined to provide a dollar figure for their spending on streaming. "Senate Majority PAC invested more this cycle in digital communications than any previous cycle, running digital campaigns in 12 states," SMP communications director Lauren French told Axios. Zoom in : Streaming and social platforms offer campaigns the power to target more specific audiences compared to traditional broadcast, and make it easier to measure the impact. "Its way more surgical than a linear broadcast buy," Zack Roday, managing director at Think Big, told Axios. But platforms can also set their own rules around which types of ads they want to accept. Some, like Netflix and TikTok, don't allow any candidate or issue ads . Republicans have complained about restrictions on ads that include transgender issues on Disney-owned platforms. Between the lines: Super PACs often pay multiple times what a campaign pays for ads on broadcast TV and radio because of laws ensuring candidates get the lowest rates. Online, super PACs can negotiate directly — and use their fat budgets and sprawling election maps as leverage. SLF works with platforms like SiriusXM, Paramount, Hulu, YouTube and others to lock in discounts based on their overall spending plans, according to the source. Groups can also experiment with different lengths and formats for ads online, breaking the 30-second broadcast mold. What to watch: Streaming ads can also be trickier for outside tracking. While Meta and Google provide public data on political ad buys, not every platform provides that kind of visibility, Streaming buys aren't covered by the same FCC filing requirements as political ad reservations on broadcast TV and radio. Broadcast filings can offer a preview of a group's targets months in advance, but streaming reservations are much harder to see. Although AI is changing the game, and there is a growing industry of companies offering better tracking tools. Super PACs still have to report independent expenditures to the FEC through 24- and 48- hour reports. Zoom out: Strong grassroots fundraising has helped Democratic candidates crush Republicans in dollars brought in directly to candidates. The GOP is hitting back with cash-flush committees and super PACs fueled by ultra-wealthy donors. In addition to super PACs moving more money to streaming, the National Republican Senatorial Committee jumped on a court decisions to coordinate ad buys with campaigns — giving them access to the candidate rate. It also allowed NRSC to negotiate with streaming platforms on behalf of multiple campaigns. The bottom line: It's just the beginning on maneuvering on streaming and coordinated buys. "That is definitely going to be the story of 2028," Kenny Day, senior vice president at IQM corporation, told Axios. He said the Supreme Court decision on coordinated spending "was too late for either party to really take advantage of the allowance of coordinated spending" in the 2026 cycle. Editor's note: This story has been corrected to show that the more than $200 million total included money spent through Texas PAC (not that it excluded that spending).

events.title: British Gas resumes force-fitting prepay meters months after £112m settlement
events.summary: Regulators lift block on supplier, enabling it to install meters in homes of people unable to afford energy bills British Gas has resumed force-fitting prepay meters in the homes of people unable to afford their energy bills months after paying the largest settlement on record for sending debt collectors into the homes of vulnerable customers. The industry regulator has lifted a block going back almost four years that prevented British Gas from clawing back unpaid bills by fitting such meters in customers’ homes after extracting a settlement worth more than £100m from the supplier for its role in the prepay scandal at the height of the Russian gas crisis. The decision means that British Gas agents will be able to force-fit prepay meters in homes from this winter as households brace for some of the highest energy bills since 2023, when the supplier first came under fire over its treatment of vulnerable customers. Debt agents working for British Gas at the time had ignored signs of vulnerability in struggling households while fitting meters in their homes, according to an investigation by the Times, including those with severe mental health issues and physical disabilities. The scandal ignited outrage among fuel poverty campaigners and across Whitehall as the government spent billions to help cut bills for energy users and prevent a collapse of the supplier industry. Within a year of the scandal, the regulator lifted its industry-wide moratorium on force-fitting meters to allow some suppliers to restart the installations , although forced fittings in homes with young children or people over the age of 75 remain banned. The regulator said that installing a prepay meter under a warrant “should only be a last resort, with rigorous checks to ensure debt is recovered lawfully, proportionately and safely”. It said smart pay-as-you-go meters were “a positive choice for many customers, helping them stay in control of their energy use and reporting high levels of satisfaction”. Campaigners have said the timing of the change is likely to increase people’s fears of falling behind on energy bills this winter, and will add to the stress that households face. Simon Francis, a coordinator of the End Fuel Poverty Coalition, said: “It’s almost as if regulators and ministers are failing to remember the lessons of the last energy price spike. “While more protections are now in place than in 2022, we know that magistrates are still approving bulk batches of applications for forced prepayment meter installs and some of the system failures identified in the original investigations are still happening.” British Gas defended its plan to claw back unpaid bills as household energy debt is forecast to exceed £7bn, adding more than £80 to the average household energy bill. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning “Our industry needs to protect and support customers who genuinely cannot afford to pay while taking appropriate action where people are able to pay but do not engage,” the company said. “We know many households are struggling with energy costs, and we offer significant support to those who need it most.” It said it planned to “engage early, offer targeted support and agree flexible, affordable repayment options” to struggling customers wherever possible, and that involuntary prepay meter fittings would “remain a last resort, with robust vulnerability and affordability checks”. Under Ofgem’s rules, all suppliers must make at least 10 attempts to contact a customer before a prepay meter is installed and carry out a welfare visit before installation. Meters should never be fitted in the homes of the highest risk customers, which include households with people over 75, under two, or those with severe health issues or medical equipment. A government spokesperson said: “This is a regulatory decision by Ofgem. We cannot allow past rogue practices to be repeated, where prepayment meters were wrongly installed in the homes of vulnerable people. We are closely watching to make sure companies protect their customers and act within Ofgem’s rules.” An Ofgem spokesperson said the regulator would continue to closely monitor suppliers and will “take action if we identify instances where our rules are not being followed”.

events.title: Read the memo from Squarespace's CEO about laying off 19% of staff
events.summary: Squarespace founder Anthony Casalena said in a memo that the cuts would mostly affect product and engineering teams. Abbie Parr/Getty Images Website-building company Squarespace is laying off 19% of staff. In a memo, CEO Anthony Casalena said most of the cuts affect product and engineering teams. Casalena added that the changes would mean "more player coaches." Squarespace is laying off 19% of its staff in a move its CEO said would help it "adapt for the modern era" with leaner teams and "more player coaches." The website-building software company is reducing its head count by about 300 employees, according to a companywide memo sent by Squarespace CEO Anthony Casalena on Monday. Most of the cuts affect product and engineering teams, according to the memo, which was seen by Business Insider. "The way we need to work is changing faster than at any point in our history, and our operating model must adapt for the modern era," wrote Casalena. "This means smaller teams, more player coaches, and a simplified organizational structure." Affected staff will get a minimum of 16 weeks of base salary plus additional weeks based on tenure and benefits through May 2027. Employees would also be able to keep their company laptops, and those on work visas would get continued support, the memo said. A spokesperson confirmed the layoffs and memo to Business Insider, adding: "The changes are intended to simplify how we operate, sharpen our priorities and enable the company to move faster as we position Squarespace for its next phase of growth." Later on Monday, Casalena hosted a livestream presentation about the layoffs for remaining employees. He reiterated the points made in his memo during the roughly one-minute livestream, which did not allow for comments. The company is planning a separate all-hands meeting, the spokesperson said. The cuts, first reported by The Verge, come after Squarespace has increasingly added AI features to its products. Squarespace joins a long list of companies that have laid off staff this year, some of which have cited the rise in AI. Last week, Microsoft offered buyouts to 60,000 employees, though the company told Business Insider it expects only 3,000 or fewer to take the offer. Casalena also joins a list of CEOs who have cited leaner teams when discussing layoffs — in February, Block CEO Jack Dorsey emphasized a shift toward smaller teams in a post on X about cutting his company nearly in half. Read the Squarespace CEO's memo to staff: All — I am writing today to announce one of the most difficult decisions I've had to make in the history of our company. We will be reducing our workforce by ~19% and saying goodbye to around 300 of our colleagues, with most of these reductions affecting Product & Engineering. Within the next twenty minutes, impacted US employees will receive an email and personal meeting invitation and potentially impacted non-US employees will receive country-specific details. This is not a decision I arrived at lightly, and I'd like to explain why it was made and what we will be doing for those leaving Squarespace. The way we need to work is changing faster than at any point in our history, and our operating model must adapt for the modern era. This means smaller teams, more player coaches, and a simplified organizational structure. This is not an exercise designed to reach a financial target — it is about reshaping our organization around how we need to work going forward. Squarespace's core business has been about empowering people to establish themselves online in a world where technology was a major barrier. Technology still is a major barrier for many, but it has changed in ways we could not have anticipated before the past 12 months. Our product and industry is undergoing a fundamental change, and our organization must too. Those who will be leaving us have been an important part of getting us to where we are today, and I'm grateful for their contributions. To support their transition, we will be offering*: A minimum of 16 weeks of base salary, plus additional weeks based on tenure Payment of the November 20, 2026 vesting of the legacy RSU cash award, where applicable Continuation of benefits through May 2027 Career coaching, resume preparation, and job search assistance Additional support for employees on work visas Impacted employees may keep their Squarespace laptops To those staying, your department leaders will reach out to ensure you understand the changes specific to you and your teams and that you have the direction and support you need to work through them. We will also have a brief livestream presentation later today, which will be added to calendars shortly. After we have had time to absorb today's changes, we will come back together to talk about the opportunity ahead of us. Today, however, I want to say thank you to those who have been a part of this journey with us. Whether staying or leaving, I understand this decision will impact all of you emotionally. I would encourage everyone to take some time to reset and digest as we move forward. Anthony (Outside the US, we will communicate further with you, follow local processes and, where applicable, seek to provide comparable support.) Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Democrats weigh ‘lawfare’ against Trump
events.summary: David’s view Before there was the other Dan Sullivan, there was the other Mike Doyle. Four years ago, when longtime Pittsburgh Democrat Mike Doyle retired from Congress, a left-wing legislator named Summer Lee won the primary to replace him. Republicans nominated a local politician from the suburbs to face her who had a fortuitous name: Mike Doyle. Some voters were perplexed . The new Doyle’s lawn signs called him “the right Mike” without explicitly identifying him as a Republican — a moniker that would be a non-starter in the safely Democratic seat. Local Democrats got worried calls, asking why Lee was running against their beloved liberal congressman. The Democrat Doyle called an emergency press conference to clarify that he was not the Republican Doyle: “My name is on the ballot, but it’s not me.” Lee won, albeit by a smaller margin than other Democrats in her district had in the past. Nothing else came of the story. There was no federal investigation of the Doyle scheme; no demands not to seat Doyle if he won; no statement from the governor saying that he might not certify the election. All of that has unfolded in Alaska this cycle. The clandestine Democratic effort to recruit a candidate who shares the name of the state’s incumbent Republican senator could have major implications for what happens after Tuesday. The plot’s exposure damaged Democrat Mary Peltola, knocking her off-message, and now threatens her party’s chances of winning control of the Senate. President Donald Trump’s administration is investigating, and also sued to block the certification of the results should Sullivan lose — though a federal judge tossed out the suit over the weekend. Those efforts, along with the announcement of investigations into candidates within 60 days of the vote, show how the Trump administration is jettisoning unwritten norms at the Justice Department. The Alaska mess is weighing heavily on Democrats who hope to win control of Congress tomorrow. Victory in either chamber would mean a two-year license on oversight powers, empowering Democrats to subpoena the Trump administration and its allies in the private sector. There is a thirst for vengeance among some Democrats that is testing their public stance that they must restore standards blown up by Trump. There’s also a shared sense, among most Democrats, that following those standards has gotten them nothing, while Republicans have benefitted from bending the rules. “Donald Trump and [House Oversight Committee Chairman] James Comer have basically written a playbook on how to politicize investigations and attack political enemies and weaponize government,” said Robert Garcia, the California Democrat who is in line to lead the House Oversight Committee in a Democratic majority. “[Attorney General] Todd Blanche? His whole job is just to grift for the president.” The argument over which party first used “lawfare” to get what it wanted is an old one. Democrats have long celebrated the Watergate investigation as an example of the Constitution and US legal system working as designed. Republicans are more likely to call the episode a coup against a president who’d just won a landslide. But the current debate begins, like so many irritating conversations, with the 2016 election. For all of Hillary Clinton’s errors, like telling coal miners that their jobs would vanish if she won, Democrats largely believe that she would have won the election against Trump had the FBI not abandoned its “60 day rule” and announced an 11th hour investigation into emails found on Huma Abedin’s laptop. Some believe that Barack Obama acted too timidly when Republicans refused to co-sign a letter warning of Russian interference in that campaign. Nobody has ever accused Trump of acting timidly. Ten years on, his Justice Department is still probing the origins of the Russia investigation into his first campaign. When Joe Biden replaced Trump, he kept on the US attorney who was investigating his son. When Trump replaced Biden, he sacked the prosecutors who’d worked on post-Jan. 6 investigations. Democrats felt like suckers. Biden publicly promised that his Justice Department would act independently. Privately, he was resentful of Attorney General Merrick Garland’s choices to hold off on investigating Trump until November 2022, after Republicans were more or less united in denouncing any Trump probe as “lawfare.” This is on many Democratic minds as they watch the Justice Department in Alaska — even though it’s not the only race where one party meddled in a way that might confuse voters. In Maine, a conservative PAC is sending out mail for a left-wing spoiler candidate for governor. In Ohio, a conservative PAC is doing the same for a socialist Senate candidate who could threaten Democrat Sherrod Brown’s chances. In Nevada, a conservative PAC… okay, you get the point. “They’re obsessed with meddling in elections,” Garcia said. “We have to put in place new rules and a new standard to get things back to a place where we don’t have the president trying to rig elections constantly.” In Pennsylvania, when I asked Gov. Josh Shapiro how Democrats should respond to Trump’s Justice Department, he was hopeful they would be the “party of law and order” — by showing that this was not the way to use the government’s bottomless resources. “I said every single day to our team and to the public that I enforce the law without fear or favor,” said Shapiro, referring to his six years as state attorney general. “That is not the case in the Trump administration.” Despite the ongoing debate of how far to go, Republicans are portraying a party intent on going after the president in order to rev up their base. “They’ve already filed articles of impeachment in this Congress,” House Speaker Mike Johnson alleged . In reality, the impeachment articles filed by Democratic Reps. Al Green and Shri Thanedar failed to accumulate broad Democratic support, and neither man will be in Congress next year. I’d expect Democrats’ thinking to reflect what happens on Tuesday. To be sure, there will be investigations of the Trump administration and its allies. But the risk assessment of any new probe will depend on voters’ appetite for it. Voters haven’t really punished a party for launching an investigation that doesn’t go anywhere. At the same time, Trump hasn’t lost much support for pardoning corrupt politicians like Rod Blagojevich, Kwame Kilpatrick, or Chris Collins. I’m confident about one thing: No Democrat with a gavel is going to want to move on from Trump oversight. Notable For Fox News, Elaine Mallon looked at how Democratic investigations could do more financial damage to their Republican targets. In his Off Message newsletter, Brian Beutler argued that Democrats should treat Blanche’s investigations the way Trump treated Garland’s — as illegitimate electioneering.

events.title: Trump Account holders to receive SpaceX stock from Gwynne Shotwell in December
events.summary: Eligible Trump Account holders will begin receiving donated shares of SpaceX stock from President and COO Gwynne Shotwell in December. The donation will go directly into about 2 million investment accounts of kids ages 11 to 17 who live in ZIP codes with median family incomes of $57,000 or less. Elon Musk in October separately pledged to give every kid in America a share of SpaceX, which could come via Trump Accounts sometime in 2027. Eligible Trump Account holders will begin receiving donated shares of SpaceX stock next month, according to an X post on Friday. "Robert and I are thrilled that our gift of over 2 million shares of SpaceX stock will be distributed to children's Trump accounts in December!" President and COO Gwynne Shotwell wrote in the post. The gift from Shotwell and her husband will provide a share apiece to around 2 million Trump Accounts holders ages 11 to 17 who live in ZIP codes with median family incomes of $57,000 or less, or in ZIP codes with too few residents for a median family income to be reported by the U.S. Census Bureau. These families should receive a notice by Monday, Shotwell wrote on X. "In a few weeks, an additional gift will be finalized for eligible 11 to 17-year-old children in military families serving overseas, children in foster care, and more children whose MFI is $90,000 or less living in counties near our home in the great state of Texas," she also wrote. Parents or guardians can check eligibility for the donation through Invest America, a nonprofit advocacy group, and track account activity with the Trump Accounts app . Children born from 2025 through 2028 may also receive a one-time $1,000 deposit from the U.S. Department of the Treasury. Other funds may also be available, depending on certain criteria. In a separate funding announcement in October, Elon Musk wrote in an X post that he plans to give every kid in America a share of SpaceX sometime in 2027, which may also come via Trump Accounts . The U.S. Department of the Treasury rolled out temporary regulations at the end of September that allow Trump Accounts to hold donated individual stocks, a change from previous guidelines that only allowed diversified, low-cost index funds . The move to permit stock donations could pave the way for more large-scale philanthropic gifts, Internal Revenue Service CEO Frank Bisignano told CNBC's " Squawk Box " on Oct. 8. events.title: Germany says lawmakers’ iPhones may have been hacked with spyware
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. The German government is warning politicians and public figures that they were targeted by government-backed spyware, days after Apple began sending out notifications warning victims that their iPhones may have been hacked. Germany’s federal cybersecurity office, known as the BSI, said in a note over the weekend that it had become aware that members of the Bundestag, Germany’s parliament, and other unnamed notable individuals had received warnings from Apple that they may have been targeted by cyberattacks. Per the Financial Times , German government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said the government in Berlin was “taking the incident and the warning very seriously,” but he did not say who in the federal government had been targeted, including whether German chancellor Friedrich Merz was among them. Apple periodically sends out threat notifications to people it thinks may have been targeted by spyware, which can steal messages, location data, and other sensitive information from their phones. This spyware often relies on zero-click exploits , which can hack individuals almost invisibly as they don’t require a victim to click on a link or open a file. Apple does not attribute attacks to specific governments or say whether someone’s phone has actually been compromised. For that reason, the BSI said that anyone who receives an Apple threat notification “should therefore assume that their device may have been compromised.” Others outside of Germany also received the recent threat alert from Apple. Radwan Mortada, a Beirut-based filmmaker, said in a post on X that he received a new threat notification warning that Apple had detected “another attack against your device,” after an earlier spyware attack targeted him in 2021. It’s unclear who is behind this latest round of spyware attacks, or which government may have orchestrated the targeting. Per the notice received by Mortada, Apple said its latest batch of threat notifications went out to users in 99 countries. The episode highlights again the murky business behind a growing number of attacks against members of civil society. Governments rarely build these tools themselves. Many buy them from private vendors, often called “mercenary spyware” makers, the best known being Israel’s NSO Group, which sells the controversial Pegasus spyware. Germany’s own central federal law agency, the BKA, reportedly bought access to Pegasus in 2019. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Residents campaign for curfew at new Sydney airport due to noise
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Blue Mountains residents unhappy at noise from Western Sydney International Airport David Lysiak has lived in Warrimoo on the footsteps of the Blue Mountains for 44 years. ( ABC News: Simon Amery ) Residents living near the new Western Sydney International Airport are reporting increasing aircraft noise linked to the new Western Sydney airport. Blue Mountains resident David Lysiak says he worries about not being able to sleep at night as flights ramp up. An expert in air traffic managements says there are "no perfect options" when determining flight routes. Residents living in the Blue Mountains say they fear an end to the area's peace and quiet following last week's opening of the Western Sydney International Airport (WSI). The airport officially opened to domestic and international passengers on October 25 amid much fanfare. But a week later, concerns are being raised about aircraft noise. David Lysiak has lived in Warrimoo, a village in the lower Blue Mountains, for 44 years. Sydney's second airport officially opened on October 25. ( ABC News: Declan Bowring ) The retired grandfather and his wife raised four children there, and they have always loved the tranquillity. "It's just beautiful, quiet. Not many people. We have one shop, a general store," he said. "I just wander into the bush and go for a bushwalk, and take your bike down the trails … You ride through a blue gum forest and it's all accessible right from here." But he fears the serenity of the last four decades could be a thing of the past because his beloved town falls under the WSI flight path. Mr Lysiak is concerned for the future of Warrimoo. ( ABC News: Simon Amery ) Freight flights began operating from the airport around the clock in July. Mr Lysiak said he has heard the noise of some freight aircraft "quite distinctly". That sound is only going to become more frequent . International airlines Air New Zealand, Singapore Airlines, Fiji Airways, Qatar Airways and Vietjet Air have so far signed up with WSI, with flights expected to ramp up over the next couple of years. The airport has one active runway. ( Supplied: Australian government ) WSI has one runway, designated as Runway 05 or Runway 23, depending on the direction of use. Flights on Runway 23 arrive from the north-east and depart to the south-west over areas in the city's west and Blue Mountains. Flights on Runway 23 arrive from the north-east and depart to the south-west. ( Supplied: Australian government ) When Runway 05 is used, flights take off to the north-east and land from the south-west. Flights take off to the north-east and land from the south-west when Runway 05 is operational. ( Supplied: Australian government ) Weighing up if a trip from Sydney's new airport is for you The doors to Western Sydney International Airport are set to soon welcome commercial passengers. Airservices Australia has previously said that, where possible, Runway 23 would be prioritised during the day to minimise overflight and noise over residential suburbs to the north-east of the airport. Marek Bekier, a lecturer in air traffic management at the University of New South Wales School of Aviation, said there were always "trade-offs" when deciding on the best flight paths. "An air route connecting an airport to the wider airway system is not just a straight line in the sky," he said. "You have to think about it as a kind of three dimensional corridor that has to fulfil certain requirements. "No option is perfect. You will never find a new route that will basically satisfy the wishes and demands of everyone, so you always have to make some trade-offs." Community treated as 'collateral damage' Julius Timmerman, who moved to the Blue Mountains town of Lawson with his wife in 1996, said people in his community had been treated as "collateral damage". "I'm worried about not being able to sleep at night, just the effect on my amenity because we bought a house in the mountains in good faith that the area would remain quiet and peaceful," he said. "It's completely unfair that the people of Western Sydney and the Blue Mountains should be just treated as collateral damage for the sake of the airline industry." Julius Timmerman says he bought his house in the area thinking it would be quiet. ( Supplied ) He is one of hundreds of people in the community who want a rethink of the flight paths and have signed the Western Sydney Airport Community Impacts Alliance petition calling for a night-time curfew. "The main thing that we want is, as mentioned in the petition, a curfew from 11pm to 6am, which lines up with Kingston Smith Airport," he said.

events.title: Web host Squarespace lays off 19% of its employees
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Squarespace, the web company that helps customers build and host their own websites, is laying off about one-fifth of its workforce, in a move that will affect hundreds of jobs. Jeff Seedman, a public relations specialist representing Squarespace, confirmed the layoffs to TechCrunch. The Verge initially reported the layoffs. “Squarespace is restructuring its organization and reducing its global workforce by approximately 19%, representing around 300 employees,” said Seedman. “The changes are intended to simplify how we operate, sharpen our priorities and enable the company to move faster as we position Squarespace for its next phase of growth.” Website building has changed immensely over the last few years as a result of the generative AI boom. “Vibe-coding” website builders, which only require simple prompts from users to spin up functional front-end designs, have largely upended the industry, making it possible for users to create sites with significantly less effort. These kinds of sites have become an increasingly central part of the website-building business. Last year, web host rival Wix bought Base44 for $80 million . Similar offerings, like Lovable, have generated significant investor interest; Lovable raised a $400 million Series C round in August that valued the company at $13.3 billion. Google also recently launched Stitch , a feature that allows users to swiftly generate user-interface designs. Squarespace has also begun a big push into AI. In 2024, the company launched an AI tool called Blueprint. The company also recently announced Forma, an upcoming AI native platform, whose waitlist users can join . Squarespace was founded in 2004 and went public in 2021 at a $10 billion valuation. However, the company struggled in the ensuing years to generate enthusiastic public market interest. Squarespace ultimately decided to go private again by way of a $7 billion private equity deal in 2024. An earlier version of this report incorrectly stated that Squarespace had not yet launched AI tools; the story has been updated.
