events.title: Hardware Defense Blocks Memory-Dependent Prefetcher Leakage (KU Leuven)
events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports Researchers at KU Leuven and EURECOM published “SecDMP: Provably Secure Data Memory-Dependent Prefetching.” Abstract Excerpt : “In this work, we address this gap by designing a defense that is both secure and efficient. First, we propose a classification of DMP leakage, categorize existing and novel attacks, and analyze which leakage classes are mitigated by existing defenses. We validate this analysis empirically by implementing the first open-source DMPs on a RISC-V processor, showing that the only existing defense that aims to preserve DMP performance fails to protect against entire leakage classes. Next, we propose SecDMP, a provably secure and efficient hardware-based defense. SecDMP requires secrets to be marked in memory and ensures that DMPs never encode these secrets in the microarchitecture—without compromising performance for public data. We formally prove that SecDMP introduces no leakage beyond a baseline semantics without DMPs. Notably, when combined with speculative-execution defenses, SecDMP restores complete microarchitectural security for constant-time code. Finally, our empirical evaluation shows that SecDMP prevents all DMP leakage while incurring minimal performance overhead and hardware cost.” Find the technical paper here . events.title: Fed will vote on rates less often. What that could mean for borrowers
events.summary: After the Federal Reserve meeting in October, Chairman Kevin Warsh unveiled changes that would reduce the number of rate-setting votes. The move could mean consumers wait longer for their borrowing costs to come down. Economists say consumers may be even more affected by the lack of transparency, as Warsh also implements measures to curtail so-called forward guidance. After the Federal Reserve held its benchmark interest rate steady last week, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh announced plans to reduce the number of rate-setting votes over the next two years. That move could potentially extend the timeline for everyday Americans to see borrowing costs adjust, some experts say. "Fewer Fed meetings in 2027 could mean consumers wait longer to see relief when borrowing costs are elevated," said James Vrachas, executive director at advisory firm Post Oak Group. Americans may feel somewhat removed from the Fed, but the central bank's moves have a ripple effect on many types of consumer products, including the borrowing rates for credit cards , home loans and auto financing. Midterm election: How affordability and the economy could affect voters' decisions These Senate races may help determine the fate of Social Security Social Security: How much money beneficiaries may lose if Congress does nothing Trump Account holders to receive SpaceX stock from Gwynne Shotwell in December CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 ranked CNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026 For example, most credit cards have variable rates tied to the prime rate, which moves with the Fed's benchmark. However, even with the central bank holding rates unchanged, credit card rates are edging higher as issuers protect themselves from risk, according to LendingTree. Card issuers are mitigating their exposure from borrowers who may fall behind on payments or default in the face of stubborn inflation in everyday expenses, said Matt Schulz, LendingTree's chief credit analyst. Generally, card issuers are slow to bring rates down, unless prompted by the Fed's actions, said Schulz: "Issuers will tinker with rates a bit at the margins at other times, but the big moves tend to only come when issuers are pushed." On Oct. 28, the central bank voted to keep the benchmark borrowing rate at the current target range of 3.75% to 4% as policymakers deliberated next steps with inflation remaining well above the Fed's 2% goal. The Fed will keep meeting eight times a year, Warsh said at the news conference following the October meeting, but next year, one of the eight meetings will not entail a vote on interest rates or include a post-meeting statement. The "strategy" meetings will increase to two the following year, leaving just six opportunities to adjust rates — with the exception of emergency meetings, if necessary. "For consumers, that could mean longer periods of uncertainty around borrowing costs," said Jordan Ricciardi, a senior wealth strategy associate at UBS. "Our clients looking to buy a home, refinance a mortgage or finance a business could be impacted as fewer scheduled opportunities means the Fed isn't as quickly responding to changing economic conditions." Borrowing rates may stay elevated for longer With fewer scheduled opportunities to adjust rates, that means borrowing rates could remain stubbornly high even if economic conditions begin to improve, Post Oak Group's Vrachas also said. As it stands, financial institutions can adjust rates whenever market conditions warrant, regardless of the Fed's meeting schedule, he said. In the meantime, though, many consumers may continue to face elevated borrowing costs for mortgages, car loans and credit card debt, among other financial products. "For consumers, the bigger concern isn't necessarily fewer meetings, but whether lenders pass along lower borrowing costs as quickly as they pass along increases," Vrachas said. 'Warsh keeps his proverbial cards closer to his chest' Consumers may be even more impacted by the lack of transparency, economists say, as Warsh implements measures to curtail so-called forward guidance, or how the Fed signals its future rate moves. Although economic conditions have become more complicated and information is more widely available, "Warsh keeps his proverbial cards closer to his chest than his recent predecessors have," said Mark Hamrick, an economic analyst and founder of The Hamrick Brief, a weekly newsletter. "I wouldn't expect consumers to see the universe of market rates change simply because the Fed votes less often," he said. "But the public may have less opportunity to hear from the source about how and why the Fed is making the decisions that shape what they pay to borrow and what they earn on their savings." In the interim, "the best protection for consumers remains shopping around, particularly for the highest yields among savings accounts and [certificates of deposit]," Hamrick said.

events.title: New York Times and other outlets sue web browser Brave over alleged content scraping
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. The New York Times sued Brave, the 11-year-old, privacy-focused browser company, on Monday, alleging it scraped the outlet’s copyrighted content and unlawfully distributed it to customers the suit names as Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI, and Cohere. Separately on Monday, the Daily News, the Chicago Tribune, and the Orlando Sentinel filed a similar lawsuit. Both were brought in federal court in Manhattan. The New York Times, which has also sued OpenAI and Perplexity over similar claims, likens Brave to a “supplier, dealer, and distributor of stolen copyrighted content” for AI companies. “In this way, Brave acts both like a burglar that misappropriates the content of publishers, and an AI ‘fence’ that sells stolen content to third parties,” the suit reads. It says Brave built an index of more than 30 billion web pages using an unidentified crawler, leaving publishers unable to block it. The suit also targets a Brave browser feature that bypasses paywalls and the company’s practice of blocking publishers’ ads while selling its own. Founded in 2015, Brave has raised roughly $250 million to date, according to private-market trackers. The Times seeks an injunction and damages. Brave did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Snap has reached a settlement in a lawsuit brought by two teenagers who accused the company of designing its platform to be addictive and contributing to their depression, anxiety, and eating disorders, as first reported by Reuters . The plaintiffs had previously reached settlements with Meta, TikTok, and YouTube. The trial was set to be Snap’s first in a broader wave of litigation over social media’s impact on young users. They said they developed compulsive usage habits, which they attributed to features such as autoplay and infinite scrolling. “The Parties are pleased to have been able to resolve this matter in an amicable manner,” a Snap spokesperson said in a statement to TechCrunch. “We’ve built safeguards, launched safety tutorials, and partnered with experts and because safety is never finished, we remain committed to continually strengthening the safety, privacy, and well-being of our community.” Social media giants are facing thousands of lawsuits in federal and state courts over claims that they knowingly designed their platforms to hook young users and fuel a youth mental health crisis involving anxiety, depression, and suicide. events.title: Who is hacking Europe’s supermarket fridges and freezers, and why?
events.summary: After a second apparent cyber-attack in weeks, we examine possible culprits and their motives Shop fridges and freezers across Europe hit by fresh suspected cyber-attack Supermarket fridges and freezers in seven European countries have malfunctioned , their thermostats remotely cranked up in some cases to 50C (122F). The EU has condemned what it said was “a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence in it”. Which supermarkets were affected and what does it mean? The attack hit fridges in Belgian branches of Carrefour, Intermarché and Ikea, Coop and ICA in Sweden, Delhaize in Luxembourg, Kesko in Finland, SuperValu in Ireland and shops in Estonia. It appeared to be a reprise of attacks three weeks ago when French retailers had to ditch huge amounts of food when their fridges suddenly overheated as a result of anonymous hackers seizing control of their internet-exposed appliance management software. Something similar may have happened in the US in early August when a series of mysterious fridge malfunctions hit commissaries at least six military bases. The Pentagon is investigating a suspected hack. This is feared to signal a new front in cyber-attack and hacking tactics. Fridges are not unique in having their controls exposed to hackers. Many ovens, washing machines, dishwashers and central heating systems are linked to the internet to allow remote access and automated control. No politically motivated “hacktivist” group has claimed responsibility and neither has a ransomware gang exploited the vulnerability to demand the supermarkets pay – which in any event would be difficult because the damage is already done when their fridges overheat. “The two most plausible attribution scenarios for me are some kind of state-based signalling and demonstration of capability or some kind of lone-wolf hacker that is conducting these attacks for their own personal reasons,” said Rafe Pilling, the senior director for threat intelligence at the cybersecurity company Sophos. The state-linked actor theory seems most likely, in part because of the obvious psychological impact on large populations of seeing food stripped from shelves. North Korea is believed to have been behind last week’s Binance cryptocurrency heist, but in this case hackers linked to Russia and China are also likely to be in the frame. Western intelligence chiefs say Moscow is waging a campaign of sabotage in Europe that takes many different forms and is likely to intensify in the coming months. Discerning the culprit is made harder by the relative simplicity of the hack. No malware was needed, which means there is no trace of a weapon at the scene of the crime. Pilling compared it to “wearing rubber gloves and messing with the switches”. The software that manages commercial fridges is connected to the internet, which means lines of code can be left vulnerable to hackers. Unlike desktop or mobile devices, on which users and IT managers are often alerted to the need to install updates that contain patches to repair constantly emerging vulnerabilities, the software in items such as fridges can be left for long periods without updates. Nick Jackson, the director of cyber-operations at the cybersecurity company Bitdefender, said one reason companies might move slowly to install patches is they can take time to run, which leaves periods when machinery needs to be offline – an obvious problem for food retailers. But he said a simpler explanation could be that the people running the fridges are not aware of the problem, “don’t think about that and it’s not top of their agenda”. In Monday’s wave of incidents, Coop in Sweden said some of its fridges were linked to a 4G mobile network that made them more exposed. ICA said its system was provided by Danfoss, the Danish company that had problems in France. What can shops do to defend themselves? The simple answer is to patch their software systems. According to the Belgian refrigerator group Sabcobel, the impact of Monday’s hack could have been far worse if they had not started patching fridges after the 12 October attack in France. In the UK, which has not yet been affected, retailers are “currently working with the National Cyber Security Centre(NSCC) to ensure their fridges and freezers are secure as possible against potential attacks” said Graham Wynn, the assistant director of regulatory affairs at the British Retail Consortium. Why have British supermarkets not been hit yet? Internet-exposed refrigeration systems are most popular in countries including France, Italy, Greece and Belgium, according to the cybersecurity company Forescout. Daniel dos Santos, its vice president of research, said: “When we checked the data for these exposed systems online of supermarkets, the UK is not in the top 10.” He said the risk was not negligible, but “I wouldn’t say it’s super-high right now for the UK specifically”.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Videostrong accused of shipping devices with a backdoor baked in Max-severity bug in widely used OT programming tool exploited to deliver Linux malware 7 hours ago Thieves pilfer environment variables from Trigger AI workflow tool 14 hours ago Token thieves costing companies $100K+ per day in illicit LLM charges 14 hours ago Nuclear threats and street brawls: Russia, Ukraine report attacks on their emergency alert apps 16 hours ago Frozen part II: Hackers remotely defrost produce in Euro supermarkets ... again 17 hours ago A coalition of private-sector security firms working with Japan’s National Police Agency has disrupted XCPE, a backdoor used to build a massive botnet comprising more than 1.3 million Android devices across more than 200 countries. Google, Lumen, Human Security, Plume, Synthient, and TrendAI participated in the disruption. “We assess with high confidence that the backdoor and botnet were intentionally developed, deployed, and operated for financial gain by Videostrong Technology,” the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said in a Monday blog. Videostrong Technology is a hardware manufacturer based in Shenzhen, China. It builds Android devices, including home TV boxes and projectors. According to Google, Videostrong deliberately embedded the XCPE backdoor in device firmware and sold access to criminal affiliates , allowing them to install additional malware modules on devices shipped to unsuspecting customers. When buyers connected these devices to their home networks, the preinstalled backdoor allowed operators to create proxy networks and hide malicious traffic using the customers' internet connections without their knowledge. The firmware’s pre-installed management agent purported to be a standard remote-management client, according to TrendAI. It pulled updates from a GitHub page, and connected to a Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) server that gave the operator full remote control of each box, allowing them to install and remove apps, change settings, and push updates to the infected devices. Between June 3 and October 1, TrendAI documented more than 3.8 million distinct home and mobile IP addresses connected to the operation. The coalition also disrupted the command-and-control domains used to manage the affiliate modules. “Because these affiliates each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE, we assess that taking down their C2 domains will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices,” according to GTIG. Google said it had since cut ties with Videostrong, and banned the OEM from making devices with preloaded Google apps. Videostrong did not immediately respond to The Register’ s inquiries. This backdoor and botnet operation is part of the same ecosystem as BadBox 2.0 , another notorious botnet that infected more than 10 million TV boxes and other devices before Human, Google, and TrendAI disrupted it in March 2025.® Open models can do 90 percent of agentic work at a twentieth of the cost of a frontier LLM: Gartner Models are commodities, harnesses are the valuable part Architect creates open-source replacement for VM migration tool VMware has hidden OpenVDDK is reportedly already being used in production, at scale From expertise to intelligence: NISCO deploys world's first swarm-intelligence steel model at scale PARTNER CONTENT: 300+ AI applications delivering surges in core metrics and annual cost reduction of over CNY100m Toyota shows off SoC that stores model weights and its OS on integrated memory Accessing external memory puts the brakes on physical AI, so carmaker has found an economical and speedy shortcut Microsoft's moolah mountain is more massive than ever.

events.title: I used to be a supermarket cake decorator. Here are 9 of my best tips for ordering a cake.
events.summary: Many supermarkets offer the option to walk in and grab a cake from their bakery case, as well as the option to order a custom cake. Molly Allen I worked as a supermarket cake decorator for two years before opening my own bakery . Ask for whipped cream if you want a less-sweet cake, or for two cake flavors to please more guests. It could be worth asking about free smash cakes or using your own toys for kids' birthday cakes . Supermarket cakes can be an easy, more affordable way to celebrate any occasion. However, not all of these cakes are served and created equally. Take it from me: I worked in the bakery section of a popular supermarket for two years, prepping treats and decorating cakes, before opening my own bakery. Here are my go-to tips for ordering the best cake from your local supermarket.  Place your order long before your party Some supermarkets bake cakes on-site, but many work with prebaked, frozen cakes. In these cases, the bakery will keep a stock of common cake flavors (vanilla, chocolate) on hand, and maybe a more limited selection of additional flavor choices (carrot, red velvet, marble).  To make sure you get the flavor you want, order your custom cake with two to three weeks' notice. This can help give the decorator and the bakery time to ensure your desired flavor is in stock. Ask for whipped cream if you think grocery-store cakes are too sweet Ask for whipped cream if the frosting on supermarket cakes is usually too sweet for you. Jasmin Merdan/Getty Images If you've stayed away from grocery-store cakes because the typical buttercream frosting is a bit too sweet for you, check if the bakery has other options.  Vanilla buttercream is often a default choice, but it's usually not the only one. Some supermarket bakeries can use fresh whipped cream for topping a cake. Other choices might include cream-cheese frosting , chocolate frosting, coconut-pecan frosting typically used for German chocolate cakes, and even chocolate ganache. Generally, you won't know for sure unless you ask. Check if the bakery can do half-and-half flavors You may not have to choose between chocolate or vanilla cake. When ordering, ask about doing half vanilla and half chocolate so everyone at your party can enjoy a slice of their preferred flavor. This is often possible with half-sheet cakes and two-layer round cakes. (And it might also work with other cake flavors, too.) Order with the cake decorator if you want something very specific Cake decorators can sometimes work early hours. gerenme/Getty Images You can generally speak with any bakery employee to order a cake, but if you have a specific or out-of-the-box request for decorations, ask when you can speak with the cake decorator by phone or in person. In my experience, they often work early shifts so they can begin preparing orders and items for the display case. Decorating is their specialty, and they can be the best person to tell you if tackling the specific design you're hoping for is achievable. And, if not, they may be able to help brainstorm an alternative. Consider bringing in your own toys for kids' cakes Supermarket bakeries usually have a look book of designs that cake decorators are trained to make, and children's cakes often include character toys from popular movies and shows. If the bakery doesn't have your child's favorite character, don't be afraid to ask staff what's possible. Depending on the store and decorator, you may be able to bring in small, washed figurines for the decorator to incorporate into the design. Or you can try asking the decorator to leave space for a specific toy when creating the design. Don't be afraid to order a plain cake if you want to dress it up yourself Remember that cake decorators don't have to dress up your cake with a border, sprinkles, and writing if you don't want them to. If you want a semi-customized dessert, just order a plain, frosted cake in your desired size. That way, you can take it home and turn it into anything you want. Add edible flowers to dress it up for a more formal occasion, or top it with candy and sprinkles in your desired shades. You can even try adding your own fun candles, toys, and knickknacks on top. Request a plastic cake container instead of a bakery box Premade birthday cakes can usually be customized. iStock / Getty Images Plus At many bakeries, custom cake orders are packaged in cardboard boxes for pickup. If you anticipate you'll have leftover cake, ask for a plastic cake container instead. This will provide an airtight solution for easily storing leftovers. Keep in mind that this tip may not work for every bakery, and it could depend on the supplies they have on hand. Ask about a free smash cake for kids If you're planning to order a birthday cake for a young child, ask if your supermarket bakery also offers free smash cakes. A smash cake is tiny, typically 4 inches in diameter, meant just for a kid to dig into on their birthday. These are usually served alongside a larger sheet cake meant for guests. Some bakeries will give you a free smash cake when you order a larger decorated cake or meet a minimum order size. Check last-minute options if you forgot to order ahead Even if you forgot to order a few weeks in advance, there may still be options the store's cake decorator can pull together for you. If it's a few days before your event, or the morning of, it doesn't hurt to ask. The decorator may be able to put together a simple design while you shop for other items in the store. Or you can grab a premade option from the bakery case and ask for writing on top and extra sprinkles along the edges to spruce it up. Just keep in mind that your options may depend on how busy the bakery is when you visit. This story was originally published on March 25, 2023, and most recently updated on November 2, 2026. events.title: Co-Optimizing Access Points Improves Analog Placement (UT Austin)
events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports Researchers at the University of Texas at Austin published “APPlace: Co-Optimizing Device Locations and Access Points for Routing-Aware Analog Placement.” Abstract “Analog layout automation remains challenging in Analog/Mixed-Signal circuit design, because parasitics and mismatches introduced during layout strongly affect circuit performance. Placement is especially critical among the layout stages, as it constrains the routing solution space and the achievable post-layout performance. Existing analytical placement methods optimize device coordinates under center-based wirelength proxies and leave access point (AP) selection to routing. In analog circuits, however, a routing pin is an extended piece of terminal metal rather than a fixed point, and the best AP on it depends on where the other connected devices are placed, so a coordinate-only placement optimizes for connection points that the router will not use. We present APPlace, a routing-aware analog placement framework that co-optimizes device locations and AP selections during global placement, followed by a legalization stage that preserves the structure established by global placement. Experimental results on four real-world analog benchmarks show that APPlace achieves better overall post-layout performance than representative baselines at comparable layout area. Ablation studies further show that removing AP co-optimization causes up to a 13 dB CMRR loss among the OTA benchmarks and a 23% increase in comparator delay.” Find the technical paper here . events.title: Approval of cheap version of HIV-prevention shot raises hopes in low-income countries
events.summary: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved a generic version of the world’s only twice-a-year shot to prevent HIV The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved a generic version of the world’s only twice-a-year shot to prevent HIV — a big step toward making the drug available inexpensively and more quickly in 120 low- and middle-income countries. The announcement was made on Monday morning by the manufacturer and organizations that helped to speed up development of the medication, called lenacapavir. The drug is expected to cost $40 a year per person in the countries where it will be available, the same price as daily preventive pills available now. But the shots are much more convenient than the pills because they’re needed much less frequently and they nearly eliminated new infections in two groundbreaking studies of people at high risk . People don’t always take their daily dose of medication, “and if you do not take it, you cannot get protected against HIV,” said Carmen Pérez Casas, HIV lead for the grant-making organization Unitaid, a global health agency. “With lenacapavir, we are much more hopeful.” Ultimately, advocates said, the medication should help drive down cases of HIV and AIDS — and deaths. According to the World Health Organization, 41 million people worldwide were living with HIV and 570,000 died from HIV-related causes last year. With an affordable, high-quality generic medication now available, “we could help to scale this to the 20 million people around the world who need PrEP,” prescription medicine taken by people at risk of HIV before being exposed to the virus, said Carolyn Amole, who leads the HIV program for the Clinton Health Access Initiative, a global health organization. “And if we scale to those levels,” she added, “we can actually begin to bring an end to the HIV epidemic.” Generic lenacapavir can’t be sold in the U.S. because a brand-name version, Yeztugo, made by Gilead Sciences and approved last year, is still protected by a patent. The U.S. list price for that version, meaning the cost before insurance, is $28,218 a year. Gilead officials say that’s similar to some other types of PrEP, which stands for pre-exposure prophylaxis. The new generic was approved by the FDA under a longstanding practice designed to ensure the quality of HIV-related drugs provided to other countries by the U.S. government. Approval of a drug by the U.S. FDA can speed regulatory approval in many other countries. The approval is considered “tentative,” the FDA's standard designation for generics while the originator remains under patent. Until now, Gilead has been the sole supplier of lenacapavir, and demand has outstripped supply in low- and middle-income countries. Last year, Gilead established royalty-free licensing agreements with six generic manufacturers to enable production. Those voluntary licenses cover a specific set of countries in sub-Saharan Africa, Asia and Latin America. “We share the sense of urgency around expanding access to lenacapavir for HIV prevention,” a Gilead spokesperson said in a statement. “We believe we have enabled the fastest and most sustainable path to expanding access for communities most affected by HIV.” The generic was developed by India-based Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories under an agreement brokered by Unitaid, the Clinton Health Access Initiative and Wits RHI, a health research institute in Africa. The partners sought to accelerate development and make the drug available at an affordable price. Learjet with 9 aboard crashes in Palm Beach County, Florida: FAA Sen. Chris Murphy hospitalized after suffering a stroke, chief of staff says 2 college students found dead after going missing while hiking, police say Common side effects with lenacapavir include injection site reactions, headache and nausea. People also must be tested for HIV prior to starting the drug and with each injection; drug-resistant HIV has been identified when used by people with an undiagnosed HIV infection. “For any kind of PrEP … you need to have HIV testing in advance,” said Saiqa Mullick, director of implementation science with Wits RHI. “For many of the low- and middle-income countries, that is a rapid test.” Generic lenacapavir should start to become available in some places within weeks, those helping with the effort said, although it could take a bit longer in countries that require the drug to go through their own approval processes before people can start taking it. Generic versions made by the other manufacturers have yet to be approved by FDA. “The work is not done. Now, we need the funding to actually buy it for everyone who needs it and then we need to do the hard work of getting it to the millions of people who need it and want it,” Amole said. “But this is a great milestone.” Casas said she’s optimistic that scientific advances — along with political will and funding — can help the world curb HIV. “Now,” she said, “we have the tools.

events.title: John Deere built an AI assistant to stop farmers from drowning in decades of field data
events.summary: John Deere announced its new AI assistant at the Farm Progress Show in Iowa. Marcin Golba/NurPhoto via Getty Images John Deere's AI assistant, unveiled in September, helps farmers analyze data quickly. JD is embedded in John Deere's Operations Center, a digital farm management system. Farmers are warming to AI, but accuracy and data privacy remain concerns. Farmers have more data than ever about their fields, equipment, and crops. But turning it into a decision could take weeks. John Deere says its new AI assistant, JD, can do it in minutes. The agricultural manufacturing company announced the tool in September at the Farm Progress Show in Iowa. JD is integrated within John Deere's Operations Center, which is a digital farm management system that connects farmers' field and machine data into one platform. Farmers can ask JD questions on their mobile devices, such as the best time to harvest based on past trends, or which sprayer covers the most acres per hour. Melissa Neuendorf, the principal product manager for customer AI solutions at John Deere, told Business Insider that JD came about because farmers consistently said they were struggling to manage their abundant data. "We're now at a point where farmers have so much data that they have a difficult time finding the insights manually themselves," Neuendorf said. While smaller agricultural tech companies such as OneSoil, VisorPro, Arable, and AgZen are developing generative AI tools to give insights on specific equipment or crop metrics, Deere is among the first major agricultural-equipment makers to put a large language model AI assistant directly inside a platform that combines farmers' field, machine, and operational data. JD's launch shows how generative AI is becoming a central part of crop management. "Prior to John Deere's announcement, this didn't exist in the industry," said Matt Darr, a professor in the agricultural and biosystems engineering department at Iowa State University, who was in the room when Deere announced JD. Why farmers are considering AI tools more than ever Farmers have been collecting data for decades. But now, modern farm equipment is outfitted with additional technology and sensors, creating large volumes of data that are difficult to keep up with. It can be stressful for farmers who must also navigate tight margins, unpredictable weather , and limited planting windows. Plus, "most farmers aren't data scientists on the side," Darr said. Neuendorf said dissecting vast datasets is complex and time-consuming, sometimes requiring weeks. That's where AI can help farmers: "AI provides them the capability to do a lot of that analysis in minutes," she said. Before coming up with JD, Deere launched an AI tool last August that allowed farmers to ask questions in natural language about Deere's help documentation and operator manuals. This replaced the manual task of farmers flipping through pages of operator manuals. The tool received positive feedback, prompting Deere to broaden its application and launch JD to answer specific questions on the spot. Farmers can input data into the Operations Center from non-John Deere equipment if they use machinery from other manufacturers. Then, if they query JD, it can analyze all of that data to deliver answers. The Operations Center and JD are free to use, Neuendorf said. The AI assistant is available through an early access program, in which interested customers sign up for a waitlist and are considered for participation. John Deere will make JD broadly available in mid-November Neuendorf told Business Insider that the feedback from farmers so far has been positive. Neuendorf said she recently spoke to a farmer who was driving past a field and noticed it had lower weed pressure, or fewer weeds present, than other fields. Through JD, the farmer was able to open John Deere's mobile app right away, ask the assistant about previous years, and understand how he managed the field differently. Winning farmer trust in AI technology A McKinsey global survey of 5,500 farmers, published in September, found that 72% expect generative AI to impact operations within five years, but only 17% use the tech right now. One reason only a minority of farmers use AI is because they're worried about data privacy and how their information could impact commodity prices, Darr said. "These are competitive businesses," Darr added. "How information is used can influence global markets and what happens to global commodity pricing." John Deere said in its release announcing JD that it doesn't sell farm data or use it for agriculture commodity trading or speculation. Katya Kheistver, the chief product and operating officer of OneSoil, an agricultural technology company, said farmers won't trust AI if it delivers generic advice rather than insights tied to specific, real field data. Farmers often start their use of AI by checking the tech's outputs against what they already know. The farmer "watches whether the answer lines up with reality," and if it does so consistently, trust grows, Kheistver said. The stakes are high if farmers make decisions based on AI-generated answers because they have "one chance a year to grow a crop," Darr said. They need to be able to trust that an AI tool is accurate. JD meshes high-quality datasets with advanced LLMs, Darr added, which sets the AI tool apart and promises a high degree of accuracy. Neuendorf said JD is configured to notify farmers when field data is missing, rather than making inaccurate assumptions or generating false advice. This configuration also encourages farmers to input additional data, so JD can derive more insights and help farmers "make better decisions for the next season," Neuendorf said. events.title: The internet's latest obsession: The end of the world
events.summary: The world seems convinced the end is near — and social media is amplifying that belief, convincing people to stock up on food, water, generators and other items. Why it matters: Online chatter is fueling viral predictions of societal collapse amid growing unease about the future. But you're probably not going to die tomorrow. What they're saying: Michael Mills, a researcher at the University of Kent who has studied doomsday prepping for more than a decade, told Axios that modern doomsday fears aren't necessarily about a specific apocalyptic scenario. "It's an overall reaction to uncertainty in most cases," Mills said. He noted that whereas Cold War-era survivalists were often focused on nuclear conflict, modern preppers worry about terrorism, climate disasters, geopolitical threats and emerging technologies. He described the modern mindset as a "multifaceted concern with uncertainty." State of play: Viral posts have repeatedly urged people around the world to stock up on food and water, following similar recommendations from various governments and warnings from former FBI Deputy Director Dan Bongino. The situation has gotten so buzzy that President Trump was asked about it in an interview Monday. He said Americans don't need to stock up because the U.S. is "in good shape. We're strong. We have a great military and we will not have those kind of problems." Separately, conservative commentator Tucker Carlson — a man with 17.9 million followers on X alone — published a lengthy post Sunday evening alleging that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is pressuring Trump to launch renewed attacks on Iran after the midterms, potentially with a nuclear weapon. For what it's worth, Carlson has been predicting similar doomsday scenarios for a while, and he's been wrong before. And the Pentagon's newly reported plan calls for U.S. military bases to prepare to operate without outside support for at least 90 days, terrifying some people into asking , "What's the government know that they're not telling us?" The big picture: Worries about financial insecurity , skyrocketing health care costs , a lack of rainy-day savings and younger generations' perceived inability to buy a house all contribute to the feeling that life is not okay. Then you've got AI , which could cut thousands of jobs, enable a cyberattack or help engineer a dangerous, and potentially deadly, biological disease. And then there's the geopolitical situation: wars, genocide and the possibility of global warfare as China continues to threaten Taiwan and rumors abound that the U.S. and Israel will reignite the Iran war with a fresh round of attacks. Zoom in: Political uncertainty can also fuel doomsday prediction culture, particularly around major elections . Mills described the prepper movement as historically right-leaning, with fears increasing during the Obama and Biden administrations and subsiding among some preppers after Trump's 2016 victory. During elections, "where it can often seem that everything is at stake... we don't know which way those contests are going to go and so naturally that uncertainty kind of flares up," Mills said. Reality check: Preparing for a catastrophe doesn't make you a conspiracy theorist. Governments commonly warn people about potential disasters, like advising them to evacuate before a hurricane. Mills distinguishes ordinary emergency readiness from prepping, which typically involves preparing for disasters lasting weeks or months, sometimes longer. The bottom line: Nobody knows what catastrophe, if any, might come next. But feeling prepared and stocking up for a couple of days without power can make sitting in the dark a little less scary. events.title: Owner of private Serbian bank detained and accused of siphoning money
events.summary: Serbian authorities have detained the owner of a private bank on suspicion he was siphoning money from the lender BELGRADE, Serbia -- BELGRADE, Serbia (AP) — Serbian authorities Monday detained the owner of a private bank on suspicion he was siphoning money from the lender that was used for some public utility payments during the previous government of former President Aleksandar Vucic. Alta Bank rose to prominence under the rule of Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party that was ousted from power in a parliamentary election last week. The bank has handled all electricity payments by millions of users in the capital Belgrade, as well as public parking accounts. On Saturday, Serbia’s Central Bank revoked Alta Bank’s operating license and launched bankruptcy proceedings to protect the bank’s depositors, saying that its liquidity “has deteriorated significantly” and “could worsen further." Serbia’s Deposit Insurance Agency, which guarantees deposits of up to 50,000 euros ($56,000), will act as Alta Bank's bankruptcy administrator, the central bank said. Davor Macura, the bank owner who initially owned an exchange office before becoming a prominent banker, was given a 48-hour detention on Monday, prosecutors said. Macura’s lawyers told local media he was present at the bank headquarters in Belgrade and fully cooperated during an hourslong police search over the weekend. Lawyers added that Macura will be questioned by the public prosecutor on Tuesday. Macura, whose businesses also span retail and construction, is suspected of illegally moving 45 billion dinars ($428 million) out of Alta Bank’s vault. Two other persons were also held for aiding and abetting the crime. The moves against Alta Bank and its owner came as part of a wave of changes triggered by Vucic’s defeat in the Oct. 25 election that also included resignations in the state-run media, arrests of several officials and an announced review of long-standing corruption cases. Former central bank governor Kori Udovicki on Sunday criticized the Serbian Central Bank moves as too slow. She said on RTS television that the central bank “lost a week in which it could have limited the bank’s ability to transfer the money abroad or to the connected individuals.” Alta Bank is a rare Serbian lender that allowed tens of thousands of Russian émigrés to open personal and business accounts. Scores of Russians have moved to Russia-friendly Serbia since the start of the invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Alta Bank's troubles resonated outside Serbia. The Central Bank of North Macedonia put Alta Bank’s subsidiary into temporary administration and limited cash withdrawals to 160 euros ($179) per week, while Montenegro's banking regulator shut down payment processing company Alta Pay. Learjet with 9 aboard crashes in Palm Beach County, Florida: FAA Sen. Chris Murphy hospitalized after suffering a stroke, chief of staff says 2 college students found dead after going missing while hiking, police say In Serbia, armed police could be seen guarding the bank's offices in Belgrade after dozens of customers stood in long lines over the weekend trying to withdraw their savings. Serbian investigative outlets in the past have described Macura as a tycoon whose political connections to Vucic and his SNS helped him win lucrative contracts with state agencies and public enterprises. In 2024, Macura’s Alta Group came under scrutiny by the European Central Bank, or ECB, when it attempted to acquire a 20% stake in Austria’s Addiko Group through two connected firms to avoid triggering the ECB’s approval requirement. The ECB spotted this and stopped the deal. It also questioned the anti-money laundering controls and the source of funds in Macura's network. The Association of Serbian Banks called Alta Bank's collapse “an individual issue” and said it would not affect other banks. The SNS, which has governed Serbia since 2012, lost the parliamentary election to the student-led Student List movement. The outgoing authorities remain in control until a formal transition of power, expected to take several weeks. Critics say the SNS has steadily taken control of state institutions since it came to power. events.title: Trump administration turns to SCOTUS in California ballot case
events.summary: The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to mandate that California separate ballots of more than 20,000 voters the government suspects are "likely" non-citizens. The big picture: A federal appeals court rejected the administration's bid to set aside mail ballots last week, erecting another roadblock in the DOJ's pre-election quest to demand the state root out claims of voter fraud in the final days of the midterm elections. Driving the news: "Once California commingles the challenged ballots with lawful ones, there is no way to get the challenged ballots back," the DOJ wrote in an application filed to the high court. "The only way to preserve the district court's ability to grant relief to the United States after a full merits proceeding, therefore, is to segregate the challenged ballots now," the application, signed by Solicitor General D. John Sauer, continued. The DOJ's initial lawsuit came after the administration threatened California officials with emergency court action unless it probed potential ineligible voters over 48 hours and set aside ballots. Catch up quick: A federal appeals court and a federal judge stymied the administration's bid. U.S. District Judge David Carter cast doubt on the government's voter lists in a late October order denying the administration's request for a temporary restraining order, citing the "vagueness" of the government's "descriptions of its procedures and the unreliability of its similar claims in other states." And in last week's 2–1 ruling, a federal appeals court found that granting the request "would provoke catastrophic change, upending the administration of the election." What they're saying: "We will continue pursuing every available legal avenue to protect the integrity of our elections and ensure federal law is enforced," Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said in a statement shared to X. The California Secretary of State's office did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters IP house believes optics demand is going to explode as Nvidia and others eye bigger systems Anthropic's compute tab could top $1T as Q3 revenue nears $17B 7 hours ago Microsoft's moolah mountain is more massive than ever. It just doesn't want the people who built it 20 hours ago Google's AI satellite sends a very expensive haiku to Earth 2 days ago Amazon sends chills through its workforce with mixed message memo about AI use 2 days ago Backbone of a beast – charting Nvidia's rise to networking titan 2 days ago Hoping to dominate the next phase of AI networking, Marvell Technology plans to acquire photonics giant Lumentum in an all-stock deal valued at $115 billion. The move will fill several key gaps in Marvell's photonics portfolio, particularly with regard to high-performance laser sources, optical transceivers, optical circuit switches, and specialized compound semiconductor manufacturing capabilities involving indium phosphide. Higher speed interconnects combined with larger compute domains are the driving forces behind the move to photonics. As interconnects push beyond 400 Gbps per lane, copper interconnects are being pushed to their limit, necessitating denser, hotter rack systems. Optics offer a reprieve from these scaling laws. Traditional copper wire can only maintain a 400 Gbps signal over about 1.25 meters. Every time the per lane speed doubles, the reach is halved. Photonics are largely immune to this and can push that signal over kilometers, enabling infrastructure providers to scale their systems across entire aisles, while also reducing the power and cooling requirements of each individual rack. Due to close in the first half of 2028, the all-stock transaction comes as AI infrastructure builders, including Nvidia and AMD, eye larger rack-scale systems, which will rely heavily on optical interconnects to stitch hundreds and even thousands of GPUs together into a single compute domain for training or inference. At Computex 2026 in Taipei earlier this year, Jensen Huang predicted that Marvell's long-term investments in photonics would catapult the IP house to a $1 trillion valuation. That hasn't happened just yet – the company’s market cap currently sits at just $180 billion – but it seems Marvell isn't above buying its way to the finish line by snapping up optics vendors before the AI boom sends their valuations skyrocketing. As we've previously reported , the move to optical scale up networks has fueled a flurry of investment in optics, silicon photonics development, and manufacturing. Nvidia itself invested $2 billion into Lumentum just eight months ago to bolster its optics manufacturing capacity. The limiting factor up to this point has been power. When Nvidia unveiled its first Blackwell-based rack systems in 2024, Huang noted the company specifically avoided optics as they would have added 20 kW of additional power draw to a system that already consumed 120 kW under load. In the years since then, Marvell has invested heavily in next-gen optics tech. One of the most notable acquisitions came in February 2026, when the company paid about $3.5 billion for photonic interconnect developer Celestial AI. Celestial's tech opened the door to more efficient optics integrations including near- and co-packaged optical interconnects that used a fraction of the power of conventional pluggable optics used in scale out networks. Marvell's Lumentum buy will position the IP house as a one-stop shop for AI infrastructure providers' photonics needs.

events.title: Virgin Australia apologises after breaking girl's $33,000 wheelchair
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Virgin Australia apologises after breaking young girl's $33,000 wheelchair Adelaide Tuimalealiifano relies on her specialised wheelchair for mobility. ( Supplied: KZ Photography ) A six-year-old could not use her wheelchair after it was damaged on a flight she was taking for medical treatment. The incident is the latest involving wheelchairs on Virgin Australia flights. Advocates want mandatory reporting for airlines on incidents involving damaged or missing mobility equipment. A girl with a rare bone disease was left without the use of her specialist wheelchair after it was damaged by an airline while she travelled to medical appointments. Adelaide Tuimalealiifano is one of about 60 people in the world diagnosed with multicentric carpotarsal osteolysis syndrome (MCTO), a genetic disorder that leads to the loss of the wrist and ankle bones. She can walk short distances but mostly relies on her wheelchair, which is worth $33,000. The damage to the wheelchair meant it couldn't be used. ( Supplied: Amanda Tuimalealiifano ) But during a flight from Townsville to Brisbane this week, the wheelchair was broken when a bracket was twisted. "It actually took quite a significant force for that bracket to twist," Adelaide's mother Amanda said. The family discovered the damage when they arrived at Brisbane Airport. Without a working wheelchair, Adelaide's father Jaster carried his six-year-old daughter through the Queensland Children's Hospital. He later fixed the chair after buying some hardware tools, but Ms Tuimalealiifano said not everyone was so fortunate. Jaster Tuimalealiifano pushing his daughter in her wheelchair. ( Supplied: KZ Photography ) "If our daughter was an adult and she was travelling solo and she couldn't walk any more … she wouldn't be able to leave the airport and she would be stranded. "It can be absolutely detrimental for people with disabilities." Ms Tuimalealiifano posted about the ordeal in a social media video that has been watched almost 100,000 times. She received many comments from people sharing similar experiences. The Tuimalealiifano family have shared their story of learning to live with disability on social media. ( Supplied: KZ Photography ) "Some people with disabilities completely refuse to travel on public transportation like airlines because their chairs are so complex … and they are so reliant on it that they can't even chance it getting damaged," Ms Tuimalealiifano said. "It is a systemic issue in the airline industry." The family received multiple apologies from Virgin Australia. In a statement, a Virgin Australia spokesperson said the airline extended immediate support and assistance to the family. "Virgin Australia is committed to improving our processes to provide an accessible and inclusive travel experience for all our guests," the spokesperson said. Ms Tuimalealiifano hopes the incident is a catalyst and "stepping stone" for conversations and meaningful change in the travel industry. The incident is the latest in a number involving wheelchairs on Virgin Australia flights, including in 2017 , two in 2023 , including when a former Queensland Australian of the Year was tipped out of a wheelchair , and another two in 2024 . In August this year, Shane Hryhorec was removed from a Virgin Australia flight in the Whitsundays because of issues with storing his portable wheelchair motor. Megan Spindler-Smith says incidents with personal mobility devices are far too common. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) People With Disability Australia (PWDA) chief executive Megan Spindler-Smith said damage to personal mobility equipment such as wheelchairs was a "long-standing issue". "It's so common that I'm not sure how it can continue to happen," they said. "How are airlines not sorting this out? "When equipment is actually damaged, passengers need more than just a 'sorry, we'll try and do this better'." Former Queensland Australian of the Year tipped out of wheelchair Dr Dinesh Palipana says a ground crew member at Brisbane Airport ignored his carers and manoeuvred his wheelchair sharply, tipping him onto the ground. They want mandatory reporting for airlines on incidents involving damaged or missing personal mobility equipment to better understand the scale of the problem and common causes. PDWA has been working with the federal government on proposed aviation disability standards. Public consultation closed on the draft standards earlier this month. Spindler-Smith wants the standards to become "practical, enforceable requirements" that change procedures at airports. "What really needs to change is the prevention of it happening," they said.

events.title: Ruby on Rails creator has a warning for 'cantankerous' coders: Learn some people skills
events.summary: David Heinemeier Hansson said engineers will need to "learn some basic people skills" in the age of AI. LAT Images/Getty Images David Heinemeier Hansson said that AI agents will bring hard times for "cantankerous" engineers. "Best learn some basic people skills," Hansson wrote. Engineers on X chimed in to wave goodbye to engineers with bad attitudes. Don't be cantankerous. David Heinemeier Hansson has some advice for engineers as they adjust to AI. Often referred to as DHH, Hansson created the webapp framework Ruby on Rails and has fashioned himself into a software sage. On Monday, Hansson shared his prediction on X: "The age of agents is going to be amazing for most programmers, but it'll be hard times for the cantankerous ones." Hansson wrote that special abilities won't save those who are difficult to work with. That would be a dramatic shift in software engineering, where some so-called "cracked" coders can get away with large egos or social awkwardness. "Best learn some basic people skills," Hansson wrote. The prediction sparked a conversation among engineers about their social habits and professionalism. One pointed out the irony: agents "don't care how cantankerous you are," but your human coworkers do. One user wrote a eulogy to the "guy whose whole job security was 'only I know how this works.'" Dart cofounder Zack Swafford wrote that teams only tolerated bad attitudes because the staffers had "arcane tribal knowledge." Others questioned how new the change was. People skills have long been valuable, from networking your way into a job to landing that big promotion. "Been true in every company forever," one X user commented. "Skills get you hired, being easy to work with keeps you around. Agents just make it obvious faster." Hansson is committed to the future of AI coding. In September, he declared " pencils down " on handwritten code. Hansson explained that writing code was an "exceptional state," performed only when something went wrong with the AI-generated code. For some engineers, Hansson's post was a vocabulary lesson. "I had to search the definition of 'cantankerous,'" one engineer commented. "First time reading that word." For the record: cantankerous means bad-tempered and uncooperative. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Readwise takes on Amazon’s Kindle and Goodreads with its new app for book lovers
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Readwise , the maker of a read-it-later app and digital reading companion that keeps track of your highlights across services, is now taking on Amazon’s e-book empire with its latest app, Readwise Books . The app is an e-book store and helps you track what you’ve read, similar to Amazon’s Goodreads. The bootstrapped startup described the new app as “a cross between Kindle and the Goodreads apps,” as it offers a single place to buy, read, and track books. However, Readwise Books aims to offer more detailed reading stats than the dates you read a book and whether you finished it. It lets readers visualize richer reading data like words read, pace, depth, immersion, and sessions. Meanwhile, its new store offers “millions” of e-books from the big five publishers and others, initially in the U.S., with more countries to come. Print books (fulfilled by Bookshop.org’s distributor) and some audiobooks are available as well, the company notes. The launch comes at a time when there’s been an explosion of new reading apps and book trackers , all hoping to challenge Goodreads by introducing new features like book clubs, widgets, improved discovery features, goal-setting, better lists and organizational tools, habit-tracking, and more. However, few indie developers have gone so far as to launch an alternative to Amazon’s Kindle e-books store, which remains the industry leader, with an 83% share of the market when Kindle+ (formerly Kindle Unlimited) is included in the stats. One of Kindle’s bigger advantages is that it offers an end-to-end solution for everything related to reading e-books, from the hardware devices to the book-tracking log. Readwise isn’t selling its own e-readers, but it is attempting to create its own community around reading, complete with tools for reading purchased and uploaded e-books, tracking them (like on Goodreads), sharing your reading progress with friends, and more. It also offers a number of ways to track books outside its ecosystem. This includes a way to track reading sessions by using Kindle’s browser-based Cloud Reader and a feature that lets you snap photos of physical books to mark your progress. Plus, you can upload any DRM-free EPUBs (a common e-book file format without copy protection). The app can read your e-books aloud via text-to-speech. Readwise believes its more in-depth metrics could be a big selling point, too, likening them to a “Strava for reading” — a reference to the metrics-heavy exercise app. “The desire to read books, like exercising and eating well, is laden with guilt,” the company explained in a blog post penned by co-founders Daniel Doyon and Tristan Homsi. “Many people feel like they should be reading more, but feeling bad about it tends to change nothing. The session tracking taps into a different psychological mechanism. It makes the reading you’re doing legible and, as the adage goes, that which is measured is improved.” The company adds that the most consistent feedback from users is that the app has led them to read more without willpower tricks like goal-setting, streaks, or scheduling. With publishers’ permission, the app will support AI-powered features as well, like session recaps, definitions and term lookups, word and phrase translations, and a location-aware ability to ask questions about the part you’re reading. (So far, only HarperCollins has opted in, though.) Unlike Goodreads’ locked-down ecosystem, Readwise is embracing open technology. This includes a public API and an MCP server. The latter supports AI agents that could be used to research book recommendations on your behalf, use your Readwise data to create a books page on your personal website, or even wire up your hackable e-reader to log your sessions automatically, depending on how involved your AI use cases may be. The new Readwise Books app will remain free, with some AI features later going behind a paywall. Its prior apps for reading and tracking highlights are either $7.99 per month each or $9.99 per month for both. events.title: Europe's fridges are getting hacked. Could America be next?
events.summary: Cyberattacks are wreaking havoc on an unlikely target across Europe: supermarket refrigerators. Why it matters: Hackers are turning everyday, internet-connected equipment into physical hazards, spoiling food and causing costly damage. U.S. supermarkets use similar technology, and the Pentagon is already investigating suspected cyberattacks involving refrigeration systems at six military commissaries. Driving the news: Suspected cyberattacks sent refrigerator and freezer temperatures soaring at dozens of European supermarkets overnight, spoiling food and threatening costly losses. Grocery chains Ahold Delhaize and Colruyt reported incidents affecting stores in Belgium and Luxembourg, while Swedish chains ICA and Coop reported similar disruptions, per Reuters . A Belgian company that operates Delhaize's refrigeration systems said hackers switched the units into defrost mode. Here's what to know. Supermarkets hacked in Europe Supermarkets in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden reported cyberattacks or IT disruptions, forcing some stores to discard spoiled food. Dozens of stores were affected, including an ICA supermarket in Sweden that said hackers set its refrigerator and freezer temperatures to 122°F, per ABC News . Authorities haven't shared who specifically is behind the attacks, per NBC News . Empty refrigerated shelves at a Proxy Delhaize supermarket in Maleizen, Belgium, following a refrigeration outage. Photo: Wiktor Dabkowski/Bloomberg via Getty Images Flashback: The incidents follow similar attacks in France last month, when hackers seized control of hundreds of refrigeration units, causing fires and spoiling food. It's unclear whether the attacks are connected. What they're saying: France's finance minister Roland Lescure said at the time that the attack "touches the heart of our food security." "It was a wake-up call for everyone," he said. How fridges get hacked How it works: Hackers aren't opening up each individual fridge and setting new temperatures. Instead, they target computer systems that control the temperatures of multiple refrigerated units remotely. Many stores use internet-connected controllers — small computer-like devices, sometimes with touchscreens — that allow maintenance workers to remotely monitor temperatures without having to visit every store. Hackers can exploit software flaws or stolen login credentials to change temperatures or activate defrost functions. Case in point: Danish manufacturer Danfoss said it identified security flaws last year and had long recommended customers install updates, according to The Guardian . In the Netherlands, some affected refrigeration systems used default passwords and were connected to unsecured networks. A supermarket manager discards spoiled food following a refrigeration outage linked to suspected cyberattacks across Europe on Nov. 2 in Belgium. Photo: Wiktor Dabkowski/Bloomberg via Getty Images The cost of hacked refrigerators Spoiled food: If temperatures rise overnight, the stores end up finding ruined meat, dairy and frozen products the next morning. In some French supermarkets, the soaring hot temperatures lasted for six hours, per Reuters. Spoiled food becomes unsafe to sell. Overheating and fires: Refrigerators can also overheat and cause fires. French prosecutors confirmed that the October attacks caused fires and food losses. Supermarkets lose money: Some stores lost more than €130,000. Two markets in the French region of Alsace reported combined losses of €270,000, per The Guardian . Intermarché's parent company estimated its nationwide losses in the tens of millions of euros. Yes, but: Not every attack causes extensive damage. In Estonia, a refrigeration company said technicians responded to the breach within minutes and halted any massive losses, per AP . Fridge attacks in the U.S. Zoom out: Many U.S. supermarkets use refrigeration technology similar to that found in Europe. Danfoss markets refrigeration monitoring and management systems in the U.S. Copeland, a U.S.-based refrigeration technology company, sells controllers that manage the grocery store display cases and walk-in refrigerators. What we're watching: The Pentagon is investigating whether cyberattacks caused freezer malfunctions at at least six U.S. military commissaries in August.

events.title: After ProPublica Investigation, House Democrats Demand Answers on U.S. Citizens Detained by Immigration Agents
events.summary: Photo illustration by ProPublica. Source images: Congress and videos obtained by ProPublica. What Happened: Citing ProPublica’s recent investigation , House Democrats are again asking the Trump administration to explain why hundreds of U.S. citizens have been held by immigration agents and how the government verifies citizenship during immigration operations. In an October letter to Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, California Rep. Lou Correa and 39 other legislators demanded the administration share the number of citizens that immigration agents have detained and how the government is tracking such encounters. They also asked for more information about how agents are trained to verify citizenship and legal status. Why It Matters: ProPublica counted more than 500 Americans detained by immigration agents — almost certainly an undercount since the government is not transparently tracking the cases. Experts told us the cases collectively show federal agents running roughshod over the constitutional rights of citizens. We found more than 100 Americans who were questioned about their citizenship, 63 Americans detained while recording, 36 Americans held for at least a day without being able to contact a lawyer or their family and roughly a dozen citizens deported, mostly children. What They Said: “We remain concerned that the Department’s actions are violating American citizens’ constitutional rights to due process, equal protection, and freedom from unreasonable search and seizure, and request transparency regarding the Department’s actions,” the representatives wrote in their letter to DHS. DHS has long insisted it is not arresting U.S. citizens, and it defended its immigration operations as “highly targeted.” “These members of Congress have shown more concern for criminal illegal aliens who’ve broken our laws and destroyed any possibility of ever remaining in our country than they ever have for Rachel Morin, Laken Riley, Jocelyn Nungaray, and the true victims of illegal alien crimes in America,” a spokesperson wrote to ProPublica. Background: Democrats have been pushing the second Trump administration for more details about how immigration agents are interacting with U.S. citizens since early 2025 . Last year, congressional Democrats announced a wide-ranging investigation into immigration agents’ detention of U.S. citizens in response to our earlier reporting that found that more than 170 citizens were detained by immigration agents . Last month, Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, a New Mexico Democrat, introduced a bill, Justice for Citizens Wrongfully Detained by ICE Act, that would make it easier for citizens to sue immigration agents for wrongful arrests. events.title: Shop freezers in seven European countries hit by cyber-attack
events.summary: 'All this food is now useless': Piles of rubbish after shop freezers hit by cyber-attack Dozens of supermarkets across seven European countries have been hit by a cyber-attack affecting their refrigerators and freezers. Around 40 Delhaize supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland. Sabcobel, a Belgian company that manufactures some of the affected refrigerators, said the units' evaporators were switched to defrost mode, causing them to warm up, in what is believed to be the same method used in last month's incident that hit hundreds of French supermarkets. Millions of euros worth of food had to be thrown away in October, local media reported at the time. Freezers have had to be emptied at several ICA grocery stores in Sweden after the cyber-attack Stephan Moelans, the CEO of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize's systems, on Monday told the Belga news agency that the incident was a cyber-attack and that the company had been "working all night and morning to disconnect the affected units from the network". He said since the French attack in early October, the company had been working to "protect our customers fridges against this vulnerability" but that the units needed physical modifications, not just software updates. Most supermarkets across Europe are linked to the internet, and maintenance and troubleshooting can be done remotely. "The simplest solution is to manage the fridges over a secure internet connection. Most of our customers switched to that after the attack in France," Moelans added. The temperature of freezers in several shops across Europe reportedly rose to as high as 50C (122F). It is unclear who is behind the latest apparent attack. In the US, authorities are investigating what caused refrigeration malfunctions at a number of American military bases in August and working together with French officials to examine whether the incidents could be linked. Both Belgium and Sweden's national cyber-security agencies said they were monitoring the incident. The UK's National Cyber Security Centre said it was working with international partners and industry to "fully understand details of an incident". No incidents have been reported in the UK. In Flanders, northern Belgium, a Delhaize branch in Hoeilaart told news website Het Laatste Nieuws it had lost €100,000 (£83,500) worth of produce. The manager said that estimate did not even take into account further losses that would result from closing the shop. Carrefour, a French-owned supermarket, said the incident had only affected 15 of its Belgian stores, adding that measures had been taken immediately to ensure all shops remained open. A spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates Spar stores in Belgium under a franchise system, told Reuters news agency five shops had their fridge systems attacked. Sweden's budget furniture retailer Ikea said refrigeration systems of its store in the western Belgian city of Mons were affected, with a spokesman quoted by Reuters as saying "we cannot rule out that additional locations may be affected". An employee at an ICA supermarket in Sweden's capital Stockholm was pictured throwing away bags of spoiled food In Sweden, several ICA and Coop shops were hit. A spokesperson for ICA confirmed the incident had affected a "small number of ICA stores operating outside ICA's central network". "ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the situation," they said. One of the ICA branches located in Sjöbo, southern Sweden, wrote on social media: "Our refrigerators and freezers have been hacked overnight and they have set the temperature to 50 degrees." The store was closed earlier but has now reopened to customers. Seven out of the 800 Coop stores in Sweden were also affected but the "situation is currently contained and under control", the company told the BBC. In neighbouring Finland, refrigerator malfunctions were detected in some K-stores. The owner of the supermarket chain Kesko was quoted by Finland's Helsingin Sanomat newspaper as saying its security experts were investigating what caused the problem. The attack is also affecting shops in Ireland, the Netherlands and Estonia. In Ireland, it impacted 13 SuperValu supermarkets. A spokesman for the owner of the chain, Musgrave Group, confirmed to The Irish Times that a "cyber incident" affected its refrigeration systems, but added that the impact was limited to a "specific model" of refrigerator. A spokesperson for Danish manufacturer Danfoss told Dutch public radio channel NOS that the freezing and cooling systems of at least 17 companies in the Netherlands were attacked overnight, affecting butcher shops and small neighbourhood stores. A Selver supermarket in Estonia was also affected and there are reports of other affected companies in the country, according to ERR.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters ISAC technology adds detection ability to existing cell networks, enabling them to track low-flying small drones London’s mobile networks fall to bottom of Europe’s capital league 13 days ago Royal Navy goes fishing for suppliers to build its Type 93 robot submarine 18 days ago British Army spends £16M on 1,000 pocket-sized eyes in the sky September 18, 2026 UK military wants lasers to stop drone swarms without running out of ammo September 4, 2026 London Tube closes the 5G gap with streets above September 2, 2026 Ericsson is bringing drone detection to mobile networks, analyzing radio signal reflections to identify and track low-altitude objects. The telecoms infrastructure maker says its Integrated Sensing and Communication (ISAC) tech adds detection to existing mobile networks, closing a security gap in tracking low-flying, fast-moving objects such as drones. Following tests over the past few months, Ericsson says it will introduce the tech commercially in phases. Small-scale, sensing-only pilots with selected customers will start in 2027, followed by broader deployments from 2028. CCS Insight research director Ian Fogg, said told The Register : REG AD "While sensing can be used for other things — like tracking boats in a port, traffic patterns or weather conditions — drone detection [in civilian areas] is the most pressing need which cannot easily be solved using other technologies. REG AD "Mobile networks are useful as drone detection solutions because their antennas are already covering low elevations, close to ground level where drones often fly, unlike traditional radar." Although it is possible to use 5G networks for sensing, a standards-based 6G method could improve precision by letting different suppliers' base stations "interoperate", alongside a mix of client devices, tracking the "smallest and fastest moving drones in difficult environments," Fogg added. "The new spectrum that should arrive with 6G will also make it easier to deploy sensing on wide channels which further improves detection accuracy," he said. Small, low-cost drones have emerged as a persistent threat, or at the very least a nuisance, closing down airports due to safety concerns - the latest incident was at Jersey Airport over the Halloween weekend. Drone activity has also been on the increase near to military bases and other sensitive sites. Dedicated sensor systems were deployed to cover sensitive sites, and in the UK, military personnel have now been granted the authority to neutralize any unwanted flying intruders . Scaling detection across larger areas, however, is more challenging, Ericsson said. ISAC transforms mobile network infrastructure into a distributed sensor array. Using sensing-enabled 5G radios, edge computing and signal processing, a cell deployment can detect objects and track them across the coverage area, complementing radar and other sensors rather than replacing them. Ericsson says the tech works by having multiple perspectives from a number of cell tower radio sites. When one transmits a signal, it reflects off the drone and is picked up by multiple receiving sites. The network then analyses the reflected signals to locate the drone and track it. REG AD ISAC requires sensing-capable radio hardware, dedicated compute resources, and software, says Ericsson. The radios have to meet specific Massive MIMO (multiple-in, multiple-out) antenna and spectrum requirements. AT&T tested ISAC at trials in Arlington, Texas, and with Erillisverkot, a state-owned special purpose company responsible for national critical communications in Finland. In both cases, the tech demonstrated it was able to detect multiple drones and track their movements, according to Ericsson. Data from ISAC - we're told - can be securely shared through standardized interfaces with authorized external systems, including security and command and control systems.
