events.title: FBI pins $6.3B Binance crypto heist on North Korean hackers
events.summary: The FBI has blamed North Korean hackers for the record-breaking $6.3 billion theft from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, pointing the finger at the notorious Lazarus Group as the exchange scrambles to replace stolen funds and reassure customers. In an alert published Saturday , the agency attributed the October 29 attack to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking operation linked to Lazarus, which has made a lucrative career out of relieving crypto exchanges of their digital assets. Pyongyang was already in the frame before the FBI weighed in. Blockchain intelligence firms TRM Labs and Elliptic had linked the theft to North Korea, with TRM reporting that most of the $6.36 billion haul disappeared in about 20 minutes. Elliptic, which puts the total closer to $6.43 billion, says it has verified that $2.85 billion of the stolen assets have been frozen or seized. According to the FBI, the hackers have started swapping their loot for Ethereum, with investigators expecting them to move the funds through decentralized finance (DeFi) platforms and instant swap services to make the money harder to trace. The agency has published a list of cryptocurrency wallet addresses linked to the theft and is urging exchanges, blockchain analytics firms, and other virtual asset providers to block transactions involving the stolen funds. The FBI's attribution comes days after Binance admitted that hackers had made off with roughly $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency. According to the exchange , the trouble started with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which gave the intruders access to a service container and allowed them to authorize withdrawals they had no business making. Binance has since resumed customer withdrawals , which it suspended after the attack, and says it has now replenished about 95 percent of the stolen assets. The remaining tokens are proving harder to replace because of their limited liquidity. The exchange has committed billions of dollars from its own reserves and emergency funds to cover the losses, with co-CEO Richard Teng promising that customers won't be left footing the bill. That hasn't stopped users from heading for the exits. Binance recorded approximately $3.64 billion in net outflows after withdrawals resumed, although the company said this represented only around 2.1 percent of its reported assets. Replacing the stolen cryptocurrency is one thing. Getting it back from North Korea is another, and investigators face the considerable task of tracking billions of dollars as the hackers attempt to move it beyond their reach. TraderTraitor has form when it comes to raiding crypto exchanges. The North Korean crew has previously been linked to a string of cryptocurrency thefts, including the $308 million attack on Japan's DMM Bitcoin exchange in 2024 . The group has previously used fake job offers and recruitment exercises to trick employees into handing over access to their employers' systems. As we reported here on Friday , crypto exchange Bitget has now confirmed that the cyberattack where hackers drained $387.5 million worth of digital assets from the exchange’s wallets also has all the hallmarks of a North Korean operation. Its CEO did not go into too much detail, but did say that “IP behavioral patterns and on-chain signatures” suggest it was Kim’s cronies at work. This isn’t Binance's first expensive encounter with hackers, either. Back in 2022, attackers exploited its BNB blockchain bridge and made off with roughly $566 million in tokens. Four years later, the sums have grown considerably. Binance may have the reserves to make its customers whole, but the attackers responsible for the latest raid still have billions of dollars to launder. ®

events.title: “Chaos” in the Air: Five Ways Voting Could Be Disrupted on Election Day
events.summary: Election workers in Los Angeles County process ballots for the state’s primary in June. Mario Tama/Getty Images As Americans head to the polls on Tuesday, voting experts are watching to see how the Trump administration’s unprecedented efforts to assert more federal control over elections will play out. Since President Donald Trump retook the White House, his administration has tried to force states to turn over their unredacted voter rolls and to restrict mail-in voting . The Department of Homeland Security has used its resources to identify and prosecute noncitizen voters , an effort that has unfolded alongside the agency’s massive crackdown on immigrants. The president has justified these steps by claiming, without evidence, that American elections are beset by fraud and that illegal voting is tipping the scales in favor of Democrats. Help Us Report on Key Election Issues ProPublica’s reporters are on the lookout for what’s going right and what isn’t. We’re monitoring voter suppression and interference, election observers and poll watchers, extremism tied to the election, and ICE activity at the polls. Have you seen something? Send Us a Tip Courts have thwarted most of the administration’s plans to date, but Trump and his top deputies have kept up the pressure. Most recently, they’ve threatened to prosecute election officials who don’t reject ballots from people that the federal government has identified as likely noncitizens. The administration hasn’t explicitly ruled out sending federal agents to the polls or seizing ballots or voting machines. Election experts say the cumulative effect has been to ramp up anxiety about the midterms and to erode voters’ trust in the system. “The administration has been creating a lot of noise, a lot of confusion, a lot of doubt,” said Ben Hovland, whom Trump fired as a commissioner for the bipartisan Election Assistance Commission earlier this year. He said he worries that this will make voters “sit it out” and “throw their hands up.” “Paper Trail” Podcast Learn more about this story on ProPublica’s podcast “ Paper Trail .” In an emailed response to questions, a DHS spokesperson said Immigration and Customs Enforcement “is not planning operations targeting polling locations,” adding that the agency would only arrest people at the polls to address a safety threat as part of “intelligence-driven targeted enforcement.” The DHS and the Justice Department “are laser focused on identifying, prosecuting and removing aliens who vote and dilute the votes of U.S. citizens,” the spokesperson added. “Our message to aliens who vote in American elections is clear: we will find you, arrest you, and you will face the consequences — including criminal charges and deportation.” Before and on Election Day, it’s typical for the major political parties to mount poll-watching operations, but both Democrats and Republicans say they’ve expanded these activities in this pressurized midterm. Republicans will focus on issues such as voter eligibility and voter-roll accuracy, according to Ally Triolo, the Republican National Committee’s election integrity communications director. Democrats will concentrate on voter intimidation and other hurdles to voting, Angelo Fernández Hernández, a Democratic National Committee spokesperson, said. Here are five issues that voting rights experts say they’re watching as this year’s election unfolds: People arrive to vote early on Oct. 27 in Coral Gables, Florida. Lynne Sladky/AP Images 1. Will There Be Federal Interference? An incident in Leon County, in the Florida Panhandle, illustrates the widespread anxiety about law enforcement at the polls. Mark Earley, the county’s supervisor of elections, told ProPublica he was “furious” when two marked U.S. Customs and Border Protection vehicles parked outside the county’s busiest early voting location last month, after he’d been repeatedly reassured by the administration that agents would not do this. He reported the sighting to the FBI, then learned that the agents, who were headed out of state, had just stopped by to try to vote themselves. The episode generated a flurry of news coverage . “Given the negative media coverage regarding federal agents at the polls, it shows pretty bad judgment that they showed up in their official vehicles,” Earley said. It’s against the law for federal law enforcement to be near polling places. Nick Brown, Washington’s attorney general, leads a group of Democratic state officials and voting rights advocates who have been planning how to respond if, indeed, there is real federal interference. The group has “war-gamed” how to react if government agents attempt to commandeer voting equipment or ballots. “We’ve seen the tension and chaos that’s in the air,” Brown said. He called the federal government “the biggest challenge to smooth elections right now, which is not the way it’s supposed to be.” A DOJ spokesperson said “the best preparation for any election official is following federal law.” It’s routine for DOJ monitors to watch over polling places, and the agency has assured states that, in the midterms, its observers will follow the law and not interfere with voting or election administration. Still, state officials remain concerned. During Wyoming’s primary election, poll workers said they felt uneasy when DOJ monitors asked about their training and to inspect voting systems. The state’s governor criticized these actions as “a bit aggressive” and “irregular.” Workers prepare ballots to be scanned for counting in Orange County, California, on Oct. 28. Apu Gomes/Getty Images 2. What Effect Will Noncitizen Voter Challenges Have? The Trump administration’s multipronged effort targeting alleged noncitizen voters has already led to eligible voters being improperly removed from the rolls. Voting rights groups fear this will block some U.S. citizens from being able to vote when they show up on Tuesday. Federal officials have made clear they plan to go after anyone they think is committing voter fraud. On the first day of early voting in Texas, Aaron Reitz, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, posted a YouTube video announcing his intentions. “If you violate federal election law,” he warned, “I will hunt you down and prosecute you.” This threat came days after the DOJ sued California, seeking to block the state from counting mail ballots from more than 20,000 voters it claims are “likely” noncitizens. The administration had obtained the state’s public voter rolls , which the DHS had blended with its own immigration information and third-party data. In a court filing , California called the claim that there are 20,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls “specious.” Los Angeles County analyzed a sampling of the likely noncitizen voters that the federal government claimed were registered there. AWS developer advocate Darko Mesaroš has connected a teletype to a modern command-line interface to revel in the delight of interacting with today's AI technology via a combination of a DECwriter and fanfold paper, or the display and keyboard of a computer whose heyday ended 40 years ago. Mesaroš' project involved AWS Kiro , a Command Line Interface (CLI) and agentic coding service. We would, however, contend that this is more about seeing what retro hardware can be made to do. Two problems needed solving: getting data to and from the teletype, and formatting the output to work on a piece of kit from another era of computing. He used Hayes modem emulation to deal with the serial connection, and Agent Client Protocol (ACP) for working with Kiro. Mesaroš used a WiModem232 for the former. The device emulates a standard Hayes-compatible modem and, according to Mesaroš, "Folks initially used this to connect Commodore 64s to BBSes in the modern era" (he started his computing journey with a Commodore 64). The latter, getting the Kiro CLI to work on a Teletype, was a little more complicated. Kiro's CLI isn't really suitable for a teleprinter capable of 30 characters per second, after all. A simple Rust application took Kiro's output (obtained via ACP) and turned it into something that a teletype, or dumb terminal, could handle. As we said, seemingly pointless, but making it work required knowledge of Rust, competence with containers, an understanding of ACP, and more than a little creative thinking. So, while one might argue it is pointless from a technical perspective, it is wonderfully educational otherwise. The repository is available and focuses on Kiro for obvious reasons (Mesaroš is an AWS developer advocate after all), but in a chat with The Register , Mesaroš said the concept was portable. He said, "Any coding assistant or any harness that supports ACP, this should work, right? I built it for Kiro, but it uses the standard ACP protocol, so I could easily plug in Claude Code or Codex. Anything that basically can serve as an ACP server should be perfectly fine. There might be some issues. "The biggest problem with this thing is that it doesn't really handle packet drops at all," he explained. "Like, if you drop packets, they're just gone. There're no retries. It's just spitting information out." And then there is buffering. Or the lack of it. Mesaroš said, "There's actually no buffering happening here. Literally, it just comes down through the fire hose through this serial device, and the bottleneck itself is the serial device." Mesaroš had toyed with using the GPIO pins on a Raspberry Pi, but settled on the serial device instead, since everything worked "out of the box." "It's kind of cheating," he admitted, "but it's also kind of good." Mesaroš collects vintage hardware, with a stash that ranges from home computers made by Commodore and Sinclair, to a 1974 Data General Eclipse minicomputer and a plethora of Sun hardware. And, of course, an old Decwriter. He is also a dab hand with the soldering iron, having learned the skills to keep old hardware operational. Unlike today's equipment. "I have this big peeve over modern computers, where you just can't fix them," he said, "and it feels like such a waste of resources that when my MacBook dies I just have to drill a hole through it so nobody steals my data, and throw it away.

events.title: Pharma's next cash cows could be specialized treatments
events.summary: Pharmaceutical companies facing a steep patent cliff are concluding the key to future profits may be customized treatments tailored to patients' genes and lifestyles — not blockbusters aimed at large patient populations. Why it matters: The pivot could influence which diseases get treated in the decades to come, and how much the health system pays. The stakes are huge. More than $500 billion in brand-name drug sales is potentially at risk from generic competition between 2026 and 2032, according to the consulting firm Evaluate. The latest: The race is on to find new treatments that each generate at least $2.4 billion in global sales, a new Iqvia Institute report finds. They're increasingly specialty treatments, biologics and rare disease drugs — with a small group of flagship products accounting for an outsized share of industry sales. GLP-1 drugs like Novo Nordisk's Ozempic and Eli Lilly's Zepbound now define that elite category. The next wave could include "biological missiles" that combine antibodies with chemotherapy to target specific cancer cells. "As precision medicine continues to advance, similar approaches may extend beyond oncology into areas such as immunology, metabolic disease and neurology," the report states. Reality check: It's not clear whether all of the innovation will cure more people, or just make health care more expensive. Novel RNA drugs and cell and gene therapies are expensive, hard to make and target small groups of patients. Challenges identifying eligible patients and getting insurers to pay for treatments have already revealed a disconnect between promising R&D and patient benefit. Widespread concern over high drug prices will force manufacturers to find more unmet needs and build sales more quickly after a drug's launch, according to the report. Context: Top-selling drugs historically were aimed at large patient populations with chronic conditions like high cholesterol. The ulcer drug Tagamet became the first to exceed $1 billion in sales in 1986. Over time, cancer and immunology drugs became major drivers of growth, followed by GLP-1s, which are sparking huge demand for conditions beyond obesity and diabetes but also driving up health costs. Iqvia found that blockbusters on average maintain a dominant market position for 12.1 years before losing market exclusivity, or nearly 80% of their commercial life. Specialty drugs for rare or complex diseases lasted even longer. Yes, but: A substantial number of top-sellers will lose patent protection and face potential competition from generics between 2028 and 2036. Bristol Myers Squibb's blood thinner Eliquis and Merck's cancer blockbuster Keytruda, which are both due to lose market exclusivity in 2028, accounted for a combined $65 billion in global sales in 2024. Follow the money: The search for new blockbusters is playing out in a highly charged environment. Drugmakers and biotechs not only have to figure out how to grow outside of crowded categories but also how much payers value new classes of drugs, Evaluate says . There's also uncertainty over China , where Western drug giants have invested tens of billions of dollars to bolster their product pipelines. Evaluate predicts that only autoimmune disease drugs will come close to rivaling GLP-1s, because of their potential to treat dozens of conditions. One example is AbbVie's injectable Skyrizi for plaque psoriasis, arthritis, Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, which could find more uses and generate more than $33 billion in sales in 2032. Iqvia identifies RNA therapeutics as a potentially important middle ground between traditional "small molecule" drugs for chronic diseases and highly specialized genetic treatments. These drugs can target disease-causing mutations across many genes and conditions, with applications for central nervous system, cardiovascular and kidney disease, as well as rare conditions. The bottom line: The success at innovating while also making sure patients have access to the new treatments "will ultimately determine whether the growth in blockbuster medicines observed over the past 25 years can continue at its extraordinary pace," Iqvia concludes.

We shared our condolences following Mr Andriesz's tragic death and our thoughts remain with his family and loved ones.The review was commissioned by our non-executive directors. It is being conducted by Lea Paterson CBE, an independent non-executive director of the FCA.When we announced the review, we said it would examine how we interacted with Mr Andriesz. The review will now also look at whether we met our responsibilities under whistleblowing law and followed our own policies and procedures when handling his whistleblowing reports, including his concerns that he had experienced detriment. It will cover the period from at least 2017 to 2026.The review will identify any lessons learned and make recommendations for improvements to our future engagement with external whistleblowers and vulnerable individuals.We previously said we aimed to publish findings in early 2027. Given this broader scope and the need to examine evidence spanning many years, more time is needed to complete the review thoroughly.A progress update will be published in January 2027, with the final report expected in spring 2027.Read the terms of reference (PDF).

events.title: JP Morgan boosts UAE presence with wealth management branch at DIFC
events.summary: JP Morgan Chase has expanded its private banking offerings in the Middle East with the opening of a dedicated wealth management branch at Dubai International Financial centre . Regulated by the Dubai Financial Services Authority, the DIFC branch will enable JP Morgan Private Bank to better serve clients across the UAE and the wider region, it said in a statement on Monday. In the 12 months leading up to the final DFSA approval, JP Morgan more than tripled the size of its Dubai-based private banking team to build capabilities before launch, it said, without specifying the number of bankers added. The team in Dubai is led by Selim Elgen, UAE market head and senior executive officer, and Karim Rekik, regional head, Middle East at JP Morgan Private Bank, the lender said. “JP Morgan Private Bank’s expansion into DIFC reinforces Dubai’s position as a global hub for private wealth,” said Arif Amiri, chief executive of the DIFC Authority. JP Morgan is the latest among major global financial institutions that have expanded in the UAE this year despite Iran war-driven uncertainty and economic headwinds. HSBC, Barclays as well as several Swiss wealth managers have also boosted their operations in the country to leverage the rapid growth of domestic wealth as well as the migration of global capital into the UAE. In October, Dubai and Abu Dhabi were ranked among the top 10 destinations for next-generation wealth despite the fallout from geopolitical tension. Dubai was ranked eighth and the UAE capital was 10th among favoured cities for the $84 trillion of wealth expected to be transferred between generations over the next two decades, consultancy Savills said in a report. Net wealth in the UAE is set to jump to $6 trillion by the end of this decade despite the short-term volatility, according to Boston Consulting Group data. In the five years to the end of 2030, net wealth in the Emirates is set to increase by more than $2.3 trillion, at an annual growth rate of 10.6 per cent, the consultancy said in a report last month. Long-term relations JP Morgan Private Bank said its dedicated money management branch is the latest chapter in the bank’s five-decade relationship with the UAE. Over the past 20 years, the company has also used DIFC as its regional base for corporate and investment banking and, more recently, broadened its activities with authorisation to provide asset management services through JP Morgan International Advisers. "The UAE and the broader Middle East represent a significant and growing opportunity for us as a business and for our clients,” said Mr Rekik.

events.title: "Arrogance": 3 GOP Senate candidates blasted over costly red-state rescues
events.summary: Republicans are burning tens of millions of last-minute ad dollars to try to rescue three red-state senators who they say ignored months of warnings that their campaigns were in danger. Why it matters: Senate races in Kansas, South Carolina and Mississippi are normally GOP layups. This year, Republicans have diverted resources from swing-state battles to defend them. The frustration with Sens. Roger Marshall (Kansas), Darline Graham (South Carolina) and Cindy Hyde-Smith (Mississippi) comes amid broader GOP finger-pointing as polls show a nationwide backlash against President Trump . "Democrats may win these seats in a wave ... but not a blue wave. It's the wave of arrogance [and] laziness ... that washed over these GOP incumbents and made them think they were invincible," said a national GOP operative involved in several key Senate races. By the numbers: National Republicans have spent $33 million in Kansas, $21 million in South Carolina and $2.4 million in Mississippi, according to data compiled by campaign finance expert Rob Pyers. Trump also has spent valuable campaign time in all three states. Behind the scenes: Republicans say the three senators ignored warnings to raise more money and build stronger campaign operations. National Republican Senatorial Committee chair Tim Scott warned all GOP senators in February 2025: "We do not need to spend time and money in places where races should not be competitive." Trump's political operation also warned Senate Republicans that they would need to pull their own weight. The most complaints center on Marshall, who has raised just $7.5 million compared with $19 million for his Democratic opponent, Adam Hamilton. Republicans blame his strained relationship with the banking and credit card industries — major GOP donors — and a lack of outreach to K Street. Republicans describe Marshall's campaign as overconfident. About a month ago, his team told aides to other GOP senators that the race would be effectively over within 10 days once it released opposition research on Hamilton. It wasn't. Strategists blame chief of staff Brent Robertson for Marshall's weak campaign operation. The campaign only recently tapped veteran Trump operative Chris Grant as part of a last-minute rescue effort. Alex DeGrasse, another veteran strategist recently hired to help Marshall, pointed to millions in spending by national Democrats and said the senator has made "hundreds of stops across all 105 counties in Kansas" and continues to "work hard for the people of Kansas." In Mississippi, Republicans have long viewed Hyde-Smith as a political underperformer. In 2020, she ran six points behind Trump. She has raised just $6.5 million despite warnings that Democratic megadonors, including George and Alex Soros, were preparing to spend heavily against her. Democratic groups have poured $13.7 million into the race. Republicans also fault Hyde-Smith for holding too few campaign events and underestimating her Democratic opponent, district attorney Scott Colom. Hyde-Smith's campaign did not respond to a request for comment. In South Carolina, Republicans fault Graham for failing to tap her late brother Lindsey Graham's donor network and showing little interest in soliciting contributions. In the first two weeks of October, Democrat Annie Andrews outraised Graham $4.2 million to $570,000. Graham spokesperson T.W. Arrighi said the senator "has faced unprecedented headwinds since losing her brother three months ago, and has risen to the occasion." Some Republicans are sympathetic to Graham, a political novice thrust into the Senate after her brother's death who faced a grueling primary and little time to campaign. They blame Trump for pushing her to run. Yes, but: Republicans point to Idaho Sen. Jim Risch, whose campaign required no spending from national GOP groups, as an example of an incumbent who took the political environment seriously. What they're saying: Representatives for the NRSC and the pro-GOP Senate Leadership Fund super PAC didn't respond to requests for comment. What's next: Top Republicans say the party needs to rethink how it deals with complacent incumbents in 2028 — and make clear that its campaign organizations can't be treated like a charity.

events.title: America's changing power grid faces a powerful El Niño
events.summary: A powerful El Niño could bring major shifts in electricity supply and demand across the U.S. this winter, posing new challenges for utilities. Why it matters: The U.S. power grid has far more solar, wind and battery storage than during the last major El Niño, and the ongoing event could reveal whether that changing energy mix has made the grid more resilient or left it vulnerable in new ways. Driving the news: A very strong El Niño is strengthening in the tropical Pacific and is expected to continue into spring 2027, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration says. NOAA's latest outlook favors wetter-than-normal conditions across California , the Southwest and much of the southern U.S. this winter, while the northern Rockies and parts of the Great Lakes lean drier and much of the northern U.S. leans warmer. The intrigue: El Niño doesn't affect every electricity resource the same way. A March study found that previous super El Niños were associated with reductions in potential solar power output of nearly 5% in parts of California over 12 months — and more than 10% in the state's north during winter. Vincent Tidwell, chief scientist at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, says a wetter California winter could boost hydropower, while reduced precipitation or snowpack in the Pacific Northwest could cut generation there. Erik Smith, a climate scientist at the Electric Power Research Institute, tells Axios the Southeast is another region to watch for reduced solar generation as El Niño favors cloudier conditions. California now has more than 21 gigawatts of battery capacity , giving the grid another tool to manage fluctuations in electricity supply — one it barely possessed during the last very strong El Niño. The Columbia and Snake river basins accounted for roughly 62% of Western U.S. hydropower generation between 2001 and 2020, according to a Pacific Northwest National Laboratory analysis . Tidwell tells Axios that the Western grid is accustomed to shifting electricity between regions when hydropower conditions differ, helping compensate for shortages. Federal water managers, states and utilities use seasonal forecasts to plan for potential hydropower availability at Hoover and Glen Canyon dams on the Colorado River, Tidwell says. Zoom in: Tidwell expects natural gas to play a larger backup role if El Niño reduces Pacific Northwest hydropower and California solar generation this winter. Other resources, including wind, geothermal and nuclear power, provide additional options, though he says El Niño's effects on wind generation remain poorly understood. The big picture: A very strong El Niño could actually ease some pressure on the electricity system, Smith says. Warmer-than-normal conditions across the northern U.S. could reduce winter heating demand, potentially offsetting some of the pressure from changing electricity supplies elsewhere. Yes, but: Even a very strong El Niño doesn't guarantee specific weather impacts. A severe cold outbreak could still stress the grid despite a warmer-than-average winter, while a few major storms could radically alter regional rainfall and snowpack, Smith says. The bottom line: "We have a lot of confidence in how the averages are going to play out, but we don't have a lot of confidence in the day-to-day, week-to-week, particular weather events that could drive those averages," Smith says. events.title: Microsoft's moolah mountain is more massive than ever. It just doesn't want the people who built it
events.summary: Capitalism can seem so perverse. Take Microsoft, which is celebrating record financial performance by inviting 60,000 employees to consider continuing their careers outside the company . Voluntary redundancy may seem to make sense when a company's running out of cash, but Microsoft is dripping with the stuff . Redmond's first quarter for fiscal 2027 was a bonanza for the tech giant. Its Azure business is up over 48 percent y-o-y, revenues are through the roof, and it has so much moolah it returned $10.2 billion to shareholders in the form of dividends and share repurchases. This latter move probably soothed CEO Satya Nadella, who recently suffered, due to the vagaries of C-suite reimbursement and incentive packages, a 6 percent cut in his pocket money . But as he’s also a stockholder with about 0.01 percent of the company, his share of the cash return presumably eased the pain. He won't have been offered redundo. Jenkins, the large wheelbarrow if you please. Microsoft, then, can afford all its employees, each of whom contributed about $1.5 million to SatNad's bottom line in the last full fiscal year. The "massive efficiencies and RoI of AI" make a great line for a company flogging magic LLM juice, but the evidence remains elusive. AI is, of course, still the reason. Nothing else matters these days. It's just that it's not today's AI. Among all the fulsome figures it put on display for Q1 2027, analysts noted that Microsoft's capital expenditure wasn't as spendy as expected. Quite a lot has been pushed into next calendar year, not because it's not there to be spent – Microsoft could build a 1:1 scale model of the Vatican filled with robot priests if it wanted – but because so much it wanted to mash the Buy Now button for was "Out of stock. More expected soon." This is bad. MS added 88 datacenters in its most recent full financial year: fiscal 2026. That’s not enough datacenters for a cloud business expected to grow by half again in 2027, and hugely not enough to do the other thing. Lags in the cadence of deforestation, dewatering and detonation of the planet can't be tolerated. Thus there are contracts signed to get things back on track PDQ, with mucho, mucho, mucho sponduiks. In its most recent Q1 earnings call, Microsoft is hinting, those selfsame analysts say, that it will have to go to the debt market and go into " negative free cash flow " territory in 2028. In other words, as well as spending its own bank, the company will be taking out massive loans. This is why Billy and Bhavya Dev have to go. The cost of borrowing depends on the financial health of the borrower, and that boils down to how much profit you're making from the money you earn. A big round of redundancies, which are very costly in themselves, sits on the books of the year they happen. The hole in expenditure left by the vanished salaries lives on. The capital must flow. Will this work? Last week, we listed the reasons why it might not — price competition between rivals and increasingly powerful local and open weight models, supply side shortages, you know the litany by now. This week is Groundhog week, with fresh stories singing the same songs from different choirs. Any sensible soul, especially developers sitting on the sharp end of AI's forcible insertion into their working lives, will know how uncertain the job market is. Voluntary redundancy is a very high stakes bet, and the game is very different if you're in an organization that's going downhill and may need to get rid of you later with far less cash available than if you're nominally making $1.5 million in a place whose biggest problem is that it physically can't move into a bigger shell. On average, only 5 percent or so of those offered voluntary redundancy take it, which Microsoft HR will have factored in. It's cold outside and snug within, so that may be on the high side. The biggest knock-on of such schemes is cultural, with only the very confident moving on out, a disproportionate loss of talent and role models. Hey, the cost of doing business, right? For those who do decide to leave and watch the fireworks from outside the tent, part of the deal is career development resources. Sounds great, if anyone knows what technical careers will look like if either AI works and does indeed do all the work, or it fails and the global financial system throws a humongous wobble. Or anything in between. So, here's an exercise in very dark humor quite fitting for the Halloween season. Ask your favorite AI what careers will be available for coders made redundant by AI. It will give you a long and plausible list. Then ask it – and yourself – why AI won't be able to do any of those jobs too. Buying a truck and a wrench and calling yourself a plumber is probably safest. Nobody will ever want AI to fix their toilet. ®

events.title: ‘No room for debate’ over human control of AI, says Sam Altman
events.summary: People, not artificial intelligence, must stay in control of the future, OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said on Monday. “There are a lot of other things we can debate, but on this one, we think there must be no room for debate,” he said in conversation with The National 's Editor-in-Chief Mina Al-Oraibi. Speaking at the opening ceremony of Adipec in Abu Dhabi, Mr Altman said there “should not be a handoff to AI” and that the technology “needs to be a tool built for people and needs to serve people, not the other way around”. “I can’t believe that this differentiates us from other AI companies, but it does,” he said. “This is a value that we intend to really go fight for. And I wish it didn’t need to be said.” The remarks followed OpenAI's agreements with Abu Dhabi, covering energy, education, investment and government. These include a deal with Adnoc and Abu Dhabi technology group G42 to use OpenAI’s most advanced models on the energy industry’s hardest problems. Mr Altman’s message was that AI has crossed a threshold. By his account, it has gone from trailing the world’s best scientists at the start of the year to mostly outperforming them. Its demand for power is growing just as fast, he said. “AI was mostly not as smart as our smartest scientists, and now it’s mostly smarter than them,” Mr Altman said, adding that AI could now do “a lot of parts” of many white-collar jobs. He said he believed society would “navigate through this all fine”. But he warned that the industry must show it can prevent harm as its systems become more capable. “How do we guarantee, and how do we give the world comfort with that guarantee, that we are going to avoid serious safety and alignment incidents?” he said. “I think that’ll be increasingly important for our industry to demonstrate.” Energy challenge In a quick-fire round, Mr Altman was asked what challenge he faces today. He answered with one word: “Energy.” He said the energy needed for each AI query had dropped sharply, but demand kept climbing . Six years ago, OpenAI’s heaviest internal user consumed about 100,000 tokens a month. Today, that figure is roughly the global per-capita average, and the top user consumes about 500 billion, he added. Costs could fall “in almost every way, except, you know, atoms are still atoms”, Mr Altman said. He called power “the very dominant factor” in how much AI the world can use. He said he hoped AI would deliver “a net gain for energy availability in the world”. Mr Altman also said OpenAI had solved one of the Millennium Prize problems, a set of unsolved mathematics problems. He said the work used 10,000 agents running an upcoming GPT model for about four days, collaborating with “no hierarchy”. The claim could not immediately be verified independently. He praised the UAE as “consistently the most forward-looking country in the world for AI adoption”, saying about 80 per cent of young people in the country were using ChatGPT .

events.title: I tested Apple's $2,000 iPhone Duo. It's a fascinating experiment, but the price is hard to justify.
events.summary: I've spent the past week trying to figure out whether Apple's $2,000 iPhone Duo is the future of smartphones or just an expensive way to do things I could already do on my regular iPhone. The answer, unsurprisingly, is a bit of both. Why it matters: Apple wasn't first to the folding smartphone party. Samsung, Google and others began making them years ago. But Apple's arrival in a category has a way of reinventing it. The big picture : The most exciting thing about Apple's first foldable iPhone isn't necessarily what it can do today but what it can become. Already, it's inspiring developers to explore possibilities that could reshape how we use our devices. Old habits die hard One of my first surprises was how little I initially used the Duo's biggest selling point: its folding screen. While other reviewers talked about endlessly opening and closing their devices, I found myself mostly using the smaller outside display. After years of conventional iPhones, it was a mix of instinct and muscle memory. Zoom in: Over time, though, I found reasons to unfold it. Watching sports was one of the clearest advantages. I pulled out the Duo at Starbucks to watch the 49ers with my son and later followed a tied World Series game in a doctor's waiting room. At the WNBA Finals, having forgotten my laptop, I managed some quick edits to a story about Anthropic's IPO . I wouldn't want to write a full article that way, but it was reassuring to have the option. Playing the New York Times' Spelling Bee alongside its Spelling Bee Buddy helper was a small but delightful example of multitasking without constantly switching apps. Between the lines: The Duo's advantages aren't always about more screen space. Sometimes they're about what you can physically do with a phone that bends. I tried watching Netflix with the phone unfolded, propped up like a tent and partially folded into a miniature laptop. I also used the Duo's ability to stand on its own to capture wide shots of the WNBA Finals from a press-box ledge without needing a tripod. Other experiences were less seamless, including getting the orientation right when trying FaceTime's option to use multiple camera views. The developer wild card Perhaps the biggest difference between the Duo and the Android foldables is the enthusiasm Apple's device has sparked among independent developers. Zoom in: Some of the early experiments are more entertaining than useful, including apps that turn the Duo into a virtual cassette player or a grilled cheese toaster . My favorite was Tiny Computers , which let it simulate a semi-functional 1984 Mac, Windows 95 PC or candy-colored iMac. Nearly two decades after the App Store debuted, we aren't all using our iPhones as virtual cigarette lighters. And I doubt we'll all be making imaginary grilled cheese sandwiches on our phones 20 years from now. Zoom out: But these early experiments offer glimpses of what might be possible when developers start thinking beyond a conventional rectangular screen. The question isn't whether today's novelties become hits. It's whether all this experimentation eventually produces genuinely new ways of using our phones — the kind of breakthroughs that make today's smartphones feel indispensable. The $2,000 question For all the fun I've had with the Duo, its price is an insurmountable obstacle. At $2,000, it's simply not a purchase I could justify for myself, much less recommend broadly. The catch: There are other compromises. I missed Face ID, occasionally fumbling for the side-mounted Touch ID sensor until I started wearing an Apple Watch to make unlocking the phone easier. And when I needed to accomplish something quickly, I often instinctively reached for my familiar, traditional iPhone. What I'm watching: On Friday, I tried putting the Duo away to see if I missed it. I didn't find myself longing for it the way I sometimes felt when I only had the Duo only and missed having a better camera. The bottom line: The Duo is a fascinating glimpse of where smartphones could go next. But early buyers are paying a steep premium to participate in an experiment whose biggest rewards may still be years away.

events.title: Tribal Leaders Warned Border Wall Construction Would Disturb Native American Remains. They Were Right.
events.summary: Quitobaquito Springs, a rare Sonoran Desert oasis imperiled by border wall construction, is located within 200 feet of the U.S.-Mexico border in Organ Pipe National Monument outside Ajo, Arizona. Anna Watts Lorraine Eiler stood in the blazing August sun, surrounded by reporters, to offer a warning. The Trump administration was racing to erect a second border wall across Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument, southwest of Tucson. If the bulldozers came, she said, they were bound to disturb the final resting places of her family and Hia-Ced O’odham tribal ancestors. “People used to live here,” the 89-year-old said. Fifteen days later, her fears were realized. ProPublica has confirmed that Native American remains were unearthed in Organ Pipe amid soil overturned by border wall contractors. The discovery, unreported until now, was made on Sept. 8, the National Park Service said in a statement. “Following established protocols, the University of Arizona conducted an assessment and confirmed that the remains are human and align with tribal cremation practices,” the agency said. The Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act governs the steps agencies must take following an inadvertent discovery of Native American remains on federal land. Those steps include halting any activity that contributed to the discovery until tribal communities are consulted. “The National Park Service is committed to respecting tribal rights and traditions,” the agency went on to say, adding that it was “working diligently to identify the culturally affiliated tribe and ensure the respectful return of the remains, so the tribe may observe their religious and cultural practices.” Eiler was alerted to the discovery by a cultural affairs specialist with the Tohono O’odham Nation, a larger tribe whose reservation is east of Organ Pipe, and later by the Organ Pipe superintendent’s office. Her family discussed what to do next. Ultimately, they decided to hold off on reburying the newly unearthed remains until construction in the area stops, fearing the work will disturb more sites. “​​Who knows what more will come up,” Eiler said in an interview. “They’re going to find remains wherever they dig.” Hia-Ced O’odham elder Lorraine Eiler stands in the shade of a giant saguaro cactus in Organ Pipe National Monument in 2022. Roberto “Bear” Guerra Customs and Border Protection contractors have bulldozed a wide swath of vegetation parallel to the international divide. The agency has fashioned staging areas for heavy equipment by knocking down, uprooting and attempting to transplant select specimens of the monument’s native plants. Eiler was told the remains were found by a park service archaeologist near the base of a saguaro cactus that was still standing. In a statement, CBP said it was advised of the discovery six days after it was made, that its cultural resource specialists examined the area and found no other remains, and that “no additional construction has occurred at this location to date.” The discovery comes amid tensions between the Department of Homeland Security and tribal communities in the Sonoran Desert. In April, border wall contractors bulldozed through a large, well-marked earthen etching, known as the Las Playas Intaglio , that was believed to be at least 6,500 years old. (CBP said the incident was accidental .) Soon after, the department awarded a $1.3 billion contract for construction of a 62-mile border wall across the entirety of the Tohono O’odham Nation. The tribe is fighting the project in federal court and has erected “no trespassing” signs to keep border wall contractors off its land. As ProPublica recently reported, DHS has responded by deploying masked federal agents as escorts for its work crews and conducting aerial surveillance of tribal members. The head of CBP has justified the need for a wall by describing the reservation as “one of the most dangerous smuggling and trafficking corridors on the Southwest border.” Verlon M. Jose, the tribe’s chairman, expressed gratitude that the park service had notified his office of the discovery, but mourned the fact that it was necessary. “When you have mass destruction and disturbance of land taking place where there are clearly sacred sites, cemeteries and other areas of cultural importance, these types of discoveries are bound to happen,” Jose said in a statement. “Every time this happens it is a wound to the heart of all members of the Tohono O’odham Nation — these are our ancestors, our family members — whose remains are being desecrated.” U.S. Rep. Adelita Grijalva, who appeared with Eiler and the chairman at the August news conference, blasted the government for failing to heed their warnings. “Tribal leaders and elders have warned DHS about the devastating consequences of bulldozing through their ancestral lands, beginning with the destruction of the Las Playas Intaglio,” she said in a statement. “For months, those warnings have fallen on deaf ears. Now, we are seeing exactly what they feared: sacred sites destroyed and ancestral burial grounds desecrated.” James T. Watson, curator of bioarcheology in the Arizona State Museum at the University of Arizona, analyzed the remains recovered in Organ Pipe in the field. While he was not authorized to discuss the details of his findings without park service approval, Watson said in an email that he confirmed the remains were human. The evidence suggested they were cremated in a manner consistent with precolonial practices in the region dating back 1,500 years, he wrote.  Under NAGPRA, the graves protection act, Native American remains inadvertently uncovered on park service lands must be immediately secured, Watson explained, and the superintendent of the jurisdiction must notify “all relevant lineal descendants” with “potential cultural affiliation or ancestral ties to the land.” “Work in the immediate discovery area must remain suspended for at least 30 calendar days,” he wrote, while the park service consults with tribal representatives “to determine the disposition and physical treatment of the remains.” Workers clear desert flora to make way for construction of a double border wall in Organ Pipe National Monument. Anna Watts In a region as rich with archaeological sites as the American Southwest, the inadvertent disturbance of Native American remains occurs with some regularity. What sets the discovery in Organ Pipe apart are the extraordinary powers the Department of Homeland Security wields to expedite wall construction in the borderlands. Following the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, Congress passed the Real ID Act, which included a provision empowering the secretary of DHS to waive any law that might slow border wall construction. In the two decades since, DHS has invoked its powers 66 times, with 60 of those instances occurring under President Donald Trump’s two administrations. events.title: Banking on innovation for a more connected future
events.summary: At Hong Kong FinTech Week 2026, Hang Seng Bank will showcase AI-enabled innovation and partnerships designed to enhance customer experiences while supporting Hong Kong's development as an international innovation and technology centre [The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.] Hang Seng Bank will bring AI-powered wealth management, digital banking, investment innovation and an interactive table tennis experience to Hong Kong FinTech Week 2026 as it makes its debut with a dedicated exhibition booth at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre on November 2 and 3. Six interactive experiences will showcase innovation across Retail Banking and Wealth Management, Commercial Banking, Markets and Securities Services, Hang Seng Indexes and the bank's partnership ecosystem. One example is Hang Seng's e-Passbook, Hong Kong's first service of its kind, launched in April 2026 with the needs of elderly customers in mind. Another demonstration is a Proof of Concept exploring the potential of bond tokenisation to make fixed-income investments more accessible to retail investors. Tokenisation holds the potential to enable fractionalisation of an underlying bond into smaller digital tokens, lowering the minimum investment required. It may also help streamline transactions and enable faster settlement. Visitors can follow a simulated demonstration investment journey, to experience the conversion of traditional bond into digital tokens. Elsewhere at the booth, visitors can take on a humanoid table tennis robot as part of an AI-wealth management experience. The game introduces visitors to AI-powered personalisation already available through the Hang Seng Mobile App, which provides tailored financial insights and suggestions based on customer profiles and preferences. Its Wealth Overview page and Goal Planner also help customers review their finances and plan ahead. The table tennis connection draws on Hang Seng's more than 35 years of support for local sporting talent. Supporting businesses and investment decisions Hang Seng will also showcase digital services designed to support businesses at different stages of development. An interactive installation takes visitors through an SME owner's journey, with three steps triggering videos covering remote account opening and daily operations, business expansion and wealth management. The bank's capabilities include digital payment solutions, a cross-bank cashflow analysis platform, Hang Seng SME Business Loan, Hang Seng TradePay, alternative data-backed financing and business mobile investment trading.Investors, meanwhile, can explore ThemeFinder, a Gen-AI-enabled solution co-developed by Hang Seng Indexes with an AI innovator from Cyberport's community. The technology identifies thematic investment trends and accelerates index development, improve the efficiency of identifying listed companies and processing relevant data by up to 5 times. The solution also helps maintain consistency across index operating processes and supports data traceability. Visitors can experience how thematic investment themes can be identified in the markets, create simulated personalised indexes and compare their performance against the Hang Seng Technology Composite Index. The showcase will also feature the Hang Seng Technology Index Family and HK-US index series, which combines Southbound Stock Connect-eligible Hong Kong tech stocks with major US-listed tech companies. Connecting Hong Kong's innovation community Its Living Lab programme with HKSTP, for example, launched a second cohort in April 2026 focused on AI applications in retail and commercial banking, providing technology ventures with opportunities to test solutions in banking environments. Such collaborations can move ideas from exploration and pilot programmes towards safe deployment, turning technological advances into solutions that can benefit customers at scale. With deep roots in Hong Kong, Hang Seng is connecting people, ideas and expertise to make banking more accessible, personalised and responsive to changing customer needs.

events.title: More than 400 jobs to be affected under Mater Pathology changes
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts More than 400 jobs affected as Mater moves to external pathology providers More than 100 positions at Mater Pathology will be lost the next two months, a spokesperson said. ( ABC News: Mark Leonardi ) More than 400 positions are expected to be affected at Mater Pathology in Brisbane and Springfield as the hospitals transition to an external pathology provider. A spokesperson for the healthcare provider blamed rising costs for the decision. More than 100 positions will be lost in the next two months, with most of the remaining positions ending in 2027. Mater has outsourced its pathology services in a move that will affect more than 400 staff. The announcement was made today, just a month before Christmas. The healthcare provider has blamed rising costs, saying Medicare subsidies have not kept pace with increasing financial pressures over the past decade. Mater says the transition to external pathology providers will affect more than 400 part-time, full-time and casual employees over the next 12 to 18 months. A spokesperson said the change will have no affect on patients. ( ABC News: Mark Leonardi ) Under the new model, pathology services at Mater's Brisbane and Springfield hospitals will be delivered through specialist providers, including Sullivan Nicolaides Pathology and Pathology Queensland. The change will not affect Mater hospitals in Townsville, Mackay, Rockhampton, Bundaberg or the Gold Coast, which already rely on external pathology service providers. A Mater spokesperson said the decision would have "no impact on the high-quality care Mater patients receive". "The pathology model Mater is adopting is used by private hospital operators across Australia and will allow more resources to be directed to the clinical care of our patients. "We are deeply grateful to our Mater Pathology people," the spokesperson said. "This decision is not a reflection on their capability, professionalism or commitment." events.title: Elections pose next test for Venezuela
events.summary: Venezuela’s next big test will be whether it can turn the Trump administration’s plan for elections into a genuine transition to democratic rule. And with the US midterms over soon, the issue will soon face renewed interest from Washington. Interim Venezuelan President Delcy Rodríguez held a rare address last week in which she vowed to hold elections — an ambitious promise for a government still navigating political upheaval following the US’ arrest of President Nicolás Maduro in January. But no election date has been set, as opposition leader María Corina Machado emphasized in her own remarks shortly afterwards. Meanwhile, Rodríguez is already signaling an interest in working with Washington, despite some of her public rhetoric, tapping former opposition aide Oliver Blanco as foreign minister. — Shelby Talcott

events.title: Election ‘war rooms’ enter the AI age
events.summary: Both OpenAI and Anthropic will have “war rooms” dedicated to ensuring their platforms provide accurate information about the midterm elections, a first for both companies. The concept of a tech platform “war room” dates back to 2018, when Meta stood one up for the first time amid concerns about the proliferation of election-related misinformation. The AI age has supercharged those threats, which now include deepfake videos and AI-powered search results spreading incorrect information. Case in point: Last week, Google’s AI Mode wouldn’t respond to a query about who won the 2020 election, which the company said they were working to fix . “Teams across the company work year-round on strengthening our election-related safeguards and enforcing our policies. Ahead of the election, we have a dedicated war room monitoring our platform for misuse and ready to quickly respond to any incidents,” an Anthropic spokesperson told Semafor. These efforts will be made more difficult by AI’s unpredictable nature, recent cybersecurity issues, and the tendency of AI search tools to reflect back results users want to see. Former Meta director of public policy Katie Harbath told Semafor that war rooms are “built for dealing with the things we can’t necessarily predict going wrong and you need a quick, established process in terms of triaging.”

events.title: Leading progressive wants Democrats to think big post-midterms
events.summary: A leading progressive lawmaker says his party colleagues need to think big and dare President Donald Trump to veto Democratic bills if they take the majority. Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, is pushing for votes on bills to tackle “price gouging, that crack down on utility rates going up, that crack down on politicians profiting off their jobs” — and though he acknowledged some might become law, “if Donald Trump vetoes them, then that’s exactly the platform upon which we beat JD Vance or whoever else in 2028.” House Democratic leaders have sketched out some early priorities for their potential majority, like restoring lapsed health insurance subsidies or reversing cuts to Medicaid; the path beyond that is fuzzier. But the scope of House Democrats’ ambitions will depend on how many seats they pick up, and on Senate control, too. Casar bristled at recent comments by Sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, who said that Democrats should table bigger policy questions until the 2028 campaign, since Trump is still in the White House and likely to veto their legislation. He argued that pushing the envelope was necessary for Democrats to prove to voters they care. “I don’t want to waste our majority by negotiating down to Trump’s level,” Casar said. And if Democrats take the Senate as well on Tuesday, party-line legislation to circumvent the filibuster should be on the table, Casar said. “We should do a reconciliation bill, or multiple reconciliation bills, and dare Trump on those issues. We should also push for policies that are 80% popular across the country and dare Senate Republicans to vote against them,” Casar added. Some incoming progressive lawmakers have threatened to withhold votes for Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries in a speaker election unless he commits to progressive policy goals. Casar sidestepped a question on that prospect. “I’ve worked very regularly with Leader Jeffries, and I am a supporter,” he said. “Everybody’s vote, of course, is their own, and I would let each member speak for themselves on that question.”

events.title: How Trump's iron grip on the Republican Party put the Senate in play
events.summary: The News Americans are angry about war and prices, and a president’s second midterm is always difficult — but a series of decisions by President Donald Trump has made Republicans’ Senate majority ever-more vulnerable. The mark Trump made on the midterms began in the summer of 2024, when he selected former Ohio Sen. JD Vance as his running mate. Since then, the president’s personnel and political decisions have reshaped the Senate battleground from what looked like an impenetrable red wall into a toss-up. His decision to pick Vance opened up a special election in Ohio that will by the end of this week cost the GOP hundreds of millions of dollars and potentially a Senate seat. Trump’s party-boss mentality in North Carolina, Texas, and South Carolina has further contributed to the yawning battleground. He endorsed Rep. Mike Collins in Georgia’s Senate race against Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff — a contest that never really got off the ground after Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp, whom Trump tried to take down in a primary in 2022, passed on the race. Ossoff is favored to win. And party insiders blame Trump’s tariffs and war with Iran for creating a volatile Senate map that has left seats in red states like Nebraska and Kansas vulnerable. Republicans could hold the chamber — or lose as many as a half-dozen seats on Tuesday. “Every negative for the GOP this cycle is a downstream effect of Iran,” said a person close to the White House. Republicans can lose up to three seats and still keep Senate control. Trump’s zeal on the campaign trail is undeniable and he helped direct huge sums of money into the midterms, albeit later than many Republicans would have liked. He spent the last weekend capping off a breakneck fall campaign schedule stumping in Iowa and Kansas, two places where the GOP was strongly favored to win a few months ago but now is struggling. “President Trump has a 97% endorsement record and he remains the best turnout machine for our base voters,” said Republican National Committee press secretary Natalie Baldassarre. Trump is hosting nearly 20 tele-rallies in the last days of the campaign, in addition to his almost-daily travel for rallies over the past month. The White House has sought to emphasize the administration’s accomplishments on issues like the border, crime, and US investment and manufacturing, as they look to encourage low-propensity voters to turn out for Republicans. “President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress,” White House spokesman Davis Ingle said. But his moves to reshape the party in his image over the past two years also often showed little regard for conventional political risk assessment. Trump created two special elections with decisions to put Vance as his vice president and Marco Rubio, a popular former Florida senator, as his secretary of state. On Tuesday, Democrats are underdogs in Florida after nominating democratic socialist Angie Nixon to face appointed GOP Sen. Ashley Moody. The race is more competitive than expected but not a five-alarm fire like Ohio, where Vance’s replacement, Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, is in a precarious position. The longtime preference of Husted, a former lieutenant governor, was to run for governor, according to multiple people familiar with internal party deliberations. He was instead appointed to the Senate and Vivek Ramaswamy ran for governor; Ramaswamy now trails Democrat Amy Action. A campaign spokesperson for Husted said that he “is completely focused on retiring Sherrod Brown once and for all this Tuesday.” “Public polls in the national media have gotten Ohio wrong every election cycle since 2016,” one Ohio GOP operative argued. drama in the south A year after selecting Vance, Trump tangled with Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., over healthcare cuts included in the tax cut law, prompting Tillis to retire. Tillis told Semafor afterward that Trump’s backing might not have helped anyway: “I’m not sure that his endorsement would have helped me in a general election in North Carolina next year, to be quite candid.” Trump quickly cleared the field for former RNC Chair Michael Whatley, avoiding a costly primary, but Whatley’s candidacy crumpled against his Democratic opponent, former Gov. Roy Cooper. Senate Majority Leader John Thune said in an interview last summer that Tillis was “established” and “knew how to run and win in North Carolina,” while also praising Whatley as a candidate who could win with Republicans united behind him. In recent weeks, however, Republicans essentially ceded the race as the battleground map expanded to places like Texas. Thune and many sitting GOP senators had hoped to convince Trump to back Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas. But Trump gave Cornyn the cold shoulder after the Texas Republican’s remarks questioning Trump’s viability heading into the 2024 election cycle. Trump instead backed Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who won the nomination. Paxton is trailing in most polls while receiving the most air support of any candidate. “Texas was an unforced error, I think, on the part of the president,” Cornyn told Semafor in previously unreported comments earlier this year. “We spent a lot of money trying to win the nomination, but the promise was that if I won the nomination, then that would be a layup in November. That’s all off the table.” Had they been nominated again, Cornyn and Tillis may have had tough races too, but most Republicans now believe they would have been closer. Paxton could still win, but the race undoubtedly opens up a shocking vulnerability in Republicans’ red wall. So too in South Carolina. After the death of his longtime ally, Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., Trump backed Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., who most senators thought would be an interim senator. Instead, Trump helped launch Graham’s run for a six-year term, even as several other prominent Republicans mounted their own campaigns. Graham defeated conservative Rep. Ralph Norman, R-S.C., in the primary runoff this summer with Trump’s help, but Graham is now in a toss-up race with Annie Andrews, who is outraising her by astronomical margins. Norman barely lifted a finger to help Graham and the race has gotten closer and closer, prompting intervention from the Senate Leadership Fund, a GOP-aligned super PAC. “There’s an incredibly divided Republican Party in South Carolina,” Andrews told Semafor in September. She added that polling clearly showed “that Darline was going to be easier for me.” Room for Disagreement Republicans say some of Trump’s impact has been positive. events.title: The agentic web is here
events.summary: In 2001, a decade after he invented the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision. Together with two colleagues, he published an article in the magazine Scientific American in which he outlined what he called the “Semantic Web” : an internet designed to be navigated by autonomous software agents that could address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves. To illustrate what this might look like, Berners-Lee and his colleagues told a story about a pair of siblings who use their agents to automatically research and book physical therapy appointments for their mother, making sure they would be covered by insurance and fit their busy calendars.  At the turn of the millennium, this vision seemed far-fetched: Google had only been online for a couple of years, and most people were still on dial-up connections. But a quarter-century on, the dream of autonomous software agents that use the internet and carry out tasks for us has finally been realized. New tools such as Meta’s blockbuster Muse agent, OpenAI’s Dots, and Anthropic’s Claude Duet are being given access to people’s email inboxes and bank accounts, Meanwhile, in a series of worrying incidents, agents created by OpenAI broke free of their sandboxes and caused havoc online. Just as the rise of smartphones sparked the development of a more atomized and attention-grabbing internet, the advent of powerful AI systems heralds a new era: We’re facing not the semantic web but the agentic web. This new web is developing out of sight and in ways that might not be entirely within our control. As it grows, the agentic web will inevitably transform the human web—and whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess. For Berners-Lee’s original vision to work, internet users would have had to annotate the pages they built with special tags so that a software agent could understand each element’s meaning—say, “street address” for the part of a physical therapy office’s web page that indicates its location and “appointment types” for the list of services. And so the idea never really caught on. “It’s a lot of labor,” says Eni Mustafaraj, a professor of computer science at Wellesley College. “And the benefits of that were not obvious.” For the next two decades, then, the internet remained a place that put humans first, with the odd Twitter reply bot or web scraper to round things out. Large language models changed that. Unlike the agents that Berners-Lee was imagining, today’s LLM-based agents don’t need any tags to understand which part of the text on a clinic’s site is its address and which details the services it offers. They can search for and process text far faster than any human, and agents with multimodal capabilities can even interpret screenshots of websites and click on specific elements such as hyperlinks and drop-down menus.  They’re also just a way more intuitive means of finding information and accomplishing tasks online. Rather than poring over pages of Google results to find a budget-friendly product dupe or a half-remembered meme, why not have Claude or ChatGPT peruse dozens of sites in just a few minutes, guided only by your vague query? Or go one step further and use a personal assistant agent like Muse to hunt down a restaurant reservation or book a flight.  As agents flood online spaces, this new user base is changing the web for good. Time magazine, for instance, is publishing versions of its articles that are easier for agents to parse and has started selling ads targeted at them. Companies from Etsy to Expedia have partnered with the major AI firms to build tools that allow agents to interface seamlessly with their services. Despite these early efforts, it’s still tough to tell exactly what forms the agentic web will take and how it will change our online experience. Depending on how it’s designed and who controls access to it, we could be in for something that’s as open and customizable as the web of the early 2000s, only far easier to use. Alternatively, we could be reduced to viewing much of the web through tiny portholes controlled by a few dominant platforms, as independent sites and creators struggle to survive the shift. And as this summer’s series of OpenAI security incidents suggests, the agents might even build their own online networks and resources—whether we want them to or not. How this plays out also depends on us: which parts of our online lives we’re happy to delegate to our agents and where we will still demand a human-centric internet. “There’s a lot we don’t know yet about how users want to use [agents],” says Ajit Varma, head of Firefox at Mozilla. But whatever does happen, the changes will be big. “It’s probably on par with getting a mobile phone,” he says. “I think things are going to change very dramatically.” Building a web for agents There are two ways to approach building the agentic web. The first involves training agents to use browsers like humans—scrolling, clicking, typing—and letting them loose on the web that we’re all used to. The second requires building tools that allow agents to interface with the internet via text and code, their preferred media. That possibility offers more separation between the human and the agentic web: designers can create different experiences for those who use text commands and those who use browsers. When Siva Reddy, a professor of computer science and linguistics at McGill University, began studying LLM agents in 2024, he focused on the first option. “At that time, we thought it should be that the best agent in the world is probably an agent that can use a browser,” he says. Such an agent would integrate seamlessly with the preexisting human web, and its owner could easily supervise it by watching as it navigated familiar interfaces. The frontier AI companies were already developing these “computer-use agents.” But they didn’t work terribly well—at least not at first. “There’s a lot of moving pieces [on the web], and they are not really optimized for automatic consumption,” says Xing Han Lu, a graduate student in Reddy’s lab at McGill. We humans are naturals at interacting with graphical interfaces using a keyboard and mouse, but agents are not. PINGNAN LU So Reddy and Lu pivoted toward the second, tool-based approach. In the summer of 2025, they expounded on this view in a preprint paper envisioning a new kind of web interface that would allow agents to interact with websites just as effectively as we do. Such a full-featured version of the agentic web doesn’t yet exist, but it is emerging in smaller ways. events.title: Britain's driverless dream hits a roundabout of awkward questions
events.summary: As robotaxis continue trials in London, an independent research group thinks the UK needs to answer some serious questions before heading any further down the road. To kick off, the sovereignty question, or "Will Britain become dependent on autonomous vehicle services for any key activities and what fallback options will exist if a supplier fails or withdraws?" as the Institute for Driverless Transport (IfDT) puts it. Another question concerns employment: "To what extent does professional driving form part of the UK's employment safety net and how will this function be recreated if demand for professional drivers is significantly reduced?" The objective for IfDT — an independent UK research and convening body focused on the consequences of autonomous vehicles — is to cast the net a bit wider than simply thinking about whether the software is sufficient to navigate London’s wiggly streets and narrow alleys. The research draws on work with operators trying to bring AVs to London and the regulators responsible for policy. It also relied on more than 30 conversations with councils, operators, industry, unions, charities, insurers, lawyers and universities. James Hutt, IfDT co-founder, said: "What struck us most in the interviews was how far this reaches: into jobs, public services, the built environment and national resilience. The people who know those areas best are rarely part of the conversation about AVs. "Our next step is to bring funding and researchers together with the businesses and public bodies that need answers. If you can fund research or offer a place to test it, we would like to hear from you." In August, Transport for London (TfL) granted private hire licences to autonomous vehicle operators provided that a human driver is present during journeys. Wayve and Uber have since launched self-driving rides in the UK capital, with 15 electric Ford Mustangs, equipped with the Wayve AI driver, set to pick up passengers with a safety driver on board. UK company Wayve also demoed a Nissan LEAF , running the Wayve AI Driver using NVIDIA DRIVE Hyperion with self-driving equipment built more closely into the car's design. IfDT points out that Waymo and Baidu are also preparing services for London, while Uber, Pony.ai and Verne have begun testing in Manchester. The research organization said UK authorities still need to answer a long list of questions in order to shape long-term infrastructure plans for local areas and prepare for AI's impact on the labor market. The question of who needs to do this also remains unanswered, as the IfDT asks: "Which are the key public bodies that should already be anticipating the impact of AVs on their own work and who within those organisations should lead a response?"®
