events.title: Asian shares are mixed and US futures advance, while oil prices retreat
events.summary: Asian shares are mixed ad oil prices have retreated, falling sharply on renewed hopes for progress in diplomatic efforts between the U.S. and Iran HONG KONG -- Asian shares were mixed and oil prices retreated Monday, falling sharply on renewed hopes for progress in diplomatic efforts between the U.S. and Iran. U.S. futures advanced after U.S. stocks fell Friday to their worst day since June as investors dumped technology- and artificial intelligence-related stocks. Japan’s Nikkei 225 gave up early gains, slipping 0.3% to 63,081.86 as some major technology companies fell. South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index rose 2.2% to 5,859.08. Samsung Electronics added 1.8%, while memory chipmaker SK Hynix jumped 3.8%. Technology stocks have been volatile as investors worry that the AI buildup may prove to be a bubble. Apple is due to report its latest earnings results later in the day. Last week, earnings reports from Google parent Alphabet Inc. and Amazon rattled markets and raised fresh questions over whether their massive AI-related spending will bring profitable returns as quickly as hoped. While recent developments do not necessarily mean that the AI boom is beginning to unravel, the debate is entering another phase, Sunil Tirumalai at UBS Global Research wrote in a recent note. Investors have become “distinctly more nervous about a handful of companies with weaker balance sheets or bigger financial commitments,” he said, rather than the technology sector as a whole. “Some cracks have appeared,” said Tirumalai. “Increasingly, the question will be whether all the money being spent on it can generate adequate financial returns.” Over the past month, the Nikkei 225 has fallen more than 7% and the Kospi dropped more than 16%. Taiwan’s Taiex was 0.7% lower, with leading chipmaker TSMC, or Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., shedding 1.7%. Learjet with 9 aboard crashes in Palm Beach County, Florida: FAA Sen. Chris Murphy hospitalized after suffering a stroke, chief of staff says 2 college students found dead after going missing while hiking, police say Hong Kong’s Hang Seng gained 0.5% to 23,411.49. The Shanghai Composite index was up 1.1% to 3,638.03, despite China reporting over the weekend that its factory activity returned to contraction territory in October indicating that the economic momentum may have slowed. China’s central bank and its securities regulatory body met with financial institutions Monday to discuss ways to support the markets, according to Chinese media reports. The Shanghai Composite index has fallen 14.6% in the past year. In Australia, the S & P/ASX 200 lost 0.6% to 8,856.50. On Friday, Wall Street’s benchmark S & P 500 fell 1.8% and the technology-heavy Nasdaq composite declined 2.9%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average slid 1.1%. Investors are watching for the outcome of Tuesday’s U.S. midterm elections . Voters across the political spectrum have shown increasing concerns about AI and data centers , along with inflation and other key issues. Oil prices dropped more than 2% early Monday, with Brent crude, the international standard, down 2.8% to $110.24 per barrel. Benchmark U.S. crude gave up 3.1%, to $100.85 a barrel. Iran’s top diplomat said in an interview shared on his Telegram channel over the weekend that Iranian negotiators were in Qatar for talks on a proposal that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if the U.S. meets several conditions. However, he said no direct talks were being held with the U.S. The final outcome of the diplomatic efforts to avoid a return to all-out war depends on answers provided by the United States to the “Iranian questions,” he said. In other dealings early Monday, the U.S. dollar rose to 157.83 Japanese yen from 157.49 yen. The euro was trading at $1.1186, up from $1.1160. events.title: Asia’s factories lose steam as AI glow meets war’s economic chill
events.summary: Manufacturing activity slowed in China, indicating the drag from Iran war may be offsetting gains from robust global demand for AI chips. Asia’s factory growth slowed in October, especially in China, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, even as chip and AI demand stayed strong. The Middle East war is lifting fuel and food prices, hurting spending and confidence, while China’s price competition is also pressuring exporters. The IMF warned Asia’s growth may ease in 2026 and 2027, and Japan’s central bank said an AI slump could hit exports, production and financial markets. TOKYO – Factory activity across Asia continued to expand in October, but growth slowed in major chip exporters, private surveys showed on Nov 2, suggesting the AI boom may be losing momentum as markets start to question the sector’s profitability. The data points to growing strains on export-led economies, as prolonged conflict in the Middle East keeps fuel and food prices elevated, hitting consumption and business confidence, even as demand for chips and artificial intelligence-related goods remains resilient. Manufacturing activity slowed in China, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, the surveys showed, indicating the drag from the US-Israeli war on Iran may be offsetting the benefits from robust global demand for chips and AI-related goods. “Strong chip and AI demand had masked soft spots in Asian and global economies. But that’s becoming hard to sustain with the Middle East war dragging on for so long, pushing up fuel and food prices,” said Toru Nishihama, chief emerging market economist at Dai-ichi Life Research Institute in Tokyo. “High inflation is hurting Asian consumption. Intensifying price competition from China is also weighing on rival exporters like Japan and South Korea,” he said. The RatingDog China general manufacturing purchasing managers’ index (PMI), compiled by S&P Global, stood at 52 in October, exceeding the 50-mark that separates growth from contraction but falling from 52.1 in September. The reading followed official data released on Oct 31 showing China’s factory activity shrank in October, marking the third contraction in four months. “The PMIs suggest that China’s economic activity lost momentum in October following September’s pick-up. Manufacturing softened a touch, but foreign demand still looks resilient,” said Nguyen Hoang Nam, China economist at Capital Economics. “More worrying was the sharp reversal in construction activity and expectations, suggesting that firms have become less confident that fiscal support will provide a substantial boost over the rest of the year.” Japan’s PMI eased to 53.3 in October from 54.1 in September, a survey by S&P Global showed, marking the slowest expansion in seven months as output and new orders lost momentum. South Korea’s factory activity grew in October at the slowest pace in eight months on weaker output and demand, with the PMI falling to 51.3 from 53.9 in September. Taiwan’s PMI stood at 54.9 in October, down from 56.7 in September. Other economies showed factory activity expanded in October at a faster pace than the previous month, including Vietnam, Indonesia and Malaysia. India’s manufacturing growth slowed in October as domestic demand eased and hiring weakened, though a surge in export orders helped cushion the slowdown. Asia has outperformed many other regions as manufacturers benefitted from brisk demand for chips and AI-related goods. But the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has projected Asia’s economic growth to moderate in 2027 , and warned of heightening risks from the Iran war-induced energy shock and a potential correction in the AI boom. The IMF said it now expects Asia’s economy to grow 4.8% in 2026 and 4.4% in 2027, higher than projections made in April but still slowing from a 5% expansion in 2025. While Japan has been among the beneficiaries of the AI boom, the central bank warned the technology also poses risks to the country’s long-term economic outlook. “If growth expectations for AI decline substantially, a tightening of global financial conditions, accompanied by a rapid repricing of stocks and a sharp slowdown in the race for AI development, could significantly hurt Japan’s economy through a plunge in exports and production,” it said. events.title: Al Habtoor Group board approves sale of all assets and investments in Lebanon
events.summary: Dubai-based Al Habtoor Group said its board of directors had approved the sale of the company's assets and investments in Lebanon , after it ceased operations there. The company, which has hotels, commercial and residential properties in Lebanon, said in January that it was ceasing operations and would terminate its employees in the country due to "prolonged instability" and an investment dispute. The conglomerate, which made investments across hospitality, retail, leisure, real estate and banking-related activities in Lebanon, said at the time that it suffered losses exceeding $1.7 billion. "Following careful consideration, the board has determined that the complete divestment of the group’s Lebanese assets represents the most appropriate course of action, consistent with its commitment to responsible investment management, capital allocation, and the protection of its interests," Al Habtoor Group said on Monday. The company said it intends to undertake the divestment "through a structured and commercially driven process, with each asset evaluated on its individual merits and transactions pursued in accordance with appropriate market conditions and valuations". In February, Al Habtoor Group said it also appointed law firm White & Case to begin arbitration proceedings against Lebanon in the US. The case is based on the dispute resolution mechanisms provided under the UAE-Lebanon bilateral investment treaty, Al Habtoor Group said at the time. The group established its presence in Lebanon with the opening of its first hotel in 2001. It said it "has made substantial investments" since then and has remained committed to the country through successive periods of economic and political uncertainty. The board’s latest decision "reflects a considered shift" in its investment strategy and its plan to concentrate resources on markets "offering greater long-term stability, investment certainty, and sustainable growth opportunities", it said. Al Habtoor Group will announce further details regarding the divestment process, it added. Lebanon has been mired in an economic crisis since 2019, one of the worst in modern history, according to the World Bank. The lender expects Lebanon's economy to contract by 6.4 per cent in 2026. The country, which is heavily reliant on imports, is also struggling from the fallout of the Iran war, as it is more exposed to shocks such as the disruption to shipping and energy supplies. The International Monetary Fund said last month that it was advancing discussions with Lebanon as part of broader efforts to support vulnerable countries in the Middle East and North Africa.

events.title: From expertise to intelligence: NISCO deploys world's first swarm-intelligence steel model at scale
events.summary: Nanjing Iron & Steel Co., Ltd. (NISCO) has worked with Huawei and ecosystem partners to commercially deploy the world's first steel model powered by swarm intelligence - the YuanYe Steel Large Model (YuanYe) - across multiple scenarios at scale. This helps NISCO transition its core operations from relying on experience to being powered by data and intelligence collaboration. As a traditional manufacturer navigating the challenges of transformation and cost efficiency, NISCO has built a robust digital and intelligent foundation by adopting industry-leading products including Ascend, Kunpeng, Huawei Cloud Stack, and Pangu models. By embedding AI into every core stage of production - ironmaking, steelmaking, rolling, and quality inspection - NISCO is forging green and high-end AI-powered super steel plants. Unlike general-purpose monolithic models, YuanYe innovatively fuses multiple AI models with the steel industry's metallurgical mechanism models to create a dual-drive, multi-model cluster architecture. This architecture features a "right brain" for probabilistic computing and a "left brain" for precise and scientific decision-making. Powered by massive amounts of sensing data aggregated from millions of operational technology (OT) data points across 26 business domains, NISCO has achieved real-time digital twin mapping within its intelligent operations center, laying solid data and scenario foundations for YuanYe. This enables the entire steelmaking process to become not only visible, but also capable of precise control and intelligent assessment. Now 100 percent of NISCO's key equipment is connected and digitally controlled and its new product R&D cycles have been shortened by 50 percent, reducing annual costs by over CNY100m (approx. US$15m). As the model continues to iterate, NISCO had launched 25 business agents by October 2026. These agents cover a wide range of scenarios, from visual quality inspection and process optimization to production scheduling and operations management, setting a new benchmark for digital and intelligent steel transformation. Breakthroughs in four core scenarios: YuanYe redefines traditional operations for significant safety, efficiency, and quality gains In the ironmaking stage, AI makes traditionally invisible blast furnaces transparent. YuanYe leverages blast furnaces' internal sensor data and metallurgical mechanism analysis to perform real-time dynamic simulations of the ironmaking process. Assisted by furnace temperature prediction and health diagnosis models, furnace operators can predict temperatures and identify issues two hours in advance, with over 90 percent accuracy. This shifts furnace operations from reactive post-event remediation to proactive pre-control, increasing prime-grade molten iron yield by over 10 percent while significantly cutting unit energy consumption. In the rolling stage, AI drives precise predictions and codifies expert experience to enhance the operational stability of steel rolling and secure leadership in product quality. To tackle the highly dynamic and complex operating conditions during the rolling process, YuanYe's rolling-force prediction model achieves millisecond-level response, narrowing the thickness tolerance to ±0.2 mm and reducing the steel thickness deviation to 1.9 percent to reach a world-leading standard. The rolling-force hit rate has jumped from 88 percent to 98 percent, supporting a steady annual output of over 2.5 million tons of steel plates and increasing the overall yield rate by 0.5 percent. Enhanced dimensional precision and physical-chemical stability allow NISCO's products to meet demanding steel specifications across diverse applications, ranging from mega stadiums and oil pipelines to 10,000-ton cruise ships and LNG storage tanks. In quality inspection, the synergy between robots and AI models serves as a discerning "eagle eye", doubling metallographic inspection efficiency. During metallographic inspection for finished steel, the integrated smart metallographic inspection system built on YuanYe has achieved full-process automation, covering sample grinding and polishing, image acquisition, and smart grading. Inspection accuracy has risen to over 95 percent, while per-sample inspection time has been shortened from 10 minutes down to 3–5 minutes. This 80 percent increase in overall inspection efficiency frees human operators to focus on anomaly analysis and high-level decision-making. In the energy and environmental control stage, NISCO leverages the YuanYe architecture to develop the S-Link Intelligent Agent for Gas and Flue Gas Sulfur Control. Integrating 602 process parameters alongside multi-modal image and knowledge capabilities, the agent achieves a smart closed loop across source prediction, process optimization, and end-of-pipe compliance. By combining mechanism inversion with time-series forecasting, it issues precise sulfur-risk warnings one hour in advance, achieving a sulfur prediction accuracy of over 95 percent. Operational optimization algorithms then calculate the optimal gas blending scheme within seconds. Finally, game-theoretic models dynamically allocate emission quotas, slashing natural gas co-firing consumption by nearly 50 percent. This has reduced downtime caused by emission exceedance by over 25 percent, and delivered more than CNY600,000 (approx. US$90,000) in annual economic benefits - securing both environmental compliance and drastic cost reduction. From automating labor to empowering people: Defining a new paradigm of inclusive AI Li Jinyan, General Manager of the Digital and Intelligent Integrated Development Department and Director of the AI Research Institute at NISCO, said: "Digital and intelligent transformation is inherently human-centric. Its purpose is not to replace people, but to unleash human potential. Our goal is to lift employees out of the endless sea of data, empowering them to direct their creative energy toward work of higher value." To date, NISCO has deployed over 300 AI models across its plants, alongside more than 1,000 low-code agents and lightweight applications built independently by frontline employees. As Cheng Yongfu, Senior Industrial Solution Expert at Huawei's Steel & Non-ferrous BU, noted: "The real value of industrial AI can only be realized when it expands from single-point applications to comprehensive integration with production, operations, and management, which can unlock sustained, scalable empowerment." Looking ahead, as model deployment expands and computing demands continue to grow, NISCO will team up with Huawei and other partners to explore the construction of dedicated data centers for smart steel plants. events.title: Shift Left Is Becoming A System-Level Problem
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Shift left is pushing beyond verification to system-level validation. Fragmented workflows with disconnected tools and models are allowing bugs to escape even though individual components have been verified. Agentic AI may improve coordination across disciplines, identify bottlenecks, and optimize tool usage, but it cannot replace fundamental processes such as simulation and emulation. Experts at the Table : Semiconductor Engineering sat down to discuss why shift left is pushing beyond verification to system-level validation, and where AI can and cannot help, with Frank Schirrmeister, executive director of strategy programs and system solutions at Synopsys ; Ronen Laviv, vice president of business development and strategic partnerships at Hiveware; Jack Berg, vice president of business development at Silvaco ; Ashish Darbari, founder and CEO of Axiomise . What follows are excerpts of that conversation. To view part one of this discussion, click here . L-R: Silvaco’s Berg; Synopsys’ Schirrmeister; Axiomise’s Darbari; Hiveware’s Laviv. SE: The focus of shift left in design has largely been about verification. But increasingly it’s also about validation, right? Darbari : Yes, and it’s influencing huge decisions that could make small companies go bankrupt if they get it wrong. We’ve seen meetings with architects, designers, UVM leads, emulation leads, FPGA and software leads, and VPs, where they’re all looking at bug escapes and asking, ‘Why did this happen?’ The architect is saying, ‘It’s supposed to be this.’ The designer is saying, ‘We didn’t know that.’ The software team says, ‘It’s supposed to be this.’ And we’re sitting there as formal verification people thinking about communication and the model not being accurate, and I don’t know how well we’ll be able to solve this unless we bring the software into the development cycle. Schirrmeister : It’s not only software. It’s all the other aspects, like multi-physics. EM, thermal, and mechanical, which all have to be integrated. To look at this differently, there are hurdles that I cannot fix in this project. But perhaps I can fix it in the next one. It’s a labyrinth. We have models that are digital twins that are irrefutable, because we’ve measured them against the real thing. We can’t overcome those. We are dependent on the application. It may be more vertical, it may be more horizontally stacked to fit into a certain form factor, like a phone or a data center. But it’s like a video game where you have these things popping up. I want to package it this way, but the packaging guy says we can’t do that, at least not today. Maybe a year from now. All of this needs to be taken into consideration as part of your model. Dabari : Absolutely correct. Laviv : Shrinking times for packaging or power estimation or simulation, or even emulation — isn’t that something we could look at? We’re shifting left using AI in order to do stuff earlier. Berg : Verification traditionally has been the longest and most expensive part of doing a design, and it would be nice to say we can take everything and shift it all left. There are chunks that are being shifted left and verified, and that’s good. But how to shift everything left is something we’re still learning. Darbari : If we pick up historical data from packaging and thermal, why can’t we start building models to say, ‘This happened last time. This time it could be done better.’ Berg : You can do that based on inference. Darbari : But we don’t have a tool that ties everything together in one frame. ‘This is the model of functional safety, security, power, packaging, thermals. Go build it.’ Berg : We have different aspects of that, and we, as an industry, are working slowly but surely to integrate all of those. But we don’t have a single workflow that does that. And it really is a workflow, not just a single tool. Laviv : Nowadays, with AI knowing everything with its skills and touching everything, there is kind of a common database for verification and emulation and all the physical stuff. It might benefit customers if they have access to everything is there to be used, potentially even cross-companies. Schirrmeister : There are certain things you can shift left, and others you have to wait for. Certain things are irrefutable. Yes, you can make them faster, but you can’t bypass them. You can be smarter about how you use them. You can figure out which things should be done in emulation, which should be done in simulation, and which should be done with FPGA-based prototyping. We have customers telling us that if they find something in simulation that should have been found in formal, or simulation beforehand, they’ll review why that happened. Laviv : Why not look at bottlenecks in formal, in verification, in emulation, and see if you can handle those bottlenecks in a way that would open the flow for faster AI? Schirrmeister : There are two views here on this whole AI stack. I’m a firm believer that the underlying portions of the stack will still be required. They will be used in different ways by the AI objects, but you don’t take away the characterization, the simulation, the emulation. You get smarter about how to use them. But at the end of the day, you need to build the emulator. That takes some time. You need to get the design into it. And there is a certain number of things which you cannot overcome. You can make the tool flow more productive, but the underlying engines still need to execute, and there are limits to how fast they can become. Darbari : We need to put all of these things in a singular context because if the manufacturing, or the physics, the heat, or the functional, are all sitting in separate context windows, and the software is sitting somewhere else, then you don’t have a complete picture of what this whole device will look like. I was coding for one project and I remember asking a designer, ‘What would happen to this processor if there was more than one outstanding transaction? Could you discard the later ones?’ And he said, ‘We’ll just discard them.’ Everything was exhaustively proved, and while I was taping, the software teams were running their own stuff. But a bug got missed. The software team had a completely different understanding of how they were going to drive the SoC. So they found a trace, and they said, ‘We are losing transactions.’ There was a complete misalignment between what the architect and the designer thought they were building, so they had to patch it at the end of the day. That’s what worries me now, because things are getting so much more complex. We’re putting all of this in the hands of an agent, but who is the master at the top leve

events.title: Putting AI To The Test
events.summary: There are an increasing number of new EDA companies these days, and this is great news. The industry needs some new vitality, new thought leaders, people willing to take risks. The same goes for established companies that cannot go outside their existing comfort zone while meeting next quarter’s financial goals. But sometimes, new startups forget the risks associated with semiconductor design. While they may be able to point to an improvement in time to market, or meeting better performance goals, they fail to understand how small that particular step is in the whole process. Today, a number of companies want us to believe that AI can do everything. Some point the way to automating design, others to verification, and some even claim it can do both at the same time, from the same source material. No, it can’t. While some of it may be possible in the future, it is far from that point today. What many of them fail to do is show proof. One example, one design, one piece of IP is not proof. When verifying any new tool or methodology, you always need to hold back a test set to apply at the end. In this case, with AI, it has to be something it has never seen before, never been trained on. That is the only thing that can provide a fair, unbiased result. As soon as you tweak your tool to do well on that test case, it is no longer a true test. This is why I was delighted to receive communications from Vikash Kumar, senior verification architect at Arm. He has 15+ years of semiconductor industry experience and is the author of the book “AI-Assisted Hardware Verification: Cognitive Verification Architecture with the VEGA Framework.” What he shared with me was his independent work on the quality of existing LLMs for the creation of testbenches. More than 20 years ago, Certess introduced the industry to mutation analysis. If you inject a bug into the design, does the testbench find it? They used the traditional stuck-at fault model and sophisticated statistical analysis to reduce the total number of faults required. The results were a slap across the face to many companies that thought they were doing a good job, only to find out how poor their testbenches were. Vikash’s approach is different. “The setup was simple — hand AI a spec and the RTL, tell it to verify and report back when it is confident the design is clean, and check what it actually found. I hand-seeded realistic, design-representative functional bugs, which keeps the ground truth clean. I know exactly which bugs were planted, so detection is measured against a known set rather than an impression.” I asked Vikash why he chose to insert bugs rather than using the stuck-at model, which has been the industry go-to since the ’80s. “The whole question with AI verification is whether it comprehends design intent well enough to catch the subtle, intent-level bugs, and that is exactly where it struggled — the misses clustered in data-path, encoding logic, and functional corners, not in anything a stuck-at pattern would have flagged.” He started with 25 hand-coded designs spanning bus protocols, DMA engines, ECC memory, control and peripheral logic, and concurrency scenarios. The RTL has never been made public. Into those he inserted 806 bugs. The models were given a specification based on published protocol standards. Three frontier AI models were chosen: Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.4, and GLM-5.2. “Without human intervention or predefined time limits, each model generated testbenches, developed coverage goals, executed simulations, identified and corrected RTL defects, and iteratively refined verification until independently declaring sign-off. All defects were seeded upfront, although some became observable only after earlier corrections.” Here are his key findings: Claude Opus 5 detected 79.2% of seeded defects, GPT-5.4 detected 76.2%, and GLM-5.2 detected 62.8%. Even the highest-performing model missed 20.8% of seeded defects, which is approximately 168 bugs. All three models reached 100% of their self-defined verification goals and declared sign-off despite remaining functional defects. In this audit, particularly high miss rates were observed in ECC memory, GPIO, and AXI DMA designs. Some missed defects involved ambiguous specifications. The agents proceeded without requesting clarification and ultimately declared verification complete. Even the best model, Claude Opus 5, did not detect roughly 168 defects. GPT-5.4 missed about 192, and GLM-5.2 missed close to 300. Perhaps even worse is that Vikash ran each model three times, and each run produced different results. But he is very optimistic about the results. “The impressive part is how much AI caught on its own,” he says. “The important part is how much it missed, and that’s where the engineer still matters.” In a similar manner, ChipAgents just released its new build-a-chip-bench tool. It goes from a workload specification to GSD. The company ranked five models. The best, Claude Fable 5.1 achieved a score of 16.6%, whilst the bottom of the pack was GLM-5.3 with a score of zero. These results look dire, but the biggest failure was their lack of understanding of performance constraints. I believe this will be an even bigger problem when it comes to writing software that has to be cognizant of the underlying hardware and its performance beyond raw speed. Real-time systems deployed within physical AI need predictable latency, at low power, over a broad range of operating conditions. None of this data is available for training today. I will finish with another comment Vikash made: “You can automate the work of verification. You cannot automate the responsibility for it.” The post Putting AI To The Test appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering .

events.title: Binance users withdraw $3.6bn after largest-ever crypto hack
events.summary: Binance customers withdrew $3.6bn (£2.7bn) of assets from the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange as it reopened on Sunday following what is believed to be the largest hack in history. The firm suspended all transactions in the wake of the incident, which impacted $6.3bn worth of digital assets. Major organisations, including the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), have accused North Korea of being responsible for the cyber-attack . The company said it has covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach but the remaining amount may take longer to source. Binance has repeatedly said it would cover all of the losses linked to the attack. Binance said on X: "Between 06:00 and 15:30 [GMT] on November 1, we processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits, resulting in a net outflow of approximately $3.64 billion." There was an "initial spike" in withdrawals, which later declined and "are stabilising as expected", it added. Sunday's net withdrawals account for just over 2% of the $171bn of assets under its management, said Binance. The firm said last week that it has reserved more than $6.3bn in funds, to deal with ​the fallout of the attack. Binance also said withdrawals of more than two dozen major cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum have resumed and that more services will resume in phases once security checks are completed. Funds linked to the Binance hack continue to be laundered, according to Alec Zebrick, senior manager in global services at Chainalysis, which has been working with the firm and governments to get the stolen money back. "We continue to see funds being laundered quite actively," he told the BBC's Today Programme. "The attackers are layering these funds across many thousands of addresses, across thousands of deposits," he added. AI discovered a massive cyber-security flaw - here's what happened Published 22 October The attack on Binance has been attributed to TraderTraitor, a North Korean cybercrime group also known as the Lazarus Group, which stole a then-record $1.5bn from crypto exchange Bybit in 2025 . The FBI on Saturday published a list of cryptocurrency wallet addresses linked to the group and urged partners in the industry to help by blocking transactions involving them. The exchange scrambled to urge cryptocurrency issuers to freeze affected assets. Binance said last week that early checks suggest the incident may have started with a compromised laptop that belonged to an engineer, allowing hackers to find a way to make unauthorised transactions. The hack hit Binance's global centralised exchange, Binance.com, while its US-facing platform has said it was not affected by the issue. Watch: What we know about Binance's $6.3bn hack and what to do if you're affected Binance said it had replaced customers' assets using a combination of sources, including its corporate treasury as well as its futures insurance and emergency reserve funds. "Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident," the firm said. Cryptocurrencies are digital assets traded on exchanges such as Binance. Unlike cash, they do not exist in physical form and are managed on computers, smartphones and other digital devices. Binance was founded in China and has hundreds of millions of registered users globally. events.title: Manager threatened to fire a colleague, then gave them a critical task – which they flubbed
events.summary: Welcome to Monday morning, an occasion The Register marks with a new instalment of " Who, Me? " It's our reader-contributed column in which you confess to workplace mistakes and share your escapes from subsequent scrapes. This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Gordon" who told us he once worked as an engineer at a major semiconductor corporation. Gordon rose to become manager of an engineering team which worked on a very popular PC chipset. One of the chaps on this team wasn't pulling his weight, so Gordon got the job of telling him to improve, or leave. "In all fairness, he was a nice guy but not a great engineer and needed to be better," Gordon told The Register. Not long after that moment of managerial unpleasantness, Gordon's team got the job of doing a full backup of the chipset's "production stepping" – the silicon equivalent of a minor point release. The idea was to create a detailed record that could be used as a restore point. "This was not a nightly backup, but a purposeful backup to retain a snapshot of the entire cleaned-up design database for future cases where we might need to spin another stepping quickly," Gordon explained. Gordon told his underperforming colleague to do the backup. "Because I was overworked, I did not think this through," he told The Register . The at-risk worker quickly proved why he was under the pump by deciding the backup wasn't necessary until the team completed the next stepping – but didn't tell anyone about that plan. Before that next stepping was done, the employee's past indiscretions caught up with him and he was let go. The story now fast-forwards six years, to a moment when Gordon learned that a customer wanted to buy the old chipset design so they could make a radiation-hardened version to use on satellites. The major semiconductor company liked the sound of that, and asked Gordon to find the backup. "My colleague and I then pieced together what had happened," he wrote. "Being good engineers, we said nothing. We searched through old nightly backup tapes until we found bits and pieces of different steppings of the design database and copied them all to one place, then handed this off to the customer." To this day, Gordon doesn't know if the customer was able to produce a useful chip from the bits of backup he cobbled together. "Did they realize they received bits and pieces of two slightly different databases? Did they care? Was the project canceled before anyone realized it?" "From then on, I was more careful about who I assigned the task of creating restore backups for each design project," he told The Register . "And I kept a record of the emails requesting backups and confirmation that backups had been done." Have you given a job to the wrong person? Or given clients slightly dodgy data? In either case, click here to send email to Who, Me? We would love to tell your tale on a future Monday. ®

( Supplied: Environmental Protection Authority Tasmania ) Tasmania's EPA says it has "disrupted an interstate waste tyre operation" it alleges unlawfully collected an estimated 4,000 to 5,000 tyres from local businesses. The operation posed as legitimate controlled waste transporters, making $50,000 in 10 days. The EPA says investigators have located six shipping containers filled with the tyres collected from businesses under false pretences. Tasmania's Environment Protection Authority says it has disrupted an interstate waste tyre operation that unlawfully collected thousands of tyres from Tasmanian dealerships and mechanics. The EPA's investigation began last year, after it received reports that an unlicensed company was approaching businesses posing as "legitimate registered controlled waste transporters" approved by the EPA and Tyre Stewardship Australia. At least 30 instances of unlawful tyre collection involving around 20 Tasmanian businesses were identified. The unlawful operators made approximately $50,000 in 10 days. Investigators located six shipping containers filled with waste tyres, four in Bridgewater and two in Launceston. ( Supplied: Environmental Protection Authority Tasmania ) Investigators uncovered a tyre network that had been operating in various Australian states over recent years, using rented vehicles, short-term shipping container leases and false credentials to collect the waste tyres. In June, six shipping containers filled with waste tyres, four in Bridgewater and two in Launceston, were located, with an estimated 4,000 to 5,000 tyres having been collected and stored across the state. The EPA said the investigation resulted in enforcement action against one operator, with warning notices issued to "retailers who should reasonably have recognised and acted on suspicious activity." Call Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000 Report anonymously via the Crime Stoppers website Evidence gathered across the investigation included alleged breaches of the Environmental Management and Pollution Control (Waste Management) Regulations 2020 and potential fraud offences. EPA chief executive and director Catherine Murdoch said the investigation would assist other jurisdictions in tackling the unlawful activity. "The EPA undertook its largest proactive industry-targeting exercise in response to organised environmental crime to date. "Waste crime can have significant financial and environmental consequences for local businesses and the wider community. events.title: 'Impossible to get ahead': ACT inflation rate rises above national average
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Small businesses feel the pinch as ACT inflation rate rises above nation's average Casey Johnston said her business had been avoiding passing on costs to consumers. ( ABC News: Luke Stephenson ) Household inflation has risen to 4.7 per cent in the ACT, with the national average being 4.3 per cent. Canberrans are continuing to curb their spending, with small businesses seeing declining foot traffic. An economics lecturer says inflation is not expected to come down anytime soon, with another rate increase on the horizon. The ACT's inflation rate jumped to 4.7 per cent in the 12 months to September this year, and now sits above the national average of 4.3 per cent. And with the RBA expected to lift the cash rate again tomorrow to 4.85 per cent — the highest rate since the 2008 global financial crisis — many households are doing all they can to curb their costs. But for some Canberra business owners that means sales are down, with no end in sight. "Nobody's out and about eating and obviously that hurts us," Casey Johnston, who runs a burrito business in Tuggeranong with her partner, said. Ms Johnston said she was used to business "fluctuating" in the hospitality sector, but sales were "a lot lower" than past years. "I feel like our foot traffic, people walking along the street just to find somewhere to eat for dinner or lunch, is definitely declining," Ms Johnston said. As the cost of living continues to bite, Canberrans are cutting back on their discretionary spending. ( ABC News: Mark Moore ) Ms Johnston said they were also absorbing rising business costs including products and rent, rather than passing those costs onto customers. "[It] is a hard battle because we can't increase our prices for our consumers, but we're definitely taking the hit of our products being more expensive ourselves," she said. "We can't always afford wages and that kind of thing. "If people aren't here then the employment is not necessarily needed all the time, and that can make things really tricky." Interest rates projected to rise again Dr John Hawkins said interest rates were predicted to continue rising. ( ABC News: Luke Stephenson ) Senior lecturer in economics at the University of Canberra Dr John Hawkins said global oil prices were the main driver for rising inflation rates. In the ACT specifically, the biggest drivers were fuel, electricity, childcare and school fees, new housing builds, and furniture, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics. "You get these variations that are quite random," Dr Hawkins said. "Our inflation's lower than Hobart, Darwin, and Adelaide, but it's a bit higher than Sydney and Melbourne." Dr Hawkins also warned the Reserve Bank of Australia was likely to once again hike up interest rates. "There's an 80 per cent chance that [homeowners] will probably be paying 0.25 per cent more on their mortgages from tomorrow, and the financial markets think if the Reserve Bank doesn't move tomorrow, they'll probably move in either December or early next year," he said. "Raising interest rates will lower inflation because it will slow down the economy. Hairdresser Elanor said people tended to spread out their appointments these days. ( ABC News: Luke Stephenson ) Elanor, a hairdresser, said she has personally already cut down "literally everything" when it comes to discretionary spending. "So no coffees out, no more expenditures," she said. "Holidaying, going away, just being able to eat out — so not going out to restaurants, even though we've got all these beautiful restaurants and everything around us — no, I don't spend on that anymore." Elanor said her workplace's clientele base had largely remained the same, but people were booking hair appointments less frequently than they normally would. "It is impossible to get ahead at the moment, especially here in Canberra," she said.

events.title: Christmas donations gift demand up, charities say
events.summary: The Christmas Sparkle appeal said demand for toys has gone up in recent years Charities giving Christmas presents to struggling families say more children need their help - but they are getting fewer donations this year. The Chard Christmas Present Appeal said it was having to deal with a high-than-normal demand this year, and blamed the problem on more people struggling financially. Martyna Lee, founder of the appeal, said a lot of families were worried about affording presents for their children due to the cost of living crisis and have "tears in their eyes" when the charity can help them. She added: "We are getting more referrals and less donations because of cost of living, so we do struggle. Cost of living is going to get harder and harder." Song urges builders to talk about mental health Published 1 day ago MP facing voice loss after surgery shows recovery signs Published 1 day ago Bid launched for 410 new homes near motorway Published 1 day ago Lee started the appeal by herself in 2019 from her living room as part of the Lord's Larder food bank in Chard. They rely completely on donations and do not receive any funding. The Chard Christmas Present Appeal said more families need their help this year "With one family, the social worker asked the children what they would like for Christmas and they asked for pencils and a colouring book," Lee said. "That broke my heart. They weren't asking for expensive gifts. "So I made sure they had a large gift package, including board games." She added that another family she remembers had a fire at their home just before Christmas and they lost "nearly everything". "We managed to get them fantastic gifts and a Christmas tree and decorations," Lee said. Meanwhile, Taunton's charity appeal Christmas Sparkle said their demand has risen sharply over the last couple of years, with 500 presents given out in 2015 to 10,000 last year. They said they are expecting even higher demand this year. Gill Harrison, founder and manager at Christmas Sparkle, said she believes the cost of living crisis is increasing the demand for their services. "When we started the project in 2015, we gave out 500 individual gifts. Last year, it was around 2,300 parcels, that's about 10,000 individual gifts," Harrison said. "We are expecting possibly even more requests this year. That's mostly because of the cost-of-living crisis." Harrison said they work with schools, social services, police, women's refuges and community nursing teams, which have all increased their referrals to Christmas Sparkle over the last few years. events.title: Christmas shoebox appeal launches to help children
events.summary: The boxes will be available in supermarkets for shoppers to pick up and pack before they are passed on to school and charities for distribution. Children across Staffordshire who might otherwise go without a Christmas present are set to receive gift-filled shoeboxes through a new appeal encouraging residents to donate locally. The initiative, organised by World Give, is asking people to pick up empty shoeboxes from supermarkets, fill them with gifts and return them for distribution to families through schools, charities and Staffordshire County Council. Trustee Adam Contoret said the appeal was launched after the charity recognised growing levels of hardship closer to home. "We look around the shops, we see everyone going about their business, but you don't see the people that aren't there," he said. School children gave feedback on what sort of items could be included so that a list could be prepared to help shoppers understand what to put in the boxes. "There's people that would be buying Christmas presents, but they can't because they haven't got the money." Over the past 20 years, the charity has helped more than 100,000 children across the world by sending shoeboxes full of gifts. This year, however, it has turned its attention to supporting children and families in Staffordshire. "It's apparently one in seven children who won't get a formal gift-wrapped Christmas present under the tree at Christmas," Contoret said. "This year we're turning around. Charity begins at home. The boxes are being done in Staffordshire for Staffordshire kids." People will be able to collect empty shoeboxes from participating supermarkets, fill them while doing their shopping and return them to be distributed through schools and local charities. The appeal comes as a Family Action survey of 2,000 parents and carers found one in five had considered cancelling Christmas because they could not afford it, while one in nine said they would not be able to afford a Christmas present for their child. Adam Contoret has previously sent shoeboxes over the world but this year after seeing the statistics, wants to shift the focus closer to home Contoret said schools and local charities were best placed to identify families who could benefit from the scheme and ensure gifts were distributed discreetly. "The schools know the families and they're the best place to hand those gifts over at the right time in a discreet and respectful way," he said. Students supporting the campaign said the shoeboxes could have a significant impact on children at Christmas. Noah said he would include practical items alongside gifts. "I think it's good to give things to everyone and relate it to the age groups," he said. "I would give them notepads, pens, calculators and a stationery set, for example pencil cases, rulers and protractors." Steven said the appeal could help children enjoy the festive season. "Christmas is a festive season of merriness, so if you don't have any presents, you don't feel that giving and love and you won't feel that much merrier," he said. Isabelle said receiving a gift-filled shoebox could help children feel valued. "They might feel special because they know someone actually put thought into putting stuff in the box for them, so they know that someone cares for them and they feel loved," she said. events.title: Dr Sultan Al Jaber urges energy security overhaul as nearly billion barrels drawn from oil markets
events.summary: The disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has drained nearly one billion barrels from global oil inventories, exposing the need for a fundamental rethink of energy security, the Adipec conference in Abu Dhabi heard on Monday. “Simply put, the world has eroded its supply buffers,” said Dr Sultan Al Jaber, UAE Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology and managing director and group chief executive of Adnoc. “But, trust me, supply is only half the story. The other half is delivery." During the event's opening ceremony, Dr Al Jaber called for greater investment in supply infrastructure and artificial intelligence to help the energy industry withstand future shocks, warning that securing production was no longer enough to guarantee that supplies reach consumers. Referring to OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman, who attended the ceremony, Dr Al Jaber said, “Sam, from the moment ChatGPT was born, the world has asked what energy can do for AI. And now, together, we will find out what AI can do for energy.” He spoke as Adnoc announced an agreement with OpenAI and G42 to become the world's first energy company to deploy OpenAI's Frontier platform, with plans to transform the Abu Dhabi energy company's field development, well management and commercial operations. The partnership, guided by Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, would make Adnoc's systems smarter, safer, more secure, more resilient and more productive, Dr Al Jaber said. The Iran war severely disrupted energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz and exposed weaknesses in global supply chains, he added. “For years, our industry optimised for just in time,” Dr Al Jaber said. “And to tell you the truth, we got very good at it. This year we got the bill for just in case.” Diesel stocks in some markets have fallen to their lowest seasonal levels in 35 years, while others face a 600 billion cubic feet gap in LNG supplies, he said. Shipping and logistics costs, which accounted for less than 5 per cent of the cost of a barrel before the disruption, now exceed 30 per cent. “Energy security is not only measured at the point of production. It is now also measured at the point of delivery,” Dr Al Jaber said. He outlined five priorities for strengthening energy security: accessible supply, routes to market, operational intelligence, investment confidence and people. He also called for intelligent energy systems capable of anticipating risks, improving performance and reducing costs. On investment, Dr Al Jaber said: “Capital follows confidence. Policy must create it … finance must accelerate it … and insurance must keep trade moving.” He said the UAE would continue to advocate dialogue, diplomacy and political solutions to support stability in energy markets and the global economy. “Talent stayed. Capital stayed. Investment kept coming … and the economy kept moving,” he said. “That is the UAE model, pressure-tested and proven by results.” Dr Al Jaber said Adnoc's preparedness had been developed years before the disruption. “We did not write our resilience playbook during this disruption. We wrote it years before,” he said. “Energy leadership is not measured by what you produce in good times. It is measured by what you deliver in hard times.” “Because when it counts the most. You can count on the UAE,” he added.

events.title: Chap who coded Google’s Pac-Man clone reveals how the game freaked out Firefox
events.summary: A designer named Marcin Wichary has revealed the story of how he freaked out a decent slab of the world’s Firefox-using population with Pac-Man. Wichary has held senior design roles at Figma, Medium, and Google. As he wrote here , in 2010 Google decided to celebrate the 30 th anniversary of Pac-Man by changing its logo at Google.com to a playable version of the game. The Google of 2010 could still mention its motto of the time, “Don’t be evil,” without making anyone who heard it guffaw incredulously. The company’s frequent changes to the logo on its homepage – called Google Doodles , and which persist to this day – were still a notable part of net culture. Wichary got the job of building the playable logo, and tweaking Pac-Man to replace its usual maze with a course that instead navigated around the letters GOOGLE. “It was, frankly, a terrifying proposition,” Wichary wrote. “The homepage was then a very important destination, and my job title was only adjacent to ‘software engineer.’ But I started researching the game and recreating it all in HTML and CSS." Google wanted a full Pac-Man experience, including sound, "because so many of Pac-Man’s sounds are beyond iconic: the starting melody, the waka-wakas, the death jingle." Wichary began work before Google sought permission from Pac-Man’s owner Namco, because the search giant was “planning to wow them with a close-to-finished doodle.” “The project was … going really well. I had fun coding the game and we seemed to have fun playing it. Namco eventually got onboard, too,” he wrote. Google liked the game work so much, higher-ups decided it would be a great idea to have it start automatically if visitors to google.com stayed idle for ten seconds. The designer liked that idea. “If there was anything scary about it at the time, it was only the thought of my code getting even more exposure – but I wasn’t worried about distraction, since the homepage was not a destination page you would ever linger on.” What Google didn’t realise was that some people lingered on the home page without ever knowing they were there. Those people used the Firefox browser with an extension called CoolPreviews that let users hover over a link to see a preview of a web page. “The extension would quietly start at the same time Firefox was opened,” Wichary explained. “And it would immediately, in the background, invisibly and unbeknownst to the user, open a website.” That website was Google’s home page, which now featured an auto-playing and version of Pac-Man that CoolPreviews users simply did not expect. Which explained why, not long after setting the Pac-Man doodle live, Google received plenty of praise, but also reports about computers making strange noises due to CoolPreviews invisibly opening the noisy game. “I pushed a patch within hours,” Wichary wrote, explaining that he added a mute button and a requirement to click something to make the game and its noises start. CoolPreviews couldn’t make those clicks, so the phantom Pac-Man sounds went away. “Ironically, I don’t believe we ever heard of normal people being bothered by the autoplay – it seemed that indeed, few people stayed on the homepage for 10 seconds doing absolutely nothing,” Wichary wrote. “The funny thing is that emergency live-patching [the] internet’s at the time most valuable homepage was perhaps the scariest part of that day for me, but that completely went over my sleep-deprived head,” he added. Google changed Wichary’s title after this incident. His post shows an image describing him as “User experience designer. The Michael Bay of doodles.” ®

events.title: Land of the free, home of the bill shock. This is life in Trump's America
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Rising cost of living to hit heavily at US midterms as bill shocks rattle Americans The decaffeinated coffee beans at a US cafe sum up how its customers feel about the rising cost of living. ( ABC News: Richard Mockler ) It's a quiet Sunday morning in Lansing, Michigan. The low autumn sun lights the interior of the Hob Nob cafe, illuminating a table of young regulars, including the flat-cap-wearing Nicholas Kolacz. He's just bought his weekly coffee. "After a tip, because I always like to tip, it's $US10," Nicholas says. "I used to come in here … probably three or four days a week. Now I come in once every Sunday because I don't have the money to spend," he says. Nicholas Kolacz rarely buys coffee out now due to the higher prices. ( ABC News: Richard Mockler ) Nicholas makes $US17.50 per hour as a delivery driver. After rent and bills, there is no spare cash. He stopped buying beer long ago and looks at every discretionary purchase through the prism of his wage. "When I do buy things, I look at like, 'Oh, how many hours am I working to get this?'" Once, America felt affordable. Now, the land of the free is also the home of the bill shock. I felt it myself at a bagel cafe on New York's Upper West Side. Twenty years ago, when I lived in Manhattan, my regular breakfast was a bargain: coffee, orange juice and a bagel with lox for $US5. This week, at a no-frills diner, the same breakfast cost me $US31 ($44). The owner of the Hob Nob cafe in Lansing, Trisha Kosloski, says her expenses have gone through the roof. She estimates her delivery costs have increased 50 per cent as shippers pass on fuel costs. But her biggest expense had nothing to do with petrol, or the US and Israel-led war with Iran. The price of coffee beans shot up just after Donald Trump was elected and announced a suite of tariffs on a number of nations where coffee was grown. The average price of coffee in the US is now $US9.33 ($13), the federal minimum wage is $US7.25 ($10.22) . "I'm an import business. We do not grow a lot of coffee in America, as much as we want to pretend that we do," Trisha says. "When we saw those first round of tariffs that were just like blanket tariffs when he first got into office, all of my coffees went up at least 30 per cent. Trisha Kosloski has passed on the cost increases to her customers. ( ABC News: Richard Mockler ) In July, Donald Trump announced 50 per cent tariffs on goods from Michigan's neighbour, Canada — which also hit the coffee industry . "A large amount of the beans roasted in America … are actually roasted in Canada. So we had to pay those tariffs to get them," Trisha says. All the extra costs have put pressure on her business. "There is no profit margin," she says. Coffee might be a discretionary purchase, but for many Americans there has been no way to avoid the most painful price increase. Petrol — or "gas" as it's known the US — is hovering at about $US4.30 per gallon ($6.10 for 3.8 litres or about $1.60 a litre), about $US1 more expensive than it averaged in 2025. That is still cheaper than Australian prices, but Americans aren't used to paying anything like this. Big cars are standard, and long journeys are unavoidable in sprawling mid-western communities like Lansing, Michigan. The city is the home of the Michigan State University Spartans college football team, and for many, a lively Saturday morning tailgate begins before dawn. The parking lots around Spartan Stadium are filled with gleaming, oversized SUVs and "trucks", like Ford F150s and Chevrolet Silverados. It's costing Americans more to fill up the tank of their big cars. ( ABC News: Richard Mockler ) "Gas is the number one thing that used to not be so much," MSU student Samson Sprague says. It's not only students feeling the pain. It's Parents' Weekend at MSU, where there are two and sometimes three generations of Americans here today. "My daughter goes to University of Kentucky, so when we drive down to see her, gas is a lot more expensive. It's almost more reasonable to fly to Kentucky than drive to Kentucky right now because of the price of our gas," Michelle Krebill says. Michelle Krebill (right) says it's costing her more to visit her daughter interstate. ( ABC News: Richard Mockler ) Tara Lukaart is another struggling with the cost of filling up tanks. Her husband operates a plumbing business with several trucks on the road. "For a small business to be able to afford that kind of increase in gas price has been a big deal," she says. Elizabeth Madigan believes the current situation should lead to political change.

events.title: Adnoc becomes first energy company to deploy OpenAI Frontier
events.summary: Adnoc has signed an agreement with OpenAI and G42 , to become the first energy company to deploy OpenAI’s Frontier technology as it seeks to expand AI use across its operations. Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi and Chairman of the Abu Dhabi Executive Council, met OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman on Monday and witnessed the agreement, signed by G42 through its subsidiary Inception42. “Abu Dhabi and the UAE are setting a bold, global standard for AI integration across both the public and private sectors to make sure the benefits of AI reach everyone,” said Mr Altman, who is in Abu Dhabi to attend Adipec . “We are proud to support the UAE’s ambition, anchored in a shared commitment to safety, accessibility and responsible innovation.” The project will integrate advanced AI capabilities across Adnoc’s operations, enabling more connected operational, investment and commercial decision-making to improve efficiency and productivity. The technology will run on OpenAI’s GPT models using inference infrastructure based in the UAE. OpenAI launched Frontier on February 5 as an enterprise platform for building, deploying and managing AI agents. HP, Intuit, Oracle, State Farm, Thermo Fisher and Uber were among its first adopters. The Frontier deal is one of four agreements signed between Abu Dhabi-based entities and OpenAI, spanning the government, energy and investment sectors. The Abu Dhabi government and OpenAI also launched what they described as the world’s first AI native Machine-Readable Government initiative , part of the emirate’s goal to become the world’s first fully AI-native government. The initiative converts government policies and regulations into a format AI systems can read, to help officials carry out routine compliance assessments, such as issuing permits and certificates. Officials retain oversight of the processes, and accountability for final decisions. Led by the Department of Government Enablement, its first pilot is already running with the Abu Dhabi Agriculture and Food Safety Authority and focuses on food imports. Mubadala , Inception42 and OpenAI signed an agreement to apply AI to investment analysis, opportunity identification and risk assessment. Inception42 and OpenAI also signed a five-year agreement to support the adoption of frontier AI across government, enterprise and education in the UAE. Adnoc has been building its AI capabilities for several years. In 2019, it agreed with G42 to set up a joint venture to develop and commercialise AI products for the oil and gas industry. The venture, AIQ , was 60 per cent owned by Adnoc and 40 per cent by G42. The agreements build on OpenAI’s long-standing ties with the UAE. G42 and OpenAI first partnered in October 2023 to apply the US company’s generative AI models in sectors including financial services, energy, healthcare and public services. In May last year, the two companies announced Stargate UAE , OpenAI’s first international deployment of its Stargate AI infrastructure and the start of its OpenAI for Countries programme. The 1-gigawatt cluster is being developed by G42’s Khazna Data Centres within the 5-gigawatts UAE-US AI Campus in Abu Dhabi, with OpenAI, Oracle, Nvidia, Cisco and SoftBank as partners. OpenAI said at launch that the first 200 megawatts were expected to go live in 2026 . Abu Dhabi has also invested in OpenAI, with MGX among the co-leads of OpenAI’s $122 billion funding round, which closed on March 31 at an $852 billion post-money valuation.

events.title: Oil prices slide more than 3% as Trump signals more time for Iran diplomacy
events.summary: Oil prices fell on Monday morning amid hopes of a diplomatic breakthrough between the US and Iran , easing concerns about further supply disruption. US President Donald Trump reportedly said he wants to give diplomacy with Iran more time before considering renewed military strikes after Tuesday’s US midterm elections. The two key benchmarks slid more than 3 per cent in morning trading. Brent, the benchmark for two thirds of the world's crude, was trading at $110 a barrel at 7.55am UAE time. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, dropped to $100.90 a barrel. Mr Trump reportedly told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during a phone call that he wanted to give diplomacy with Tehran more time before considering further strikes, Axios reported, quoting sources. CBS News reported that Mr Trump said he believed the US would soon end the war with Iran, "one way or the other". The US President was speaking to Right Side Broadcasting Network before a campaign rally in Iowa on Sunday, according to the report. "We've had such a victory, and we'll put it away very soon, one way or the other," Mr Trump was quoted as saying. "Either they'll make a deal, or we'll just end it … The job we've done is amazing." On Saturday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said no decision had been made on renewed strikes and that Mr Trump preferred a diplomatic resolution. On Sunday, the UK Maritime Trade Operations said it received a report that a ship had been struck by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz , after an attack on a liquefied natural gas tanker on Friday. The UKMTO also reported a vessel was struck east of Ras Al Khafji, along Saudi Arabia's Gulf coast. An Iranian delegation was in Qatar for discussions with mediators on Saturday, according to a Bloomberg report. Fears of US strikes on Iran have maintained upward pressure on crude, keeping supply risk premiums elevated. Oil prices started sliding on Monday after hitting a six-month high last week on Hormuz strikes and a US threat to hit Iran. Over the past week, both Brent and WTI increased by about 0.8 per cent. On a monthly basis, the benchmarks surged by about 15 per cent and 12 per cent, respectively, to hit their highest levels since April. Meanwhile, Swiss lender UBS said in a report recently it expected Brent crude prices to remain elevated, near $110 a barrel at the end of the year, as Middle Eastern supply remains volatile and geopolitical uncertainty persists. "Record freight costs, constrained tanker capacity, and recovering Chinese imports are other factors likely to keep oil prices high," UBS commodity analyst Giovanni Staunovo said.

events.title: India floats AI plan under which ‘The model travels to the data, rather than the data travelling to the model’
events.summary: As debate and legal argument continue over the extent to which developers of large language models are entitled to feed the world’s data into their systems without paying for it, India’s government has come up with an idea to regulate and secure the flow of information. India’s motive is to create AI models trained on local data, because it thinks offshore model-makers won’t be motivated to address the nation’s issues or to ensure owners of data stay in control. The scheme India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) thinks can make that happen is called the “Data Empowerment and Protection Architecture (DEPA) for AI Training.” As described by Professor Ajay Kumar Sood, Principal Scientific Adviser to the Government of India, DEPA means “the model travels to the data, rather than the data travelling to the model.” The scheme envisions “Training Data Providers” (TDPs) – examples of which include hospitals, banks, and government agencies – sharing anonymized and encrypted data with a “Data Exchange Platform” (DEP). Entities called “Training Data Consumers” (TDCs) access the data stored at the DEPs to train their models. DEPs will operate what MeitY calls “hardware-based Secure Data Environments” in which “data remains encrypted and isolated even during processing.” They also enforce rules set by TDPs that describe how TDCs can use data. MeitY’s DEPA framework [PDF] says this scheme means “Differential privacy techniques are systematically applied to prevent the model from learning or revealing individual specific information,” adding “All activities inside the secure data environments are immutably logged for audit purposes, ensuring that the process is both secure and transparent.” India’s government already operates several data exchanges, but it is unclear how much work remains to make DEPA a reality. Once DEPA is working, MeitY envisions model-makers will use it to do things like “unlock currently fragmented health data to power breakthroughs in AI-driven diagnostics, drug discovery, and public health management.” The optimism extends to financial services. India is home to literally thousands of banks, and MeitY thinks “DEPA can enable secure sharing of diverse financial data, potentially extending formal credit to 400 million underserved individuals and MSMEs and fueling next-generation fintech innovation.” India’s government has long believed that if financial services companies can lend to more people, it will boost economic development. “Similarly, in Education, DEPA can overcome data interoperability challenges to enable AI-powered personalized learning for millions and create portable skill credentials essential for a future-ready workforce of its 250 million students in a $29 billion EdTech sector,” the framework states. “The successful adoption of DEPA Training across these domains is the essential catalyst for realizing India’s vision of inclusive growth and responsible AI leadership on the global stage.” While the purpose of the framework is to build Indian AIs for Indians, the document also has half an eye on the nation’s international standing. “DEPA is India’s contribution to global science diplomacy, advancing the efforts of institutions such as the World Bank and the United Nations to shape a more inclusive and responsible global AI ecosystem,” the framework states. It also makes several mentions of digital public infrastructure (DPI), an idea pioneered by India that involves government funding creation of tools like the Unified Payments Interface payment systems and the Bharat Taxi zero-commission ride-sharing platform, to ensure Big Tech companies don’t dominate the local market. India also uses its DPI as a diplomatic tool, by giving it away to friendly nations. ®

events.title: Alterra's investments designed to hedge against AI bubble, says chief executive
events.summary: Alterra, the UAE's $30 billion climate vehicle , has designed its artificial intelligence investment strategy to protect it against a much talked about bubble in the sector, its chief executive has told The National . The fund's focus on investing in energy systems powered by AI and not directly into the technology is serving as a “hedge” against any potential bubble that may burst in the booming industry, Majid Al Suwaidi said. “We're investing in the only place that our portfolio touches the AI story – through the energy systems. What is great with our investment thesis is that we don't invest directly in AI infrastructure,” he said in an interview. “Those energy systems, regardless of whether it's powering AI or powering a factory, homes, schools, or hospitals, that power will still be needed. So, in a way, Alterra and the investments we make are a really good hedge against a bubble in AI.” Mr Al Suwaidi's comments come as Abu Dhabi-based Alterra gives a vote of confidence to the technology by partnering with one of Europe's biggest sovereign AI companies. On Monday, Alterra announced that it had partnered with Milan-based Domyn to develop a proprietary climate intelligence system that the former will own and control, which will pave the way towards becoming an AI-native company, Mr Al Suwaidi said. “Once we've built that core system, we can then extend that to other aspects of the business and truly become an AI-native organisation,” he said. The system, which will be developed in phases, will “come into the fore” next year, he added. “To pick up these technologies and apply them very early in our development means that we will be able to use AI or our analytics to … take advantage of the power of this technology.” Alterra did not disclose the value of its partnership with Domyn, which was formerly known as iGenius and founded by former Apple employee Uljan Sharka. Domyn has raised $1.1 billion in debt financing over the past two years and is valued at about $2 billion. In June, the European Commission chose Europa, a project led by Domyn, to develop an open-source AI model covering all 24 official languages in the EU. “The way we're designing the system is that it can be evergreen in the sense that as new models are being built or as new developments happen within the technology that they can be plugged in immediately and we can upgrade our system,” Mr Al Suwaidi said. The partnership with Domyn mirrors his confidence in the AI sector, where the bubble debate is hot. Recently, two of the biggest names in asset management, Citadel chief executive Ken Griffin and Blackstone president Jon Gray, gave negative and positive views, respectively. Mr Al Suwaidi acknowledged that there is a bubble “in some ways”, but managing expectations and doing due diligence to make sound investment decisions will help contain potential ill-effects. “Any time you have a new asset class, a bubble is developed … and bubbles can be good if managed and bad if they burst … it just remains to be seen how long it will continue to grow and whether we can manage it in a prudent way so that it doesn't burst with negative consequences,” he said. “We know for sure that this technology is going to be critical to our future economic development, and how we use it becomes increasingly important, and we're discovering that, so there's going to be winners and losers in that process.” Alterra's mandate is to raise $250 billion globally by 2030 to create a fairer climate finance system. Its chairman is Dr Sultan Al Jaber, Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology and managing director and group chief executive of Adnoc. It is less than three years since Alterra's launch at the Cop28 climate conference hosted by the UAE. Since then, Alterra has grown into three funds – Acceleration, Transformation and Opportunity – with five global investment partners: Brookfield Asset Management, BlackRock, Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners, KKR and TPG. It also has more than 60 direct and indirect portfolio companies across more than 40 countries, supporting more than 100GW of renewable energy capacity. Alterra's capital activity is also accelerating. More than $51 billion in expected equity capital across its fund and co-investment activities has been mobilised, with preliminary mobilisation ratios of more than 10 times for its Acceleration Fund and over four times for the Transformation Fund, excluding Alterra's own capital and deal-level debt. Recent investments also show the breadth of Alterra's expansion, including Inkia in Peru, Wireless Logic alongside General Atlantic, and Jeppesen ForeFlight with Thoma Bravo. “What Alterra has shown through our success in the climate realm is that you can achieve the same goals, but in an economically prudent way,” Mr Al Suwaidi said. “Something that is very unique, and very underreported is how successful we've been in our model.”
