Chris Murphy hospitalized after suffering a stroke, chief of staff says 2 college students found dead after going missing while hiking, police say The Election Commission and Modi’s administration deny the allegations and say the revision is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible entries. Human Rights Watch on Thursday said that the accusations over the voter roll revision raise “serious questions about the fairness of future Indian elections.” “The authorities should immediately scrap the voter roll revision process that has denied India’s most marginalized people their right to vote and other government services,” said Elaine Pearson, the group’s Asia director, in a statement. For weeks, the call for Kumar’s resignation has been a rallying cry for opposition parties and supporters of the Cockroach Janta Party seeking to challenge Modi’s Hindu nationalist BJP. Opposition parties, mainly the Congress, say the governing BJP has undertaken systemic manipulation of the electoral process, accusing the party of “vote chori,” or vote theft. Modi hasn't publicly commented on the protests. Some of his party leaders have dismissed the demonstrators as “anarchists” and suggested, without offering evidence, that they are backed by foreign powers. In July, protests led by the youth “cockroach” movement forced the resignation of Modi’s education minister , a rare setback for Modi, who has been in power for more than 12 years. The movement began as an online satirical campaign this summer after India’s chief justice compared unemployed young people to parasites. Suresh Sharma, a protester from northern Haryana state, said that the country’s system needed reform because democracy was being throttled. The process of voter roll revision needs to be scrapped, Sharma said. “We demand that Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar resign and be arrested,” he said. events.title: Virgin Media O2 set to cut thousands of jobs to reduce costs
events.summary: Thousands of Virgin Media O2 staff are facing redundancy as the telecoms firm attempts to save money in the face of billions of pounds of debt and tougher competition. The broadband provider has not finalised the number of roles to be cut but it is likely be a sizeable chunk of its 16,000-strong workforce, the BBC understands. Virgin Media O2 has billions in debt on its balance sheet and is tackling both smaller providers as well as giants like BT, which has agreed a deal to acquire rival TalkTalk, which Virgin Media O2 has firmly opposed. The company declined to comment. Prospect, a union which represents Virgin Media O2 staff, said the cuts were "disappointing and very unsettling". Noel McClean. deputy general secretary at Prospect, said the union was "committed to supporting our members through what is a difficult time, as well as also working with employers to explore ways to mitigate the number of redundancies and ensure retraining and redeployment of staff affected". The majority of the affected staff are in roles that are not customer-facing and a number of senior leadership changes are already under way, the BBC has been told. Virgin Media O2 is also expected to review its use of contractors and suppliers in conjunction with the job cuts. As of 30 June, Virgin Media O2's total liabilities stands at £27.2bn while it holds assets worth £45.9bn, according to the firm's latest accounts. Meanwhile, the company is dealing with fierce competition from cheaper "altnets" like Hyperoptic, Community Fibre, Gigaclear and YouFibre. Virgin Media O2 had attempted to respond to this growing threat by buying altnet competitor Netomnia for £2bn via nexfibre, a joint venture owned by Virgin Media O2's owners. However, the Competition Markets Authority (CMA) has provisionally found competition concerns in the deal , external , with a final decision to come in December, sparking anger from Virgin Media O2. In October, Virgin Media O2 called the BT's agreed takeover of TalkTalk a "stitch-up" that had allowed its rival to "tighten its grip" over the market. BT said its deal provided "a safety net" for TalkTalk customers as their broadband provider faced collapse without the takeover. On Friday, BT's share price jumped 7% after the Financial Times reported Virgin Media O2 was close to agreeing a deal , external to use its rival's fibre broadband network. The BBC has been told the deal was very close and that Virgin Media O2 was highly likely to announce it will stop all investment in fibre in its results on Tuesday. Do you work for Virgin or O2? events.title: Global energy giants gather in Abu Dhabi as Adipec prepares for record exhibition
events.summary: Some of the world's biggest energy companies will converge on Abu Dhabi on Monday as Adipec prepares to stage what organisers say will be its largest exhibition yet, bringing together industry leaders, ministers and investors amid heightened concerns over energy security and global supply disruptions. The four-day event, running from November 2 to 5, is expected to feature a record 2,260 exhibiting companies, including 54 national and international energy companies, as well as more than 40 government ministers. Organisers expect more than 239,000 attendees from more than 170 countries, with all 16 exhibition halls at Adnec Centre Abu Dhabi booked, prompting them to build additional structures and relocate the opening ceremony to accommodate demand. BP, Shell, TotalEnergies, Eni, ExxonMobil, Chevron and Occidental Petroleum are among the major energy companies listed as exhibitors, alongside technology and industrial groups including Siemens, IBM and Microsoft. “The industry's commitment to Adipec is clear,” Christopher Hudson, president of organiser dmg events, said. “We have a record-breaking 2,260 exhibiting companies, with the exhibition venue fully sold out and additional structures built to accommodate demand.” The gathering comes as governments and companies reassess energy supplies, infrastructure investment and trade routes following months of disruption to global oil and gas markets. Energy security, AI, electricity demand and the financing of new infrastructure are expected to dominate discussions. Energy giants showcase new technology Several major companies have independently confirmed their participation, outlining plans to demonstrate technologies designed to improve operational efficiency, strengthen infrastructure and reduce emissions. US oilfield services company Halliburton said it would showcase advanced drilling and completions technologies, production optimisation systems and AI-powered tools. Its chairman and chief executive, Jeff Miller, is scheduled to address the conference on Tuesday, discussing how energy companies can navigate volatility while maintaining profitability. Industrial automation group Emerson has also confirmed its attendance, with plans to demonstrate AI-enabled software, autonomous operations and advanced instrumentation aimed at improving reliability and project execution. GE Vernova, the US energy equipment manufacturer, said it would showcase advanced gas turbines, electricity grid modernisation and carbon management technologies. Schneider Electric, meanwhile, will focus on autonomous operations and AI-driven technologies. Research released by the French company ahead of Adipec found that 76 per cent of surveyed Middle East energy leaders had increased investment in autonomous technology over the past year. SLB, another major US oilfield services group, plans to demonstrate AI-enabled drilling, reservoir management and digital technologies aimed at improving production efficiency. Industrial software company Aveva will showcase digital twins and connected industrial intelligence, while Honeywell is expected to demonstrate AI-driven autonomous upstream operations. The technology focus comes as energy companies increase their AI spending , with an Adnoc and Microsoft study finding that 89 per cent of surveyed energy leaders had raised investment over the past year. However, the industry's growing reliance on AI presents challenges of its own, with a separate Adipec survey finding that 81 per cent of energy executives believe electricity demand from AI will exceed existing forecasts. Abu Dhabi's Enersol, the energy technology investment platform jointly owned by Adnoc Drilling and Alpha Dhabi Holding, will also highlight technologies developed and manufactured in the UAE. Asia's growing influence Asia will send its largest delegation yet , with 353 companies and six national pavilions representing China, India, Japan, Malaysia, Singapore and South Korea. Participants include China's Sinopec, CNPC and CNOOC, battery manufacturer Catl, Malaysia's Petronas and Japan's Inpex and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries. The record Asian presence follows major disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical route for global oil and gas supplies. Before the war, nearly 90 per cent of crude oil and condensate shipments passing through the waterway were destined for Asia, according to the US Energy Information Administration, with China accounting for 38 per cent. The disruption to shipping earlier this year triggered what the International Energy Agency described as the largest supply disruption in oil market history. For Asian energy buyers, Adipec offers an opportunity to engage with Gulf producers on supply security, infrastructure investment and long-term partnerships. “Asia is at the centre of global energy demand growth,” Abdulmunim Al Kindy, chairman of Adipec 2026, said last month. Mr Al Kindy has also highlighted how Adnoc's contingency planning helped maintain production during the Iran war. The opening day's programme will feature an address by Dr Sultan Al Jaber, Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology and managing director and group chief executive of Adnoc. Adipec 2026: Opening ceremony A ministerial discussion on energy security will bring together UAE Energy Minister Suhail Al Mazrouei and his counterparts from Germany, Turkey and Egypt. Other executives scheduled to speak include BP chief executive Meg O'Neill, Siemens chief executive Roland Busch, Baker Hughes chief executive Lorenzo Simonelli and Inpex chief executive Takayuki Ueda. The exhibition also follows Adnoc's announcement of Dh60 billion in manufacturing opportunities for UAE suppliers, aimed at strengthening domestic supply chains and reducing dependence on imports. Commercial agreements will also be in focus. Last year's Adipec recorded 49,131 agreements worth $53 billion, according to organisers, with further announcements expected during this year's event.

events.title: Guarding the Gates of Knowledge
events.summary: A recent scroll through social media got me thinking about trust. About half my feed was filled with AI slop that astute users would call out as being machine-generated, often to the embarrassment of the rube who unknowingly spread it and sometimes to the delight of the poster who shared it deliberately because they found it amusing or useful for sowing confusion. Remember the good old days of GPT-3 when we could ask the chatbot anything and it would almost instantly and very confidently spit back a plausible but false answer? That’s when the word “hallucination” as applied to AI answers entered the lexicon. Six years and several versions of a few different chatbots later, I still can’t trust the answers I get, even though Claude or Gemini often do useful work for me. That’s the thing about current AI: Trust but verify. And verify you must. Apply that maxim at scale to maintain the integrity of the scientific record and you get an idea of the challenge facing publishers of peer-reviewed scholarship. In “ I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper ,” freelance writer and doctor of applied mathematics Benjamin Skuse tells the story of the human gatekeepers trying to beat back the rising tide of AI slop by attempting to get his own AI-generated papers past IEEE’s defenses. “He basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper.’ And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it.” —Eliza Strickland As features and AI beat editor Eliza Strickland told me, Skuse was surprised at just how effortless it was to generate a paper that was more or less plausible and more or less science. For one of his experiments, “he basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper,’” she said. “And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it. He just launched it into the maw of the publishing engine.” Skuse discovered that the combination of IEEE’s human-review processes and research-integrity checker programs are currently keeping pace in what amounts to a cat-and-mouse game against people using free tools. But the more advanced LLMs are no longer making the same dumb mistakes the free versions do. That leaves publishers locked in an arms race between increasingly plausible slop and the systems aimed at detecting it. Scholarly publishers aren’t the only ones trying to hold the line against slop. So is that global depository of human-generated knowledge, Wikipedia. For this month’s Five Questions , Strickland interviewed Ellia Lebleu, a founding member of WikiProject AI Cleanup , a volunteer effort to detect and delete AI-generated material from the platform. Lebleu’s team is confronting the same problem as commercial publishers, but with fewer people and fewer tools. “Wikipedia is known as a repository of human-generated information, and they want to hold on to that,” says Strickland. “Who knows how long they’ll be able to do that.” If we can’t collectively assume that the scientific record is trustworthy or that basic facts about the world are accurate, then our understanding of what is real unspools into uncertainty . Perhaps that delights quantum scientists and the grifters who thrive in an information environment where there is no shared reality. But that uncertainty ultimately undermines trust in the institutions that exist to curate the corpus of human knowledge and to promote the advancement of science and technology for the benefit of humanity. Or maybe in a world where AI is doing the science and writing the papers, it won’t matter whether or not humans trust the outputs. As Strickland put it, “Doesn’t it just feel crazy that we’ll have AI writing for other AIs at some point? We’ll just get left out of the loop.”

events.title: Behind the Curtain: OpenAI's post-election power play
events.summary: Right after Tuesday's midterms, OpenAI will unleash a policy and PR blitz to try to get in sync with the new Washington, including an effort to rebrand data centers as "AI compute campuses." Why it matters: After two years of a friendly White House, AI companies will face a harsher Washington after Tuesday, when Democrats will likely win the House. OpenAI also aims to help frame the AI debate for the big field of 2028 presidential contenders that'll start forming on Wednesday. "You can try to chase the moment, or seek to inform the moment via the power of ideas," OpenAI chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane tells us, calling Tuesday an "electoral portal from one era to the next." Since August, Lehane and his team have been stockpiling policy proposals, some new and some repackaged, to drive urgency and steer the AI debate. It'll all start during the lame-duck session of Congress — the awkward but often consequential weeks between the election and the swearing-in of new members and senators on Jan. 3. This year's lame duck opens Nov. 9. The big picture: Other tech companies are also positioning themselves for a potential blue wave. Meta is taking steps to strengthen its ties with Democrats, Axios' Sara Fischer scooped Saturday . Other big AI and tech players can be expected to do the same. Tech titans who enjoy close relationships with President Trump will be top targets for Democrats, who are eager to ramp up scrutiny and regulatory pressure on the industry. OpenAI's plans, being revealed here for the first time, all involve control — trying to send the message that AI is being built for people, not to displace people. The proposals include: Speed limits: Building on earlier proposals , OpenAI plans to unveil new ideas for mandatory safeguards for the most powerful AI systems — speed limits for AI that will allow humans to keep their hands on the wheel. This'll include a more aggressive congressional drive. "You're going to see us talk more and more about the concept of speed limits," Lehane said. "Our belief is people should always remain in control of this technology. AI should be built by and for people, and people should have more control over how the technology shapes their lives and communities." Data centers: OpenAI hopes to stem the nationwide, bipartisan backlash by offering new community compacts and commitments to smooth the way for future data centers. In addition, the company will try to set a new industry standard by proposing state legislation that gives people a meaningful say in how projects are built and what benefits they receive. In an intentionally provocative rebranding effort, OpenAI will argue that the infrastructure it's building, in contrast to legacy data centers, should be called "AI compute campuses" that can economically transform host communities. OpenAI points to its role in developing a huge data center project that promises to bring thousands of jobs to Pike County in Ohio's Appalachian region. "We think the conversation is good and healthy," Lehane said. "It's democracy in action. Communities should hold companies responsible and accountable so they really and truly get a transformative benefit from these projects." Economic opportunity: OpenAI is developing ideas to help more people see AI as empowering for their daily lives and on the job, including supporting workers through disruption, widening access to education and training, and making it easier to start and grow a business. International cooperation: OpenAI will push for the U.S. to shape global standards with AI built on democratic values. Between the lines: OpenAI is trying to stake out a human-centered "third path" in a debate that often defaults to an artificial binary of doomers vs. accelerationists. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, speaking to the UN Security Council in September, called for an AI approach that leads to a "new Renaissance of creativity and discovery." What we're watching: OpenAI's overtures are aimed partly at 2028 presidential hopefuls, who'll be increasingly vocal about their plans starting Wednesday. "AI is going to be the issue in 2028," Lehane said, calling the midterms a "bit of a movie trailer for what you're going to see in 2028." "I don't think it's going to be good enough just to say 'AI bad,'" Lehane added. "The public gets that this is a much more complex, nuanced conversation. They're going to be looking for whoever their FDR or Lincoln is who's actually going to want to try to lead them through this journey." Lehane said candidates should ask: "How do we start to think about trust? How do we think about the incredible anxiety that exists in modernity? How do we think about the fact that people are profoundly unhappy with where their social contract is, where the American dream is?" The bottom line: The plans for the coming months are just the beginning of OpenAI's effort to inject more urgency in Washington and push the industry on frontier safety. Remember: Every day, AI models get more powerful — and tougher to corral. "Our policy priorities — and urgency, especially on frontier safety — are about meeting the moment in response to the rapidly advancing capabilities," Lehane said. "And we expect that to continue as a new Congress ramps up." Axios' Bradley Olson contributed. Disclosure: Axios has a content licensing and technology agreement with OpenAI, emphasizing expansion of local news coverage. Go deeper : "AI governing the AI world."

events.title: Why Florida Republicans are "white-knuckled" about Tuesday
events.summary: Florida Republicans aren't panicking about sluggish turnout for the midterms , but in the words of one GOP elder: "We're white-knuckled." Why it matters: Florida once looked like a much safer Republican bet for the midterms. Losing any statewide race would stun and embarrass its elite Republican residents, starting with President Trump . "I don't necessarily want to be the bearer of bad news, but I don't think the turnout is as strong as we would like to see," Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis fretted last week. The biggest GOP concern is U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds' campaign for governor, though most polls show him narrowly leading Democrat David Jolly. Donalds has raised $176 million; Jolly just $28 million. Zoom in : The GOP's jitters are rooted in early turnout data. Republicans led Democrats in early ballots cast by 3 percentage points as of Sunday morning. That's much lower than in the past two general elections — and it's despite a much-bigger Republican registration advantage over Democrats: 11 points. Republican turnout is weakest in parts of the conservative Panhandle and rural North Florida, including many of the 17 counties Donalds lost in the Republican primary. In those 17 counties, GOP turnout is 3.2 points below 2022, compared with 1.1 points below in counties that Donalds won, University of Florida political scientist Michael McDonald found. Between the lines: Republican turnout is made up of more habitual voters, while Democrats and independents are banking ballots from people who don't always show up. That could benefit Jolly if polls underestimate those voters. Democrats already have surpassed their entire 2022 early and mail-in vote totals in 15 counties, compared with four counties for Republicans. Nearly every poll shows independent voters favoring Democrats by double digits, so Republicans need a heavy turnout advantage. About two-thirds of Florida voters typically cast ballots before Election Day, making the early and absentee margins critical. Among voters who waited until Election Day in 2022, roughly 60,000 more Republicans than Democrats have already voted this year, Democratic strategist Steve Schale found. That means some voters Republicans rely on for their Election Day surge in 2022 have already cast ballots — potentially shrinking their usual Tuesday advantage. The big picture: Donalds could enter Election Day down by as many as 500,000 votes, according to internal Democratic and GOP estimates shared with Axios. To overcome that deficit, Donalds could need to win the Election Day vote by a 2:1 ratio. It's a tall order, but Republicans have delivered huge Election Day margins before, notably in 2022. By the numbers: Black and Hispanic voters, who are leaning more toward Democrats this year in Florida polling, are making up a growing share of the early electorate, accounting for a larger share of newly reported ballots. Across racial and ethnic groups , Democrats are voting at higher rates than Republicans. Among active Democrats, 50% of white voters, 39% of Black voters and 34% of Hispanic voters have cast ballots, compared with 35%, 21% and 28% of Republicans in those groups. Young voters show another substantial gap: 25% of active registered Democrats under 30 have voted, compared with just 9% of Republicans. Yes, but: Florida Republicans still outnumber Democrats by 1.5 million, with a larger pool of reliable voters. Florida's GOP is better funded and organized than the state's Democratic Party. Even in 2018, when a blue wave flooded the nation, Florida's red wall held. By razor-thin margins, DeSantis won the governor's race and then-Gov. Rick Scott was elected to the Senate. "We always win Election Day, and we know how to do this," state GOP chair Evan Power said. "A lot of the nerves here are because the last time we had a close election was eight years ago, and people forgot what a close election looks like here." Zoom out: Republicans face a different political climate than in 2018, when Trump was ascendant in the GOP and the economy was improving. Today, Trump's approval with Republicans is lower and gas prices are higher. Republicans worry they could lose 10 to 15 state House seats, jeopardizing their supermajority. In Miami's 27th Congressional District, voting patterns are flashing warning signs for Republican Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar in her race against Democrat Eliot Rodriguez. As for the three statewide Florida Cabinet posts (attorney general, chief financial officer, agriculture commissioner), "no one should feel safe, but there's reason to feel OK," said a Republican involved one of the races. Nationwide , the atmosphere is so bad for the GOP that Texas, Kansas, Alaska, Ohio and even South Carolina look in play. Behind the scenes : The early voting data sent a chill through Republican ranks in Tallahassee last week: What if the polling assumptions about stronger Republican turnout were wrong? "Just a few weeks ago I didn't think I would be feeling like this," a top consultant for one of the statewide races said. "It's not panic. At least not yet." Republicans remain more confident about Sen. Ashley Moody's race against state Rep. Angie Nixon, who's widely seen as too progressive for the red state's voters. Friction point: Republicans have quietly fretted that racism could hurt Donalds just as it may hurt Nixon. Donalds and Nixon are Black. "We're about to run the biggest experiment to see how racist some of our voters are," a longtime Republican consultant said, calling the counties Donalds lost "more culturally Confederate" than the rest of Florida. "During the primary, he underperformed in the Panhandle and if people think skin color didn't play a role in that, they are naive," MAGA influencer Laura Loomer posted Saturday on X.

events.title: Opec+ holds December oil output targets steady as Iran war disrupts supply
events.summary: The Opec+ bloc kept its oil production targets unchanged for December, maintaining September's required production levels as the war in the Middle East continues to disrupt global energy supplies. The group's seven core members – Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Kuwait, Oman, Algeria, Russia and Kazakhstan – decided during a meeting on Sunday to “maintain September 2026 required production for December 2026” after reviewing global market conditions and the outlook, a statement said. The group finished unwinding 1.65 million barrels per day of voluntary cuts from 2023 in September. It is keeping a further two million bpd of cuts, agreed to in 2022, in place until the end of the year. It is also reviewing members' production capacity to set quotas for 2027. The seven Opec+ countries “reiterated their collective commitment to achieve full conformity with the Declaration of Co-operation”, the statement said. The producers will continue holding monthly meetings to review market conditions, with the next scheduled for November 29. The joint production targets for the seven members amount to about 31 million bpd for December, unchanged from September, October and November. Saudi Arabia has the largest allocation at 10.478 million bpd, followed by Russia at 9.949 million bpd and Iraq at 4.431 million bpd. Kuwait's target is 2.676 million bpd, Kazakhstan's at 1.628 million bpd, Algeria's at 1.007 million bpd and Oman's at 841,000 bpd. But most members are producing below their targets because of the war. The group reaffirmed its commitment to market stability, although the statement did not announce any additional production adjustments or provide a timetable for increasing output. The Strait of Hormuz , which carried about a fifth of the world's crude oil and liquefied natural gas, has been effectively shut since fighting between the US and Iran started on February 28. The conflict, now in its ninth month, has no clear endgame in sight. Fears are growing that the US might resume hostilities on Iran after the midterm elections, with President Donald Trump saying the war “will be wrapped up soon”. Israeli media reports, meanwhile, claim that the country's military is preparing for the possibility of another round of conflict with Iran, although Mr Trump has yet to make a decision on launching a new military campaign. Attacks on commercial vessels in and around the strait reached their highest monthly level in the Iran-US war in October, with at least 35 attacks reported, according to maritime incident tracking data. Increasing attacks from Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi rebels on Saudi Arabia have also added to regional tension. On Saturday, Riyadh said its air defences had “intercepted and destroyed a hostile drone” in the Saudi capital. That followed dozens of Houthi strikes on Saudi assets over the past weeks. Oil prices settled up more than 2 per cent on Friday to hit six-month highs and post a fourth straight monthly gain. Brent was up 2.4 per cent at $117.64 a barrel, after briefly touching $118, while West Texas Intermediate gained 2.08 per cent to settle at $104.12 a barrel.

events.title: Trump's election probes find an opening in Georgia
events.summary: On the eve of midterms, President Trump is facing setbacks left and right in his push to investigate alleged election fraud . But in Georgia, he has an opening. Why it matters: Six years ago, Georgia was at the epicenter of Trump's efforts to overturn the 2020 presidential election. Now the state's own election board has invited his administration to investigate its voting system. Georgia features two high-stakes statewide campaigns: Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) against Rep. Mike Collins (R) for Senate, and former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms (D) against businessman Rick Jackson (R) for governor. The big picture: The Justice Department disclosed in court on Friday that the administration has sent letters to officials in California, Washington, Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Nevada, asking some states to segregate mail-in ballots from suspected noncitizen voters. A federal judge on Friday issued an emergency order that blocks federal officials from threatening to charge election officials who count ballots from voters the DOJ claims are ineligible. In October, a federal judge restricted the Department of Homeland Security's investigations into suspected noncitizen voters. But Georgia is different . "We've managed with duct tape and bubble gum to be able to bootstrap our way through one last round, but that's not a way of running elections," a Georgia election official told Axios. Georgia's State Election Board asked the Justice and Homeland Security departments to review and potentially investigate the state's voting system and handling of election data. The Sept. 30 letter cited outdated software, threats to ballot secrecy and QR-code ballots it says may violate the Help America Vote Act. A DOJ spokesperson said in response to the letter: "We take seriously allegations that election officials have failed to adequately maintain election equipment and otherwise comply with federal law. We are evaluating the request and will investigate and, if appropriate, bring an enforcement action consistent with federal law." The other side: Georgia State Election Board Chair John Fevrier , appointed by Gov. Brian Kemp (R), opposed the letter and told Axios that a majority of the board now believes it "far exceeded what was in the resolution." Michon Lindstrom, senior director of communications for Georgia's secretary of state, said: "It's unfortunate that the state election board sought to inject chaos in the 11th hour of the election." In 2020, Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger rebuffed Trump's efforts to overturn Georgia's presidential election results. Friction point: Georgia has spent years debating how to address vulnerabilities in its voting system. The secretary of state's office said Georgia's machines haven't been updated since they were purchased in 2019. The state said it's starting a procurement process for new machines for the next election cycle. The state's legislature passed a law in 2024 to move away from a QR-code ballot system to hand-marked paper ballots. This transition was supposed to be implemented by this July, but lawmakers passed a deadline extension. A software glitch on the state's tabulators that could impact ballot secrecy has been known to the state since 2022. But an available fix hasn't been installed. Between the lines: "There are no clean hands in this," the Georgia election official told Axios. "The secretary of state could have fought harder for the funding... [The] legislature could have funded it when the secretary of state asked for it. But ... they all have pissed each other off so much." In 2025, Raffensperger urged lawmakers to reconsider a $47 million voting-machine upgrade, proposing a software update costing less than $15 million or delaying any purchases until the existing contract expired. In 2026, Raffensperger told legislators that there wasn't money for any election upgrades. No upgrades were funded. What they're saying: "Money allocation is ultimately the function of the legislative branch, and any questions about why they did not deem it necessary to fund 'election infrastructure improvements' should be directed to the legislature," Lindstrom told Axios. Fevrier told Axios: "I blame the legislature. If the legislature thought it was an issue, they would have fixed it, and they didn't." The Department of Homeland Security didn't respond to Axios's request for comment. The bottom line: The Trump administration suffered a setback in California on Friday, with an appeals court rejecting its demand to set aside mail-in ballots. But the dispute in Georgia shows that the fight over federal intervention in state elections is far from over.

events.title: Dems and GOP quietly bankroll dozens of third-party spoilers
events.summary: More than 40 third-party candidates in pivotal House and Senate races across the country are receiving support from outside super PACs, many of which have ties to the two major parties, an Axios analysis has found. Why it matters: The sums being thrown around, which total more than $16.5 million, are far greater than virtually any of those candidates have raised or spent on their own. The super PACs have spent an average of $375,000 more than the third-party candidates they are supporting. More than half of the 43 candidates haven't filed any financial paperwork with the Federal Election Commission. While it is a comparative drop in the bucket for a midterm that has already seen billions in ad spending nationally, the money will likely play an outsized role in races that are set to be decided by razor-thin margins. Those races, in turn, will help decide the balance of power in Congress next year. Data: Federal Election Commission; Note: Heikes is a self-identified Republican, but Sen. Dan S. Sullivan is the Republican Party-endorsed candidate in the race; Table: Andrew Solender/Axios The top spenders nationwide have been a pair of obscure groups which, like many of the other "pop-up" super PACs in this story, were formed this month and therefore won't have to disclose their donors until after Election Day. Buckeye Freedom PAC has reported spending more than $3.8 million on ads in Ohio's U.S. Senate election supporting Libertarian Bill Redpath and opposing Republican Sen. Jon Husted, who is in a tight race with Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown. Alaska Values PAC has disclosed spending $3.8 million backing Gerald Heikes, a self-identified Republican running on Alaska's ranked-choice U.S. Senate ballot with Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola. Between the lines : Third-party candidates in Alaska are facing national scrutiny after the New York Times reported that Heikes and another self-proclaimed Republican on the ballot, Dan J. Sullivan, were recruited into the race. Republicans have long accused Dan J. Sullivan of being a spoiler meant to siphon votes from the incumbent senator by confusing voters with their shared name. The "double-Dan" case is unique in that it reportedly included direct involvement from a political operative working with the Peltola campaign, who allegedly used pseudonyms as part of the effort. The Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee have denied recruiting any third-party candidates into the race. Enough Promises Ohio is another huge spender, putting $2.6 million behind supporting independent Senate candidate Greg Levy in Ohio, per its FEC filings. The group's mailers encourage voters to "join the revolution" and "send a worker to the Senate" by voting for Levy, a member of the Party for Socialism and Liberation who has disavowed the support . The group's FEC filings offer hints as to its partisan affiliation: It shares vendors with several Republican candidates and groups including MAGA Inc. Principled Patriots PAC has reported spending over $600,000 on digital ads supporting right-leaning and Libertarian candidates in 15 battleground House and Senate races, according to FEC filings and Google's Ad Transparency Center. The group's vendor for its ads, Movement Labs LLC, has primarily serviced Democratic clients, filings show. It touts itself as working for "progressive change everywhere." "Washington is spending money it doesn't have. Republicans raised the debt limit $5 trillion. Darline Graham is one of them," says a Principled Patriots' ad in the South Carolina Senate race — part of a $110,000 ad buy. Constitution Party candidate Mark Hackett, the ad continues, "lives here, works here, owes party bosses nothing. Not a Democrat, not a Republican. He'll end the waste, cut spending." "I have spent no money and asked for no help in my campaign," Hackett said in an email to Axios. He said of the PACs supporting him: "I still don't know who they are." Hackett said he will "remain" in the race and suggested he is not concerned about being a spoiler for Graham "since neither Graham nor Andrews have made defunding the wars in Ukraine and Iran an issue." Progressive Champions PAC , a group Republicans used to boost their preferred Democratic primary candidates in several battleground House districts, has quietly resurfaced in a pair of hotly contested general elections. In Virginia's 2nd District, the group has reported spending over $480,000 supporting independent Matthew Baker. One of its mailers, reported by the New York Times , highlights Baker's liberal positions on issues such as abortion. Baker, a self-described "radical centrist," told the Times the mailer makes him "mad as hell" because the group is "only telling half my story" and "trying to use me to trick people." Progressive Champions PAC also spent more than $500,000 on texts and mailers boosting Green Party candidate Shafina Barnett in Michigan's 4th District, according to filings. Our Heritage Matters has reported spending nearly $3.7 million to support third-party candidates in more than two dozen House and Senate races, per FEC filings. Most of the candidates are Libertarians. The group's mailers advertise the candidates as the conservative alternative to the Republicans in each race. Much of its spending is also listed in FEC filings as being in opposition to the GOP candidates. The Nebraska Senate race has seen easily the most separate instances of super PACs boosting third-party candidates — somewhat ironically, given Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts' chief rival is independent Dan Osborn. Outside groups have reported spending more than $450,000 supporting Robin Richards of the Working People Party and $115,000 boosting Mike Marvin of the Legal Marijuana Now Party. The group supporting Marvin, High Time Nebraska, shares a treasurer with a Republican House candidate in California, per filings. One of the other candidates, Chuck Conboy of the America First Party, is supported by Principled Patriots PAC. The intrigue: Axios reported last week that the House Democratic campaign arm put messaging guidance on its website laying out how to boost third-party candidates in several key races. It may have come in handy. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee's page on VA-02 — known as a redbox — says white, college-educated men should see that Matthew Baker is "a staunch supporter of the 2nd amendment." Our Heritage Matters began spending for Baker on Wednesday with an initial $18,000 digital ad buy, according to filings. The redbox on Nevada's 2nd District says Republican women in the district should be informed Independent American Party candidate Lynn Chapman "has spent decades fighting for conservative values." events.title: 'Mother of all editors' Emacs is 50
events.summary: No lesser authority than the MIT Technology Review says that the Emacs editor has turned 50 years old. But then, it is biased — Emacs was invented in MIT's AI lab. Simson Garfinkel's article is simply called EMACS turns 50, but the sub-heading explains why it matters more: "How the MIT AI Lab's text editor gave birth to the free software movement." There are multiple timelines and accounts of the origins of Emacs, and it is not a single monolithic application. The name is an abbreviation for " E diting MAC ro S ", and the original editor for which this set of macros was developed was TECO – "Text Editor and COrrector," written by Dan Murphy in 1962. Murphy died earlier this year at the age of 83. The inimitable Jamie Zawinski has an encyclopedic Emacs Timeline – as he mentions at the start, his interest being that he long ago maintained a fork of GNU Emacs, originally called Lucid Emacs . It's still around, under its later name XEmacs. There are a lot of forks and re-implementations of Emacs out there, and we are not going to go into all of them, or this article would become a book – one only interesting to programmer-archeologists (to use a term coined by the late great Vernor Vinge ). As for who originally wrote those Editing Macros, though, another history has quotations from several of the people involved: On the Origin of Emacs in 1976 . (Note – some of the quotes still contain the | symbols that marked quoted text.) This credits Lisp boffin Guy L. Steele Jr with the original work in 1975, but in it, Steele says: "RMS is responsible for the names 'E' and 'EMACS'. RMS still deserves 99% or 99.9% or 99.99% or 99.999% of the credit for taking a package of TECO macros and turning it into the most powerful editor on the planet." RMS is of course Richard Stallman, and the page also quotes some emails from RMS on October 23 and 31, 1976. Mind you, just a few years after the event, in a 1981 talk now preserved on the GNU website, Stallman said, "I began the development of EMACS in 1974 with an improvement to TECO". Like all the best FOSS, even in its very early stages, it was a collaborative effort – but around late October 1976 is when RMS took over the bulk of the development. Of the many forks of Emacs over its half a century of development, some are still just about hanging on in there. When we looked up the link for XEmacs, we were surprised to see that there was a new release: XEmacs 21.5.37 "lettuce" appeared just last month. And even the forks have forks: in this case, SXEmacs , last updated in 2020. Most of the changes in XEmacs and SXEmacs eventually made their way back upstream to GNU Emacs, which is still in active development, although as The Register reported in 2008 , RMS is no longer the primary maintainer. GNU Emacs 31.1 appeared in August. Cards on the metaphorical table: this vulture is not an Emacs user. We have tried. A major influence was one of the Reg FOSS desk's favorite writers, Neal Stephenson, who in 1999 published an essay called In the Beginning… Was the Command Line . (It was later republished as a rather short book, but the text is still online .) In it, he says: "In the GNU/Linux world there are two major text editing programs: the minimalist vi (known in some implementations as elvis ) and the maximalist emacs . I use emacs, which might be thought of as a thermonuclear word processor. It was created by Richard Stallman; enough said. It is written in Lisp, which is the only computer language that is beautiful. It is colossal, and yet it only edits straight ASCII text files, which is to say, no fonts, no boldface, no underlining. In other words, the engineer-hours that, in the case of Microsoft Word, were devoted to features like mail merge, and the ability to embed feature-length motion pictures in corporate memoranda, were, in the case of emacs, focused with maniacal intensity on the deceptively simple-seeming problem of editing text. If you are a professional writer–i.e., if someone else is getting paid to worry about how your words are formatted and printed–emacs outshines all other editing software in approximately the same way that the noonday sun does the stars." Emacs is 50-plus-year-old software, and it shows. This is a huge and complicated program: decades ago, the joke was that EMACS stood for "Eight Megs And Constantly Swapping". It is not an easy program to learn. Despite lavish documentation and a built-in tutorial, this is software so old that its terminology predates microprocessors and the personal computer. Its exhaustive manual is 804 pages long, and to pick some trivial examples, its terms for parts of the screen use “frame” to mean what’s now called a window, and “window” to mean what’s now called a pane. In the section on Keys , it discusses the Control and Meta keys. That’s a slight snag: you don’t have a Meta key, and neither do the authors of Emacs. It was a key on the now almost legendarily rare Space Cadet Keyboard, of which the Deskthority keyboard wiki says: “It is known as the holy grail of keyboards.” You can buy a modern replica, the Keymacs keyboard . They are hand-made in the Czech Republic, and depending on exactly what model and specifications you want, they cost from €2,998 for the Lispsaver up to €6,878 for the A624N Space Cadet . In other words, you can have a keyboard with a real Meta key if you want, but it is going to cost you. However, KDE also uses the Meta key – but what the KDE documentation calls "Meta " is the Windows key – or Command on Macs. Like most Linux folks, the GNOME documentation calls it the Super key. Names are important. They matter. Who's right, the Emacs folks or the KDE folks? Well, neither: nobody has Meta keys any more. We have Ctrl, Alt, and Cmd/Super/Windows. events.title: Hundreds of thousands of young protesters take to the streets across France
events.summary: Thousands of young protesters take to the streets of France for a third weekend. PARIS -- Hundreds of thousands of protesters inspired by frustrated high school students took to the streets across France on Saturday in a third consecutive weekend of demonstrations over living costs and education. Youth-led protests were also held elsewhere in Europe , including in Germany and Portugal. France's protests were overwhelmingly peaceful, with whimsical Halloween costumes lightening the mood, but gatherings in Paris and other cities ended in clouds of tear gas and scattered fires set by small groups on the margins. About 70,000 police and gendarmes were deployed across the country after French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez warned of a “very high risk” of disorder, especially after dark on Halloween. Paris marches were rerouted to the capital’s edge to protect stores, government buildings and touristed areas in the city center. France's government estimated that 320,000 people protested nationwide Saturday, fewer than in previous protests but still a significant turnout. Mass protests on Oct. 17 that deteriorated into some of France's worst rioting in years drew 550,000 people around France, and demonstrations on Oct. 24 drew 410,000, according to government estimates. Organizers’ turnout estimates are higher. Authorities in France reported more than 560 arrests nationwide by Saturday night. Police had arrested thousands of people following riots and looting that marred marches the previous two Saturdays. In the main Paris march, each group carried its own banner: high school students, climate activists and people angry about the cost of living. Corentin Cabreux, a 21-year-old student, said that he lives in a state-run student residence where “there are damp stains all along the bottom of my walls, whole sections peeling off, cockroaches everywhere, rats.” An information technology worker protested in solidarity with the students and her mother, who was struggling with a minimum wage job. A gray-haired woman carried a sign reading ‘’The Old are Fed Up Too.'' Halloween costumes reflected the mood. Cléo Farenc, a 30-year-old gallery assistant, came dressed as a beheaded Marie-Antoinette. “It’s about embodying a figure of power who was brought down by the people,” she said. “It’s a very strong symbol in French culture.'' The rallies in France were started last month by high school students protesting neglected buildings, teacher shortages and a university admissions system seen as unfair to disadvantaged students. Labor unions and others angry at the leadership of President Emmanuel Macron joined in with a variety of demands. On Saturday, the crowd streamed along the Boulevards des Maréchaux, avenues that ring the edge of Paris, in a march that was joyful for hours. Techno music blasted from speakers, and some marchers went trick-or-treating. A police helicopter hovered overhead as the sun set slowly over the city. Later, clashes broke out near Porte de Charenton, where the march ended. Protesters hurled glass bottles and fireworks at police. Officers responded with volleys of stun grenades and tear gas. The blasts echoed through the streets, and smoke filled the air as dusk fell. Many peaceful marchers turned back, coughing, their eyes streaming with tears, and left the march, some scattering into the nearby Bois de Vincennes, one of the largest parks in Paris. While the vast majority of protesters have been peaceful, groups of troublemakers routinely target police with fireworks and projectiles. Police use tear gas, dispersion grenades, water cannons and other tactics that have resulted in severe injuries . Learjet with 9 aboard crashes in Palm Beach County, Florida: FAA Sen. Chris Murphy hospitalized after suffering a stroke, chief of staff says 2 college students found dead after going missing while hiking, police say Paris police barred people from entering Place de la Republique and Les Halles — neighborhoods popular among young people — from 11 p.m. to 6 a.m. Saturday and Sunday. Unaccompanied minors face a separate 9 p.m. curfew around the Champs-Elysees. A Paris court on Wednesday suspended an earlier curfew on minors as a serious and illegal infringement of freedom of movement. In Germany, a youth initiative called “Gen Z regelt” — roughly “Gen Z’s got this” — rallied in more than 30 cities “for education, health, climate protection and an affordable life,” and against any return of military conscription. Organizers said that tens of thousands participated in the protests across the country, but official figures weren't immediately available. In Berlin, young protesters gathered at Brandenburg Gate on Saturday afternoon, demanding more investments in education and housing.

events.title: Fight over race questions intensifies ahead of 2030 Census deadline
events.summary: A fight over whether the 2030 Census should stop asking about race and ethnicity has drawn more than 100,000 public comments, according to advocates tracking the federal docket. Why it matters: The change could weaken the nation's most complete snapshot of race — data used in civil rights enforcement and redistricting — just as America grows more multiracial. Catch up quick: The Census Bureau proposed in September to stop asking Americans about their race and ethnicity on the once-a-decade census. The Census Bureau says a shorter form could encourage more people to respond, while greater use of existing government records would reduce the need to ask certain questions. The proposal wouldn't end federal race data: Census could obtain demographic data from government records and other sources and ask about race and ethnicity on the American Community Survey (ACS) and other surveys. But civil rights advocates say that would give the federal government more power to determine people's race and ethnicity , rather than the respondents, leading to inaccurate data. State of play: Census extended the comment deadline from Oct. 13 to Nov. 2. An outside analysis of 52,424 published comments through Oct. 16 found 86% opposed the overall proposal, while 88% addressed removing race and ethnicity questions. This week, an advocacy alert citing Regulations.gov said the docket had topped 108,000 submissions . These comments are not meant to be treated like a survey or poll, but show that people who feel strongly enough to comment tend to be opposed. What they're saying: "If you've ever fought for political maps or explained why race or data matters...it is vital that you tell the Census Bureau what losing that information is going to mean to your work and to your community," said NC Counts Coalition executive director Stacey Carless. The big picture: Race has appeared in some form in every decennial census since 1790, but how Americans identify themselves has changed dramatically. The number of Americans reporting two or more races rose from 9 million, or 2.9%, in 2010 to 33.8 million, or 10.2%, in 2020. Census says improvements in question design, coding and processing accounted for a substantial share of that increase, along with demographic change. The bottom line: The Census Bureau hasn't explained how it would produce detailed racial population counts without asking Americans to identify themselves. The agency already combines information from government and other records to determine people's race and ethnicity when working with administrative data. But its proposal doesn't say whether that system would replace people's own answers in the 2030 Census.

The partnership marks another step in Dewa International's efforts to establish itself as a global energy and water infrastructure developer. In the presence of HE Saeed Mohammed Al Tayer, MD & CEO of DEWA and Chairman of DEWA International, he MoU was signed by Waleed bin Salman, Executive Vice President of Business Development and Excellence at DEWA and Vice Chairman of DEWA International, and Zhao Hui, Managing Director of Shanghai Electric Group in the Middle East and North Africa. #DEWANews — DEWA | Official Page (@DEWAOfficial) November 1, 2026 Dewa established its international subsidiary in June to pursue overseas projects and partnerships, drawing on Dubai's experience in developing large-scale electricity, water and clean energy infrastructure. Dewa has previously invested in green hydrogen production , including a pilot facility developed with Siemens Energy at the solar park. However, the partnership remains exploratory, with no specific overseas projects, investment commitments or development timelines announced.

events.title: Landline phones will switch off across Britland in 100 days, no extensions – Openreach
events.summary: Openreach has issued a stark reminder to customers that the legacy phone network is being officially switched off on January 31, and says the deadline will not be postponed. The infrastructure arm of BT Group, Britain’s biggest telecoms biz, circulated the warning this week in a letter to comms providers that use its network to deliver their services. It informs them that any customers still on legacy public switched telephone network (PSTN) connections are at risk of disruption when these are retired at the end of January, 2027. The switch-off could affect businesses and consumers alike. Beyond the plain old telephone, systems that rely on PSTN connectivity include point-of-sale terminals, fire and security alarms, and personal care alarms for elderly and vulnerable people. The move is part of a wider government scheme to get the UK onto all-digital high-speed networks running on fiber-optic infrastructure, and the legacy phone service – with its dependency on copper cabling – was standing in the way. Many households have now ditched landline handsets and instead use only mobile phones, yet for those who still want a landline, the changeover means plugging the phone into the back of a broadband router to access a Digital Voice service. Openreach has been planning this move for the best part of a decade . It has already pushed back the deadline at least once, after the government asked telecoms providers not to force vulnerable customers who use phone-network systems such as TeleCare to switch until fixes are in place. Nevertheless, public awareness seems low that analog phone services will soon be disconnected. "Openreach and all providers need to coordinate a much more cohesive campaign that reaches customers directly," said telecoms analyst Paolo Pescatore at PP Foresight. "TV, billboards and newspaper advertising should reinforce a consistent message, supported by targeted letters, calls and door-to-door support for older and vulnerable people who need extra help," he told The Register . "Customers need to understand what is changing, what action to take, and who will help them. Providers must take responsibility for ensuring people remain safely connected, especially those who rely on their landline or a care alarm." Caroline Abrahams, charity director at Age UK, agreed. "With only three months to go, the digital landline switchover is entering a critical final phase. Most people have moved over without major problems, but nobody who relies on their landline or TeleCare should be left behind," she told us. "Anyone with concerns should contact their provider, but the responsibility cannot rest with customers alone. Providers must not give up on people who have not responded. They need to keep trying to reach them and offer practical, individual support, recognizing that some may be unwell, living with dementia, worried about scams or without anyone nearby to help." Openreach has a webpage with information regarding the switch-off . This advises consumers to call their service provider as soon as possible to ensure service is not interrupted. The company previously told The Register that customers without a fiber connection will likely be switched to SOTAP for Analog (Single Order Transitional Access Product), where equipment is installed in the local telephone exchange to allow them to continue to use their old phone line as before. Openreach has warned that commercial customers delaying migration risk significant disruption and unnecessary costs - leaving it until the last minute could make it harder to secure the requisite engineering support before the deadline hits. "Businesses and organizations that delay action are making things harder for themselves," said James Lilley, Openreach Director of All-IP. "The straightforward migrations have largely been completed. What's left are the complex connections that underpin critical operations, requiring careful planning, supplier coordination, and thorough testing. We are urging businesses to act now, audit their remaining analog services, and work with their communications provider on a migration plan today." Earlier this year, the firm tried to drive home the message by announcing it was stepping up its charges to service providers and companies still operating legacy business lines, who will by now be paying double the rental cost compared to last year. ®

events.title: UAE updates e-invoicing penalties for businesses
events.summary: The UAE Ministry of Finance has issued new rules to update fines for e-invoicing to support businesses and reduce duplicate penalties. Structured invoices are issued and exchanged digitally between a supplier and a buyer and reported online to the UAE Federal Tax Authority . The latest amendments – following a cabinet decision – aim to provide businesses with greater regulatory certainty and reduce administrative burdens by introducing more proportionate fines. A penalty of Dh5,000 ($1,360) applies for an initial accounting violation, followed by Dh5,000 for each month during which the non-compliance continues. Fines are subject to a maximum aggregate penalty of Dh50,000 for these breaches in any 12 consecutive months. Administrative penalties for the issuer's or the recipient's failure to notify the authority of a system failure have also been removed. This change aims to ensure that penalties are applied more appropriately, taking into account the respective responsibilities of the different parties within the e-invoicing system. The changes support the UAE's wider digital transformation objectives and reinforce the country's commitment to implementing a modern tax administration framework. A pilot phase and voluntary e-invoicing adoption launched in July, with a full introduction planned for October 1, 2027.

events.title: Binance to resume withdrawals after covering 95% of $6.3bn crypto heist
events.summary: Binance , the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, is preparing to resume cryptocurrency withdrawals in phases after covering 95 per cent of the $6.3 billion in tokens stolen in what has been described as the world’s largest digital heist . The first phase of withdrawals is scheduled to begin between 6am and 9am GMT on Sunday, covering Bitcoin , ether, BNB, Solana, XRP, dogecoin and other digital assets, Binance said in a post on X late on Saturday. The remaining 5 per cent of the stolen tokens consists of less liquid assets that may take longer to source in the required amounts, the exchange said. https://t.co/pBJaht1UGV — Binance (@binance) November 1, 2026 “Since the incident, our teams have taken precautionary measures to safeguard the platform, conducted security assessments, and worked to verify the readiness of affected services. We aim to restore withdrawals progressively as we complete security and readiness checks,” the Binance post on X said. “Deposit services remain open and are not affected by the incident,” it added. The resumption follows security assessments and precautionary measures taken by the cryptocurrency exchange to safeguard its platform and verify the readiness of affected services. Binance said it would absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds rather than passing the losses on to customers. “As we have said throughout this incident: user funds remain safe,” Binance said. The FBI on Saturday attributed the attack to TraderTraitor , a North Korean state-sponsored hacking unit. Members of the group were observed by law enforcement converting the stolen assets into ether, the FBI said in a statement, adding that it expected further laundering through related technology. Binance said on X that withdrawals were temporarily suspended as a precaution, “while our teams worked to contain the incident loss, assess its impact, restore affected services and complete security checks”. “We did not take this decision lightly. We understand how important reliable access to withdrawals is for our users. However, our priority was to protect users, safeguard the platform, and complete the necessary security checks before restoring services.” Despite its reputation for robust security, the cryptocurrency industry has suffered several high-profile hacks and collapses over the years. In 2014, the Mt. Gox exchange, then the world's largest Bitcoin trading platform, collapsed after hackers stole hundreds of thousands of Bitcoins, alongside a series of technical and operational failures. Eight years later, FTX, then the world's second-largest cryptocurrency exchange, imploded amid revelations of fraud and the misuse of customer funds. Its founder, Sam Bankman-Fried , was later sentenced to 25 years in prison. More recently, the FBI attributed a $1.5 billion theft from cryptocurrency exchange Bybit to North Korea, highlighting the persistent security threats facing the industry.

events.title: No more washing up: How Airbnb's new house rules have divided hosts and guests
events.summary: Airbnb host Lisa says her Welsh holiday let was left 'a complete mess' by a group of guests When Lisa Clewes returned to her Welsh holiday let after a group of guests checked out, she was horrified by the mess. Just days earlier, she had met the group in person and helped with their luggage. But after a dinner party, the house was left "in a complete mess" with broken glasses, drinks cans on the floor, pans full of food on the table and fish guts left in the garden. "It was really unbelievable. Had I had another booking the same day, I would have had to cancel or delay check-in," says Clewes. She charges a cleaning fee that covers around 75% of the cost of a cleaner and asks guests to empty the fridge, put rubbish in the bins and load the dishwasher. Clewes says it typically takes cleaners four hours to turn around her property and fears that guests leaving more mess could mean increasing costs But Airbnb's new rules mean hosts can no longer ask guests to do jobs normally carried out by cleaners, including washing and putting away dishes, stripping beds and taking rubbish off site. The updated guidelines, which apply to bookings made globally from 20 November, state that hosts can now set seven standard house rules and add other "reasonable" requests. Clewes says it typically takes cleaners four hours to turn around her three-bedroom property. She fears guests leaving more mess could mean hiring extra cleaners and increasing costs – expenses that may ultimately be passed on to her guests. The changes have come as a relief to guests like Jessica Newhook, who says she has been faced with lengthy checkout lists, often on top of hefty cleaning fees. She booked an Airbnb in Florida for a family reunion of 11 guests and says they had to "leave the property move-in ready for the cleaners", despite paying a $250 (£187) cleaning fee. Newhook says the host told them to wash and fold towels, clean the bedding and kitchen, and sweep and mop the floors. She was also warned by the host that their behaviour needed to improve or they could be told to leave, because they had left chairs blocking bins. "We had rules about everything and it was not relaxing at all." While Newhook likes the home comforts of staying in an Airbnb, she says the combination of relentless rules and rising cleaning fees has taken away much of its appeal. "It is getting to the point where a hotel is cheaper and I know what to expect." Krissi Foskett, 46, from Glasgow, runs a national cleaning company and regularly stays in Airbnb properties so "can see the issue from both sides". Krissi says there's a difference between being a respectful guest and being expected to help run the business you've just paid to stay in During a recent stay in Stafford, she paid a £35 cleaning fee but was still asked to strip the beds, put on a wash, empty bins and carry rubbish down a long track to a recycling area. "I don't particularly mind doing those things, but it did make me question what exactly I was paying the additional cleaning fee for," she says. For Foskett, there is a difference between being a considerate guest – "putting your dirty dishes in the dishwasher" – and being "expected to prepare the property for the next guests". Through her cleaning business, she has also seen the other extreme, with teams arriving to find broken furniture, vomit and pet urine. While she sympathises with hosts facing tight turnarounds and rising cleaning costs, these should not be passed on to guests, she says. "If you're running an Airbnb as a business, professional cleaning is a cost of doing business." Anthony Marsh, who co-owns a cabin retreat in North Yorkshire with his husband, used to list five of their 12 properties on Airbnb, but says the new rules have prompted him to reduce this number to just two. His concern with the changes is that "Airbnb has effectively given guests permission to come and leave properties a tip, and a host can't do anything about it". Anthony and his husband used to list five of their 12 cabins in North Yorkshire on Airbnb... ... but will now list just two in light of the new rules He believes asking guests to wash their pots and put out the bins is hardly unreasonable and, with a small cleaning team and tight turnaround times, he worries extra mess could leave properties unready for the next arrivals. "It's common sense and common decency," he says. His company does not charge a cleaning fee, and Marsh says most guests are respectful. But fees are more common than not. Some 63.2% of Airbnb listings charge a cleaning fee, with an average cost of £55 according to data from AirROI , external . Laura Lewis runs a directory that helps holiday-let owners market their properties and connect with potential guests. Many of her clients also list on Airbnb and she says most are unhappy with the new rules, arguing that asking guests to wash up is a matter of basic respect.

events.title: Judge tosses Trump lawsuit against WSJ, Murdoch over Epstein story
events.summary: A federal judge on Saturday threw out President Trump's lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal and Rupert Murdoch over the paper's reporting on Trump's ties to Jeffrey Epstein, Why it matters: It's the second time this year courts have blocked Trump's efforts to sue the paper over stories about his relationship with the disgraced financier. As with the first one, courts found the president did not clear the high bar set by New York Times vs. Sullivan for allegations of defamation in critical reporting on public figures. Driving the news: Judge Darrin Gayles of the southern district of Florida issued the 20-page ruling Saturday afternoon, finding that Trump failed to prove the paper acted with "actual malice" by reporting on his links to Epstein. Gayles dismissed the amended complaint with prejudice, meaning it can't be refiled. "We're pleased with the court's decision," a representative of WSJ parent Dow Jones said. Zoom out: Trump first filed suit against the paper and Murdoch in July 2025, seeking $20 billion in damages. At issue was a story describing a "bawdy" letter, bearing Trump's name and given to Epstein for his birthday, which the president insisted was fake. Gayles tossed the initial suit last April, but allowed Trump to file an amended complaint — which was the one he dismissed Saturday, saying it fell short of the burden to prove the paper acted maliciously. What they're saying: "Indeed, the allegations regarding malice are conclusory, vague, sometimes inconsistent with the Article, and often irrelevant to whether Defendants knew or should have known that the statements in the Article were purportedly false," Gayles wrote. For the record: " President Trump will continue to press forward in his powerhouse lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal and all of the other defendants. The President will continue to hold those who mislead the American People with Fake News and smears accountable for their actions," a spokesman for his legal team said in a statement. Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details. Sara Fischer contributed.

events.title: Tusk defends suspension of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal president as protesters gather again
events.summary: Prime Minister Donald Tusk says his government is acting to restore judicial independence in Poland WARSAW, Poland -- Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Saturday that his government would press ahead with efforts to restore the independence of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal, as hundreds of protesters gathered for a second night against the suspension of the court’s president . The pro-European government said the suspension is necessary to restore judicial independence, while critics from the opposition have likened it to a “coup d’etat.” President Karol Nawrocki — who opposes the pro-European government — turned back his plane during a flight to Senegal on Friday evening and returned home. On Friday night, he made his way to the Constitutional Tribunal despite the chaos and said he helped the suspended court president enter the building. Police said they detained three protesters on Friday night after some threw objects at officers and tried to break through the security fence around the court. The dispute over the long-embattled Constitutional Tribunal is likely to deepen political polarization in Poland a year before a parliamentary election, further intensifying the standoff between the pro-European government and the national-conservative opposition party Law and Justice , or PiS. Critics in Poland and the European Union accuse PiS, which led the country between 2015 and 2023, of imposing political control over key judicial institutions. Reforms introduced under the PiS government prompted the EU to impose fines on Poland. Tusk’s pro-European government came to power in 2023 with a promise to restore the independence of the judiciary. Since then, its efforts have been blocked by vetoes from two successive presidents aligned with PiS, including Nawrocki. “Restoring the rule of law is our obligation,” Tusk wrote on X on Friday evening. “After years of lawlessness under PiS this is a difficult process, sometimes painful and it requires decisive action. There is no other way.” Tusk had earlier pledged that his government would ensure the tribunal was again staffed with lawfully appointed judges while acknowledging that his methods may not be to everyone’s liking. The functioning of the Constitutional Tribunal had been impaired for years. The Court of Justice of the European Union, the EU's top court, had said it was no longer an impartial court after PiS appointments. Even after Tusk took power, efforts to balance the court were hampered by Nawrocki and the tribunal's president, Bogdan Święczkowski. On Friday evening, the Constitutional Tribunal’s website announced the suspension of Święczkowski. Shortly after, the protesters — including PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński and far-right politicians — began rallying outside the building. Chris Murphy hospitalized after suffering a stroke, chief of staff says 2 college students found dead after going missing while hiking, police say The government says Święczkowski repeatedly broke the law and jeopardized the tribunal’s work. Święczkowski became head of the court under the former PiS government. Tusk has accused him of blocking judges elected by the parliamentary majority from taking up their posts at the tribunal. “Since last night, we’re dealing with a massive constitutional crisis in Poland, the result of an illegal, forceful attempt to take over an important institution,” Marcin Przydacz, a top aide to the Polish president, told The Associated Press. Przydacz said that the president had invited all parliamentary parties to talks on Saturday in an effort to defuse tensions and find a solution to the crisis. The government is a broad coalition made up of Tusk's centrist Civic Coalition, the Left, and two more conservative groupings, Poland 2050 and the Polish People’s Party, or PSL. Representatives of Poland 2050 and PSL, along with several opposition parties, met with Nawrocki on Saturday, while Tusk didn't attend. The president’s camp is hoping that the crisis surrounding the Constitutional Tribunal will erode Tusk’s parliamentary majority. “Everything depends on those political parties who supported Donald Tusk so far,” Przydacz said. Speaking on Saturday night, Tusk compared PiS to a man who steals an elderly woman’s purse and then claims to be the victim when police catch him and take it back. PiS' response to the suspension of Święczkowski, including the attempts to forcefully enter the Tribunal on Friday, represents “another stage in the process of destroying the rule of law in Poland” by PiS and the president, Tusk said. events.title: D.C., Virginia sue to block Trump's 250-foot arch
events.summary: The governments of Washington D.C. and Virginia asked a federal court to block construction of President Trump's planned " triumphal arch ," claiming it's unlawfully tall and would snarl traffic for years. Why it matters: It's a last-minute gambit to stop construction before the multi-year project begins, potentially as soon as this coming week. What they're saying: " This project is flagrantly unlawful," the two governments said in a Saturday filing in D.C. federal court, first reported by the Washington Post. "During the three-year period of construction, the Arch project will inevitably snarl traffic between the jurisdictions, produce pollution and stormwater runoff in the Potomac, interfere with emergency services, and pose numerous other challenges," they argue. They further claim that the defendants — the National Park Service and the Interior Department — have rushed the project without the proper consultations. The city and state are asking a judge to issue injunctions to stop any site preparation or construction on the project. Zoom out: The proposed 250-foot arch would be one of the largest such monuments in the world, sparking concerns that it could interfere with other national symbols, block views and even complicate landings for pilots at nearby airports. (The FAA found otherwise.) The Park Service's own August report indicated the construction of the arch would have adverse effects on nearby monuments and landmarks. The other side: The administration has argued it will be a major tourist attraction — but also vital to national security, serving as a base for snipers and drones. "The Triumphal Arch in Memorial Circle is going to be one of the most iconic landmarks not only in Washington, D.C., but throughout the world," White House spokesman Davis Ingle said in a statement. What's next: A federal judge held a hearing Friday on a separate challenge to the arch, and indicated she may block construction at least temporarily.

events.title: Binance covers 90 per cent of assets stolen in $6.3 billion hack
events.summary: Cryptocurrency exchange Binance said on ​Saturday that ​it has ​been able to cover ⁠90 per cent of the amount stolen in ⁠ an unprecedented hack ​on its platform. In an update on its website, Binance said the amount to cover the stolen funds would come out of three sources: a partial use of the Secure Asset Fund for Users; a portion of the Futures insurance fund; and Binance's own corporate treasury. Users were also invited to check the balances of the first two funds online. The outstanding 10 per cent consists of tokens that are less liquid, which means they may take longer to source in the required amounts, the company added. The exchange said withdrawal services for users are expected to resume on November 1, with more details to be confirmed later. What happened? Binance Holdings, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, lost an estimated $6.3 billion to hackers early on Friday, in what has been described as the single biggest theft of cryptocurrency on record, exceeding the $1.5 billion stolen from Bybit in February 2025 . Funds began leaving Binance's hot wallets, which are connected to the internet to process customer withdrawals, at about 12.24am UAE time on October 30. A single transaction moved about 167,464 Ether, worth about $388 million, along with 63 other tokens, to an address created hours earlier and funded through the Tornado Cash mixing service, according to Etherscan data. Bitcoin shares plunged after the news, and have now fallen to about $76,450, data from CoinMarketCap shows.
